items.t: 1 · Framework: how to analyse the decline
items.x: Story so far: a State at its peak in 1707. Because the decline hit five kinds of power at once, learn the five-part equation and the two lenses first. Ask: which lens fits each event, vertical or horizontal? This is where Modern Indian History (MIH) starts. The Mughal State reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07 and began collapsing right after. Within about four decades it was a small area around Delhi–Agra under Maratha protection. Chapter 2 timeline: Babur 26-30 to Zafar 37-57; foundation of decline at Aurangzeb 58-07 MIH starts here. Later Mughals are weak: Bahadur Shah (1707-12) in the 1700s to Zafar (1837-57) in the 1800s. Power moves from the Mughal down to the Mansabdars. Foundation of decline was laid at Aurangzeb 58-07; after him, weak emperors either could not revive the State or contributed to its decline. The five-part equation State power = Political + Economic + Military + Social + Technological. The Mughal decline is a simultaneous weakening across all five. By 1707 the Mughal empire reached its peak (territory), but not its economic power peak, and not its social power peak. Travancore was never part of the Mughal State. Assam also not. Two analytical tools (apply to every decline question) Vertical power shift = decentralisation The emperor weakens and power moves downward After 1707 the emperors were weak personalities, so the Mansabdars under them became the real centre of power Horizontal power shift = replacement One entity replaces another at the same level Delhi Sultanate replaced by the Mughals at Panipat 1526; British super-power replaced by US-USSR at the end of WW2 (1945) The handout says to apply both lenses to every exam question on decline. The teacher's components board (what each form of power means) Political power = the emperor's word is rule ("vachan hi hai shasan": decision + rule). Teacher: political power is proportional to the territory of the State. Economic power = the treasury, or public exchequer = the name of the bank account of the State. Military power has four parts: number of soldiers / size of the army; technology; no military corruption; strong military leadership. Framework: political, economic and military power The teacher's World War examples: 1945, USSR had the largest army; 1945, atomic bomb (USA). Social power: awe and love, security, revolt Social power = awe / love in people's hearts. The common man wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural), not to be an MP, MLA or minister. Social power falls = chance of revolt rises; social power rises = chance of revolt falls. Example: 1971, Indira Gandhi, and the film song of the time. The teacher's list of factors Reasons for decline of the Mughals Factors tree: Aurangzeb, institutional, economic, military, weak emperors 1. Role of Aurangzeb 58-07: wars, religious policy. 2. Weak emperors post-1707. 3. Military weakened: external (Nadir Shah) and internal (rebel states, e.g. the Marathas). 4. Institutional decline: disloyalty of Mansabdars, military corruption. 5. Jagirdari crisis of the 18th century. 6. Lack of reform (tech and organisation), all ending in territorial decline. "We have covered the concepts of decline of the Mughals. Now let's look at factual data and events to support the concepts." Concepts first, then facts: org = concept + fact. Concepts of decline: factionalism, weak personality, military weakness Concept summary: Factionalism (Royal vs Royal, Royal vs Noble, Noble vs Noble); Weak personality (Rangila, 1719-48 = Muhammad Shah 19-48); Military weakness plus shrinking of territory (external: Nadir Shah 1738-40; internal: Marathas).

items.t: 2 · Why did Aurangzeb 58-07's wars sow the seeds of decline?
items.x: Because the peak hid weak economic and social power, the story begins with Aurangzeb's wars. Ask: was the return on investment positive, and did peace follow? Aurangzeb 58-07 came to power in 1658 after a brutal succession war (he killed his elder brother Dara Shikoh). He governed as an empire-builder on a mission: to conquer all of India, particularly the Deccan. War helps a State only if ROI (return on investment) is positive and a period of peace follows the conquest. If wars never stop and territory won is eventually lost, it becomes an economic disaster. War as rapid investment; victory as slow ROI War = rapid investment of money: recruit more men and horses, produce more weapons, logistics (costs of moving men, food, weapons), attrition of soldiers, horses and elephants. Domestic economy suffers if the war is fought in the homeland. Victory = long, slow ROI: gain of territory (more LR, ports, trade) and geopolitical gains such as a natural frontier. Example: Hitler wanted territory up to the Urals. What he won, and what it cost Bijapur (annexed 1686; Adil Shahi dynasty 1489–1686) and Golconda (annexed 1687; Qutb Shahi dynasty 1518–1687). Both were successor kingdoms of the Bahmani Sultanate (1347–1527). In Bijapur it was a three-way fight: Mughals, Bijapur, and the Marathas, who never accepted Mughal authority. By 1705 the Marathas were winning; by the 1750s they had reversed most of Aurangzeb 58-07's gains and some of Akbar 56-05's as well. 40 years of warfare drained the treasury (the government's bank account), broke the Mansabdars financially (they had to maintain armies), and translated directly into later military corruption (Mansabdars not maintaining the army as per Sawar). Role of Aurangzeb 58-07 versus Akbar 56-05 Role of Aurangzeb 58-07 (1658-1707, about 50 years) versus Akbar 56-05 (about 50 years). Aurangzeb, four lines: (1) Religious orthodoxy: Jizya (1679), temple policy → social power sad. (2) Execution of leaders: GTB (1675), Sambhaji 80-89 (1689) → social power sad. (3) Contribution to the Jagirdari crisis. (4) Continuous wars of about 45 years → economy sad (high LR demand; military corruption → weak military; wars proved useless ultimately; future emperors inherit a weak treasury). Akbar 56-05 = foundation of rise. Universal peace, syncretic policies, religious harmony → social power happy. LR system fair, no Ijaradari, economic security. Strong state machinery (Mansabdari system) → military happy. Deccan wars table and the fight triangle Deccan triangle: Bijapur (1686), Golconda (1687), Goa, and the old Vijayanagara (1336–1646) region below them. Fight triangle = Aurangzeb 58-07 (external power) + Marathas (domestic rebels) + Bijapur (existing State). Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur: Adil Shahi dynasty (1489-1686) Golconda Fort, Hyderabad: Qutb Shahi dynasty (1518-1687) Gol Gumbaz is the mausoleum (burial building, like the Taj Mahal) of Muhammad Adil Shah (1627–56) of the Adil Shahi dynasty. How 40 years of war drained the State Forty years of war: treasury, Mansabdars, military corruption Aurangzeb's long wars lead to Mansabdar losses and military weakness 40 years of war, step by step Endless Deccan campaigns; conquest without lasting peace; Marathas continue rebellion Treasury drained by perpetual warfare Mansabdars forced to maintain armies in continuous wars; financially crippled Military corruption post-1707: troops not maintained as per Sawar rank Military weakened; loss of territory for the Mughals

items.t: 3 · Religious policies and the social foundation
items.x: Because the wars cost money, the emperor also lost the people. Ask: which of the four dates hit social power, and who became a martyr? State power needs social support. Aurangzeb 58-07 followed an orthodox interpretation of Islam in his personal life and his governance, systematically alienating non-Muslim subjects. 3.1 Jizya (1679) and its long history The most damaging measure was the re-introduction of Jizya in 1679 (abolished in 1564): an additional tax on non-Muslim adult males. Beyond the money, the manner of collection made people feel religiously discriminated against, and resentment ran deep. Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 first introduced Jizya in an institutionalised manner. He was the first Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) and founder of the Mamluk dynasty (1206–1290; Mamluk = military slave). Babur 26-30 and Humayun 30-40 continued it. Akbar 56-05 abolished it in 1564 as part of his Sulh-i-Kul (Universal Peace) policy. Aurangzeb 58-07 reintroduced it in 1679. Zulfiqar Khan (Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13 abolished it again in 1712. The handout says Farukhsiyar (1713–19) re-introduced it in 1717. As the empire weakened, Jizya faded with it. Jizya in India: timeline from 712 CE to 1719 Who first introduced Jizya? Muhammad bin Qasim introduced it in 712 CE after conquering Sindh. By paying it, the non-Muslim population was granted the status of Zimmis (Dhimmis), "protected people", allowed to practise their religion and exempted from military service. (Handout aside: is this a gain or a loss of employment opportunity for the masses?) Who first institutionalised Jizya? Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10. Discrepancy. Handout: Farukhsiyar re-introduced Jizya in 1717. Class slide: Farukhsiyar continued the abolition but later re-imposed it, and Jizya fades from 1719. Both agree: abolished 1712, re-imposed by Farukhsiyar, gone by 1719. 3.2 Temple policy: Kashi Vishwanath (1669) Aurangzeb 58-07 refused temple repairs and reduced their land grants. More significantly he demolished important temples. Best-known case: the Kashi Vishwanath temple at Varanasi, demolished 1669, replaced on the same site by the Gyanvapi Mosque. His own court record, the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, documents his order. The temple's troubled history: razed earlier by Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 (1194, then slave-general of Md Ghori, before he became first Sultan in 1206) and Sikandar Lodi (1490). Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore rebuilt it in 1780 near the original site. Kashi Vishwanath Temple and Gyanvapi Mosque, Varanasi 3.3 Executions that backfired 1675: Guru Tegh Bahadur (GTB), the 9th Sikh Guru. 1689: Chhatrapati Sambhaji 80-89, elder son of Shivaji 74-80, after weeks of torture. Both were offered convert-or-die; both refused. The executions did not suppress resistance: they created martyrs, hardening anti-Mughal sentiment among Sikhs and Marathas. GTB (1675) and Sambhaji 80-89 (1689) = the "execution of leaders" line, under social power sad.

items.t: 4 · Why did the Mansabdari system turn against the empire?
items.x: Because the treasury and the people were weaker, the nobles who served the emperor came under strain. Ask: what is different for an unhappy Mansabdar under a strong and a weak emperor? The Mansabdari system ran on personal loyalty to the emperor as an individual, not impersonal loyalty to the empire as an institution. It was a give-and-take: the emperor granted Mansabs and Jagirs; nobles gave military service and loyalty. Strong emperors made this work; weak emperors could not. After 1707 the Later Mughals could not control powerful Mansabdars. When the emperor could not grant the desired Mansabs and Jagirs, the Mansabdars became disloyal and acted upon that disloyalty (earlier, either fear or belief in the fairness of a strong emperor kept them in line): they engaged in court politics for the best Mansabs and Jagirs, or tried replacing the emperor with their favourite from the royal family. Court politics crippled governance. Those who should have led reforms (economic, administrative and military) were consumed by factional rivalry. "Busy in court politics and not on work" = the reason reform slowed down. Disloyalty under strong versus weak emperors; factionalism Why the Mansabdari bargain failed Mansabdar does not get the desired Mansab and Jagir Feeling of disloyalty Strong emperor: good strong = faith in future fairness; bad strong = fear; so no action by the Mansabdar Weak emperor: the Mansabdar acts on his feeling of disloyalty Factionalism = group politics = court politics: lobbying the emperor, backbiting, plot/coup (takhtapalat), bringing the favourite as emperor

items.t: 5 · Why did the Mughal military weaken?
items.x: Because nobles were busy in court politics, the army was left unreformed. Ask: which of the three problems is a matter of people, and which of method? Three interconnected problems: 5.1 No technological or organisational reform European powers succeeded with smaller numbers because of better command, tighter discipline, and tactical innovations: File firing: rotating lines for continuous fire. Grapeshot artillery: multiple bullets in one shot; lethal at close range. Bayonet (a knife) on the Brown Bess musket (so a rifle became a sword at close range). Haider Ali 61-82, Mysore) reorganised his military on the European model and stayed formidable. The Mughals, paralysed by factionalism, reformed nothing. Why the Mughal military collapsed No reform while Indian rivals upgraded the military with European help. Example: Haider Ali 61-82 reorganised on the French model (class slide: "on the French model"; handout: "European model"). 5.2 Weak war commanders Under the Later Mughals (1707–1858), court politics, not merit, decided military appointments. 5.3 Military corruption Under weak supervision Mansabdars maintained far fewer cavalry than their Sawar rank required, pocketing the difference. Aurangzeb 58-07's war drain and the Jagirdari crisis compounded this. By the early 18th century the army was corrupt, under-equipped, poorly led and technologically frozen. The Jagirdari crisis increased the chances of military corruption.

items.t: 6 · Factionalism: how it operated in the Mughal court
items.x: Because loyalty was personal, nobles formed groups to control the emperor. Ask: which group does each named noble belong to? Factionalism = Royal vs Royal + Royal vs Noble + Noble vs Noble. It is group politics. Irani Shia Persian Zulfiqar Khan (Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13; ended Jizya) Turani Sunni Turkish-Uzbek (like the Mughals) Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (1724–48), Governor / Subadar / Nawab of Hyderabad Suba Hindustani Converted Indian Muslims Sayyid Brothers (brought Farukhsiyar 13-19 to power) Hindu Rajputs and Jats Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 Deccani Nobles absorbed from Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) none given After 1707 weak emperors could not control these groups. Mansabdars competed to dominate the sitting emperor or install their preferred candidate: whoever controlled the emperor controlled Mansabs and Jagirs. No clear succession rule: every emperor's death was potentially a new power struggle. Some Mansabdars who could have stabilised the centre chose not to, and instead used the chaos to carve out their own principalities (the successor states). Factionalism: Royal vs Royal, Royal vs Noble, Noble vs Noble

items.t: 7 · The Jagirdari crisis: why did it hit so hard?
items.x: Because there were more claimants than land, tenure became unsafe and everything below it cracked. Ask: why does the teacher call this the most important cause? The Jagirdari crisis was a structural mismatch: supply of Jagirs and demand for them fell dangerously out of balance. Jagirdari crisis: Mansabdars up, land down Water-crisis analogy: number of people up, water down. Jagirdari crisis = number of Mansabdars up + land down. What? (1) Over-recruitment of Mansabdars. (2) Land is the same in the kingdom; it shrunk because of loss of territory in wars (post-1705, the Marathas winning). Why over-recruitment? (a) Role of Aurangzeb 58-07: he declared most lands of Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687 as Khalisa (LR to the King), but the Deccani group came in as Mansabdars. (b) Post-1707 factionalism: either to be in power or to come to power, emperors over-recruited. Mansabdars maintain the army from their Jagirs The crisis High number of Mansabdars but less land for distribution as Jagirs: demand-supply mismatch The origin After taking Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687), Aurangzeb 58-07 declared most of their lands Khalisa to be self-sufficient in funding the war vs the Marathas. Mansabdars rose, the Jagir lands did not Over-recruitment Later Mughals kept appointing Mansabdars to buy the loyalty of Mansdar groups while land under Mughal control kept shrinking Gross inequality 5% of Mansabdars controlled 61% of Jagir revenue Luxury inflation Inflation in luxury goods (partly from EIC exports of Indian goods) meant many could not sustain an elite life The consequences Impact of the Jagirdari crisis = most important in the decline of the Mughals. Chain: factionalism (noble vs noble for Jagirs) → political instability (emperor of choice to power) → pressure on the emperor → change in Jagir tenure (many Naqdi Mansabdars waiting) → insecurity of tenure (kal ho na ho Jagir) → military corruption, and greater, more frequent Ijaradari → over-extraction of LR → Zamindar-led peasant revolts. Military corruption → victories for rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) plus an external power (e.g. Nadir Shah) → loss of territory (State = organisation = rules + territory). The Jagirdari spiral Frequent transfers: Jagirs shuffled to satisfy disgruntled Naqdi Mansabdars Tenure insecurity: no Jagirdar knew how long he would hold the land (kal ho na ho Jagir) Ruthless extraction: maximum in minimum time; no incentive to invest in the land Ijaradari spreads: revenue-farming strips collection from Zamindars, the rural stabilisers Impact of the Jagirdari crisis: most important in decline Peasant revolts: over-extraction leads to Zamindar-led revolts (Jat Kingdom from the 1695 revolt under Churaman 95-21 Jat) Effect on the peasantry: over-extraction, stagnation, revolts led by alienated Zamindars. Direct example: the Jat Kingdom emerged from a 1695 peasant revolt under Churaman 95-21 Jat, a Zamindar. Meanwhile Mansabdars did not maintain the army as per Sawar, to maximise their earnings, as no one knew when the emperor would transfer the Jagir (kal ho na ho Jagir). The teacher ties the military consequences together: military corruption → victories for rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) + an external power (Nadir Shah) → loss of territory.

items.t: 8 · Proof of decline: factionalism in practice
items.x: Because factionalism was a concept, the teacher now gives facts. Ask: which round of the boxing match is each emperor in? Royal vs Royal Bahadur Shah (1707–12) fought his brothers to be in power. Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power backed by Zulfiqar Khan (Irani), but only after executing the father of Farukhsiyar. Reward: Zulfiqar became Wazir. Farukhsiyar (with the Sayyids) removed and executed Jahandar Shah 12-13. Jahandar Shah 12-13 Back the right claimant, extract the reward Royal vs Noble Farukhsiyar rose with the Sayyid Brothers (Abdullah Khan became Wazir; Hussain Ali Khan became Mir Bakshi). He refused to be their puppet and built rival alliances. The Sayyids reached outside the court, allied with the Marathas under Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath 13-20; 15,000 Maratha cavalry temporarily took over Delhi in 1719), killed him, and installed Muhammad Shah 19-48 as a puppet Farukhsiyar (1713–19) The price of noble support is being a puppet Noble vs Noble Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Turani) allied with the Irani group and defeated the Sayyids. He served as Wazir 1722–24, then, seeing the centre was beyond saving, took the Mansab of Governor of Hyderabad Suba in 1724. In 1740 he left Delhi permanently Md Shah (1719–48) "Delhi to gayo, at least save my Hyderabad" Bahadur Shah 07-12: fought brothers to be in power. Jahandar Shah 12-13: Royal vs Royal. Farukhsiyar 13-19: Royal vs Noble. Md Shah 19-48: "totally uninterested in ruling." Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48: Noble vs Noble; Wazir 1722-24, quits Delhi for Hyderabad. Mir Bakshi = Chief Military Paymaster / Commander (defence minister + defence finance authority, the handout adds). On the decline arc, succession turmoil is corrected from "1719-24" to "1707-19": it runs from Aurangzeb 58-07's death to Muhammad Shah 19-48's installation.

items.t: 9 · How the Marathas exposed the military collapse
items.x: Because Delhi was weak inside, the Marathas could measure it from outside. Ask: what did each step, 1737 and 1738, take from Mughal prestige? The military decline is best measured by what the Marathas achieved. Marathas expose the military collapse From 1705 they systematically defeated Mughal forces. By the mid-18th century they had not only recovered Aurangzeb 58-07's Deccan gains but taken lands annexed under Akbar 56-05, including Gujarat. Only Hyderabad (formerly Golconda) stayed outside Maratha control, held by Nizam as a successor State. 1737: Peshwa Bajirao 20-40 marched to Delhi, plundered the capital, and briefly held Md Shah prisoner. 1738: the Marathas defeated a large Mughal army commanded by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48. Formalised in the Treaty of Bhopal (1738): the Marathas received legal recognition of control over all lands between the Chambal and Narmada and the Subah of Malwa. Imagine the Mughal emperor became a hostage in his own capital. 1737: "prestige", "military prestige ↓↓↓". 1738 map: Chambal above, Malwa in the middle, Narmada below. 1752: the Mughal came under Maratha protection, because of fear of Afghan (Abdali) invasions.

items.t: 10 · Nadir Shah's invasion (1738–40): the five-pillar blow
items.x: Because the Marathas had gone south, a Persian raider met Delhi alone. Ask: how did one snub undo a 50 lakh deal, and which pillars did he hit? Nadir Shah: route and cost-benefit of war A State has a territory motive, but does a cost-benefit analysis: (+) own resources (economic, military) and (+) geography. Ruling territory = a cost; maintaining territory = a cost. War aims: annexation, or less than annexation, e.g. plunder (attack and loot). Nadir Shah's aim was plunder. Route: Iran → Afghanistan (Kabul) → Khyber Pass → Peshawar → Lahore → Karnal → Panipat → Kurukshetra → Thanesar → Delhi. Nadir Shah ruled a Persian empire stretching into Afghanistan (Mughal-claimed territory) and desired India's wealth. His victory was easier because of the weakened Mughal empire plus factionalism. Map: Nadir Shah's route to Karnal and Delhi What happened, step by step Battle of Karnal 1739 and Nizam's negotiation Karnal to the fall of Delhi (1739) Battle of Karnal: Mughal army routed; Sadat Khan 22-39 taken prisoner; the Mir Bakshi died fighting Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, now Mir Bakshi, negotiates: Rs 50 lakh and Nadir Shah does not enter Delhi Factionalism: snubbed over the Mir Bakshi post, Sadat Khan 22-39 goads Nadir Shah to attack Delhi for bigger plunder Delhi falls; Md Shah imprisoned; Nadir Shah rules as emperor of Delhi for 60 days Sadat Khan 22-39, insulted by Nadir Shah after the victory instead of being rewarded, takes his own life Nizam appointed Mir Bakshi = military intelligence + war paymaster. Recent war expenditure had risen (Marathas 1738). Factionalism: Sadat Khan 22-39 wanted to be Mir Bakshi, but the post was given to Nizam. Nadir Shah's loot and Mughal prestige The five pillars Political Md Shah (1719–48) was publicly humiliated and did not stand up for his own dignity. For Mansabdars watching, an emperor who could not stand for his dignity wasn't worth defending. Social Nadir Shah's forces massacred roughly two lakh civilians of Delhi. Whatever social legitimacy remained evaporated in the streets of the capital. Military A State that can't defend its capital invites more attacks. The defeat directly encouraged the First Afghan Invasion of 1748 by Ahmed Shah Abdali. (Board: 1748, "attacks".) Economic Wealth estimated at about 100 crore rupees of the time (x250-300 for present value) extracted, plus irreplaceable assets, most famously the Peacock Throne with the Kohinoor diamond. Mansabdars were forced to contribute from personal wealth. The empire, already in the Jagirdari crisis, now lacked means to rebuild a strong army. Technological Funds that might have bought reform were gone, locking in the existing technology gap, so a weak military. Peacock Throne and Kohinoor, taken 1739 Nadir Shah = the lowest point ("Nadir") of Mughal power (pun on the name). Loot: gems, gold and silver, horses and elephants, artisans, Shah Jahan 27-58's Peacock Throne. Mansabdars' loss → future military corruption; treasury down → a military that could no longer maintain a strong army. Student doubt (handout). If the Marathas plundered Delhi in 1737 and defeated Nizam in 1738, why were they not fighting Nadir Shah in 1739? Because the Marathas had returned South to their HQ after the Treaty of Bhopal (1738). They had already extracted maximum concessions through the treaty. Allow the rival State to get weak; why interfere unless there is a deal, like in 1752? That strategic patience is exactly what gave them the Maratha Protectorate of the Mughal Emperor in 1752.

Because the centre collapsed, power moved to many hands. Ask: which regional powers are successors, rebels or already autonomous, and who is No. 1? Decline arc: 1707, 1719-24, 1752, 1754 Arc board: 1707 "but foundation of decline (1707+)"; 1752 "Ahmed Shah Bahadur 48-54, Mughal came under Maratha protection because of fear of Afghan invasion (Abdali)"; 1754 "Alamgir II 54-59 of Marathas". Handout diagram: Mughal decline arc 1707-1754 1752: the Mughal emperor came under Maratha protection, accepting Maratha military guardianship against further Afghan invasions. The protector had become the protected. 1754: the Marathas installed Alamgir II 54-59 as their puppet emperor, a Mughal ruler chosen by the very people the Mughals had spent decades trying to suppress. By the mid-18th c the Mughal Empire as a functional State had ceased to exist. What remained was a collection of regional powers, each with its own territory, army and foreign policy. The Maratha State stood at the top. The emperor continued to sit in Delhi, technically retaining symbolic sovereignty until 1858, but his actual authority extended little beyond Delhi and Agra. A ceremonial figurehead kept alive because his symbolic legitimacy was useful to others. Mughal rule limited to Delhi and Agra by the mid-18th century By the mid-18th century the Mughal emperor's rule is limited to a small area around Delhi and Agra; symbolically he is emperor of Hindustan until 1858. Sovereignty = symbolic power + power on external and domestic affairs (= rule). Rule in different parts is by different regional States (next chapter). India by the mid-18th century: regional powers Multiple regional powers = Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad (successor states); Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand and Farukhabad (rebel states; the Afghans); Mysore, Rajputs, Travancore (already autonomous). No. 1 power = Marathas. Stressed: the emperor's symbolic sovereignty and the regional powers. Beside the Shah Alam II line: "Factionalism: R vs N". The Prelims 2003 pin: Shah Alam II 60-06 Worth pinning (Prelims 2003). Shah Alam II 60-06 spent the initial years of his reign away from Delhi because of fear of his own Wazir, Imad-ul-Mulk, not fear of foreign invasion from the North-West frontier. The question: Assertion (A): Shah Alam II 60-06 spent the initial years as an Emperor far away from his capital. Reason (R): There was always a lurking danger of foreign invasion from the North-West frontier. (a) Both true and R explains A Wrong: R is false; the threat was internal (Wazir), not external (frontier) (b) Both true but R does not explain A Wrong: R is false (same reason) (c) A is true, R is false Answer (c) (d) A false, R true Wrong: A is true Teacher's lesson on Assertion-Reason questions Method: read as independent statements. (i) Read A and mark T/F. (ii) Read R and mark T/F. (iii) If both are True, THEN THINK: is R the reason for A? On this PYQ both A and R are True (the word "always" in R is stressed) and the board marks (b) ("both true but R is not the correct explanation"). Note: UPSC was not bringing any answer key. Coaching institutes have brought out keys: both (c) and (b) appear. Conflict. Handout and class slides give (c) (R false: the cause was fear of the Wazir). The board's own marking points to (b), and coaching keys are split between (c) and (b). Learn both the facts and the dispute. Fact to hold: Shah Alam II 60-06's cause was fear of his Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk.

items.t: 12 · Exam strategy: how to turn a PYQ into a FYQ
items.x: Because the same facts serve different questions, learn to read the protagonist. Ask: who is the question about, and who therefore gets the 70%? The key skill is identifying the protagonist of a question, what it is actually centred on. Once you know the protagonist, you know where to put your emphasis. PYQ (Mains 2017) "By mid-18th century, India was a spectre of fragmented polity. Elaborate." Fragmented polity 30% Mughal decline (cause), 70% rise of regional powers (evidence) FYQ (illustrative) "In the first half of the 18th century, the Mughal Empire was reduced to a figment of imagination. Elaborate." The Mughal Empire's own collapse 70% Mughal decline (Maratha victories, Nadir Shah's invasion, Karnal, Bhopal, emperor-as-puppet), 30% regional powers (supporting evidence of Mughal irrelevance) Assertion-Reason method Same body of knowledge. Two different protagonists. Two very different answers.

712 Muhammad bin Qasim imposes Jizya in Sindh (first) 1206 Aibak (1206-10) institutionalises Jizya 1336 Vijayanagara begins (1336-1646) 1347 Bahmani Sultanate begins (1347-1527) 1489 Adil Shahi dynasty of Bijapur begins (1489-1686) 1518 Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda begins (1518-1687) 1564 Akbar 56-05 abolishes Jizya (Sulh-i-Kul) ★ 1658 Aurangzeb 58-07 comes to power after the succession war (Dara Shikoh killed) 1669 Kashi Vishwanath demolished; Gyanvapi Mosque built ★ 1675 Guru Tegh Bahadur executed ★ 1679 Aurangzeb 58-07 re-introduces Jizya ★ 1686 Aurangzeb 58-07 annexes Bijapur ★ 1687 Aurangzeb 58-07 annexes Golconda ★ 1689 Sambhaji 80-89 executed ★ 1695 Jat revolt under Churaman 95-21 (Jat Kingdom) 1705 Marathas begin winning against the Mughals 1707 Aurangzeb 58-07 dies; Mughal territory at its peak; the decline begins ★ 1712 Zulfiqar Khan (Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13) abolishes Jizya 1717 Handout: Farukhsiyar re-introduces Jizya 1719 Muhammad Shah 19-48 installed as puppet; 15,000 Maratha cavalry in Delhi ★ 1722 Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 Wazir (to 1724) 1724 Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 takes the Mansab of Governor of Hyderabad Suba ★ 1737 Peshwa Bajirao 20-40 plunders Delhi ★ 1738 Marathas defeat Nizam; Treaty of Bhopal (Chambal-Narmada and Malwa) ★ 1739 Nadir Shah: Battle of Karnal; Delhi ruled for 60 days; Peacock Throne and Kohinoor taken ★ 1740 Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 leaves Delhi for good 1748 Abdali's first Afghan invasion ★ 1752 Mughal emperor under Maratha protection ★ 1754 Marathas install Alamgir II 54-59 as puppet ★ 1760 Shah Alam II 60-06; early years away from Delhi (fear of Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk) 1858 Symbolic sovereignty of the Mughal emperor ends

The peak that hid the rot (1707). By 1707 the Mughal State has its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07, yet the teacher says its economic power and social power have not peaked. State power is Political + Economic + Military + Social + Technological, and the decline will weaken all five at once. Aurangzeb laid the foundation of decline; the weak emperors after him could not revive the State or added to the decline. The emperor who never stopped fighting. Aurangzeb 58-07 comes to power in 1658 after killing his elder brother Dara Shikoh, and wants all India, above all the Deccan. He annexes Bijapur in 1686 (Adil Shahi, 1489-1686) and Golconda in 1687 (Qutb Shahi, 1518-1687), but the Marathas never accept Mughal authority. About 40 years of war drain the treasury and cripple the Mansabdars, who must maintain armies; by 1705 the Marathas are winning. The people turn away. Aurangzeb 58-07 follows an orthodox Islam in his governance. He re-introduces Jizya in 1679 (Akbar 56-05 had abolished it in 1564) and demolishes the Kashi Vishwanath temple in 1669 (his court record, the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, documents it). He executes Guru Tegh Bahadur in 1675 and Sambhaji 80-89 in 1689; both refuse to convert and become martyrs, hardening Sikh and Maratha feeling. The bargain breaks. The Mansabdari system runs on personal loyalty to the emperor and a give-and-take: Mansabs and Jagirs for military service. A strong emperor keeps even an unhappy Mansabdar quiet through faith in fairness or through fear. A weak emperor cannot, so the Mansabdar acts on his disloyalty: lobbying, backbiting, a takhtapalat to bring his favourite to the throne. A paper army. Europeans win with smaller numbers using file firing, grapeshot and the bayonet on the Brown Bess musket; Haider Ali 61-82 reforms on a European model, but the Mughals, paralysed by factionalism, reform nothing. Commanders are chosen by court politics, not merit, and Mansabdars keep far fewer cavalry than their Sawar rank requires. Too many Mansabdars, too little land. The Jagirdari crisis is like a water crisis: the number of Mansabdars goes up and the land goes down. After 1686 and 1687 Aurangzeb 58-07 makes most Bijapur and Golconda land Khalisa yet absorbs the Deccani nobles; later Mughals over-recruit to buy loyalty; land shrinks as the Marathas win. Then 5% of Mansabdars control 61% of Jagir revenue, and luxury inflation hurts the rest. The teacher calls its impact the most important in the decline. Kal ho na ho Jagir. Jagirs are shuffled to satisfy disgruntled Naqdi Mansabdars, so no Jagirdar knows how long he holds his land. He extracts the maximum in the minimum time, Ijaradari spreads, and Zamindar-led revolts follow: the Jat Kingdom grows from the 1695 revolt of Churaman 95-21 Jat. Military corruption brings victories to rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) and to an outsider like Nadir Shah. Five factions, three rounds. The court splits into Irani, Turani, Hindustani, Hindu and Deccani groups. Bahadur Shah 07-12 fights his brothers; Jahandar Shah 12-13 rules with Zulfiqar Khan and is executed by Farukhsiyar 13-19, who rises with the Sayyid Brothers. He refuses to be their puppet, so the Sayyids ally with the Marathas (15,000 cavalry in Delhi, 1719), kill him and install Muhammad Shah 19-48. Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 beats the Sayyids with the Irani group, then takes Hyderabad in 1724. The Marathas test Delhi. From 1705 the Marathas defeat Mughal forces; by the mid-18th century they recover Aurangzeb 58-07's gains and take Akbar 56-05's Gujarat, and only Hyderabad holds out. In 1737 Peshwa Bajirao 20-40 plunders Delhi and briefly holds Md Shah prisoner. In 1738 they beat the army led by Nizam, and the Treaty of Bhopal gives them the Chambal-Narmada lands and Malwa. Nadir Shah, the lowest point (1739). Nadir Shah wants plunder, not annexation. At Karnal the Mughal army is routed and Sadat Khan 22-39 is captured; Nizam, now Mir Bakshi, buys peace for Rs 50 lakh. But Sadat Khan, passed over for that post, goads Nadir Shah to attack Delhi: he rules for 60 days, about 2 lakh civilians die, about 100 crore is looted, including the Peacock Throne with the Kohinoor. The Marathas, home in the South after Bhopal, simply wait. Protector and puppet (1752-54). Nadir Shah's victory encourages Abdali's first invasion of 1748. In 1752 the emperor comes under Maratha protection for fear of Afghan invasions, and in 1754 the Marathas install Alamgir II 54-59 as their puppet. By the mid-18th century there are many States, not one: successors (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), rebels (Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farukhabad) and the already autonomous (Mysore, Rajputs, Travancore), with the Marathas as No. 1 power. The emperor keeps symbolic sovereignty until 1858. How the exam asks it. Prelims 2003: Shah Alam II 60-06 stayed away from Delhi in his early years for fear of his Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk, not a frontier invasion; read A and R separately, then think. Mains 2017 asked about a fragmented polity: find the protagonist and weight 30% Mughal decline and 70% regional powers, and flip the weights if the Mughal Empire itself is the subject.
Prelims 2021 The relation between the Carnatic and Hyderabad Do not treat the Carnatic as a separate independent State. It was the southern part of the Hyderabad Subah The Carnatic inside Hyderabad

Story so far: before any State is built, the teacher fixes one idea, control is not rule. Hold it: Plassey is control, Buxar is rule. Control versus Rule: absentee colonialism; Plassey and Buxar Control ≠ Rule. Control is possible without ruling (absentee colonialism, e.g. Angola, Mozambique: raw materials extracted, few people on the ground). Rule = doing L, E, J (making and implementing laws) plus governance of local health, education, infrastructure through IAS, IPS. EIC in Bengal: Plassey 1757 = control / conquest began; Buxar 1764 = rule began.

items.t: 1 · Framework: the three classes of regional State
items.x: Because the Mughal State stopped working as one polity, power spread out. Ask: which of the three classes fought the emperor, and which only took his authority? By the mid-18th century the Mughal State had ceased to function as a single unified polity. What remained was a patchwork of regional powers. Power decentralises (1707-1800) to three kinds of State Successor States Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad Powerful Mansabdars who extracted governing authority over a Subah from the emperor (this chapter) Rebel States Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Afghans (Farukhabad, Rohilkhand) Formed by those who openly rebelled against the empire Already Autonomous Rajputs, Mysore, Travancore Never under effective Mughal control to begin with Successor states: "the Mughal emperor is stabbed in the back by his provincial governors / Subadars", who set up their own rule in B, A, H but never declared independence formally. Rebel states: they FOUGHT the Mughal State, took some territory and built their own State on it. Already autonomous: "even when the Mughal was powerful, he did not rule here." Maps of 18th-century India: regions and European settlements Handout map marked 1700-95. The list of later emperors (teacher's proof of decline) Later Mughal emperors: successor States arose in 1713-48 Bahadur Shah 1707–12 Jahandar Shah 12-13 1712–13 Farukhsiyar 1713–19 Muhammad Shah 19-48 (Rangila) 1719–48 Ahmad Shah Bahadur 1748–54 Alamgir II 54-59 1754–59 Shah Alam II 60-06 1760–1806 Akbar II 06-37 1806–37 Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 1837–57 FS 13-19 and Md Shah 19-48 are the reigns in which the Successor States arose. "Proof of decline of Mughal."

items.t: 2 · Why autonomous but never formally independent?
items.x: Because the governors held real power, why did they not simply declare independence? Four reasons, and one founder holds two Delhi posts. Bengal was set up as a successor state by Murshid Quli Khan (MQK, 1717–27) in 1717; Awadh by Sadat Khan 22-39 in 1722; Hyderabad by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 in 1724. Each ruled de facto as sovereign; none declared independence. Founders of the successor States and the EIC column De facto = on-ground reality. De jure = on paper. All of these were Mansabdars, some ministers in the Central Govt, some in the Provincial Govt (a Head of State with three branches at the Centre; a similar tree in each Province). The board's "EIC" column lists 1757, 1764, 1798 against Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad. Neither slides nor handout explain 1798; check your own notes. Why B, A, H did not declare independence Symbolic legitimacy (Social power) A Mughal Subahdar's title commanded the obedience of local nobles If you declare independence, opponents may unite against you in the name of the emperor Ambitions at Delhi (Political power) Prized Mansabs at the Centre: Wazir (PM / Imperial Diwan) and Mir Bakshi (War Paymaster). Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 was Wazir 1722–24 while also Subahdar of Hyderabad, and became Mir Bakshi in 1739–40 while still Subahdar of Hyderabad Independent Hyderabad has no influence; Hyderabad with a minister at the Centre has some influence on the rest of the Mughal empire Military assistance (Military power) Provinces could rely on each other's help in times of war If independent, an attack on Hyderabad is no longer an attack on the Mughal empire, so the help is gone Trade barriers (Economic power) Political independence could hurt trade, because tariffs may then apply. (Think EU members giving up partial sovereignty for open borders and trade.) Domestic trade is easier, cheaper, lower taxes

items.t: 3 · Mughal provincial titles and the Bengal Subah's structure
items.x: Because a governor could only rule a province by taking its offices, learn the offices first: Sword, Purse and Eyes, each with a different boss at Delhi. Ask: who reported to whom? Subahdar (Nazim / Nawab) Nizamat: defence, peace, criminal justice (the Sword) the Emperor Diwan Diwani: land revenue and civil justice (the Purse) the Imperial Diwan (Wazir), bypassing the Nazim Bakshi of the Subah Military audit and intelligence the Mir Bakshi at the Centre, bypassing the Nazim The design (Akbar 56-05 Checks and balances. Every successor State's founder dismantled it none Akbar's Mansabdari system: checks and balances Akbar 56-05's Mansabdari system = checks and balances in any province. Nazim / Subadar = gun power (military head). Diwan = political + finance power (CM + FM). Bakshi = intelligence power. Each reports to a different officer at Delhi, all under the King. To end the emperor's authority in a province: end the checks and balances; concentrate all power in yourself or your supporters. This is the recipe in Section 4. Vocabulary: Mansabdar, Nazim, Subadar, Nawab, Naib Mansabdar is the general term (like "animal"); Mir Bakshi, Nazim, Naib Nazim are particular posts (like lion, tiger, cheetah). Naib = Deputy. Nazim = Subadar = Nawab of Suba = Governor. "Nizam" was the title of the Nazim of the Hyderabad Suba. Nawab ≠ Subahdar always. A Nawab could run a sub-region within a Suba: Alivardi Khan 40-56 was Nawab of Patna (inside the Bengal Subah) / Naib Nazim of Bihar before becoming Subahdar of all Bengal in 1740. Naib Nazim = Deputy Subahdar. The Diwan did not report to the Subahdar but directly to the Imperial Diwan at Delhi. Akbar 56-05 made the two co-equal. This separation of the Sword (Nizamat) from the Purse (Diwani) kept the Mughal Empire stable for over a century. Every successor State founder had to dismantle it. 3.1 Geographical administration of the Bengal Subah (handout tables) Territory: Bengal Subah (West Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, East Bengal). Capital: Murshidabad (in West Bengal). Nizamat (Home Minister: law and order, criminal justice, defence / war commander) = Nazim (Subahdar), directly answerable to the Emperor. Diwani (revenue, civil administration, civil justice) = Diwan, directly answerable to the Emperor (under the supervision of the Imperial Diwan, i.e. the Wazir). Parallel audit and intelligence officer = Bakshi of the Subah, reports directly to the Mir Bakshi at Delhi, bypassing the Nazim. The Nazim, the Diwan and the Bakshi were mutually independent. None could overrule the others. All three reported only to their imperial counterparts at Delhi. Chain of command (handout table 3.2) Nizamat Home Minister (law and order, criminal justice) plus defence (war commander) Naib Nazim Nazim (Subahdar) Emperor (direct reporting; no intermediate minister) Diwani Revenue, civil administration, civil justice Naib Diwan Diwan Wazir-i-Mumalik / Imperial Diwan (Diwan-i-Ala), then the Emperor Bakshi (parallel audit and intelligence line) Mansabdari records, military payroll, anti-corruption inspection (dagh and chehra), intelligence (waqia-navis) Subordinate Bakshis (attached to Faujdars and contingents) Bakshi of Bengal Subah Mir Bakshi (Bakhshi-ul-Mumalik), then the Emperor Regional breakdown within the Subah of Bengal (handout table 3.3) West Bengal Murshidabad Nazim Diwan Direct rule Bihar Patna Naib Nazim Naib Diwan (reports to Murshidabad) Delegated rule Orissa Cuttack Naib Nazim Naib Diwan (reports to Murshidabad) Delegated rule East Bengal Dacca Naib Nazim Naib Diwan (reports to Murshidabad) Delegated rule The Bakshi line operated as a parallel vertical, reporting only to Delhi. The Bakshi's four functions 1 Mansabdari records Who holds what rank, who got promoted, demoted, joined or died; registers updated constantly 2 Military payroll Calculating each Mansabdar's entitlement, assigning him a Jagir of the right value, transferring Jagirs every 2-3 years to prevent local roots, and in wartime controlling war expenditure 3 Anti-corruption inspection Two mechanisms by Akbar 56-05: Dagh ("branding": every horse branded with an imperial mark on its flank; at inspection only branded horses counted) and Chehra ("face": each soldier's face, height, complexion and marks recorded in a register) 4 Intelligence (waqia-navis) Information collectors in every province, district and significant town, sending daily reports to Delhi: court intrigues, market prices, harvest conditions, military movements, suspicious behaviour by the Nazim or Diwan, rebellions brewing, foreign travellers arriving. Reports flowed up through the Bakshi system, the Mir Bakshi being the chief recipient The Bakshi knew who every noble was (records), what they were paid (payroll), whether they were honest (dagh-chehra) and what they were doing (intelligence). That is why he was the second-highest official in the Empire.

items.t: 4 · How all three successor States were built: the recipe
items.x: Because every founder had to break the design of the last section, a five-step recipe appears. Ask: which step ends the checks, and which buys the men of money? How a successor State was built: the recipe The recipe for a successor State 1 Extract the Subahdari: take the Mansab of Subahdar from the emperor, who depended on powerful Mansabdars (their army) to stay in power 2 End checks and balances: fill the Diwan, Naib Nazim and war commander posts with personal loyalists 3 Build revenue strength: strong revenue administration; field survey, efficient LR system; finance is crucial for everything else 4 Co-opt the men of money: merchants, bankers and Ijaradars get Mansabs, fusing wealth with political power (teacher: intermediary Zamindars) 5 Convert Tankha Jagirs into Vatan Jagirs: hereditary, for the loyalty of other powerful Mansabdars in the province Result: a diffused autonomous polity: a Nawab on top of a network of powerful actors, with the Mughal link kept as a symbol Handout diagram: six-step successor State formation Step 4 in the handout: convert Tankha Jagirs (temporary, transferable) into Vatan Jagirs (hereditary). Vatan = hereditary. The emperor's historic tool of control (shifting Jagirs at will) was traded away for local loyalty of provincial Mansabdars to the regional ruler. Step 5 in the handout (co-opting): intermediary Zamindars, revenue farmers, merchants, moneylenders and bankers were promised security of property and reasonable taxes and, most unprecedentedly, given Mansabs. The Mansabdari system was traditionally lineage-based (military / noble bloodlines only). Appointing merchants and bankers to Mansabs was a structural transformation: administrative rank and commercial wealth, historically kept apart, now merged. All the steps were taken while accepting the symbolic sovereignty of the Mughal Emperor. Count check. Handout heading says "four-step process", its text lists Steps 1 to 5, its diagram shows six steps (adds "keep the Mughal symbolic link"). The slide has five steps plus the result. Learn the recipe, not the number.

Because the recipe worked first in Bengal, watch MQK wear two hats. Ask: whose money makes the Zamindars loyal? Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) Bengal Subah = Bengal, Orissa and Bihar: vast and commercially rich. Capital: Murshidabad, on the banks of the Hooghly, then the major port (the British later developed Calcutta as an alternative). MQK was the last Bengal Governor appointed as per the wish of the Emperor. His path (handout): Diwan from 1700; under Farukhsiyar (1713–19) he also became Deputy Governor of Bengal Suba and Governor of Orissa. In 1717, when elevated to the Mansab of Nazim of Bengal Subah, he already was Diwan (combining finance and executive in one man = ending Akbar 56-05's checks and balances). He still sent tribute to Delhi, but the emperor's approval for appointments in Bengal Suba was now a paper formality. Revenue: brilliant administrator. Collected LR through intermediary Zamindars and got detailed field surveys done for fair assessment. The intermediaries grew powerful: by 1727 just fifteen were collecting 50% of Bengal Suba's LR. Coercion: Mansabdars who resisted had their Tankha Jagirs in Bengal taken and were given Jagirs in Orissa; resisting Zamindars were punished by reducing the land from which they collected LR. MQK's rise = finance + executive + military power in one man. Field surveys gave a "justified / right LR demand." LR chain: ryots → intermediary Zamindars (I2) → Diwan of Suba → Imperial Diwan, money going to the King or to a Jagirdar (J). "Co-opting" powerful people = the 15 Zamindars. Map: Bengal and its neighbours, 1750

items.t: 6 · The Jagat Seths: why Bengal's power was diffused, not centralised
items.x: Because the Nawab's power rested on a network, the bankers matter. Ask: what does the 1740 coup prove about who really chose the Nawab? "Jagat Seth" was a hereditary title, not a personal name, held by successive heads of a banking family: Manikchand under MQK; Mehtab Rai and Swarup Chand under Alivardi Khan 40-56. Already powerful before 1717, under the successor State they rose to what Dutch records called the richest banking house in the world. They loaned to Zamindars (so revenue reached the State on time), loaned to merchants, and ran Hundi services (pre-modern wire transfer). Under Shuja-ud-din Md Khan (1727–39) a Jagat Seth was appointed Treasurer of Bengal and Daroga of the Royal Mint: central bank plus the Nawab's personal banker in one family. Power was diffused, not centralised: a network of Nawab + intermediary Zamindars + merchants + bankers, with the Nawab on top but dependent on their cooperation. Proof: the coup of 1740. Alivardi Khan 40-56 (Nawab of Patna) overthrew and killed the sitting Nawab Sarfaraz Khan (1739–40) with the Jagat Seth's backing. He secured formal approval by promising Emperor Md Shah one crore rupees plus Sarfaraz's personal wealth, and approval was duly given. The emperor had been reduced to a transactional figure.

items.t: 7 · Bengal's virtual break: the Maratha raids and Alivardi Khan 40-56
items.x: Because an outside raider took a share of the revenue, Bengal stopped paying Delhi. Ask: which three provinces does Nagpur pull from? Under MQK, Bengal was autonomous but tribute still was sent to Delhi. Under Alivardi the break deepened, triggered by an external shock. Bengal's virtual break: Raghuji Bhonsle and Alivardi Khan 40-56 The virtual break of Bengal 1745-51: Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raids Bengal repeatedly; Alivardi cannot defeat him 1751 settlement: Bhonsle gets annual Chauth (one-fourth of revenues) of Bengal and Bihar plus direct control of Orissa Part of the revenue now flows to Nagpur Alivardi stops sending revenue to Delhi and stops seeking the emperor's approval for provincial Mansabdar appointments Virtual break complete, but independence never declared The succession chain after Alivardi

items.t: 8 · Awadh: from Sadat Khan 22-39 to the virtual break of 1753
items.x: Because Awadh's founders kept their eyes on Delhi, its break came through a Wazir's misstep. Ask: who is Sadat, who is Safdar, who is Shuja? Founder: Sadat Ali Khan (1722–39), appointed Subahdar in 1722 as a reward for suppressing local revolts. He installed his nephew and son-in-law Safdar Jung 39-54 as Deputy Governor (Naib Nazim) and his own loyalist as Diwan; tribute to Delhi was reduced. Revenue grew from efficient land assessment and taxes on trade. He created a new loyal class of local elites (Indian Muslims, Afghans, Hindus) by giving them Mansabs and Jagirs. Unlike MQK, Sadat Khan 22-39 kept ambitions at the centre: he wanted a senior Mansab at Delhi (the Central Government). He convinced Nadir Shah to invade Delhi in 1739 because the Mir Bakshi post had gone to Chin Qulich Khan (another name of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48) instead of him. Nadir Shah ill-treated him after the victory; he committed suicide. Safdar Jung 39-54 was appointed Wazir by Ahmad Shah Bahadur (1748–54) in 1748. He misused the office to annex Farukhabad into Awadh. Other Mansabdars opposed, and in 1753 he was forced to resign. The resignation was Awadh's virtual break: no more revenue to Delhi, no imperial authority inside Awadh, though legally still part of the empire. Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 was appointed Wazir by Shah Alam II 60-06. He fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) and was later defeated by the EIC at the Battle of Buxar (1764). Awadh survived nominally until EIC annexation in 1856 from Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. Discrepancy to check. The slide calls Safdar Jung 39-54 the nephew of Sadat Khan 22-39; the handout calls him nephew and son-in-law. The handout in Chapter 2 also calls Sadat Khan 22-39 "of Irani group" in the Karnal passage.

items.t: 9 · Hyderabad: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48's path from Delhi to the Deccan
items.x: Because the Nizam failed at the centre, he turned south. Ask: which two posts did he hold at Delhi, and when did he give up? Hyderabad was set up within the empire in 1724 by Chin Qulich Khan, aka Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, aka Asaf Jah I (Nizam, 1724–48), after defeating Mubariz Khan, the sitting Nazim of the Deccan. He was the leader of the Turani group. In Aurangzeb 58-07's Deccan wars he and his father built strong roots in the region. 1720: the Turani and Irani groups removed the Sayyid Brothers, kingmakers who controlled Md Shah, and formally restored imperial authority. But the structural problem remained: Md Shah was uninterested in governance. (Remember: 5% of Mansabdars controlled 61% of all Jagir land revenue.) As Wazir (1722–24) Nizam tried to redistribute Jagirs from big Mansabdars to smaller ones to ease the Jagirdari crisis, but the bigger Mansabdars did not agree. The Marathas defeated him in 1728 and 1738, forcing him to pay Chauth and Sardeshmukhi (10% hereditary Maratha claim in the Deccan). He served as Mir Bakshi (1739–40) during Nadir Shah's invasion. By 1740 he gave up on reforming the centre and moved to Hyderabad permanently. Succession after Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48: Nazir Jung (1748–50) → Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (1750–51, 3 months) → Salabat Jung 51-62, French dominated under Bussy) → Nizam-Ali-Khan (1762–1803). The 1720 removal of the Sayyids = "Factionalism: Noble vs Noble."

items.t: 10 · How Nizam established Hyderabad as a successor State
items.x: Because Hyderabad moved furthest from the Mughal system, it shows the recipe at its most aggressive. Ask: what are the three marks of this State? Symbolic sovereignty (by 1748) The emperor's name on coins and in the Friday Khutba, but zero influence over war, peace, treaties or appointments Tolerance The Hindu majority was economically powerful, so Nizam followed religious tolerance and punished opponents regardless of community Most aggressive change Of the three States, Hyderabad converted Tankha to Vatan Jagirs most aggressively and made merchants, moneylenders and Ijaradars Mansabdars ("upstarts") on the largest scale Merchants and moneylenders got property security and became Mansabdars (called upstarts), and in return gave financial support. The most pronounced transformation of the Mansabdari system was in Hyderabad. Result: the same diffused polity: Nawab at top, influential sections under him.

items.t: 11 · The Carnatic: a State within a State
items.x: Because Hyderabad had a smaller State inside it, the Prelims 2021 trap lives here. Ask: is the Carnatic independent, or the southern part of the Hyderabad Subah? Hyderabad had a smaller State inside its borders, the Carnatic. By law it was part of the Hyderabad province. But it had its own ruler, the Nawab, and ran its own government. Parallels for a State within a State Parallels for the Carnatic: India → J&K (Art. 370); Assam → Meghalaya as an autonomous State within Assam (Art. 244A); Hyderabad → Carnatic, practically autonomous. 11.1 Backstory: the Vijayanagar Empire (1336–1646) For three hundred years the Vijayanagar Empire was the strongest power in South India, and the Carnatic was part of it. Provinces were ruled by Nayaks (teacher: Nayak = CM), Telugu Hindu governors from warrior families. Nayaks divided their provinces into Palayams, each run by a local chief called a Poligar (Palayakkarar) with his own private army and fort. Vijayanagar Empire: Empire, Nayaks, Palayams 11.2 The long decline (1565–1698) Hampi / Vijayanagar ruins: the capital whose 1565 sack ended the empire as a major power. 1. A. Defeat of Vijayanagar at Talikota (1565). A four-state alliance of the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) destroyed the Vijayanagar army. The empire officially continued until 1646, but this defeat was the real end of its power. 2. B. Nayaks independent, then defeated. After 1565 the southern Nayaks of Madurai, Tanjore and Gingee ruled autonomously; distance protected them for a while. By 1646 Bijapur and Golconda conquered and divided the Carnatic between themselves. 3. C. Sultanates defeated by the Mughals. Aurangzeb 58-07 conquered Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687). The whole Carnatic now came under Mughal rule. 4. D. Gingee under the Marathas, then lost to the Mughals. Shivaji 74-80 captured Gingee Fort from Bijapur in 1677. After the Mughals executed Sambhaji 80-89 in 1689, the next Chhatrapati, Rajaram 89-00, made Gingee his base against the Mughals. In 1690 Zulfiqar Khan (Nawab of Carnatic) surrounded the fort. The siege lasted eight years (the longest by the Mughals); the Mughals finally captured Gingee in 1698. (Zulfiqar Khan later became Wazir under Jahandar Shah 12-13, 1712, until his execution in February 1713.) 11.3 Dividing the region Prelims 2021 trap: the Carnatic and Hyderabad relation. Do not treat the Carnatic as a separate independent State; it was the southern part of the Hyderabad Subah. Hyderabad Subah divided: Hyderabad and the Carnatic Hyderabad North of the Krishna river Ruled directly by the Mughal Governor (the Nizam) Carnatic (Hyderabad-Karnatic) Twelve districts south of the Krishna; capital Gingee (covered the old Nayak kingdoms of Gingee, Tanjore and Madurai; on 18th-century maps, simply the "Carnatic") Had its own Nawab, but he reported to the Nizam: a "state within a state" 11.4 and 11.5 Towards autonomy: the Carnatic Nawabs Saadatullah Khan (1710–32) The last Nawab directly chosen by the Mughal Emperor (1710). Two big steps: he moved the capital from Gingee to Arcot and made the Nawab post hereditary in his family without asking the emperor. He was childless and adopted his brother Ghulam Ali's son, Dost Ali. In name the Carnatic was still under the Nizam Dost Ali Khan (1732–40) His adopted nephew. Killed in 1740 by the Marathas under Raghuji Bhonsle in the Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh, close to the Tamil Nadu border Anwar-ud-din Khan (from 1744) Chosen by the Nizam, ending Saadatullah Khan's dynastic rule. But he too emerged autonomous of the Nizam The handout diagram carries the later steps: Anwar-ud-din killed at the Battle of Ambur (1749), 2nd Carnatic War, French versus British; Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah (1752–95), British-backed, leading to dependency on the EIC. The handout text stops at Anwar-ud-din (1744).

items.t: 12 · Synthesis: the common pattern and what it made possible
items.x: Because all three States share one pattern, the EIC faced a gap between paper and power. Ask: what did the emperor become? Concentration of power Across Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad (and the Carnatic): a powerful Mansabdar extracts the Subahdari, dismantles checks and balances, builds revenue strength, converts Tankha to Vatan, and co-opts merchants and bankers into the Mansabdari system No independence None declared it: the Mughal umbrella served their interests; practically independent, including decisions of war and peace. Each developed its own diplomacy, army and fisc Unique Carnatic Part of the Hyderabad Suba but autonomous: a successor State inside a successor State. Fragmentation was not only horizontal (Subahs breaking from the empire) but also vertical (sub-regions within a successor State developing their own semi-autonomous identity) Mughal authority The emperor became a constitutional monarch with no executive power: a ceremonial head of State whose legitimacy was still useful to others The India into which the EIC was stepping: competing, partially autonomous States, each with its own elite coalition and its own fiscal and military interests, and, critically, a world where legitimacy and real power had come apart. That gap between formal authority and actual power is exactly what made the subcontinent vulnerable to outside penetration. Founder and year Murshid Quli Khan, 1717 Sadat Khan 22-39, 1722 Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Asaf Jah I), 1724 Founder's reign 1717–27 1722–39 1724–48 Earlier post Diwan (from 1700) Subahdar as reward for crushing revolts Leader of the Turani group; Wazir 1722–24 Key feature Field surveys; 15 Zamindars collected 50% of LR; Jagat Seths as bankers New loyal elite of Indian Muslims, Afghans and Hindus; kept ambitions at the centre Most aggressive Tankha to Vatan; merchants and moneylenders as Mansabdars; Carnatic inside Link to Nadir Shah 1739 - Sadat Khan 22-39 urged the attack on Delhi Nizam as Mir Bakshi bought Nadir off with Rs 50 lakh (attempt) Virtual break Alivardi Khan 40-56, after 1751 settlement with Raghuji Bhonsle 1753, Safdar Jung 39-54 forced to resign After 1740, Nizam moves to Hyderabad for good EIC link Plassey 1757; Diwani 1765 Buxar 1764; annexed 1856 Succession: French-dominated under Bussy (Salabat Jung 51-62)

1717 MQK becomes Nazim of Bengal (already Diwan) ★ 1727 MQK dies; by now 15 Zamindars collect 50% of Bengal LR; Shuja-ud-din Md Khan (1727-39) 1739 Sarfaraz Khan (1739-40) 1740 Alivardi Khan 40-56's coup with Jagat Seth's backing ★ 1745 Raghuji Bhonsle's raids begin (to 1751) 1751 Settlement: Chauth of Bengal and Bihar, Orissa to Bhonsle ★ 1756 Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 1757 Battle of Plassey; Mir Jafar 57-60 EIC puppet ★ 1760 Mir Qasim 60-63 1763 Mir Jafar 57-60 restored (1763-65) 1765 Bengal's Diwani passes to the EIC ★

Control is not rule. The teacher opens with a warning: control can exist without rule (absentee colonialism, like Angola and Mozambique, where raw materials leave and few people live on the ground). Rule means doing L, E, J, making and implementing laws, plus governance of health, education and infrastructure. For the EIC in Bengal, Plassey 1757 was control and Buxar 1764 was rule. A patchwork. By the mid-18th century the Mughal State no longer worked as one unified polity. Power decentralised from 1707 to 1800 into three classes of State: Successor, Rebel and Already Autonomous. The teacher lists the later emperors as proof of decline, circling FS 13-19 and Md Shah 19-48 as the reigns in which the Successor States arose. Three founders, three years. Bengal was set up by Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) in 1717, Awadh by Sadat Khan 22-39 in 1722, Hyderabad by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 in 1724. Each ruled de facto as sovereign, yet none declared independence. Four reasons: symbolic legitimacy, ambitions at Delhi (Nizam was Wazir 1722-24 and Mir Bakshi 1739-40), military assistance and trade barriers. Sword, Purse, Eyes. Akbar 56-05's system split a province in three. The Subahdar (Nizamat) held the Sword and reported to the Emperor; the Diwan (Diwani) held the Purse and reported to the Imperial Diwan; the Bakshi held military audit and intelligence and reported to the Mir Bakshi. The Diwan and the Bakshi both bypassed the Nazim: checks and balances. The recipe. Extract the Subahdari, end the checks and balances with personal loyalists, build revenue strength (field survey, efficient LR system), co-opt the men of money (merchants, bankers and Ijaradars given Mansabs) and convert Tankha Jagirs into Vatan Jagirs. The result is a diffused autonomous polity: a Nawab on top of a network of powerful actors, with the Mughal link kept as a symbol. Bengal: two hats and fifteen friends. In 1717 MQK 17-27 became Nazim while already Diwan, ending Akbar 56-05's checks. His field surveys and intermediary Zamindars paid off: by 1727 just fifteen collected 50% of Bengal Suba's LR. The Jagat Seths, a hereditary title of a banking family, funded it all. Proof of diffusion: in 1740 Alivardi Khan 40-56 toppled Sarfaraz Khan with a Jagat Seth's backing and bought the emperor's approval with a promised crore. Bengal breaks away. From 1745 to 1751 Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raided Bengal and Alivardi could not beat him. The 1751 settlement gave Bhonsle the Chauth (one-fourth of revenues) of Bengal and Bihar plus direct control of Orissa. Alivardi stopped sending revenue to Delhi and stopped seeking approval for appointments. After him came Siraj 56-57, Mir Jafar 57-60, Mir Qasim 60-63, Mir Jafar again, and in 1765 the Diwani passed to the EIC. Awadh: Sadat, Safdar, Shuja. Sadat Khan 22-39 became Subahdar in 1722 as a reward for crushing revolts and kept ambitions at the centre. Passed over for Mir Bakshi, he convinced Nadir Shah to invade Delhi in 1739, and died by suicide. Safdar Jung 39-54, Wazir in 1748, annexed Farukhabad and was forced to resign in 1753: Awadh's virtual break. Shuja 54-75 fought at Panipat (1761) and lost at Buxar (1764); Awadh was annexed in 1856. Hyderabad: the Nizam goes home. Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Chin Qulich Khan, Asaf Jah I) led the Turani group, helped remove the Sayyid Brothers in 1720, and took Hyderabad in 1724 after beating Mubariz Khan. The Marathas beat him in 1728 and 1738. After serving as Mir Bakshi (1739-40) he gave up on the centre. Hyderabad kept the emperor's name on coins and the Khutba, tolerated its Hindu majority, and converted Tankha to Vatan Jagirs most aggressively. The Carnatic: a tenant downstairs. The Hyderabad Subah had two parts: Hyderabad north of the Krishna, and the Carnatic (Hyderabad-Karnatic), twelve districts south with capital Gingee and its own Nawab who reported to the Nizam. Saadatullah Khan (1710-32) moved the capital to Arcot and made the post hereditary; Dost Ali Khan (1732-40) was killed by the Marathas; Anwar-ud-din Khan (from 1744) was the Nizam's pick but became autonomous too. This is the Prelims 2021 trap. The gap the EIC stepped into. Across all three, a powerful Mansabdar concentrated power, none declared independence, the Carnatic was a successor State inside a successor State, and the emperor became a constitutional monarch with no executive power. Legitimacy and real power had come apart, which made the subcontinent vulnerable to outside penetration.
