items.t: 0 · Where the Marathas fit, and the teacher's opening boards
items.x: Story so far: the Marathas are the first of the Rebel States on the teacher's board, followed by the Sikhs, Jats and Afghans. Ask: which three kinds of regional power did the teacher draw? Chapter 4 title: regional powers and the Marathas as Rebel States Regional powers = SS (Successor States) + Rebel S (Rebel States) + AA S (Already Autonomous States). The Marathas head the Rebel States, followed by the Sikhs, Jats, Afghans. Zat and Sawar: net importance of a Mansabdar Mansabdari refresher: Zat = personal seniority, Sawar = horsemen to be maintained; together they give a Mansabdar's net importance (e.g. Zat 4000 + Sawar 2000 = 6000; Zat 3000 + Sawar 3000 = 6000). See Chapter 1.

items.t: 1 · Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80: who he was and why he rose
items.x: Chapter 1 of the story: a boy of 16 with a fort. Because Bijapur was oppressive and the Mughals were closing in, he rose. Ask: what were the two issues against Bijapur? Shivaji 74-80: who he was and the Deccan setting 1.1 Who he was Shivaji 74-80 Bhonsle was born on 19 February 1630 to Shahji Bhonsle and Jijabai. His father was a Jagirdar of Poona and served as a General and Mansabdar in Bijapur (1489-1686), ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty. This dynasty, together with the Qutub Shahi (1518-1687), had replaced the Bahmani Sultanate (1347-1527) in the Deccan. Early training came from his guardian Dadaji Kondadev, who shaped him as a soldier and administrator. The deeper inspiration came from his mother Jijabai and his own fierce ambition. He captured his first fort at the age of 16, in 1646. Working from the Maval region, a hilly, forested terrain in today's Pune district running through the Sahyadri range, he gathered an army of local warriors and peasants. 1.2 Guerrilla warfare: the teacher's boards Tactics = guerrilla warfare: hide and seek, attack and withdraw, sabotage; not traditional warfare. It uses surprise attacks, speed and geography and creates shock and awe. The only way to defeat a much stronger opponent. Guerrilla warfare is a tool for positive, neutral or negative goals. Examples: Naxals in India; Spain (1808-12) against Napoleon; 1857 Revolt (Kunwar Singh, Tatya Tope); Ganimi Kava of the Marathas; Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922-24). 1.3 Why he rose against Bijapur and the Mughals From 1657 onwards, Shivaji 74-80 launched systematic attacks on the Kingdom of Bijapur (1489-1686), which followed economically oppressive and religiously discriminatory policies. This was also the period when Aurangzeb 58-07 became Mughal emperor. In 1659, Ali Adil Shah II, Sultan of Bijapur, sent his General Afzal Khan to kill Shivaji 74-80 under the pretext of negotiations. Instead, Shivaji 74-80 killed the seven-feet-tall Afzal Khan using his concealed Bagh Nakh (Tiger Claws) and a Bichhwa (dagger). Shivaji versus Bijapur and the Mughals When Aurangzeb 58-07 launched his campaign for the conquest of the Deccan, Shivaji 74-80 defeated the Mughal General Shaista Khan 64-88 in 1663 and sacked the wealthy port of Surat, which enraged Aurangzeb 58-07. Aurangzeb 58-07 sent General Jai Singh 99-43, who used an encirclement strategy to cut off supplies to Maratha territories. In 1665 Jai Singh 99-43 laid siege to Fort Purandhar (40-50 km southeast of Pune). Triangle: Aurangzeb 58-07, the Marathas, Bijapur. The Marathas' goal = Swarajya. 1674 = coronation of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80; 1686 = Aurangzeb 58-07 annexes Bijapur. BG Tilak (1890s) used this cultural history (a Maratha against a Mughal general) to arouse nationalism against the British. Fort Purandhar: Jai Singh's siege and the Treaty of Purandhar 1665 Gherao = starve the enemy. Jai Singh 99-43 = a powerful Hindu Mansabdar of the Mughal State. Standard books say Shivaji 74-80 never accepted Mughal sovereignty; correction: the Treaty of Purandhar 1665 was a temporary tactic. 1.4 Treaty of Purandhar 1665: a tactical pause, not a permanent defeat To prevent the massacre of his soldiers and people, Shivaji 74-80 negotiated the Treaty of Purandhar (1665). Under its terms: 1. He surrendered 23 of his 35 forts to the Mughals. 2. He accepted Aurangzeb 58-07 as Emperor but declined a personal mansab for himself. 3. His son Sambhaji 80-89 was made a Mughal Mansabdar with a rank of 5,000. 4. He agreed to support the Mughals in their war against Bijapur. Treaty of Purandhar 1665, Agra 1666 and the 1674 coronation In 1666, Shivaji 74-80 and Sambhaji 80-89 visited the Mughal court at Agra. They were insulted and imprisoned. Their escape became legendary: disguised as Sadhus with bodies smeared in ash, they went to Mathura. Shivaji 74-80 left Sambhaji 80-89 there with a Brahmin family and took a long route back to his capital. Aurangzeb 58-07 marched to the Deccan in 1681, when his own son Prince Akbar 56-05 defected to Chhatrapati Sambhaji 80-89. Treaties are named after the place where they were signed. Coronation = legal reversal of the Treaty of Purandhar: a fully independent kingdom. Jat kingdom, Svarajya and the Sikh state share one feature: the result of people / mass participation (the Jat kingdom = peasant revolts). After the escape: rebellion resumes. 1.5 The 1674 coronation at Raigarh: Svarajya In 1674, Shivaji 74-80 was coronated at Raigarh as Chhatrapati, legally declaring himself independent from the Mughals. His kingdom, called Svarajya ("own rule"), covered the Marathi-speaking region. (The handout's heading places the headquarters at Satara; see the capital note in section 8.) The Maratha kingdom had thus been founded in the second half of the 17th century, built through wars against both Bijapur and Aurangzeb 58-07. Raigarh Fort and Vatan rights Shivaji 74-80 died of natural causes in 1680. Vatan = hereditary. A Mughal Vatan right could be: LR of a Jagir (a Vatan Jagir); collecting LR for a commission (Zamindar); a job such as Qanungo (maintaining land records); or Khudkasht cultivation of a plot.

items.t: 2 · Military tactics: army, Jagirs, navy and forts
items.x: Because the Marathas could not match Mughal strength, Shivaji 74-80 built a light, fast army, a coastal navy and sea-forts. Ask: why was copying European deep-sea ships a strategic disaster in the Konkan? 2.1 The army: light cavalry and guerrilla warfare Shivaji 74-80 built a well-organised army of around 30,000 to 40,000 cavalry. He used the mountainous terrain and dense forests to master guerrilla warfare and captured 240 forts, many of them in the Konkan. Their strategy was built on surprise (shock and awe) combined with guerrilla tactics. The major fighting force was a horse-mounted army with light cavalry for faster movement, in sharp contrast to the Mughals, who relied on heavy cavalry (elephants carrying a support system like food). Heavy cavalry = elephants plus horses carrying supplies, slow. Light cavalry = horses only, food and shelter on the way (by love or force). Speed = the focus of guerrilla warfare. 2.2 The Saranjami system: military land grants Unlike the Mughals, Maratha civil officials did not hold military roles. Shivaji 74-80 never gave Jagirs and paid officials in cash, leading to a centralised polity. Later Chhatrapati Shahu 19-49 gave Tankha Jagirs to military commanders called Saranjams, but never Vatan Jagirs. This prevented military loyalty from getting tied to hereditary land grants and gave the ruler more control. Jagirs: Tankha versus Vatan, and Shivaji 74-80's cash system Under this system revenue assignments on Jagirs were given to the Maratha Sardars, the Peshwa (Prime Minister of the Chhatrapati) and various military commanders, each drawing income from designated territories to maintain troops and administration. This led to a fragmented polity as revenue and military power were dispersed rather than centralised. Saranjam (a Tankha Jagir) Military commanders Temporary, tied to service, NOT heritable Vatan / Watan Civil officials such as Patils (village head) and Deshmukhs (revenue collectors like Zamindars) A hereditary right, passed within the family Land = the source of power; whoever controls land and its resources is more powerful, hence greater concentration of power under Shivaji 74-80. A Saranjam is taken away if not in service. 2.3 The navy: Father of the Modern Indian Navy Shivaji 74-80 established a naval force of 20 ships in 1657, a full navy of 200 ships by 1664, and the peak Maratha navy reached 700 ships. His doctrine was not about matching the British or Portuguese in deep-ocean warfare. It was a specialised, asymmetric coastal defence strategy designed to: 1. Protect Maratha merchant ships. Shivaji 74-80's navy: Father of the Modern Indian Navy 2. Secure the Konkan coastline from the Siddis of Janjira. 3. Prevent European powers from dominating Konkan trade routes. He built forts in coastal areas, established naval bases in the Arabian Sea, and focused on intelligence gathering at sea. In 1668 Shivaji 74-80 allowed the French to establish a trading factory at Rajapur. In return he secured high-quality military supplies: European cannons, lead and saltpetre for gunpowder. He is called the Father of the Modern Indian Navy because he relied entirely on indigenous human resources, engineering and strategy, never on European naval architects or shipbuilders. He recruited from local coastal communities, the Kolis and Bhandaris, master seafarers who knew the tides, hidden rocks and shallow creeks of the Konkan. He appointed commanders like Mayanak Bhandari and Daulat Khan. Saltpetre = potassium nitrate, used in gunpowder. Desi = indigenous tech, human resources, tactics. "Enemy's enemy = friend": the British were the common enemy. The Maratha navy was comparable in tech and strength to European navies ("modern"). 2.4 The fleet: tactical ship design Konkan coast: Jaladurg patrol and coastal forts Coast and shallow waters as navy hiding places Navy serves Merchant and Military. Patrol = Jaladurg: forts in coastal areas and on islands. The land coast and shallow waters are hiding places for small Maratha boats against British ships. A key insight was tactical ship design. Copying the massive deep-water (blue water) ships of the Europeans would have been a strategic disaster in the shallow estuaries of the Konkan coast. Instead he built a lighter, faster fleet for coastal defence and hit-and-run: Ghurabs Gunboats carrying heavy artillery Galbats Fast, highly manoeuvrable rowboats with light sails that could tow the Ghurabs into position during dead winds or chase fleeing enemy ships Shibars and Pals Larger vessels for transport and heavier engagements To ensure self-reliance, Shivaji 74-80 set up shipbuilding yards, sourcing timber from the teak forests of the Sahyadri. 2.5 The forts: the Jaladurg doctrine His greatest strategic innovation was the Jaladurg doctrine: sea forts on rocky islands or peninsulas along the coast. They provided security to docked vessels, and cannons in these forts and along the coast kept enemy ships at a distance. Key examples: Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg and Suvarnadurg. In Gujarat the EIC so feared the Marathas that they made Bombay their main base for trade, leading to the Bombay Presidency in 1687. Fleet, Jaladurg sea-forts and the shift from Surat to Bombay The Marathas actively captured ports from the Portuguese: in 1736 they removed the Portuguese and Ethiopian Muslims from the Konkan coast, and by 1739 effectively controlled Salsette and Bassein. 1668: EIC already in Bombay. 1687: Bombay becomes the Presidency (HQ); Bombay = a group of seven islands. Why shift from Surat: British navy strong, goods better protected at Bombay; Surat feared (Maratha) cavalry. Britain became the No. 1 naval power. China: chaos, kingdom wars and plunder, so goods go through Hong Kong (British, ringed by navy); India: goods go through Bombay (British). Britain as No. 1 naval power: Hong Kong and Bombay Maratha Military Landscapes: 12 UNESCO Heritage Forts (site #1739) Sindhudurg, the island sea-fort 2.6 After Shivaji 74-80: Admiral Kanhoji Angre Handout map: 12 UNESCO Heritage Forts After Shivaji 74-80 the dominant naval figure was Admiral Kanhoji Angre, called the "Shivaji 74-80 of the Seas", who dominated the Arabian Sea for 30 years in the early 1700s until his death in 1729. Kanhoji fought the British, Portuguese, Dutch, the Sawants (a small kingdom since 1627) and the Siddis or Habshis (people of African ancestry, now found in Gujarat, Karnataka, Andhra and parts of Sindh and Baluchistan in Pakistan). From 1714 to 1724 he frequently attacked the EIC in Bombay with guerrilla warfare at sea. The bigger, heavier British ships could not pursue the small, fast Maratha vessels in shallow waters. Admiral Kanhoji Angre: Shivaji of the Seas The result was a stalemate, and Kanhoji eventually offered peace to the British. The British defeated the Maratha Navy in 1756, one year before the EIC defeated the Bengal Suba at Plassey (1757).

items.t: 3 · Sambhaji 80-89 and Rajaram 89-00: the troubled succession
items.x: Because everything rested on one man, his death in 1680 opened a succession crisis. Ask: who ruled as regent in the name of the infant Shivaji II? Chhatrapati means Emperor. Shivaji 74-80 was the first Chhatrapati, ruling from 1674 until his death from natural causes in 1680. After him, his elder son Sambhaji 80-89 took charge. He was captured by Aurangzeb 58-07 and, after weeks of torture, was assassinated in 1689. The younger son Rajaram 89-00 then took over but died of tuberculosis in 1700 at just 30 years of age. With no adult male heir ready, Rajaram 89-00's widow Tarabai stepped in. She ruled as regent in the name of their infant son Shivaji II. This held until 1707, when the Mughals released Shahu 19-49, the elder son of Sambhaji 80-89, who had been in Mughal imprisonment. Shahu 19-49's release triggered a civil war between Shahu 19-49 and Tarabai that lasted until 1719 (section 6). Family tree: Shivaji 74-80 to Shahu 19-49 and Tarabai Regent = rules in the name of the king, because the king cannot rule (age, health). A war is internal (civil war) or external.

Because a Chhatrapati was not an absolute ruler, he governed with eight ministers. Ask: which of the eight was the Prime Minister? 4.1 The Chhatrapati was not an absolute ruler The Chhatrapati governed with a council of eight ministers, the Ashtapradhan. This was similar in concept to the British Monarch and his Privy Council, or the Mughal Emperor and his Darbar. Separation of powers (a separate legislature, executive, judiciary) is a modern concept. The Ashtapradhan was simply a council of ministers serving the Chhatrapati. 4.2 The eight ministers Ashtapradhan: the eight ministers Peshwa Prime Minister (the right hand of the Chhatrapati) Amatya Finance Sachiv Correspondence Sumanta Foreign Affairs Senapati Military Commander Panditrao Religious Affairs Nyayadhish Justice Waqenavis Intelligence The Chhatrapati was like a British monarch with a Privy Council (ministers); the Mughal emperor had a Darbar of Mansabdars (Irani, Turani, Hindu, Deccani and others). Today = Prime Minister plus Council of Ministers. 4.3 The Peshwa's own council: Darakhdars and the Barbhai Mandal Chhatrapati, Ashtapradhan and Peshwa's Darakhdars Maratha administration: centre, provinces and villages Just as the British PM had his own Council of Ministers beneath the monarch, the Peshwa had his own council of senior civil servants, the Darakhdars. In 1774, twelve of these powerful men came together under Nana Fadnavis to form the Council of Twelve Ministers, the Barbhai Mandal. The Peshwa's secretariat at Poona was the Hazur Daftar. Around 200 people worked there; all records important for governance, including financial records, were kept there. Barbhai = "12 Bros". Power drifted downwards: as the Chhatrapati weakened after Shahu 19-49, it moved to the Peshwa, like the British monarch's power moving to the PM and Council of Ministers as democracy grew. 4.4 Provincial and village administration Within Svarajya the territory was divided into Sarkars (provinces), each under a Governor. Notably, the office of Governor was auctioned. There were checks: many hereditary officers had dual reporting lines, to the Governor and directly to the Peshwa. The Governor's accounts submitted to the Peshwa were tallied against those submitted independently by the Deshmukhi directly to the Peshwa. This cross-checking prevented Governors from manipulating revenue figures. At the lowest level villages functioned as self-contained units. Each was under a Patil, who held all powers (financial, executive, judicial) including revenue collection, and reported directly to the Peshwa. Village accounts were kept by Kulkarnis. Both Patils and Deshmukhi (revenue collectors) held heritable Vatan rights. Mughal terminology: Sarkar = District. The Governor got a share of LR during his term, recovering his auction price plus some profit. Deshmukhs collected LR and kept a 10% commission. 4.5 The judicial system In Svarajya the final judicial decision rested with the Peshwa; in Samrajya, with the respective Maratha Sardar. There was a hierarchy of courts from the Panch at the village level up to the Peshwa. The Peshwa, as far as possible, respected the decisions of the Panchs. The law used was from the Dharma Shastras. Justice and revenue in Maratha administration The policing was as efficient as the London Police of that era, with a very good information network. Crucially there was a rule of law: even the highest authorities could be and were imprisoned for violations. 4.6 Sources of revenue Land revenue was the primary source, fixed on the basis of the quality of soil, irrigation facilities and the crop sown. Beyond this: (1) customs duty and octroi on trade; (2) judicial proceeds: Nazrana paid by the winning party and Jurmana paid by the losing party; (3) fees from permits and licences for cutting wood, manufacturing drugs and private minting of coins. To support peasants, dams and canals were built and loans given at low interest. The Deshmukhi and Patils were kept under check so they would not oppress the peasantry. Octroi = taxes on local / domestic trade; customs = international trade. Maratha LR assessment used proper field surveys, like MQK's in Bengal (1717-27) (Chapter 3). Canals serve transport (e.g. the Suez Canal) and irrigation.

items.t: 5 · Shahu 19-49's release (1707): was the Mughal "pacifist policy" really pacifist?
items.x: Because the Mughals released Shahu 19-49, people call it a pacifist policy. Ask: why does the chapter call it real-politik with divide and rule? After the death of Aurangzeb 58-07 it is often said the Mughals adopted a pacifist policy towards adversaries, including the Sikhs and Marathas, the policy under which Shahu 19-49 was released in 1707. This is a flawed interpretation. What emerged was pragmatic real-politik: reconciliation plus opportunism plus divide-and-rule. The Mughals were weakened and relied more on diplomacy, but the diplomacy included conspiracies and manipulation. It was nominal pacifism with plausible deniability for hostile acts by Mughal Governors. The Sikh case (1707-08): in 1707 Bahadur Shah (1707-12) granted Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 a high Mansab and promised him Anandpur. Very soon after, the Faujdar of Sirhind, Wazir Khan, had the Guru assassinated in 1708 at Nanded, Maharashtra, where the Guru had accompanied Bahadur Shah. No action was taken against Wazir Khan and Anandpur was never handed over. Note from the handout: Sirhind was a Sarkar (a district) within the Lahore Suba, and a Faujdar held military, judicial and land-revenue functions over a district. He was not a Governor, as some books incorrectly describe him, though Wazir Khan had much greater influence than a typical Faujdar. The Maratha case (1707 onwards): Shahu 19-49's release was a gesture of reconciliation, yet the Mughals did not stop attacking the Marathas, and his release triggered a civil war with Tarabai. The Mughals encouraged divided loyalties among Maratha Sardars and Deshmukhs, who kept switching sides between Shahu 19-49, Tarabai and the Mughals. This was shrewd diplomacy, not pacifism. Why release Shahu 19-49? For better relations with a rival, and because a Maratha civil war (1707-19) would weaken the enemy from within.

items.t: 6 · Tarabai and the Maratha civil war (1707-1719)
items.x: Because Shahu 19-49 returned, he and Tarabai fought a civil war until 1719. Ask: what settled the family dispute in 1731? 6.1 Why the civil war broke out After Rajaram 89-00's death from TB in 1700, Tarabai stepped in as regent for infant Shivaji II. This arrangement held the Maratha state together for seven years. In 1707 the Mughals released Shahu 19-49, the elder son of Sambhaji 80-89. This triggered a civil war between Shahu 19-49 and Tarabai that lasted till 1719. Sardars and Deshmukhs kept switching sides between Shahu 19-49, Tarabai and the Mughals, which the Mughals deliberately encouraged. By 1705 the Marathas had begun winning against the Mughals; credit to Tarabai (1700+). 6.2 Treaty of Warna 1731: the family settlement The dispute was finally settled by the Treaty of Warna (1731). Shahu 19-49 gave Kolhapur to Sambhaji II, the son of Rajaram 89-00 from his second wife Rajasbai, who had taken control from Shivaji II around 1714. From this point there were two Chhatrapati dynasties: Shahu 19-49's line at Satara and Sambhaji II's line at Kolhapur. 6.3 After Shahu 19-49: the Chhatrapati becomes ceremonial After Shahu 19-49 his adopted son Ramraja (Rajaram II) ruled 1749-77. From here the Chhatrapatis became largely ceremonial, like a powerless President. Real power had moved to the Peshwa (section 8). The last Chhatrapati of the Satara line was Shahaji (1839-48), when the EIC annexed Satara. Kolhapur survived much longer, as a Princely State from 1858 until its merger into India in 1947.

items.t: 7 · Why Shahu 19-49 won, and who the Maratha Sardars were
items.x: Because Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 won the bankers and the new Sardars, Shahu 19-49 won. Ask: which four Sardars, and which four capitals (Prelims 1995)? Reasons for victory in any war: technology, leadership, tactics, geography, money, number of soldiers / army size (alliances), military infrastructure (forts). Use as a checklist on any war question. 7.1 Why Shahu 19-49 prevailed A critical reason was the sixth Peshwa, Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, a highly able leader who won for Shahu 19-49: 1. The support of powerful Brahmin banking families. 2. The support of the new independent Maratha Sardars (who emerged precisely in this period). Telling example: during the civil war Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 convinced Admiral Kanhoji Angre to switch from Tarabai to Shahu 19-49 in 1714. Without Kanhoji's coastal and naval power, Shahu 19-49's victory would have been far harder. 7.2 Who were the Maratha Sardars? The Maratha Sardars were local chiefs, essentially mini-kings, who held their own armies and forts and dominated smaller territories. Post-1719 some expanded dramatically to a king-like status. These four became the kingmakers of the Confederacy: Gaikwad Baroda Holkar Indore Scindia (Shinde) Gwalior Bhonsle Nagpur Local chief = Misl chief = Sardar = Poligar Prelims 1995 (map detail): Sardar-capital pairings: Gaikwad = Baroda, Holkar = Indore, Scindia (Shinde) = Gwalior, Bhonsle = Nagpur. Local chief = Shivalik hill chiefs = Misl chiefs = Bundela chiefs = Rajput chiefs = Maratha Sardars = Poligars: a "mini mini king" with a private army and his own fort, dominating the politics and wealth of a small area (today's negative version: Bahubali; Kaleen Bhaiya of Mirzapur). Power tends to centralise in a strong personality. Every first king began as a local chief, e.g. Maharaja Ranjit Singh 01-39, chief of the Sukerchakia misl. Strong Maratha Sardars became kings: Holkar, Bhonsle, Scindia, Gaikwad. The Maratha Empire can be visualised as five provinces (Peshwa plus four Sardars as rulers) with the Chhatrapati as head of state. By 1750 it was effectively a Confederation: weak centre, strong provinces. Unitary Centre about 75% or more / provinces 25% or less China Federalism About 50 / 50 USA Confederation Centre 25% or less / provinces 75% or more European Union Quasi (semi) federalism 60 / 40 India (and 40 / 60 for Belgium) Maratha empire 1750s: Svarajya and Samrajya Maratha empire 1750s: centre and provinces Maratha empire, 1750s. Svarajya (1650s): set up by Shivaji 74-80 against Aurangzeb 58-07, in the Konkan. Samrajya (1719+): Gujarat, Rajputana, Malwa, Awadh, Bihar, Bengal, Orissa, brought under the Maratha State in Shahu 19-49's time, against Md Shah 19-48. Centre: Chhatrapati (powerless). Provinces: Svarajya (Poona) under the Peshwa; Samrajya under Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Gaikwad (Baroda), Bhonsle (Nagpur). Treaty of Sangola 1750: all the Chhatrapati's powers to the Peshwa, so the Chhatrapati is symbolic.

items.t: 8 · Svarajya and Samrajya, Chauth and Sardeshmukhi, the Peshwa as the real authority
items.x: Because the Sardars ruled outside Maharashtra, the empire lived on tribute. Ask: why is Chauth a tool of empire-building, and which of the two tributes is collected only externally? 8.1 Svarajya versus Samrajya Territory The original kingdom inside Maharashtra Lands outside Maharashtra (from 1719) Ruled by The Chhatrapati / Peshwa, directly The Maratha Sardars, in their own right Capital / HQ Raigarh, then Jinji, then Satara; Peshwa at Poona Varies by Sardar Character Culturally homogeneous and governed Real administration only in parts (Gujarat, Khandesh, Malwa); elsewhere mainly Chauth / Sardeshmukhi collection Svarajya versus Samrajya: capitals and Sardars Svarajya: the original Maratha kingdom established by Shivaji 74-80, capital Raigarh (1647-1689); then conquered by Aurangzeb 58-07, so capital = Jinji (1689-1698); capital = Satara under Rajaram 89-00 (as the handout prints it), with the Peshwa's headquarters at Poona. It was the territory within Maharashtra, under direct rule, and culturally homogeneous. Samrajya: the territory outside Maharashtra, ruled by the Confederate chiefs (the Maratha Sardars); administration varied from one Sardar to another. Effective administration existed only in parts of Samrajya, notably Gujarat, Khandesh and Malwa. Elsewhere the primary concern was not governance but collection of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. From 1719 onwards the territories added beyond the original Svarajya were called Samrajya, governed not by the Chhatrapati but by the Sardars who held power in their own right. Capital conflict: handout section 1.4 says Svarajya's headquarters was Satara (and "Capital = Satara by Rajaram 89-00"); section 8.1 and the teacher's boards give Raigarh, then Jinji (1689-98), then Satara, tying Jinji to Rajaram 89-00 and Satara to Shahu 19-49. Use Raigarh, Jinji, Satara. Jinji / Ginjee (Carnatic) = an important fort; after Sambhaji 80-89 the Marathas under Rajaram 89-00 set up their capital there. Sardars conquered Samrajya largely with their own resources and efforts: autonomous from the beginning, but within the Maratha empire. Chauth is collected until the state is annexed, not thereafter. 8.2 Chauth: one-fourth, externally collected Both Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were tribute systems that existed even before the Marathas. Chauth = one-fourth (25%) of the revenue paid by a protected state to the Marathas in exchange for military protection. It was also a deliberate tool of foreign policy: the annual payment weakened the protected state economically and militarily over time. When it could no longer pay, the Marathas annexed it. Chauth thus functioned as a tool of empire-building. Chauth versus Sardeshmukhi: the ideal case 8.3 Sardeshmukhi: an additional 10%, internal and external Sardeshmukhi was an additional levy of 10% of land revenue, collected over and above the regular land revenue. Deshmukhs collected Sardeshmukhi from the ryots and deposited it to the Chhatrapati. Shivaji 74-80 declared himself Sardeshmukh, the head of all Deshmukhs, so payment by the Deshmukhs was a symbol of their recognition of the Chhatrapati's authority. When extracted from states outside the Maratha Empire, Sardeshmukhi served as a symbol of Maratha authority being recognised by that state. Important distinction: Chauth was collected only externally, while Sardeshmukhi could be collected both internally and externally. 8.4 The teacher's boards: how Chauth and Sardeshmukhi work Prelims. Tributes are of two kinds: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi (1/10). Other tribute names seen earlier: Nazrana, Abwab, Peshkash. Chauth: on states outside the Maratha Empire, 1/4 of the external state's annual revenue. "If paid, Marathas will not attack" (protection). Steps: (1) the Marathas defeat the external state; (2) the peace treaty makes it agree to pay Chauth. Sardeshmukhi internally: a Deshmukh collects Rs 100 LR from ryots; commission = Rs 10; Rs 90 to the state. Sardeshmukhi = 10% of the Deshmukh's Rs 10 = Rs 1 to the Chhatrapati. State or Chhatrapati gets Rs 90 + Rs 1 = Rs 91. Sardeshmukhi externally: after defeat, the peace treaty makes the state pay Chauth + Sardeshmukhi = 25% + 10% = 35% of its annual revenue. Two descriptions of Sardeshmukhi. Handout and slide table: an extra 10% of land revenue. Teacher's worked example: 10% of the Deshmukh's Rs 10 commission when collected internally (the Deshmukh pays respect to the Chhatrapati). Learn the table wording and the Rs 100 / Rs 10 / Rs 1 / Rs 91 example for the internal case. Sardeshmukhi applied internally Chauth and Sardeshmukhi: the worked example Why pay Sardeshmukhi internally? When Person A pays money to Person B, it establishes that B is respected. The Chhatrapati = the Sardar (head) of the Deshmukhs; Shivaji 74-80 declared himself so (Sardeshmukh), hence Sardeshmukhi internally. Ideal: the Deshmukh bears the burden. 8.5 How Chauth was divided Revenue from Chauth and Sardeshmukhi collected outside the Maratha Empire helped reduce the tax burden on the people within the empire. When Chauth was extracted by the Chhatrapati / Peshwa, all of it was retained by Svarajya. When Maratha Sardars extracted it from a state outside the empire, they retained two-thirds and sent one-third to Svarajya: Mokasa 66% (about 2/3) Kept by the Maratha Sardars to maintain troops and cavalry contingents Babti 25% (1/4) Sent directly to the Chhatrapati for personal use and the royal treasury Sahotra 6% Allocated to the Pant Sachiv, head of the royal secretariat and a member of the Ashtapradhan Nadgaunda 3% At the Chhatrapati's discretion: charitable grants, royal gifts or minor officials Division of Chauth A Maratha Sardar defeats an external state, a peace treaty follows, annual Chauth is extracted. The Chhatrapati gets 1/3 of the Chauth. 8.6 Chauth as a tool of empire-building: the teacher's boards Peace treaty harshness scale 1 Chauth 2 Chauth + Sardeshmukhi 3 Chauth x 2 + Sardeshmukhi (note: 1727, Gujarat made to pay 60% of its revenue annually) 4 Annexation of territory After a war comes a peace treaty; how harsh it is for the loser depends on the power differential between winner and loser: the bigger the gap, the harsher the treaty. Peace treaty today: Russia-Ukraine example Peace treaty today (Russia-Ukraine example), mild to severe: 1 war reparation; 2 no import duty on Russian exports to Ukraine, or preferential treatment to Russian goods and services; 3 non-aggression pact, Ukraine never joins NATO; 4 imposed military alliance, Ukraine a protectorate of Russia; 5 some territory; 6 significant territory; 7 full annexation. Chauth and the external state's budget Chauth as a tool of empire-building How Chauth became a tool of empire-building (teacher's boards) Short war: the Marathas defeat the external state quickly and offer peace Peace treaty: the external state agrees to pay Chauth (25% of annual revenue) The drain: Rs 25 of every Rs 100 leaves, so less investment, less spent on the army, GDP and revenue fall (Rs 90 instead of Rs 100), yet 25% is still due Over the years: a weak economy and weak army, the state is unable to pay Chauth Short war, easy total victory: the Marathas annex, avoiding the long, costly, high-casualty war of direct annexation Scenario 1: straight annexation = long war, expensive, high loss of men. Scenario 2: a short war, peace, Chauth extracted; after ten years of Chauth the state has a weak economy and weak army, cannot pay, and a short war means easy total victory and annexation. The 25% drain means less invested in the economy and less on the army: of Rs 100 revenue, Rs 25 goes to the Marathas and Rs 75 is left for army, agriculture, irrigation, technical reforms; falling revenue (e.g. Rs 90) still owes 25%: DRAIN. 8.7 How the Peshwa office became hereditary; the power shift and Sangola 1750 The Peshwa's office was originally not hereditary. Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, the sixth Peshwa, changed this in practice. His son Baji Rao 20-40 became the next Peshwa, then his son Balaji Bajirao 20-40 / Nana Saheb (1740-61) followed. Once this custom held across three generations, the office became hereditary in effect. Shahu 19-49 was an effective ruler but progressively delegated more and more power to the Peshwa. After his death a crisis emerged when Tarabai claimed that Shahu 19-49's adopted son Ramraja was not her grandson, as had been stated at the time of adoption. To prevent the state being left without a Chhatrapati, Peshwa Nana Saheb (1740-61) backed Ramraja, but made him sign the Treaty of Sangola in February 1750, which transferred all real power from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa. Power shift from Chhatrapati to Peshwa Sangola 1750: the family-table analogy Shahu 19-49 = powerful personality and effective Chhatrapati, BUT he over-delegated to the Peshwa because of trust (the Peshwa also never backstabbed Shahu 19-49). Ramraja (1749-77) was adopted with controversy over his identity, and a weak personality, so his legitimacy as Chhatrapati fell, leading to Sangola 1750: the Chhatrapati purely symbolic, all power with the Peshwa. Whenever real power shifts downward to a lower authority: (1) factionalism increases (Peshwa versus Sardars, Sardars versus Sardars; e.g. Bhonsle did not fight at the Third Battle of Panipat, 1761), and (2) there is more dependence on the lower authority's personality to prevent factionalism. Family analogy: the Chhatrapati is the father and the Peshwa (B1), Gaikwad (B2), Scindia (B3), Bhonsle (B4), Holkar (B5) are brothers; after 1750 the eldest brother (Peshwa) takes the father's seat at the head of the table. 8.8 The series of Peshwas Baji Rao 20-40 had a brother, Chimaji Appa, whose son Sadasiv Rao Bhau commanded the Maratha army at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) and died fighting. Nana Saheb (1740-61) did not fight but died within weeks of the defeat. His elder son Vishwas Rao also died fighting at Panipat. Peshwa family tree Svarajya (minus Satara and Kolhapur) was annexed by the EIC after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19); Satara and Kolhapur were left out to signal that the Chhatrapatis are respected. 1 Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 Sixth Peshwa; backed Shahu 19-49 and made the post hereditary in practice 2 Baji Rao 20-40 Son of Balaji Vishwanath 13-20; plundered Delhi (1737); Treaty of Bhopal (1738) 3 Balaji Bajirao 20-40 / Nana Saheb (1740-61) Son of Baji Rao 20-40; Panipat era; died within weeks of the 1761 defeat; signed the Treaty of Sangola (1750) with Ramraja 4 Madhav Rao 61-72 Younger son of Nana Saheb (elder son Vishwas Rao died at Panipat); "young" = also inexperienced; young but able, a temporary revival; died naturally 1772 5 Narayan Rao 72-73 Brother of Madhav Rao 61-72; murdered in 1773 in a conspiracy by his uncle Raghunath Rao 73-74 6 Raghunath Rao 73-74 Uncle, the conspirator; usurped the office 7 Madhav Rao II 74-95 Infant Peshwa, son of the murdered Narayan Rao 72-73; Nana Fadnavis regent; his overbearing control drove him to suicide in 1795 8 Baji Rao II 96-18 Last Peshwa, son of Raghunath Rao 73-74 (his claim rested on bloodline); ended by the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19) The Peshwas: treaties of Bhopal and Sangola, Barbhai Mandal Nana Fadnavis: the man who led the Barbhai conspiracy removing Raghunath Rao 73-74 as revenge for Narayan Rao 72-73's murder. He had fought at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) and is regarded as a "modern Chanakya." Crucially, he was the first to recognise that the EIC had territorial ambitions in India and was not merely a commercial enterprise. 8.9 The three broad phases of Maratha polity after Shivaji 74-80 1 1680-1719 Turmoil: continuous Mughal warfare after Shivaji 74-80's death; civil war 1707-19 2 1719-1761 Growth and expansion 3 1761 onwards Decline, with a temporary revival in the 1770s, notably the First Anglo-Maratha War of 1775-82

items.t: 9 · Wars, treaties and territories up to the Third Battle of Panipat (1761)
items.x: Because the Sayyid deal of 1719 gave the Marathas rights in six Deccan provinces, the Nizam's refusal in 1724 sparked a decade of expansion. Ask: which three gains of 1719 did the teacher box for Prelims? 9.1 The 1719 turning point: alliance with the Sayyid Brothers 1719 was a turning point. Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 allied with the Sayyid Brothers, the kingmakers of the Mughal court. Together they removed Farrukhsiyar 13-19 and placed Muhammad Shah 19-48 on the throne as a puppet. In return the Marathas secured three concessions: 1. The Mughals formally recognised Maratha autonomous status in Maharashtra. 2. The Marathas received the Chauth of Malwa and Gujarat. 3. They gained the right to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi from six Mughal provinces of the Deccan: Khandesh, Hyderabad, Aurangabad, Berar, Bidar and Bijapur. Since Bijapur was later merged into Golconda, some sources name Golconda as the sixth instead. The Nizam's Hyderabad State was later constituted from precisely these six erstwhile Mughal provinces. This did not last. In 1720 the Nizam (1724-48), Governor of Hyderabad Suba, defeated the Sayyid Brothers. Muhammad Shah 19-48 became a joint puppet of the Irani and Turani factions of Mansabdars. When the Nizam established Hyderabad Suba as an independent successor state in 1724, he refused to pay Chauth and Sardeshmukhi to the Marathas. 1719 gains: the six Deccan provinces Map c.1700: Malwa, Deccan provinces, European settlements Historical map: Malwa and the six Deccan provinces 9.2 The Maratha decade of expansion (1727-39) Handout map: Deccan provinces, Malwa, coastal settlements The Marathas responded to the Nizam's refusal with a decade of relentless military expansion: 1. 1727-28: defeated the Mughals in Gujarat and extracted 60% of revenue as annual tribute. 2. 1728: defeated Hyderabad and regained the Chauth and Sardeshmukhi of the Deccan. 3. 1729: captured Malwa and pushed their reach into Rajasthan. Decade of Expansion: Malwa and Treaty of Bhopal 4. 1731: defeated a joint attack by the Nizam and local Gujarat chiefs. 5. 1736: defeated the Portuguese and Ethiopian Muslims on the Konkan coast. 6. 1737: Peshwa Baji Rao 20-40 plundered Delhi itself and held Muhammad Shah 19-48 prisoner temporarily. 7. 1738: defeated a large Mughal army commanded by the Nizam and signed the Treaty of Bhopal (1738), under which the Marathas received the Suba of Malwa (formalising what they had controlled de facto since 1729) and sovereignty over all lands between the rivers Chambal and Narmada. 8. 1739: Treaty of Bassein with the Portuguese led to the annexation of Bassein (Vasai). 1729: the Mughals did not accept Maratha control of Malwa; conflict continued. 1739: Salsette and Bassein, near Bombay (trade). 9.3 Expansion continues on many fronts (1745-54) 1. 1745-51: Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur regularly attacked Bengal Suba and forced Alivardi Khan 40-56 to give up Odisha and pay the Chauth of Bengal and Bihar, paid until Plassey (1757). 2. 1751: Peshwa Nana Saheb attacked Hyderabad and forced Salabat Jung 51-62 to cede Khandesh via the Treaty of Bhalke. 3. 1752: the Marathas took Ahmedabad, completing the annexation of Gujarat. The Peshwa appointed Damaji Gaikwad as Chief and Governor of Gujarat, HQ Baroda. Expansion 1745-54: Bhalke and Gujarat 4. From 1751 the Marathas regularly attacked the Rajputs, extracting annual tributes and interfering in succession disputes, but never fully conquered Rajputana. They also failed to dominate the Sikhs. 5. 1752: the weakened Mughal Empire came under Maratha protection, driven by fear of Afghan invasions. 6. Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 launched at least seven invasions between 1748 and 1767. The first, 1748, was checked at the Battle of Manupur, where the Mughal army fought the pitched battle while the Sikh misls harassed his supply lines. 7. 1754: the Marathas interfered in the Mughal succession and installed Alamgir II 54-59 as their puppet. By the mid-18th century the Maratha State had emerged as the top power in India. Regional map of India in the 1750s Handout map: Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas Two ways to capture power Two ways to capture power: (a) replace the rival (annexation) = costly but fast; (b) capture the enemy from within = less costly but slow. By 1752 the Marathas stood where Zulfiqar Khan, the Sayyid Brothers and the Nizam (Wazir 1722-24) once stood. Homework on the last map: plot Annexation, Control (and the total). 1751 Bhalke: Hyderabad lost its access to the Arabian Sea. 1752: annexation, with the Maratha army in Delhi for fear of Afghan invasion. Not imp (the 1745-54 table).

Because by 1752 the Marathas stood where the Sayyids once did, the Afghan threat had to be met. Ask: what was Abdali's immediate reason (Prelims 2010)? 10.1 Sides and background If Awadh was part of the Mughal empire yet joined Abdali's alliance, what does that prove? (1) Factionalism (Mughal against Mughal); (2) a weak centre / emperor; (3) Awadh being a successor state. Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72, also known as Durrani, founded the modern borders of the Afghan State in 1747, declaring himself independent King after the death of Nadir Shah, Emperor of Iran and Afghanistan. Before 1747 he had been a trusted commander of Nadir Shah and Governor of Afghanistan, and took part in Nadir Shah's invasion of India in 1738-40. His invasion of 1756 culminated in the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Panipat III sides: Abdali's rise and Awadh's role The two sides: the Marathas (about 50,000) and an alliance of Abdali (about 60,000) comprising Abdali himself; the Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 of Rohilkhand; the Bangash Pathans under Ahmad Khan (1750-82) of Farrukhabad; and Awadh under Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75. By 1752 the weakened Mughal Emperor was under Maratha military protection and the Marathas effectively controlled Delhi. From 1756 Abdali's forces frequently raided north India. Abdali had installed his eleven-year-old son Timur Shah as Governor of Punjab and Kashmir. In 1758 Nana Saheb sent his brother Raghunath Rao 73-74, who removed Timur from Lahore. This was the peak of Maratha power, the maximum territory ever under Maratha domination. Nana Saheb even contemplated making his son Vishwas Rao the Emperor of Hindustan. Then the Third Battle of Panipat changed everything. Prelims 2010: immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 to invade India and fight the Third Battle of Panipat? Answer (a): to avenge the Marathas' expulsion of his viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore (March 1758). Wrong: (b) fast Maratha expansion is only general background; (c) there was no Mughal tribute dispute; (d) there was no "Sultan of Punjab" refusing safe passage. After Timur Shah's expulsion the Marathas made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year; on his death Sabaji Scindia took charge and held the Maratha garrisons at Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border. This conquest of Punjab was the direct challenge Abdali could not ignore. 10.2 Why Abdali won: six factors Why Abdali won: alliance, logistics, terrain 1 Strength of his alliance Awadh felt strategically encircled by the Marathas (Chauth from Bihar and Bengal since 1751 in the east, control of Delhi in the west since 1752, Samrajya to the south) and, when the Marathas sought an alliance with Shuja, he chose the Islamic alliance. The Indian Afghan kingdoms of Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad backed Abdali hoping for greater influence under an Afghan emperor. Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats stayed neutral, a direct consequence of years of Maratha plundering and tribute extraction. 60,000 versus 50,000. 2 Logistics Abdali cut the supply routes between the Maratha camp at Panipat and Delhi. Famine-like conditions: no food for men, no fodder for horses. 3 Terrain Panipat's vast open plains gave no advantage to Maratha guerrilla tactics, which depended on hills, forests and narrow passes. 4 Firepower Abdali's horse-mounted swivel guns could pierce Maratha armour. 5 Military leadership Abdali and Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 provided strong, coordinated command. 6 Maratha factionalism Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur refused to fight, being opposed to Nana Saheb as Peshwa. In 1765 the Peshwa even plundered Nagpur in retaliation. Bhonsle also did not take part in the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). Horse-mounted swivel gun Swivel gun: stability and aim Why the mounted swivel gun was better: better stability and better aiming, because it is attached to the seat. Alliance: Jats offered help to the Marathas, but the alliance failed over tactics: Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla war; Sadashiv Rao Bhau did not; the Jats still sent supplies. Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad hoped for greater political influence under an Afghan emperor (ethnicity = soft power). Maratha plunder = attack, then loot = Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. Logistics and terrain both fall under TACTICS. 10.3 Impact of the defeat Military losses: Sadasiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao died fighting. Nana Saheb had not fought (someone was needed to guard other frontiers in the south); he arrived with reinforcements when the battle was already lost and died within weeks. The Marathas lost 50,000 men in total, combatants and non-combatants. Factionalism deepened: young, inexperienced Peshwas followed one another: the young but brilliant Madhav Rao 61-72, then the incompetent Narayan Rao 72-73, then the infant Madhav Rao II 74-95. Abdali too paid a heavy price: serious losses and an anti-Abdali revolt among his own generals back in Afghanistan. He went home with his loot but could not consolidate any lasting presence in India. The deeper consequence: a power vacuum at the centre. Panipat did not decide who would rule India; it decided that neither the Marathas nor Abdali would. The vacuum was eventually filled by the British EIC, which defeated the regional Indian states one by one.

items.t: 11 · After Panipat: decline with moments of strength (1761-1819, about 60 years)
items.x: Because Panipat left a power vacuum, decline followed, with moments of strength. Ask: which Anglo-Maratha war did the Marathas win, and which one ended Svarajya? After Panipat: Delhi, Salbai and the Campoo 1. 1765: the Marathas defeated Mysore and extracted tribute. 2. 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: Hyderabad gave the Northern Sarkars to the EIC for an annual payment of seven lakh rupees and protection against both the Marathas and Mysore. The Northern Sarkars (Northern Circars) were initially four districts: Chicacole (Srikakulam), Rajmandri (Rajahmundry), Ellore (Eluru) and MustafaNagar (Kondapalli), with MurtuzaNagar (Guntur) added later as a fifth. Guntur was not transferred to the EIC in 1766. 3. 1771: Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptured Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans, who had taken it in 1761. 4. 1775-82 First Anglo-Maratha War: the Marathas defeated the EIC, the only war in this period the EIC lost. 5. 1782 Treaty of Salbai: a Maratha-EIC military alliance. 6. 1784: Mahadji Shinde (Scindia) hired the French military adventurer Benoit de Boigne, who raised and trained the Fauj-i-Hind, also called the Campoo system (each Campoo was an integrated force with its own infantry, own cavalry, own artillery, thus self-sufficient units). It transformed the army from a traditional light-cavalry force into a modern, disciplined European-style infantry-cavalry-artillery machine (similar to Haider Ali 61-82's army (1761-82), also modernised with French help). Other Sardars followed: Holkar hired the Frenchman Dudrenec. 7. 1795 Battle of Kharda: a Maratha victory over Hyderabad. The EIC stayed neutral as the Marathas were still its ally under Salbai 1782. The last battle between Hyderabad and the Marathas. 8. 1798: Hyderabad became the first Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance (also called a subordinate alliance) with the EIC, securing guaranteed protection and ending its vulnerability to Maratha pressure. 9. 1803: the EIC captured Delhi in the Second Anglo-Maratha War. 10. 1817-19 Third Anglo-Maratha War: Svarajya was annexed by the EIC, ending the last Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18's rule. 1761-1819 = about 60 years. 1765: Haider Ali 61-82 strong. Delhi was with the Marathas 1752-1803 (minus 1761-71), the Rohillas holding it in between. 1782 Salbai (near Gwalior) was signed by Mahadji Scindia. 1803 and 1817-19 are marked as Maratha losses. Salbai alliance length: handout says it held until 1795 (tied to the Battle of Kharda, EIC neutral); the teacher's Lecture 7 note says it held until the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Both are in the class material; the teacher's version places the breakdown at the next Anglo-Maratha war. The Campoo system Campoo = "multiple regiments, and every regiment is like a mini army": self-sufficient, with its own transport, infantry, cavalry, supplies and weapons. Benefits: speed; political stability, as chances of a coup by a commander go down. Later link: the Risala system of Haider Ali 61-82. "Today, we are doing this again" (modern integrated, self-sufficient military units).

items.t: 12 · Why couldn't the Marathas establish all-India rule?
items.x: Because the Marathas controlled but did not rule, all-India rule slipped away. Ask: why is extracting tribute not ruling? Why no all-India Maratha rule (Mains) The Marathas came closer than any other power in the 18th century to an all-India empire, but the reasons they never crossed that threshold are structural: 1. Tribute, not annexation. Often after a victory they limited themselves to Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rather than annexing and establishing direct rule. Extracting tribute is not ruling. Ruling means making and implementing policies through your own administration on the ground; for one central authority to rule effectively, power must be centralised: one country, one ruler, one law, rule of law. 2. Weak centre, strong Sardars. The centre was never strong enough and factionalism weakened it further; the Sardars had always been autonomous. Shivaji 74-80 never gave Jagirs to his officers and Shahu 19-49 never gave Vatan Jagirs to military commanders, so ambitious Sardars seeking their own principalities ventured out on their own to build Samrajya. In territories brought under Maratha control through the Sardars' own efforts, the Chhatrapati's authority would naturally be weak. 3. The Treaty of Sangola 1750. As power shifted down to the Peshwa, the Sardars felt even less constrained and factionalism grew; after 1761 a succession of weak Peshwas accelerated this. 4. Power was not properly centralised even in Svarajya: local assemblies of Vatan right-holders (Deshmukhs and Patils) asserted themselves and pressured the Peshwa. 5. In Samrajya, effective centralised rule did not exist at all in many areas: certain areas were under a Maratha Sardar militarily, but no effective government machinery was present on the ground. "Rule" = administration on the ground: making and implementing laws by the King (= the Centre). Control yes; Rule no: not 100%. Even in Svarajya, local assemblies of Vatan-holders show a "democratic spirit" but not a "strong centre." Mains 2014: why so many battles at Panipat? Mains 2014: why have so many empire-shaking battles been fought near Panipat? Not for the city itself: the region is the gateway to Delhi. Any power from Central Asia or Afghanistan came through the Khyber Pass, and the natural staging ground before the final push runs through Panipat, Karnal, Kurukshetra and Thanesar; a Delhi ruler's sound move was to stop the enemy at these gates. Supporting factors: (1) vast open fields for set-piece battles; (2) weather supporting prolonged campaigns; (3) many warrior communities easing recruitment; (4) agricultural productivity plus proximity to Delhi easing supply. Thanesar 1014 Mahmud of Ghazni fought here and had built an empire from Iran to today's Pakistan by 1030 Thanesar 1191 Muhammad Ghori First Battle of Panipat 1526 Shook the Delhi Sultanate Second Battle of Panipat 1556 Ended the rule of Hemu Battle of Karnal 1739 Shook the Mughals Third Battle of Panipat 1761 Shook the Marathas From Shivaji 74-80 to Panipat: the big picture 1674-80 Shivaji 74-80: coronation at Raigarh, Svarajya, army, navy, forts, guerrilla warfare 1680-1719 Turmoil: Sambhaji 80-89 killed (1689), Rajaram 89-00 dies (1700), Tarabai regent, Shahu 19-49 released 1707, civil war to 1719 1719 Shahu 19-49 wins, Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 rises: Sayyid alliance, recognition of autonomy, Chauth and Sardeshmukhi 1719-61 Growth: Gujarat, Malwa, Delhi raid 1737, Bhopal 1738, Odisha, Khandesh, Alamgir II 54-59 1754; Sangola 1750 moves power to the Peshwa 1761 Third Panipat: Abdali's alliance wins; factionalism, weak Peshwas, power vacuum After 1761: Mysore, Delhi 1771, First Anglo-Maratha War won 1775-82, Campoo 1784, then annexation 1803 and 1817-19 Why Abdali won at Panipat Alliance: Awadh, Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad join; Sikhs, Rajputs, Jats neutral; 60k versus 50k Logistics: supply line Panipat-Delhi cut, famine Terrain: open plains, no hills for guerrilla tactics Firepower: horse-mounted swivel guns pierce armour Leadership: Abdali and Najib coordinate Factionalism: Raghuji Bhonsle refuses to fight Result: a power vacuum; neither the Marathas nor Abdali rule India; EIC fills it Area or scope Inside Maharashtra, direct rule Outside Maharashtra (from 1719), Sardars External only Internal and external Rate Not applicable Not applicable 25% of revenue Extra 10% of land revenue Meaning Culturally homogeneous, governed Real administration only in parts Tool of empire-building Symbol of recognising the Chhatrapati

A boy from the Maval. Shivaji 74-80 Bhonsle is born on 19 February 1630 to Shahji (Jagirdar of Poona, a General and Mansabdar in Bijapur) and Jijabai. Guided by Dadaji Kondadev, he takes his first fort at 16, in 1646, working from the hilly, forested Maval region with local warriors and peasants. Guerrilla war and the Purandhar squeeze. From 1657 he attacks oppressive Bijapur, and in 1659 he kills Afzal Khan with the concealed Bagh Nakh and a Bichhwa. In 1663 he defeats Shaista Khan 64-88 and sacks Surat, so Aurangzeb 58-07 sends Jai Singh 99-43, who cuts off supplies and in 1665 besieges Purandhar. To spare his soldiers and people Shivaji 74-80 signs the Treaty of Purandhar: 23 of 35 forts go, Sambhaji 80-89 becomes a Mansabdar of 5,000, and he backs the Mughals against Bijapur. Crown, army and navy. In 1666 he and Sambhaji 80-89 are insulted and imprisoned at Agra, and escape disguised as Sadhus. In 1674 he is crowned at Raigarh as Chhatrapati, declaring himself independent of the Mughals, and Svarajya covers the Marathi-speaking region. His army of 30,000 to 40,000 light cavalry holds 240 forts; his navy grows from 20 ships in 1657 to 200 by 1664 (peak 700), guarded by Jaladurg sea-forts, and he pays officials in cash, never in Jagirs. How the Chhatrapati ruled. He governs with the Ashtapradhan, eight ministers headed by the Peshwa as Prime Minister, like a British monarch with a Privy Council. Under the Peshwa sit the Darakhdars, and in 1774 twelve of them form the Barbhai Mandal under Nana Fadnavis. Provinces (Sarkars) have Governors whose office is auctioned, cross-checked by the Deshmukhi, while villages run under a Patil and justice climbs from the Panch to the Peshwa. A troubled succession. Sambhaji 80-89 is captured by Aurangzeb 58-07 and killed in 1689 after weeks of torture, and Rajaram 89-00 dies of tuberculosis in 1700, aged 30. His widow Tarabai rules as regent for the infant Shivaji II until 1707, when the Mughals release Shahu 19-49, the elder son of Sambhaji 80-89. The release triggers a civil war that lasts until 1719, while Sardars and Deshmukhs keep switching sides, which the Mughals encourage. Shahu wins, the Sardars rise. The sixth Peshwa, Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, wins Brahmin banking families and the new Sardars for Shahu 19-49 and persuades Admiral Kanhoji Angre to switch in 1714. The Treaty of Warna (1731) splits the house into Satara and Kolhapur. Four Sardars become kingmakers, Gaikwad at Baroda, Holkar at Indore, Scindia at Gwalior and Bhonsle at Nagpur, so Svarajya (inside Maharashtra) is ruled by the Peshwa and Samrajya (outside, from 1719) by the Sardars. Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. Chauth is 25% of the revenue of a protected state, paid for military protection; the annual drain weakens that state until it cannot pay and is annexed after a short war, which beats a long, costly war of direct annexation. Sardeshmukhi is an extra 10%, collected both inside and outside. When Sardars collect Chauth abroad they keep 66% (Mokasa), send 25% (Babti) to the Chhatrapati, give 6% (Sahotra) to the Pant Sachiv and 3% (Nadgaunda) to the Chhatrapati's discretion. The bargain of 1719 and the decade of growth. In 1719 Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 allies with the Sayyid Brothers, who remove Farrukhsiyar 13-19 and install Muhammad Shah 19-48 as a puppet. The Marathas win autonomy in Maharashtra, the Chauth of Malwa and Gujarat, and Chauth plus Sardeshmukhi of six Deccan provinces, but the Nizam beats the Sayyids in 1720 and stops paying in 1724. A decade of expansion follows (1727-39): Gujarat at 60%, Malwa in 1729, Delhi plundered in 1737 by Baji Rao 20-40, the Treaty of Bhopal in 1738 and Bassein in 1739, then Odisha, Khandesh, Ahmedabad and Alamgir II 54-59 as a puppet in 1754. Sangola 1750. Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, then Baji Rao 20-40, then Nana Saheb (1740-61) hold the Peshwa's chair, so after three generations it is hereditary in effect, and Shahu 19-49 keeps delegating to him. When Tarabai says Shahu's adopted son Ramraja is not her grandson, Nana Saheb backs Ramraja but makes him sign the Treaty of Sangola in February 1750, and all real power passes to the Peshwa. The teacher's family table shows the eldest brother taking the father's seat. Panipat, 1761. From 1756 Abdali invaded, took Lahore and Kashmir and made his son Timur Shah Governor, but in March 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 expelled Timur from Lahore, the peak of Maratha power and Abdali's immediate reason to return. Abdali (60,000) joins the Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, the Bangash Pathans under Ahmad Khan (1750-82) and Awadh under Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75, while the Marathas (50,000) under Sadasiv Rao Bhau face them with the Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats neutral and their supply route from Delhi cut at Panipat. Swivel guns pierce their armour, Raghuji Bhonsle refuses to fight, and about 50,000 Marathas die. Decline, and why no all-India rule. Young and weak Peshwas follow (Madhav Rao 61-72, Narayan Rao 72-73, the infant Madhav Rao II 74-95), though the Marathas win the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes Delhi in 1771 and builds the Campoo army in 1784. The EIC takes Delhi in 1803 and annexes Svarajya in 1817-19. The Marathas never ruled all India because they took tribute instead of ruling, and their centre was weak: they had control but not rule.

Prelims 2010 The immediate reason for Abdali's invasion and Third Panipat To avenge the expulsion of his son Timur Shah from Lahore (March 1758) by Raghunath Rao 73-74. Abdali's son was Governor of Punjab and Kashmir The Prelims 2010 alert and the slides that show the question, the answer and the reason
