items.t: 1 · The middle path between king and rebel
items.x: Because the Mughals were too weak to crush every rebel, they offered a deal. Ask: what does each side give, and whose core interest is met? The middle path when rebels establish their rule Rebels establish their rule in an area: the emperor has two options: (1) continue fighting and end the rebellion; (2) lose the territory (T) and let the rebel establish an independent kingdom. The middle path: the rebel accepts to be a Mansabdar, accepts the Mughal as emperor, sends tribute to Delhi, and agrees to maintain an army / help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, and non-interference in the rebel's rule. Middle path: the core interest of each side Core interests. Emperor: the empire's territory shall not shrink; revenue and military come from that territory. Rebel: king of that territory, with dynastic rule in it. Middle path: king and rebel; regional powers sorted King (Mughal) The rebel provides an army; the empire does not shrink Rebel Opportunity as a Mansabdar at the centre (recall successor states); dynastic governor status; the king accepts the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir Except for the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once, in 1707), this pattern appears among the Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad, Mysore and Rajputs. Board link: Article 370 status (a state within a state on special terms). Sorting: SS (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad); RS (Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad; plus the Sikhs); AAS (Rajputs, Mysore; plus Travancore). The Sikhs [RS] and Travancore [AAS] were not legally in the Mughal empire.

Because the deal was on offer, three more rebel States used it. Ask: which three, and what did none of them manage to build? Apart from the Marathas, there were three more Rebel States in the 18th century: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan, and the two Afghan kingdoms, Farrukhabad (est. 1714) and Rohilkhand (crystallised 1737-40). All three used the opportunity created by the weakening Mughal Empire to convert local military power into territorial rule, but none could establish a large, sustainable empire.

Because harsh land revenue and lost autonomy angered the Zamindars, the first rebel State grew from the soil. Ask: which two names did the teacher mark imp, and why? 3.1 Who were the Jats and why did they resist? The Jats were primarily an agrarian community of North India, with cultivation as their traditional occupation. Their hostility to the Mughal State stretched back to the reign of Jahangir 05-27, when harsh land revenue policies and the Mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed the Zamindars, the traditional leaders of rural society, toward organised resistance. 3.2 How the resistance developed The first organised Jat revolt came in 1669 (teacher's slide: 1669-70), led by the Zamindar Gokla. The torch passed through Rajaram 89-00 to Churaman 95-21, then Badan Singh (1722-55, consolidation), then Surajmal 56-63, each pushing resistance further. Their preferred method was guerrilla warfare: fast, decentralised and hard for a large Mughal army to counter. The Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur, in East Rajasthan, south of Delhi, bordering the Mathura and Agra districts, was formally established by Churaman 95-21 Jat (1695-1721). Like many rebel-state founders (Marathas, Sikhs), Churaman 95-21 turned peasant discontent over high land revenue into political and military power. Two names marked imp: Churaman 95-21 = establishment of the Jat kingdom; Surajmal 56-63 = the most powerful. Hostility is about LR (high land revenue) and ending local autonomy. Lohagarh Fort, Bharatpur: the Iron Fort, never conquered 3.3 Surajmal 56-63: the peak Under Maharaja Surajmal 56-63 the Jat State reached its peak. He built a strong, centralised State and forced the Mughal emperor to formally recognise him as an autonomous ruler (within the Mughal Empire). His reforms: 1. He recruited European soldiers to modernise his military. 2. He introduced a Mughal-style revenue system for administrative efficiency. 3. He removed relatives from court positions to reduce factionalism. At its peak the Jat State stretched from Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal River to the Ganga, across present-day Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. After Surajmal 56-63's death in 1763 the Jat State collapsed. Panipat 1761: Surajmal 56-63 offered help to the Marathas before the Third Battle of Panipat, but the alliance could not be established because of differences on war strategy and tactics. Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla warfare, but the Maratha commander Sadasiv Rao Bhau disagreed. The Jats still sent essential supplies to the Marathas during the war. Status: "the same thing was accepted during Churaman 95-21 Jat" (recognition as an autonomous ruler within the Mughal Empire). Panipat link: Alamgir II 54-59 was a puppet of the Marathas. Reform 1: Mahadji Scindia 68-94's Campoo = Fauj-i-Hind is the same kind of modernisation (Chapter 4). Reform 3: contrast with the Mughal family's infighting (R vs R). Map: the Jat State at its peak, Delhi to Agra, Chambal to Ganga 3.4 Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant? Handout diagram 1: the Jat Kingdom, Gokla to Surajmal and collapse Though the kingdom was the result of peasant revolts, it was no peasant utopia. Land revenue remained high, and real power rested with Zamindars, not with the ryots. The Jat State replicated the same extractive structure it had risen against. No peasant utopia = "Dreamland." Keywords: land revenue, peasant revolt, same extractive structure. Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant?

items.t: 4 · The Afghans: migration and the rise of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45
items.x: Because the Afghans were soldiers for hire, one of them once ruled Delhi himself. Ask: what did Sher Shah 40-45 learn from the Mughals, and what did he build in five years? The Afghans: migration and the rise of Sher Shah Suri 4.1 Who were the Afghans and what brought them to North India? Afghans had been migrating into North India since the 15th century, driven by poor economic conditions and political instability back home. In the military labour markets of North India they functioned largely as wandering warlords, skilled fighters available to whoever could pay. 4.2 Was there ever a moment when Afghans actually ruled Delhi? The story of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 is the story of all these Afghan migrants compressed into one life. His family, the Suris, a clan of the Pashtun tribe, had migrated from the Sur region of Afghanistan to India during the Lodi Sultanate in the late 15th century. His grandfather had received a small jagir in Sasaram (present-day Bihar) in service of the Lodi Sultans. Sher Shah 40-45, born Farid Khan around 1486 in Sasaram, grew up not in Afghanistan but in Bihar, as a second-generation Indian Afghan, a product of the North Indian military labour market. He served under various masters, rising through ability rather than birth. He served as an administrator under the Afghan governor of Bihar, then briefly under the Mughals after Babur 26-30 defeated the Lodis in 1526. During this Mughal service he closely studied Mughal administrative methods, knowledge he later turned against them. He built his power base in Bihar and Bengal and by 1540 had defeated Humayun 30-40, first reign) at the Battle of Kanauj, driving him into exile in Persia and seizing the throne of Delhi. Handout comparison: compare Suri with the Bangash Pathans of Farrukhabad (same Afghan migrant background, same military-labour-market entry), but a very different ceiling on what they could achieve, partly because the political window available to them was much narrower. The Suri family were Mansabdars in the Delhi Sultanate (Bihar). Afghan markers timeline: Suris 1540-55; Farrukhabad 1714; Rohilkhand 1737-40; Abdali 1748-61. 4.3 What Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 achieved in five years Administrative hierarchy Centre, Province (Suba), District (Sarkar), Sub-district (Pargana) Akbar 56-05 later adopted it almost wholesale Grand Trunk Road Upgraded the Uttarapath connecting Bengal to the North-West Frontier Boosts economy and trade Dak Chowki A reliable postal-relay system "Like a relay race" The Rupiya A standardised (by weight and value) silver coin, the basis of Indian currency for centuries Important: the degree of trust between buyer and seller; standardisation needs a central authority Revenue Land surveys and a fair land revenue demand fixed directly with the peasant, cutting out the middleman Zamindar Recorded in a Patta (with the ryot) and a Qubuliat (with the government): "head and tail," one document in two copies Handout: Suri was in a sense the first ruler to seriously attempt "administrative reform": streamlining the State machinery to make it efficient and fair. Unfortunately he had only five years. His successors could not hold together what he built. After his death in 1545 the Afghans fragmented again into competing warlord groups. The period 1540 to 1555, the Suri Interregnum, was a brief Afghan interruption of Mughal rule, ending when Humayun 30-40 recaptured Delhi in 1555 after the Battle of Sirhind and briefly restored Mughal authority before his death in 1556. Map: Sher Shah Suri's empire, Bengal to the Indus, Sindh and Malwa Sher Shah Suri's tomb at Sasaram, Bihar: red sandstone, set in a lake The Suri empire's extent is similar to Babur 26-30's (1526-30) and to the Delhi Sultanate (1208-1526).

items.t: 5 · The 18th century: a new surge of Afghan migration
items.x: Because the Mughal State weakened again, a second Afghan wave came. Ask: which two Afghan kingdoms emerged, and which clan founded each? The 18th century brought a new surge of Afghan migration as political instability in their homeland intensified. The progressive weakening of the Mughal State created exactly the opportunity these groups had been waiting for. Two Afghan kingdoms emerged: Farrukhabad (today a district in Uttar Pradesh; Bangash Pathans) and Rohilkhand (also called Rampur, with capital Bareilly; Rohilla Afghans). Map: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand between Awadh and the Marathas Map labels: Rohilkhand [1737-40] = Rampur (Rohilla Afghans); Farrukhabad (1714) = Bangash Pathans. Both lie between Awadh and the Marathas. Afghan kingdoms within the Mughal Empire (Article 370-type status). Farrukhabad (Bangash Pathans), 1714-43, Md Khan Bangash. Rohilkhand (Rohillas), 1721-48, Ali Md Khan; 1737-40 = Marathas and Nadir Shah weaken the Mughals. Mughal interests: territory does not shrink; military and money. Rebels' interest: dynastic rule over some territory. Factionalism (R vs R): Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother; Farrukhsiyar 13-19 killed Jahandar Shah 12-13. Both kingdoms supported Abdali at Panipat (1761); Awadh annexed both.

Because court politics left vacuums, a warlord with troops could buy a title. Ask: what did Md Khan Bangash get, and who swallowed his son's kingdom? 6.1 How did a Bangash Pathan warlord found a kingdom near Agra? The founding of Farrukhabad shows how factional Mughal court politics created vacuums that outsiders could exploit. It was structurally weak from the start, sitting between powerful neighbours, principally Awadh, which preyed on it whenever it could. Its history is best understood as a sequence across three rulers. Md Khan Bangash (1714-43) A Pathan warlord who backed Farrukhsiyar 13-19 with 12,000 troops; rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue assignments near the Ganga; founded Farrukhabad (1714), naming it after the emperor. Died 1743, succeeded by his son Qaim Khan. Qaim Khan (1743-49) In 1749 Safdar Jung 39-54 (Nawab of Awadh and Wazir of the emperor) engineered his death in battle; Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered. Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71 Retook it in 1750; driven out in 1751-52 by Marathas and Jats; fought beside Abdali at Panipat (1761) to recover it; the EIC annexed it in 1802. The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated. Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19: the handout (section 4.2) says Jahandar Shah 12-13 seized power in 1712-13 by killing the father of Farrukhsiyar 13-19, who avenged this by removing him; the board says Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother. Both are in the class material; for answers, write Mughal succession violence (R vs R). Md Khan Bangash's gesture (handout): he first founded a town called Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Farrukhabad ("the city of Farrukh") was the diplomatic correction: the classic pattern of a rebel State acknowledging Mughal sovereignty in name while building real autonomy on the ground. Nawab = a mansabdar rank; revenue near the Ganga = a Jagir; the Mughal followed the "mid path." Safdar Jung 39-54 (Wazir of Ahmed Shah Bahadur 48-54) misused his position; other Mansabdars accused him and he was forced to resign: the virtual break of Awadh from the Mughal empire (Chapter 3). Qaim Khan (handout): the textbook example of the Wazir's loyalty being to his own State, not the Emperor he nominally served; the highest Mughal Mansab had become a tool for personal and regional ambition. 6.2 Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750 onwards Ahmad Khan fought back and retook Farrukhabad in 1750. In 1751-52 the Marathas, specifically Malhar Rao Holkar and Jayappaji Rao Scindia sent by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao 40-61, along with Jats under Surajmal 56-63, drove him out. (Note: Awadh had requested the Marathas and Jats in 1751.) As Abdali's invasion progressed, the Marathas signed a treaty in 1752 that allowed him to return and resume rule, at the price of handing half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia. In 1761 he fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 at the Third Battle of Panipat. With the Marathas defeated, he recovered his full dominions, including the half ceded in 1752. Once Abdali left India in 1761, Farrukhabad weakened. In 1802 the EIC annexed Farrukhabad. (The "Ceded Provinces" refers to territories Awadh was forced to hand over under the Subsidiary Alliance of 1801; Farrukhabad was merged into the Ceded Provinces after annexation.) The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated. Ahmad Khan's dates: the handout heading reads "Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750-1802", the Panipat line-up (Chapter 4) writes 50-82, and the slide table reads 1750-1802. The short form is inconsistent, so remember the anchors: retook Farrukhabad 1750; EIC annexed it 1802.

Because Nadir Shah paralysed Delhi in 1739, a slow ground-level builder could finally declare independence. Ask: how did the Mughals respond to what they could not defeat? 7.1 How Afghan mercenaries became rulers The region that became Rohilkhand was originally called Katehr: western Uttar Pradesh, around Bareilly and Moradabad. In the 17th and early 18th century, as Mughal authority weakened, local Zamindars and regional governors in Katehr hired Afghan mercenaries to settle disputes and enforce authority. These Afghan fighters, called Rohillas, became a dominant armed presence. Note: Rohilkhand was formed by settled Afghan mercenaries consolidating power from within the region, already entrenched in Katehr long before Abdali entered India. The word "Rohilla" comes from "Roh," the Afghan homeland, so Rohilkhand means the land of the Rohillas. 7.2 1721: the starting point When Daud Khan, the Afghan commander who had consolidated the mercenary groups, died in 1721, his adopted son and protege Ali Md Khan (1721-48) took over leadership. This is the starting point, not yet an independent State, but the moment one man gained control of a significant armed force. After 1721 he moved methodically: for two decades he consolidated, slowly absorbing lands from the very Zamindars his men had been hired to protect and uniting the scattered Afghan groups under his sole command. 7.3 What finally pushed Ali Md Khan to declare independence? Nadir Shah's devastating invasion of Delhi in 1739. With the Mughal State paralysed, Ali Md Khan stopped paying taxes to Delhi and began ruling Katehr as an independent power, capturing key districts including Bareilly and Moradabad. Handout comparison with Farrukhabad: both Afghan kingdoms used the same window (Mughal paralysis) to convert military presence into territorial control. Md Khan Bangash did it earlier and more formally through Mughal court politics; Ali Md Khan did it through slow ground-level consolidation followed by outright defiance during the 1739 crisis. 7.4 How the Mughals responded Too weak to crush him, the Mughal State fell back on its standard strategy: co-opt what you cannot defeat. In 1740 Emperor Md Shah (1719-48) formally granted Ali Md Khan the title of Subadar. From 1740 Katehr was officially renamed Rohilkhand and functioned as an autonomous State under nominal Mughal sovereignty. (Ali Md Khan took control in 1721 but was officially recognised as Nawab of Rohilkhand by the Mughals in 1740.) The title gave the rebel legitimacy; it gave the Mughals the illusion of control. Both sides understood the fiction. 7.5 How Rohilkhand ended The arc is the same as Farrukhabad: rise on Afghan military power, peak during the Abdali alliance, collapse once that external prop was removed. 1761: under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, Rohilkhand actively supported Abdali at the Third Battle of Panipat. 1761-71: Delhi was effectively under Rohilla influence (the Mughal emperor was in Awadh). 1770: Najib dies; with no Abdali to support since 1761, Rohilkhand weakens. 1771: Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptured Delhi and allowed Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06 to return home (the Red Fort). 1774: Most of Rohilkhand was annexed by Awadh with EIC help, because of the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), which led to a military alliance. The rest, a small part, became the autonomous State of Rampur with capital Bareilly, legally under Awadh, and from 1801 under the EIC when Awadh gave half of Awadh in the Subsidiary Alliance.

items.t: 8 · Why Abdali came: the immediate trigger
items.x: Because both Afghan kingdoms backed Abdali at Panipat, we ask why he came at all. Ask: why is 'the expulsion of Timur Shah' the answer and Maratha expansion not? Prelims 2010. Abdali's immediate reason for the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was to avenge the Marathas' expulsion of his son Timur Shah from Lahore. March 1758: Raghunath Rao 73-74 crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah (Governor of Punjab and Kashmir). The Marathas made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year; on his death Sabaji Scindia took charge, holding the garrisons at Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border against Abdali. The Maratha conquest of Punjab was a challenge Abdali could not ignore: the immediate trigger. Link to the previous lecture: auctioning of office (e.g. a governorship). The Marathas gave Punjab to Adina Beg Khan for Rs 75 lakh a year. Phrase for Maratha reach: "Attock se Cuttack" (Orissa). Prelims 2010 options: (a) to avenge the expulsion by the Marathas of his viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore (correct); (b) fast expansion of the Maratha Empire; (c) Mughal Emperor's refusal to pay annual tribute; (d) Sultan of Punjab's refusal to grant safe passage. Why (a): in March 1758 the Marathas drove Timur Shah out of Lahore, the immediate, personal reason. Why not the rest: (b) general background, not the trigger; (c) no Mughal tribute dispute caused this invasion; (d) there was no Sultan of Punjab refusing safe passage.

items.t: 9 · Synthesis: three Rebel States, one pattern
items.x: Because each story had the same shape, the teacher joins them. Ask: what was the prop in each case, and what happened when it was removed? The Jats From an agrarian base upward: Zamindar-led revolt, then territory, then a reforming ruler (Surajmal 56-63) Farrukhabad From Mughal court politics downward: 12,000 troops for Farrukhsiyar 13-19, then a Nawab title, then a city, then a dynasty Rohilkhand From the ground up over two decades: hired mercenaries, then consolidation, then independence in the 1739 Delhi paralysis The common rule Each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal 56-63), and each collapsed once that support was removed How a Rebel State was built (the pattern) Opportunity: the Mughal Empire weakens, factional court politics or paralysis (1739) creates a vacuum Local military power: peasant Zamindars (Jats), Afghan mercenaries (Rohillas), a warlord with troops (Bangash) The middle path: accept Mansabdar status, Mughal sovereignty in name, tribute and troops; get dynastic governorship and a Watan Jagir Dependence: each needed external support to peak (Abdali; Maratha tactical backing) Collapse: support removed (1761 Abdali leaves; 1763 Surajmal 56-63 dies), neighbours annex (Awadh, then the EIC) Founder and year Churaman 95-21, 1695 Md Khan Bangash, 1714 Ali Md Khan, 1721 (recognised 1740) Base Agrarian Zamindars, peasant discontent over LR Pathan warlord with 12,000 troops, court politics Afghan mercenaries hired in Katehr Peak Surajmal 56-63, 1756-63 Ahmad Khan with Abdali, 1761 Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, 1761-71 (Delhi influence) Collapse 1763, Surajmal 56-63 dies 1749 annexed by Awadh; 1802 EIC 1774 Awadh plus EIC; Rampur remains

1486 Farid Khan (Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45) born at Sasaram (around) 1526 Babur 26-30 defeats the Lodis; Suri serves the Mughals 1540 Battle of Kanauj: Sher Shah 40-45 defeats Humayun 30-40, takes Delhi ★ 1545 Sher Shah 40-45 dies; Suri Interregnum (1540-55) continues 1555 Humayun 30-40 retakes Delhi after the Battle of Sirhind 1605 Jahangir 05-27's reign begins (Jat hostility traced from here) 1669 Gokla leads the first organised Jat revolt 1695 Churaman 95-21 founds the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur ★ 1714 Md Khan Bangash founds Farrukhabad ★ 1721 Daud Khan dies; Ali Md Khan takes over Katehr 1722 Badan Singh consolidates the Jat State 1739 Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi; Ali Md Khan stops paying taxes 1740 Md Shah grants Ali Md Khan the Subadar title; Rohilkhand ★ 1743 Md Khan Bangash dies; Qaim Khan 1749 Safdar Jung 39-54 engineers Qaim Khan's death; Farrukhabad annexed to Awadh 1750 Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71 retakes Farrukhabad 1751 Marathas and Jats drive Ahmad Khan out (to 1752) 1756 Surajmal 56-63's reign begins 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 expels Timur Shah from Lahore ★ 1761 Third Panipat: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand back Abdali ★ 1763 Surajmal 56-63 dies; the Jat State collapses 1765 Treaty of Allahabad (Awadh-EIC military alliance) 1770 Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 dies 1771 Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes Delhi 1774 Awadh with EIC help annexes most of Rohilkhand; Rampur remains 1801 Awadh's Subsidiary Alliance; Rampur under the EIC 1802 EIC annexes Farrukhabad 1857 Bangash Pathans join the Revolt

Two bad options and a middle path. When rebels establish their rule in an area, the emperor can fight on and end the rebellion, or lose the territory and let the rebel set up an independent kingdom. The middle path: the rebel accepts Mansabdar status, the Mughal as emperor, tribute to Delhi and a duty to maintain an army and help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, and non-interference. Both core interests are met; only the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once, in 1707), stand outside. Three more Rebel States. Apart from the Marathas, the 18th century saw three more: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan, Farrukhabad (est. 1714, Bangash Pathans) and Rohilkhand (process began 1721, completed 1737-40, Rohilla Afghans). All three turned local military power into territorial rule as the Mughal Empire weakened, yet none built a large, sustainable empire. The Jats rise from the soil. The Jats were an agrarian community, hostile to the Mughals since Jahangir 05-27, when harsh land revenue and the drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed their Zamindars into organised resistance, mainly by guerrilla warfare. The chain runs Gokla (first revolt, 1669), Rajaram 89-00, Churaman 95-21, who formally founds the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in 1695, and Badan Singh (1722-55), who consolidates it. Surajmal's peak, and the fall. Surajmal 56-63 builds a strong, centralised State and forces the Mughal emperor to recognise him as autonomous. He recruits European soldiers, introduces a Mughal-style revenue system and removes relatives from court posts; the State stretches from Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal to the Ganga, with the Iron Fort Lohagarh as his pride. At Panipat 1761 he wanted guerrilla warfare, Sadasiv Rao Bhau did not, yet the Jats still sent supplies. After he dies in 1763 the State collapses: it was no peasant utopia, since land revenue stayed high and power stayed with Zamindars. The Afghan who ruled Delhi. Afghans had been migrating into North India since the 15th century, driven by poor economy and instability at home, and worked as wandering warlords in its military labour markets. Farid Khan, born around 1486 at Sasaram in Bihar to the Sur clan, rises through ability, serves the Mughals after 1526 and studies their administration. By 1540, as Sher Shah 40-45, he defeats Humayun 30-40 at Kanauj and seizes Delhi. Five years that mattered (1540-45). Sher Shah 40-45 builds the Suba-Sarkar-Pargana hierarchy (Akbar 56-05 later adopts it), upgrades the Uttarapath into the Grand Trunk Road, sets up the Dak Chowki relay post, issues the standard silver Rupiya and fixes a fair land revenue directly with the peasant, recorded in a Patta and a Qubuliat. After he dies in 1545 the Afghans fragment; the Suri Interregnum (1540-55) ends when Humayun 30-40 retakes Delhi after Sirhind in 1555. Farrukhabad: a warlord and a flattering name. Md Khan Bangash, a Pathan warlord, backs Farrukhsiyar 13-19 with 12,000 troops and is rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue near the Ganga; he founds Farrukhabad in 1714, after first naming a town Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed the emperor. His son Qaim Khan is killed in 1749 through the scheme of Safdar Jung 39-54, and Farrukhabad is annexed to Awadh and plundered. Ahmad Khan's see-saw. Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71 retakes Farrukhabad in 1750, is driven out in 1751-52 by Marathas (Holkar and Scindia) and Jats at Awadh's request, and returns by a treaty that hands half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia. In 1761 he fights beside Abdali 47-72 at Third Panipat and recovers his full dominions. The EIC annexes Farrukhabad in 1802. Rohilkhand: hired guns become rulers. Zamindars of Katehr (around Bareilly and Moradabad) hire Afghan mercenaries, the Rohillas, who grow dominant under Daud Khan. When he dies in 1721 his adopted son Ali Md Khan takes over and spends two decades absorbing lands. In 1739 Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi, so Ali stops paying taxes; in 1740 Md Shah 19-48 co-opts him with the Subadar title and Katehr is renamed Rohilkhand. The end of Rohilkhand. Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 backs Abdali at Panipat in 1761 and Delhi is under Rohilla influence until 1771, when Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes it. Najib dies in 1770; in 1774 Awadh, with EIC help (allies since the Treaty of Allahabad 1765), annexes most of Rohilkhand. A small remainder becomes the State of Rampur, under the EIC from 1801. Why Abdali came (Prelims 2010). In March 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah, Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir. The Marathas made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year, and later Sabaji Scindia held Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border. The immediate reason for Third Panipat was to avenge Timur Shah. One pattern, one prop. The Jats rose from an agrarian base upward, Farrukhabad from court politics downward, Rohilkhand from the ground up over two decades. The common rule: each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal 56-63) and each collapsed once that support was removed: Abdali left in 1761 and Surajmal died in 1763.
