items.t: 1 · How did Sikhism begin, and what were its core beliefs?
items.x: Chapter 1 of the story: a peaceful faith with four ideas. Ask: what did Nanak teach that a State could not tolerate? Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539) was a contemporary of Babur 26-30. Sikhism rose from 1500 onwards, built on four core principles: 1. One supreme and formless God. 2. Direct access to God without rituals or priests. 3. Rejection of the caste system. 4. Emphasis on honest living and selfless service. Guru Nanak undertook four major spiritual journeys (Udasis) over 30 years, covering about 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet and Arabia. He finally settled in Kartarpur (present-day Pakistan), where he established the Langar, the free communal kitchen designed to promote equality.

items.t: 2 · When did conflict begin between the Sikhs and the Mughal State?
items.x: Because the Sikhs began to demand a State at Anandpur, the Mughals struck twice. Ask: why does 1606 turn a movement martial? Initially there was no conflict. But as the Sikh population grew and Sikhs began demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla and south of Chamba), an area under the Shivalik Hill Chiefs who were Mughal allies, religious and political tensions built up. First flashpoint, 1606: the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, was executed by Jahangir 05-27. A turning point: a peaceful spiritual movement began its transformation into a martial community. Second flashpoint, 1675: the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, was executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07.

Because two Gurus were killed, the tenth Guru built an army. Ask: why is it compared to NSG or STF? In 1699, at Anandpur, the 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08, established the Khalsa, a Sikh military organisation created to defend the Sikh Panth and struggle for a Sikh State. The handout compares it to an NSG/STF: its creation marked the formal militarisation of the Sikh community's political ambitions.

items.t: 4 · December 1704 to October 1708: the Sahibzadas and the Guru's death
items.x: Because the Khalsa threatened the Mughal order, the Guru's family paid. Ask: who promised, and who broke the promise? December 1704, Battle of Chamkaur: the Guru's two elder sons, Sahibzada Ajit Singh (aged 18) and Sahibzada Jujhar Singh (aged 14), died in battle. The same month his two younger sons, Sahibzada Zorawar Singh (aged 9) and Sahibzada Fateh Singh (aged 6), were buried alive in a wall on the orders of Wazir Khan, the Mughal Faujdar of Sirhind. (A Faujdar = a district military commander, comparable in local authority to a Superintendent of Police today. Since 2022, 26 December is observed as Veer Bal Divas in memory of the younger Sahibzadas.) 1707: the new emperor Bahadur Shah (1707-12), following the pacifist policy (diplomacy more than war), granted the Guru a high Mansab and promised a Sikh State in and around Anandpur. The promise was never fulfilled. 7 October 1708: Wazir Khan arranged assassins to attack the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib Gurdwara in Nanded, Maharashtra, where he had accompanied Bahadur Shah. The Guru killed the assassins himself but later succumbed to his injuries, dying at the age of 42. No action was taken against Wazir Khan; Anandpur was never given to the Sikhs. 1707 pacifist policy, Anandpur promised, 1708 Nanded 1707: Aurangzeb 58-07 dies; the Mughal pacifist policy follows: "better relations with rivals." For the Guru: a very high Mansab [Zat] and Anandpur promised (Article 370-like status, like Rohilkhand, Jats, Farrukhabad, the Marathas under Shahu 19-49, Mysore, Rajputs). 1708: at Nanded the Guru is killed by men sent by Wazir Khan [Faujdar of Sirhind], also responsible for the death of the Guru's four sons. Wazir Khan was not punished by the Mughals; Anandpur was not given. Same pacifist-policy argument: Chapter 4, section 5.

items.t: 5 · Why the Guru declared the Guru Granth Sahib the final Guru
items.x: Because a living successor could inflame Jats against Khatris, the Guru chose a Book. Ask: why is a Book neutral? Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) and the Akal Takht, Amritsar A few days before his death, at Abchal Nagar Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 declared that he would be the last living Guru and that all spiritual authority would henceforth be vested in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the holy book he had compiled. The decision was deliberate: to prevent community tensions between the Jat community, which dominated the Khalsa, and the Khatri community of traders, to which all ten Gurus had belonged. By vesting authority in the holy book rather than a human successor, the question of community dominance was permanently closed. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji was installed at the Akal Takht in the Golden Temple complex, Amritsar. From the Akal Takht the Gurus issued Hukumnamas (formal orders) and Sikh warriors took blessings before going into battle against the Mughals. The 19th-century sects of Nirankaris and Namdharis believe in a living Guru, which has historically led to serious conflicts within the community. Guru Granth Sahib as final Guru; Jat-Khatri rivalry; Banda Bahadur Guru Granth Sahib has two aspects: the Holy Book and the Guru itself. Disrespect = Beadbi (very sensitive today also). Jats dominated the Khalsa; Khatris = men of money (merchants, moneylenders, ijaradars) [Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari in Punjab and Bengal]; all the Gurus were Khatris. Banda Bahadur 08-15: a small state "in and around Patiala"; took revenge by executing Wazir Khan.

items.t: 6 · Banda Bahadur 08-15: the first Sikh State, and why it collapsed
items.x: Because the Guru was dead, Banda took revenge and built a State. Ask: what makes a State real (coins, officials, seal)? From 1708 the rebellion was carried forward by Banda Bahadur 08-15. He defeated and killed Wazir Khan at the Battle of Chappar Chiri on 10 May 1710, which also led to the conquest of Sirhind. He established a Sikh State over territories between the River Ravi and the River Jamuna, with its own coins, its own officials and its own seal for administrative orders (= full independence). Farrukhsiyar 13-19 appointed Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore specifically to suppress this Sikh State. By 1715 Banda Bahadur 08-15 was defeated; captured and executed in Delhi in 1716 by Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Territory flag: the handout places Banda's State between the Ravi and the Jamuna; the board says "a small state in and around Patiala." Both are in the class material; the handout's wording is the answer-writing one. Why his State fell (three reasons): 1. Khatri traders turned against him. Constant warfare hurt trade, and the commercial class needs decisive victors and political stability to function. 2. Divide and rule. Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari (the revenue-farming system) in Punjab specifically to co-opt Khatri traders with business opportunities. Both Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 offered Mansabs to Khatri traders, who switched sides. (Note: this further increased the number of Mansabdars, adding to the Jagirdari Crisis; see Chapter 2.) 3. Hindu Jat zamindars switched sides. Churaman 95-21 Jat (1695-1721), for instance, went over to the Mughals after they recognised his Jat Kingdom, granting him conditional dynastic autonomy in exchange for loyalty. Why Banda Bahadur 08-15 lost: Khatris, Jats, divide and rule Khatris stopped supporting him (money); Churaman 95-21 Jat likewise (guns / military), co-opted by accepting a Jat kingdom within the Mughal empire. The Khatris wanted peace as trade was hurt by constant wars, so they chose the stronger side. Banda Bahadur 08-15 was not a Guru, so he lacked the Gurus' authority. Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari in Punjab and Bengal (business opportunity); he and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 made Khatris Mansabdars. Rule (double-starred): when a personality weakens, power leaves (downward or sideways), and factionalism rises (Khatris against Banda Bahadur 08-15).

items.t: 7 · What kept the Sikh State alive: the Misl confederacy
items.x: Because Banda fell but the Mughals were weak, power spread to Misl chiefs. Ask: is a confederacy strength or weakness? The defeat of Banda Bahadur 08-15 did not end the Sikh State. The Mughals were too weak to fully reassert control over Punjab, and power became decentralised among Misl Chiefs. Misls are kinship-based clans. They united during wars, particularly against Afghan invasions, but otherwise operated independently. Whenever a Misl conquered territory, the lands were distributed among its members in proportion to their military and monetary contribution. Even the lowest-ranking soldier received a share of land. By 1770 there were 12 major Misls in Punjab, with the Dal Khalsa at the centre under a leader chosen by the Misl chiefs: a confederacy structure with a weak centre and strong constituent units. Takeaway (handout): compare it to the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, where a nominal centre held together largely autonomous regional chiefs. Decentralisation was both a source of resilience and, ultimately, a vulnerability. Misl confederacy: weak centre, Dal Khalsa, Manupur 1748 Death of Banda Bahadur 08-15 = no strong centre, so power decentralised to the misl chiefs. Polity structure: a Confederacy (of misls); fragmented. Board figure: one big circle (Punjab) with about a dozen circles (misls) inside, "roughly 40-60 misls" (handout's formal count: 12 major Misls by 1770). Dal Khalsa = assembly of misl chiefs: on Abdali's 1748 invasion it meets and prepares a joint defence, e.g. Manupur 1748, where Abdali was defeated (Chapter 4). Fragmented polity PYQ: UPSC Mains and State PCS PYQ (UPSC Mains): "By the mid-18th century India was a spectre of fragmented polity." State PCS FYQ: "By 1715 Punjab was a spectre of fragmented polity." In today's language this is a weak centre, as with coalition governments at the Centre: factionalism, instability, shorter tenures, a weak PM. Nature of power: it centralises in a strong personality "It is in the nature of power to centralise in a strong personality." Power cycles between centralised and fragmented; "today" sits at a trough. PSIR links: multi-polar world, balance of power, fragmented world order, confederalism.

Because power gathers in a strong personality, Ranjit Singh 01-39 unifies the Misls. Ask: which crisis became his opportunity? Portrait of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Sukerchakia Misl, coronated 1801 Ranjit Singh 01-39 of the Sukerchakia Misl played a crucial role in defeating Zaman Shah's third Afghan invasion of 1799 (the slide reads: he rose during Zaman Shah's Afghan invasions of 1796-1799). This gave him the platform to establish dominance over the other Misls, and he was coronated King (Maharaja) of the Sikh State in 1801. The other Misl chiefs were reduced to tribute-paying vassals, retaining conditional control of their lands in return for loyalty and tribute to the King (lands held as Jagirs, not Watan). Zaman Shah (Abdali's successor) invaded: "crisis = opportunity." The Sukerchakia misl of Ranjit Singh 01-39 emerged the most powerful. 1801: coronation. 1809: Treaty of Amritsar made the Sutlej the border with the Company State (British India) and brought a military alliance with the EIC. The Misl chiefs' lands: Jagirs, not Watan. 8.1 Territorial expansion: rapid and systematic Handout diagram 3: Ranjit Singh's expansion and administration 1. 1801: conquered Lahore (handout list); the slides place the capture of Lahore in 1799 from the Bhangi Misl. 2. 1808: conquered Jammu from the Dogras (the handout adds: in 1819 he returned Jammu to the Dogras but within the Sikh Empire: the Dogras became vassals; the slide adds: Jammu later granted as a jagir to Kishore Singh in 1820, and his son Gulab Singh formally made Raja of Jammu in 1822). 3. 1809: the handout lists "conquered the whole of Punjab" as the third step; the slide reads: "signed the Treaty of Amritsar ... secured his eastern frontier." Flags on the Ranjit Singh 01-39 dates: the handout gives Lahore 1801 and Jammu returned to the Dogras in 1819; the slides give Lahore 1799 (captured from the Bhangi Misl) and Jammu given as a jagir to Kishore Singh in 1820 and Gulab Singh made Raja in 1822. Also, the handout says Zaman Shah's third invasion of 1799, the slide says the invasions of 1796-1799. For answers, anchor on: coronation 1801; Treaty of Amritsar 1809; Multan 1818; Kashmir 1819; Peshawar 1834; Tripartite Treaty 1838.

Because he now borders the EIC, he settles the frontier. Ask: what did he gain, and which way did he then expand? In 1809 Ranjit Singh 01-39 signed the Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC, represented by Charles Metcalfe, the EIC's Resident in the Delhi court. (Recall that the Scindias had been removed from Delhi in 1803 and the EIC had set up indirect rule there through a British Resident.) Four outcomes: 1. The EIC recognised Ranjit Singh 01-39 as the sovereign ruler of Punjab. 2. It led to a military alliance (later link to the EIC's Policy of Ring Fence). 3. The Sutlej River was fixed as the border between the Sikh State and the Company State. 4. Ranjit Singh 01-39 was free to expand on his side of the Sutlej without British interference. Map of Punjab: Sutlej border, north Ranjit Singh, south EIC Punjab map: north of the Sutlej = Ranjit Singh 01-39 (RJ 01-39); south of the Sutlej = the EIC.

items.t: 10 · How far did Ranjit Singh 01-39 expand after 1809?
items.x: Because the east was secured, he turned west and north. Ask: which conquest completed what the Marathas left unfinished? With his eastern border secured, Ranjit Singh 01-39 turned west and north: 1. 1818: removed the Afghans from Multan. 2. 1819: conquered Kashmir. (Recall that Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 captured Punjab and Kashmir; Punjab was taken back by the Marathas in 1758 but not Kashmir; Ranjit Singh 01-39 completed what the Marathas left unfinished.) 3. 1834: conquered Peshawar (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, bordering Afghanistan along the Durand Line). Peshawar was conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa, whose reputation was so fearsome that Afghan mothers used his name to frighten unruly children: "If you don't stop crying, Haria Ragle will turn up." Board keywords: Khyber Pass, Peshawar. 10.1 The 1838 Tripartite Treaty In 1838 Ranjit Singh 01-39 signed the Tripartite Treaty between the Sikh State, the EIC and Shah Shuja of Afghanistan. The design: to establish British indirect rule in Afghanistan through Shah Shuja as a puppet ruler. The aim: to create a buffer of Afghanistan and Punjab against the feared Russian invasion of British India from the north-west. British fear of Russia. Chain: Russia → Afghanistan → Khyber Pass → Sikh State → Company State (British India). Afghanistan and Punjab are the buffer. The 1838 Tripartite Treaty: Sikh State, EIC, Shah Shuja

items.t: 11 · What kind of State did Ranjit Singh 01-39 build?
items.x: Last scene: how did he hold it together? Ask: which four groups did he balance, and what did the Kardar do? How power was built Coercion, diplomacy and careful balance between Misl chiefs, the Khalsa army, Khatri traders and non-Sikh nobles such as the Dogras (similar to the successor States) Character Militarily strong and economically prosperous Revenue policy Fair for the masses; trade flourished; a strong State delivered law and order Land Only 40% of land under the Jagirdari system; from the rest revenue went directly to the King Kardar Main income source LR collected by Kardars, the chief administrative officer at the Taluqa (district) level: revenue collector, local magistrate (judge), police chief and customs officer Ijaradari Relied on Ijaradari: instead of a fixed cash salary a Kardar often acted as an Ijaradar, but it was ensured the ryot was not oppressed by very high LR Village autonomy State authority stopped at the village level; local chiefs and clans respected (connects to the Mahalwari Settlement in Punjab, where even the British respected village autonomy) Secular cabinet Fakir Azizuddin (Muslim) as Foreign Minister; Dewan Dina Nath (Hindu) as Finance Minister Culturally broad Sahajdhari (non-Khalsa) Sikhs included; they do not keep the five Ks How Chapter 6 feeds UPSC. The chapter carries no mapped UPSC Prelims questions (1995-2025). It feeds two Mains answers, where Sikh-State facts are a supporting strand: Mains 2014: why were so many empire-shaking battles fought at Panipat? (see Chapter 4) and Mains 2017: the spectre of a fragmented polity in mid-18th-century India (the Misl confederacy is your Punjab example). From Guru Nanak to Ranjit Singh 01-39 Faith: Guru Nanak's formless God, anti-caste, Langar Two flashpoints: 1606 Arjan Dev, 1675 Teg Bahadur: a peaceful movement turns martial 1699 Khalsa: a military organisation for a Sikh State at Anandpur 1704-08: Sahibzadas killed, the promise of Anandpur broken, the Guru killed at Nanded; Guru Granth Sahib declared final Guru 1708-15 Banda Bahadur 08-15: a first Sikh State (Ravi to Jamuna) that falls when Khatris and Jats defect 1715-1801 Misls: confederacy of 12 major Misls with the Dal Khalsa 1801-39 Ranjit Singh 01-39: unified Sikh State, treaty with the EIC, expansion west and north Commercial class Khatri traders turned against him (trade hurt, co-opted by Ijaradari and Mansabs) Khatri traders balanced among the pillars of his State Landed groups Jat zamindars switched (Churaman 95-21 recognised) Misl chiefs as tribute-paying vassals; Dogras and local chiefs respected Centre No Guru authority; Mughals' Governor of Lahore sent against him Strong king: coronation 1801, treaty with the EIC 1809 Outcome Captured 1715, executed 1716 Prosperous State, expansion to Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar

1469 Guru Nanak born (1469-1539) 1606 5th Guru Arjan Dev executed by Jahangir 05-27: first flashpoint ★ 1675 9th Guru Teg Bahadur executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07: second flashpoint ★ 1699 Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 founds the Khalsa at Anandpur ★ 1704 Battle of Chamkaur; Sahibzadas die 1707 Bahadur Shah grants high Mansab, promises Anandpur 1708 Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 killed at Nanded (7 October); Banda Bahadur 08-15 takes up the struggle ★ 1710 Chappar Chiri: Wazir Khan killed; Sirhind conquered ★ 1715 Banda Bahadur 08-15 defeated 1716 Banda Bahadur 08-15 executed in Delhi 1748 Dal Khalsa prepares joint defence; Manupur 1770 12 major Misls with the Dal Khalsa 1799 Ranjit Singh 01-39 helps defeat Zaman Shah; takes Lahore (slide dating) 1801 Ranjit Singh 01-39 coronated Maharaja of the Sikh State ★ 1808 Jammu conquered from the Dogras 1809 Treaty of Amritsar (Charles Metcalfe); Sutlej as border ★ 1818 Afghans removed from Multan 1819 Kashmir conquered 1834 Peshawar conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa 1838 Tripartite Treaty: Sikhs, EIC and Shah Shuja ★

A peaceful faith. Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539), a contemporary of Babur 26-30, teaches four things: one formless God, direct access without rituals or priests, no caste, honest living and selfless service. He makes four Udasis over 30 years (about 30,000 km), then settles at Kartarpur and starts the Langar, a free kitchen for equality. Territory, and the first blow (1606). The teacher says a State is an organisation with a territory motive, and until the Sikhs wanted territory there was no dispute. They begin demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla, south of Chamba), land held by Shivalik hill chiefs who are Mughal allies. In 1606 Jahangir 05-27 executes the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, and a peaceful movement starts turning martial. The Khalsa (1675-1699). In 1675 Aurangzeb 58-07 has the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, executed in Delhi. In 1699 the 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08, founds the Khalsa at Anandpur: a Sikh military organisation, something like an NSG or STF, to defend the Panth and struggle for a Sikh State. Its identity is the five Ks. The Sahibzadas and a broken promise (1704-1707). In December 1704 the two elder sons, Ajit Singh (18) and Jujhar Singh (14), die at Chamkaur. The same month the two younger, Zorawar Singh (9) and Fateh Singh (6), are buried alive in a wall on the orders of Wazir Khan, Faujdar of Sirhind. In 1707 Bahadur Shah 07-12, on a pacifist policy, gives the Guru a high Mansab and promises Anandpur, but never keeps it. Nanded and the Book (1708). On 7 October 1708 Wazir Khan's assassins strike the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib in Nanded; he kills them but dies of his injuries at 42, and Wazir Khan is not punished. A few days before, he had declared the Guru Granth Sahib the final Guru, to stop Jat versus Khatri tension: Jats dominated the Khalsa and all ten Gurus were Khatri traders. The Book was installed at the Akal Takht. Banda Bahadur 08-15's State. From 1708 Banda Bahadur 08-15 carries on. On 10 May 1710 at Chappar Chiri he kills Wazir Khan and takes Sirhind. His State between the Ravi and the Jamuna has its own coins, officials and seal, which the teacher reads as full independence. Farrukhsiyar 13-19 sends Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore to crush it. Why it fell (1715-1716). The Khatri traders, hurt by constant war, turned away. Jahandar Shah 12-13 brought Ijaradari to Punjab to co-opt them, and he and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 offered them Mansabs. Hindu Jat zamindars switched too: Churaman 95-21 went over when the Mughals recognised his Jat Kingdom. Banda Bahadur 08-15 was also not a Guru. He was defeated in 1715 and executed in 1716. The Misl confederacy. The Mughals are too weak to take Punjab back, so power spreads to Misl chiefs: kinship clans that unite in wars, especially against Afghan invasions, and otherwise act alone. Conquered land is shared by contribution. By 1770 there are 12 major Misls with the Dal Khalsa at the centre; at Manupur 1748 it prepares a joint defence and Abdali is defeated. This is a weak centre, a fragmented polity, like the Maratha Confederacy. Ranjit Singh 01-39 centralises. Zaman Shah's invasions are a crisis that becomes an opportunity for Ranjit Singh 01-39 of the Sukerchakia Misl, who takes Lahore from the Bhangi Misl and is crowned Maharaja in 1801. The other Misl chiefs become tribute-paying vassals holding Jagirs, not Watan. The handout dates Lahore to 1801, the slides to 1799. Treaties and conquests (1809-1838). In 1809 Charles Metcalfe, the EIC's Resident at Delhi, signs the Treaty of Amritsar: Ranjit Singh 01-39 is recognised as sovereign, there is a military alliance, the Sutlej is the border, and he is free to expand on his side. He then takes Multan (1818), Kashmir (1819) and Peshawar (1834, Hari Singh Nalwa). The 1838 Tripartite Treaty with Shah Shuja makes Afghanistan and Punjab a buffer against feared Russian invasion. A balanced, secular State. Ranjit Singh 01-39 built power by coercion, diplomacy and balance between Misl chiefs, the Khalsa army, Khatri traders and non-Sikh nobles such as the Dogras. Only 40% of land was Jagirdari; the rest paid the King directly, collected by Kardars (collector, magistrate, police chief, customs officer). Village autonomy was respected, Fakir Azizuddin was Foreign Minister, Dewan Dina Nath Finance Minister, and Sahajdhari Sikhs were included.

Prelims 2001 Which Indian ruler established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? (d) Tipu 82-99 Sultan: embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, with new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. The distractors were Haider Ali 61-82, Mir Qasim 60-63 and Shah Alam II 60-06 Mysore: Tipu 82-99's innovations

Story so far: nothing yet. These three States stood outside the middle path of Mughal rule. Ask: which is Rajput, which southern, which grew from Vijayanagar? [Part of the Vijayanagar empire, 1336-1646]. Mysore's roots are in the Vijayanagar Empire (section 6). These are the third class of regional States from Chapter 3: Already Autonomous States, where even when the Mughal was powerful he did not rule. The Rajputs were brought into the Mughal system by Akbar 56-05 but kept their home territories; Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire; Mysore grew out of the Vijayanagar world.

Because Rajputana had no single centre and fighting all clans was costly, Akbar made a deal. Ask: what did each side get? Akbar 56-05 and the Rajputs: Mansabdars and Vatan Jagirs 16th-century Rajputana No single central power; roughly 20 major Rajput clans, each controlling its own territory (in modern IR terms a multi-polar world: many power centres, no single dominant one) Akbar 56-05's approach Defeating all would be expensive and uncertain, so he co-opted the more powerful Rajput chiefs Mansabdars The chosen chiefs became ranked nobles with military and administrative responsibilities Vatan Jagirs Their home territories were recognised as Vatan Jagirs: the land remained theirs but within the Mughal framework Obligations Accepted the Mughal Emperor as sovereign, paid tributes, contributed troops Hindu bloc As a group they formed the Hindu bloc within the Mansabdari system (about 15% of all Mansabdars) In return Akbar 56-05 helped them subdue the smaller Rajput chiefs Result A partial consolidation of power 20 clans, with a few strong ones (Mewar, Marwar) swallowing the smaller: only a partial (Centralization). The whole of Rajputana was never under one king (no single pyramid of power).

items.t: 2 · Rajputs against Aurangzeb 58-07, and the Marathas
items.x: Because the bargain rested on balance, Mewar's growth upset it. Ask: why did the 1680 revolt collapse? The 1680 Rajput revolt Mewar expands: under Raj Singh, aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states Aurangzeb 58-07 is uneasy: he did not want one Rajput power to dominate all Rajputana and rival the Mughals 1680, the trigger: a child comes to the throne in Marwar (astride the Delhi/Agra to Ahmedabad trade route); Aurangzeb 58-07 interferes in the succession Marwar and Mewar revolt The rebellion collapses: the other Rajput chiefs refuse to join, fearing Mewar would dominate them Rajputana after Aurangzeb 58-07: Marathas, then Subordinate Alliances Handout diagram 1: Rajputs from Akbar to the EIC This arrangement held through most of the 17th century. Trouble came under Aurangzeb 58-07. Mewar, under Raj Singh, had been expanding aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states; Aurangzeb 58-07 grew uneasy, not wanting one Rajput power to dominate Rajputana and rival the Mughal State. 1680: a child came to the throne in Marwar, a kingdom astride the important trade route connecting Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad. Aurangzeb 58-07 interfered in the succession: the trigger. Marwar and Mewar both revolted, but the revolt failed. The other Rajput chiefs refused to join, fearing that if the revolt succeeded Mewar would dominate them. After Aurangzeb 58-07's death in 1707 the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms. The most prominent figure was Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber, who ruled Jaipur and remained a powerful Mansabdar in Delhi, but on his own conditions. From 1751 the Marathas began regular raids into Rajputana, extracting tribute and interfering in succession disputes, but could never fully conquer the region. After the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the EIC replaced the Marathas as the regional power and signed Subordinate Alliances (also called Subsidiary Alliances) with the Rajput states. Subordinate Alliance is like World History's Protectorate: the Indian ruler kept his throne but surrendered foreign policy and defence to the EIC, which stationed its own troops, paid for by the Indian ruler. Under suzerainty = loss of external sovereign functions plus loss of symbolic sovereignty. "Will do in future" (Subsidiary Alliance is taken up in Chapter 11).

Because after 1707 the Rajputs acted on their own terms, one of them is worth knowing in detail. Ask: what are his four roles? "Sawai" A title (1.25 times more able than any contemporary ruler) conferred by Aurangzeb 58-07 Four roles at once Mughal Mansabdar, regional state-builder, astronomer and town planner Subedar Held the Subedari of Malwa (1729-37) and Agra (Governor) Hurda conference, 1734 A conference of Rajput rulers at Hurda to forge a united front against the Marathas; it collapsed due to internal Rajput rivalries Treaty of Bhopal 1738: Malwa annexed by the Marathas (the teacher: Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 = the Mughal Governor of Malwa) Jaipur founded, 1727 Designed by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya on Vastu Shastra principles, grid-pattern layout; the first planned city of modern India; Sawai Ram Singh painted it pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales Social reform Tried to curb dowry and excessive marriage expenditure among Rajputs; limited success Last Yajnas The last Indian ruler to perform the Ashvamedha and Vajapeya Yajnas: a conscious assertion of Hindu Chakravartin status as Mughal authority collapsed Flagged: "astronomer and town planner" (for Prelims). Memorise Jaipur 1727, Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, grid-pattern layout, the first planned city, and the pink colour of 1876. 3.1 The Jantar Mantars and astronomy Five observatories (Jantar Mantars) were built at Delhi (1724), Jaipur (1734), Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi. Jaipur's is the largest: a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2010). The Samrat Yantra there, the largest sundial in the world, could measure local time to an accuracy of 2 seconds. Astronomical tables tell where a celestial body (sun, moon, planet, star) will be at any given date and time. The existing tables, the Zij-i-Ulugh Begi (Islamic) and the Siddhantic (Hindu), had accumulated errors over centuries. The Jantar Mantars generated fresh observational data to correct them in the form of the Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi (1733), dedicated to Muhammad Shah 19-48. He also sent a scientific delegation to Portugal (1730) and commissioned Sanskrit astronomical works. He chose stone instruments over brass for greater accuracy: Samrat Yantra Sundial for time Jai Prakash Yantra Celestial mapper Ram Yantra Altitude meter for the Sun's position

Because the Mughals never reached the far south, a small State could build itself on trade. Ask: where did the trade money go? Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire. The Mughal State simply never expanded far enough south to include it. By the 1740s, Marthanda Varma 29-58 had built a strong, centralised State by subjugating local chiefs across the region, and a European-style military: modern weapons, trained soldiers. Takeaway: Travancore established a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast. The revenues were reinvested into the military, irrigation works and transport infrastructure: a classic example of a small State using trade income to build State capacity. 4.1 Colachel 1741 and the fall of the Dutch Since 1663 The Dutch East India Company's Malabar headquarters at Cochin (central Kerala), captured from the Portuguese 1741 Battle of Colachel: a landmark in the history of Kerala; Marthanda Varma 29-58's army crushed the Dutch East India Company Effect Terminal: it permanently ended Dutch political and military ambitions in Kerala, reducing them to mere merchants in Cochin 1759 Battle of Bedara (also called Battle of Chinsura): the British EIC defeated the Dutch in Bengal, crushing their remaining ambitions in India 1795 Final expulsion from South Asia by the British (Ceylon / Sri Lanka)

items.t: 5 · Travancore against Mysore and the EIC
items.x: Because the military declined after Marthanda Varma, the neighbours and then the Company moved in. Ask: which year did Malabar go? Under Rama Varma 58-98 Travancore became a centre of art and scholarship, but military strength declined. The consequences were quick: in 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 of Mysore annexed Malabar and Calicut. (Malabar was the heart of the spice trade: pepper, cardamom, ginger. Whoever controlled Malabar's ports controlled a significant share of Indian Ocean commerce, which is why both Mysore and the British were so interested.) After 1798 Travancore came steadily under British influence. Travancore's loss of independence 1805 Nair mutiny: troops unpaid Travancore seeks British help In return it signs the Subsidiary Alliance (1805): independence effectively ends Anger: heavy financial burden and interference in internal affairs; Velu Thampi Dalawa leads resistance 1809 revolt: against the British Resident, Kundara Proclamation calls the people to rise Suppressed: Velu Thampi, seeing no escape, takes his own life A light note: Shashi Tharoor is from the Nair community. Dalawa = Prime Minister and Chief of the Armed Forces; books may use Dewan for the PM of a State subordinated by the British = Head of all administration (revenue, civil, police, criminal justice), the military being with the British. Handout: one of the earliest organised resistance movements by an Indian ruler against the Subsidiary Alliance system; directly tested in UPSC.

items.t: 6 · Mysore: from Vijayanagar to Haider Ali 61-82
items.x: Because Vijayanagar broke at Talikota, Mysore became autonomous, and a strongman took it over. Ask: how did Haider Ali rise? Mysore was part of the Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646). The Empire's effective power was shattered at the Battle of Talikota (also called Rakkasa-Tangadi) in 1565, when a coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeated Vijayanagar. The dynasty lingered until 1646, but 1565 marks the operational end of Vijayanagar as a major power. After Vijayanagar's decline Mysore gradually became autonomous under the Wodeyar dynasty. Under Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar (1672-1704) it was militarily powerful and centrally governed. By 1761 the Wodeyars had been reduced to figureheads by a powerful and corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj. Haider Ali 61-82 ended that. He began as a junior military officer, his early career made possible partly because the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts. Capable, ambitious and strategic, in 1761 he overthrew NanjRaj and seized effective power, keeping the Wodeyar as a nominal head of State. Pattern at the 18th century: the king becomes a puppet as personality weakens. Recall the Peshwa and Chhatrapati (Chapter 4). 6.1 Haider Ali 61-82's military machine Haider Ali 61-82 took French assistance for military training, technology transfer and organisational reform. The army was now on a European model, organised into Risalas (regiments): Each Risala's commander was directly appointed by the King, ensuring personal loyalty upward. Each unit had a clear chain of command. Each was self-sufficient: its own weapons, transport and supplies (recall the Campoo system of Scindia, Chapter 4). Result: a fast, efficient military with regiments capable of independent action. He then spent roughly twenty years subjugating the Poligars (local chiefs and landlords who controlled land, the wealth of temples and had their own armed men, the real rulers of the countryside since the Vijayanagar era) and the Deshmukhs (revenue collectors who functioned like primary zamindars). Non-State power was systematically dismantled. 6.2 How Mysore funded this machine: Military Fiscalism Khalisa land expanded More revenue went directly to the State treasury Jagirdari minimised Maximised State income, reducing the nobles' independent economic power Direct collection Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries; State officials collected taxes and got salaries (far smaller than commissions) Detailed field surveys Assessed LR by soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access and past production trends; prevented over-assessment Investing in agriculture Canals repaired and built; cash crops promoted; sericulture introduced Boosted tax collection More peasant income meant a larger tax base; even enemies admitted Mysore's population was among the most prosperous These policies are called Military Fiscalism: the systematic generation of State wealth as a foundation for military power. (The handout's analogy: replacing a commission-based agent with a salaried employee; the State kept far more of the revenue.) Khalisa land = land whose revenue went directly to the State treasury. Jagirdari land = land whose revenue was assigned to nobles or commanders.

items.t: 7 · Tipu 82-99 Sultan (1782-99): innovations and why he still lost
items.x: Because his father built the machine, Tipu took it abroad and also overreached. Ask: which innovation answers Prelims 2001? Modern navy and trading company: a government-owned trading company modelled on the EIC, trading in sandalwood, sulphur, rice, pepper, silk and cardamom, with 30 trading centres inside and outside India, including Muscat, Oman. (Before the age of machines a "factory" meant a warehouse or trading depot, not a production facility; a trading settlement meant warehouses, homes, offices and sometimes a fort. Details in Chapter 8.) Iron-cased rocket artillery: developed by Haider Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99, 100% indigenous, range 2 km; the iron cylinder casings did not burst and could take high pressure compared with cardboard-cased rockets (fireworks), which existed for centuries in India and China. The British studied them closely: William Congreve's rockets, deployed in the early 19th century, drew directly from Tipu 82-99's designs. 1785: Tipu 82-99 formally declared independence from both the Wodeyars and the Mughal Emperor, and requested a sanad from the Khalifa recognising him as independent of Mughal authority. Modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, alongside new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. 7.1 Tipu 82-99 and Revolutionary France In the 1790s Tipu 82-99 sent an ambassador to France seeking military technology and a formal alliance against the British. Since 1789 the French Revolution had set France on a collision course with the monarchies of Europe, including Britain (the 23-year wars, 1792-1815). In 1798 Napoleon attacked Egypt and the Middle East, partly to disrupt British trade in the Arabian Sea. Tipu 82-99 exchanged communications with Napoleon and planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore (a symbol of the French Revolution), and joined the Jacobin Club. The alliance did not materialise into military support. The British were alarmed, and it became a reason for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War of 1799. Prelims 2001: who established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? (d) Tipu 82-99 Sultan. Embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, plus new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. Jacobin membership and the Tree of Liberty made him an ideological adversary to the British, not merely a military one. 7.2 Why Mysore lost Mysore's long-term ambition was to dominate all of South India and control its international trade (Vijayanagar 2.0). But constant warfare against neighbouring Indian powers and the EIC drained the State's resources faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish them. The ambition was real; the capacity, ultimately, was not enough. 1766: Haider Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar and Calicut, triggering the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), as the EIC feared losing coastal trade access through Malabar. Four Anglo-Mysore Wars: 1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799. The Fourth (1799) ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam; Mysore's power was broken. Conflict on Travancore: the handout (section 7) says Haider Ali 61-82 in 1766 "invaded Travancore and annexed Malabar and Calicut"; section 4 and the slide say he annexed Malabar and Calicut and "could not successfully invade Travancore." Use the slide: Malabar and Calicut annexed; Travancore not successfully invaded. Mysore's rise and fall Handout diagram 3: Mysore's rise and collapse 1761 Haider Ali 61-82 overthrows NanjRaj; the Wodeyar stays nominal French-assisted Risalas: self-sufficient regiments under commanders loyal to the King Military Fiscalism: Khalisa expanded, Deshmukhs removed, surveys, canals, sericulture: wealth for war Tipu 82-99: navy, government trading company, iron-cased rockets, 1785 independence, modern embassies, French link Overreach: ambition to dominate all South India (Vijayanagar 2.0); constant war drains the State faster than fiscalism refills it 1799: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu 82-99 dies at Seringapatam; Mysore's power broken Relation to the Mughals Co-opted by Akbar 56-05: Mansabdars with Vatan Jagirs; Hindu bloc (15%) Never part of the Mughal Empire Part of Vijayanagar, then autonomous under the Wodeyars Key figure Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 Marthanda Varma 29-58 Haider Ali 61-82, Tipu 82-99 Strength Astronomy, Jaipur, politics on own terms Trade monopoly, centralised State, Colachel 1741 Risalas, Military Fiscalism, rockets, trade company End Subordinate Alliances after 1803-05 Subsidiary Alliance 1805; revolt 1809 Four wars; Tipu 82-99 dies 1799

1336 Vijayanagar Empire begins (to 1646) 1565 Battle of Talikota: Deccan Sultanates defeat Vijayanagar ★ 1663 Dutch take Cochin from the Portuguese 1672 Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar (to 1704) makes Mysore powerful 1680 Marwar and Mewar revolt; it collapses ★ 1699 Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber (rule 1699-1743) 1724 Delhi Jantar Mantar built 1727 Jaipur founded ★ 1729 Marthanda Varma 29-58 begins (1729-58); Jai Singh 99-43 Subedar of Malwa (to 1737) 1733 Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi 1734 Hurda conference; Jaipur Jantar Mantar 1738 Treaty of Bhopal: Malwa passes to the Marathas 1741 Battle of Colachel: Travancore crushes the Dutch ★ 1751 Maratha raids on Rajputana begin 1759 Battle of Bedara (Chinsura): EIC defeats the Dutch in Bengal 1761 Haider Ali 61-82 overthrows NanjRaj ★ 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 annexes Malabar and Calicut 1767 First Anglo-Mysore War (to 1769) 1785 Tipu 82-99 declares independence; Khalifa sanad request 1795 Final Dutch expulsion from South Asia (Ceylon) 1798 Travancore comes under British influence 1799 Fourth Anglo-Mysore War: Tipu 82-99 dies at Seringapatam ★ 1805 Nair mutiny; Travancore signs Subsidiary Alliance ★ 1809 Velu Thampi revolt and Kundara Proclamation ★

Outside the middle path. These are the third class of regional States from Chapter 3: Already Autonomous States, where even when the Mughal was powerful he did not rule. The Rajputs were brought into the Mughal system but kept their homes, Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire, and Mysore grew out of the Vijayanagar world. Akbar's Rajput bargain. Rajputana had no single centre, only roughly 20 major clans (a multi-polar world). Defeating them all would be expensive and uncertain, so Akbar 56-05 co-opted the powerful chiefs as Mansabdars with Vatan Jagirs, and in return they accepted the Emperor, paid tribute and sent troops. They formed a Hindu bloc of about 15% of the Mansabdars, and Akbar helped them subdue smaller chiefs: a partial consolidation. 1680. Mewar under Raj Singh began expanding aggressively, and Aurangzeb 58-07 grew uneasy at one Rajput power dominating Rajputana. In 1680 a child came to the throne of Marwar, which lay astride the trade route from Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad, and Aurangzeb interfered. Marwar and Mewar revolted, but the other chiefs refused to join for fear of Mewar, and the revolt collapsed. Own terms, then new masters. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms, most prominently Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber. From 1751 the Marathas began regular raids for tribute but never fully conquered the region. After the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the EIC replaced them and signed Subordinate Alliances: the ruler keeps his throne but surrenders foreign policy and defence. Four hats. Sawai means 1.25 times more able than any contemporary ruler, a title from Aurangzeb 58-07. Jai Singh was a Mughal Mansabdar, state-builder, astronomer and town planner, Subedar of Malwa (1729-37) and Agra. His Hurda conference of 1734 collapsed, and the Treaty of Bhopal (1738) gave Malwa to the Marathas. He founded Jaipur in 1727 (Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, Vastu Shastra, grid, the first planned city of modern India), and was the last Indian ruler to perform the Ashvamedha and Vajapeya Yajnas. Stone and sky. Five Jantar Mantars stand at Delhi (1724), Jaipur (1734), Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi; Jaipur's is the largest, a UNESCO site (2010), and its Samrat Yantra measures time to 2 seconds. The old tables (Zij-i-Ulugh Begi, Siddhantic) had accumulated errors, so fresh observations gave the Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi (1733), dedicated to Muhammad Shah 19-48, and a delegation went to Portugal (1730). The Samrat, Jai Prakash and Ram Yantras were stone, not brass, for accuracy. Travancore builds on trade. Marthanda Varma 29-58 subjugated local chiefs, built a centralised State and a European-style military, and held a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast. The revenues went into the military, irrigation works and transport. In 1741 his army crushed the Dutch East India Company at Colachel, leaving them as mere merchants in Cochin; Bedara (1759) and the 1795 expulsion finished the Dutch. Malabar slips, the Company arrives. Under Rama Varma 58-98 Travancore became a centre of art and scholarship but its military declined. In 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar and Calicut, the heart of the spice trade. After 1798 British influence grew; in 1805 the Nair troops mutinied over unpaid salaries and Travancore signed a Subsidiary Alliance. In 1809 Velu Thampi Dalawa issued the Kundara Proclamation, and when it was suppressed he took his own life. From Vijayanagar to Haider Ali. Mysore was part of the Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646), which Deccan Sultanates shattered at Talikota in 1565. The Wodeyars then made Mysore autonomous, and Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar made it militarily powerful. By 1761 a corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj, had made the Wodeyars figureheads, and Haider Ali 61-82, a junior officer, overthrew him and kept the Wodeyar as nominal head. The machine and the money. With French help Haider Ali 61-82 built Risalas on a European model and spent roughly twenty years subjugating the Poligars and Deshmukhs. To pay for it Mysore practised Military Fiscalism: Khalisa land expanded, Jagirdari minimised, Deshmukhs removed so State officials collected directly, field surveys, canals, cash crops and sericulture. Tipu looks abroad. Tipu 82-99 ran a government-owned trading company with 30 centres including Muscat, and used indigenous iron-cased rockets (range 2 km) that inspired Congreve's. In 1785 he declared independence and asked the Khalifa for a sanad; he set up embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt (Prelims 2001). He also planted a Tree of Liberty and joined the Jacobin Club, but the French alliance gave no military support. Why Mysore lost. Mysore wanted to dominate all of South India and its trade (Vijayanagar 2.0), but constant war drained the State faster than Military Fiscalism could refill it. The 1766 annexation of Malabar and Calicut triggered the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), and four wars (1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799) ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam.

Prelims 2021 Where St Francis Xavier died Shangchuan Island (off China), 1552, not Goa. His body was brought to Goa (Basilica of Bom Jesus) 4.6 Religious intolerance Prelims 2022 The claim that the Dutch received land from the Gajapati dynasty Incorrect. The Gajapatis (15th-century Odisha) had declined long before the Dutch arrived 6. The Dutch VOC

Story so far: this is a Prelims chapter, and the teacher says UPSC asks three things. Ask: where, who, roughly when, and which came first? Very important chapter (Prelims). Learn tables T1, T2, T3 and T5 as place + who + rough year + order. The handout for Chapter 8 ends with an index for the next chapter (Carnatic Wars). That belongs to Chapter 9. Two Prelims traps are inside this chapter: St Francis Xavier died at Shangchuan Island, not Goa (Prelims 2021) and the Dutch did not get land from the Gajapati dynasty (Prelims 2022). Both are flagged where they occur. Lecture 10 covers Sections 1 to 4 of the handout (up to the decline of the Portuguese). Lecture 11 adds ink on the tables and on the Dutch, English, Danes, Surat and Roe sections. Lecture 12 (slides 1 to 55) covers Sections 12 to 19 and then the Chapter 8 PYQs (section 21). Sections 5 to 9 are mostly handout text.

items.t: 1 · Asia, the economic power of the world
items.x: Because Europe wanted what only Asia made, the whole chapter starts with goods and profit, not conquest. Ask: who carried the goods before the Europeans? Asia, the economic power of the world Three main attractions Indonesia (Java and Sumatra) for spices; India for textiles (plus Malabar for spices); China for silk and tea Routes China: land route (the Silk Route). India and Indonesia: a mix of land and sea, through the Middle East and the Arabian Sea Who controlled trade Arab traders dominated the Arabian Sea leg. Then Italian merchants of Genoa and Venice carried goods across the Mediterranean into Europe. Both earned enormous profits at each handoff Over Indonesia: "islands." Trade = two funnels (Mediterranean Sea and Arabian Sea) meeting at a point; the "new route" from Europe (Portugal) goes round the Cape of Good Hope (CoGH). Beside the Arabian Sea leg: "The empire of Arabs and Ottoman." Silk and spice trade routes Medieval European trade routes: Genoa and Venice Who gained: the teacher's board on "no political control" No political control (no colonialism or imperialism) = trade was good for India. [1757: colonialism began; Goa an exception.] Imp: Europeans came to purchase Indian FINISHED GOODS; there was competition among Europeans and between Arabs and Europeans. Good for: exports of India; forex for India; strength of Indian kingdoms; India getting a BETTER PRICE; Indian merchants; Indian artisans. Flow of goods from ryots to the coast If no political control: who gained Flow of goods on the teacher's board Ryots and artisans (villages) produce Indian merchant (city, town) collects and sells inside Indian territory: domestic trade Coastal area: goods meet Arabs / Europeans: international trade Europeans pay export duty (tax) to the Indian ruler OUT OF INDIA Europe was not wealthy; spices and the 800% profit Europe not wealthy; spices; 800% profit Europe was not wealthy Eastern goods were luxuries only the rich could afford. A common European could not afford Indian cotton or Chinese silk. The profit came from supplying Europe's wealthy classes, and Genoa and Venice guarded this position zealously Spices held a special place Until the 1600s European food was as spiced as Indian food. Spices preserved and made palatable the meat stored through winter (no industrial refrigerator: clove and pepper did the job) Profit was staggering Da Gama's 1498 cargo sold in Europe at 800% profit; by the 1600s, 1 kg of clove cost the equivalent of 1 kg of gold 6 months = average journey time from EU to India. Indonesia did not want anything from the EU (see the triangle trade). Trade: a buyer gives Gold or Silver to the seller, which depletes the forex reserves of a country. Side note: [Savings Bank A/c: 4%; 6-7%] (a comparison of rates of return; the handout does not explain it). The handout's aside: had the present been the 1650s, most of us would have been "spitting gold" as children, with the cloves our mothers tucked into rice that we picked out and pushed to the side of the plate. (memory hook for clove = gold) Forex versus domestic currency, and the triangle Forex versus domestic currency; triangle trade Used in the international market; a country buying from another country; import-export transactions Within the borders of a state, domestic transactions must be done (ideally) in domestic currency Till 1971: Gold. 1971 onwards: the Dollar replaced Gold  The EIC triangle trade (teacher's triangle) (1) Buy goods: the EIC buys goods (cloth) from India (2) Sell Indian goods: the EIC sells Indian goods to Indonesia (3) Sell goods: Indonesian goods (spices) come back to the EIC (4) The EIC sells Indonesian goods to the rest of Europe for profit Shift over time: as European incomes rose in the 17th and 18th centuries and spices became more widely available, Indian cotton textiles became the most sought-after commodity from the East. But in the beginning it was spice that started everything. Demand rose "as people came out of poverty / as the size of the middle class expanded" (incomes rose).

items.t: 2 · The Ottoman blockade (1453) and the Age of Discovery
items.x: Because the land road closed in 1453, Europe had to find a sea road. Ask: which two powers led, and which inventions made the voyage possible? 1453: interruption The Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople (today's Istanbul) and blockaded the traditional land trade routes connecting Europe to Asia. European traders needed a new way east Age of Discovery (16th century) This necessity became the engine of one of history's great turning points. European powers, led initially by Portugal and Spain, sent ships into the Atlantic searching for a direct sea route to the East What the era gave (1) Better use of the astrolabe (location) and the magnetic compass (direction) What the era gave (2) The system of latitudes and longitudes and the modern world map What the era gave (3) Geography as a formal discipline What the era gave (4) The invention of the Caravel: a ship able to sail at an angle against the wind Blockaded "effectively," not literally: the Ottomans demanded a share of the profits on trade, making trade unviable for Europeans. Caravel: sails at an angle to the wind. The Caravel and routes after the Age of Discovery

Because two powers claimed the same ocean, a Pope drew a line. Ask: which side of the line is Brazil, and why? Rivalry and mediator Portugal and Spain competed over who owned the new sea routes and lands. Pope Alexander VI mediated the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 The line An imaginary line in the Atlantic Ocean, about 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands East Lands EAST of the line went to Portugal West Lands WEST of the line went to Spain Why Brazil is Portuguese Brazil's eastern tip fell on the Portuguese side, so it became the only Portuguese colony in the Americas; the rest of the continent became Spanish Cape Verde islands, the Tordesillas reference point Tordesillas map: Spain west, Portugal east 1492: Columbus reached Central America (Spain went west). Portugal went east round the Cape of Good Hope to the "East Indies" = mid-east, India, China, Indonesia and South East Asia. Brazil = the only Portugal colony (in the Americas). The handout defines the East Indies as all lands east of the Cape of Good Hope. Tordesillas, 1494 Portugal and Spain compete over new sea routes and lands Pope Alexander VI mediates Line ~1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands East of the line: Portugal West of the line: Spain Brazil's eastern tip falls on the Portuguese side: the only Portuguese colony in the Americas

Because Tordesillas gave them the east, the Portuguese reached India first. Ask: how did a State, not a company, run the trade? 4.0 · Da Gama at Calicut (1498) Portuguese arrive: Da Gama at Calicut, 1498 Da Gama at Calicut (1498) Armed with the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) and backed by the Portuguese Crown, Vasco Da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode, Kerala) in 1498, sailing round the Cape of Good Hope, the southernmost point of Africa He traded and left Received permission to trade from the Zamorin of Calicut but faced heavy opposition from Arab traders. No factory or permanent settlement on this voyage The handout adds: the Cape was named "Cape of Good Hope" by Portugal's King John II, as it represented hope of finally finding a sea route to India. Board: "NOT COCHIN." Da Gama landed at Calicut (1498); the first permanent factory was at Cochin (1500). Zamorin = "King of Calicut kingdom." Vasco da Gama monument, Kappad Beach Why trade, not empire? (the teacher's board) Primary purpose of Europeans = Trade, not empire building. Empire building happened in the Americas (weak states); India had strong states (land powers, i.e. strong armies). Gains of empire building: resources from mining (gold, silver); greater trade profits (+); land revenue (LR) and other taxes. With political control, as government in any territory, you can export goods to the home country at a low price. Why South India was vulnerable (handout): when the Portuguese arrived, the Mughal Empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist in India. South India was divided between the Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, without a unified central naval power. This fragmentation let the Portuguese dominate trade and some territory in the 16th century. Character of the Portuguese approach: part commerce, part conquest, part coercion. West coast map with European settlement dates Learn the west coast north to south: Diu, Surat, Daman, Bombay, Goa, Mahe, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore. Also on the map: Broach/Bharuch. Calicut = small kingdom; Cochin = small kingdom on the northern border of Travancore. Map dates: Diu 1535 (P), Surat 1612 (British), Daman 1558 (P), Bassein 1533 (P), Bombay 1638 (B), Goa 1610 (P), Cannanore 1501 (P), Mahe 1725 (French), Calicut 1498 (P), Cochin 1500 (P; Dutch 1669), Colombo 1505 (P; Dutch 1656). These differ from the handout text (Goa 1610 on the map against 1510 in the text; Bombay 1638 against 1668). Use the handout text and tables (T1) for exam dates; use the map for locating places. 4.1 · Structure of trade: a State enterprise Unlike the private joint-stock companies the British and Dutch later set up, Portuguese trade was a State enterprise called the Estado da India, directly controlled by the Portuguese Crown through its official administration. The Portuguese government was the trader. Estado da India = "like a PSU / Govt." English EIC and Dutch VOC = private companies. French EIC = initially private; later taken over by the French Govt. Depot, Factory, Settlement In this period a "factory" did not mean a manufacturing unit. It was a trading post: warehouses for storing goods, offices for trade, homes for company employees, and often a fort for protection. The word comes from "factor," a merchant agent; the factory was where factors worked. Depot vs Factory vs Settlement Portuguese trade: a State enterprise (Estado da India) Depot = "think bus depot": "for going out of India" (goods waiting for the ship). Factory = trading post; function "Office." Settlement = multiple factories and warehouses; "collects LR (land revenue) and consumes LR." Don't confuse with "LEJ" here: a depot has no (L)egislative, (E)xecutive, (J)udicial jurisdiction; a settlement has sovereign territorial rights, L E J. Taxes can be charged only by the Ruler / Govt. Farman, Parwana, Nishan Farman, Parwana, Nishan The handout defines these when discussing the Danes: Farman (Imperial Decree by the Mughal Emperor), Nishan (Princely Decree by a Prince of the Royal Blood), Parwana (Provincial Decree or Order by a Provincial Governor). What UPSC Prelims asks about factories and forts 4.2 · Early factories, the first fort and the aggression (1498-1503) Because Da Gama left no factory, the next steps matter: 98, 00, 02, 03. Ask: where is the first permanent factory, and where the first fort? Early factories, Fort Manuel and aggression, 1498-1503 Early Portuguese moves, 1498 to 1503 1498: Da Gama at Calicut; trade permission from the Zamorin; no factory 1500, Cabral: first Portuguese factory, Calicut (permission of the Samoothiri/Zamorin); destroyed by Arab merchants (about 50 Portuguese killed) Cabral bombards Calicut (the Zamorin would not evict the Arabs) and sails south 1500: first PERMANENT factory, Cochin (protection of the Raja of Cochin) 1502, Da Gama's 2nd voyage: bombards Calicut, massacres innocent fishermen; aims: avenge Cabral, subdue the Zamorin, expel Arab rivals 1503: Fort Manuel, Cochin (Albuquerque 09-15, then a naval commander): first European fort in India Cochin = first capital of Portuguese India until the HQ shifted to Goa in 1530 Order along the coast: Zamorin, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore. (1st - 1498) is marked beside Da Gama's 2nd voyage. "Notice the nature of the Portuguese" (the violence). Albuquerque 09-15: 1504-15. [Goa annexed in 1510], then 1530 (HQ shift). The 2nd voyage disrupted the Arab-Venetian domination of the trade; Europe could now trade directly with India (Portugal a player in the Indian Ocean trade). Handout: the second voyage forcibly integrated Indian Ocean trade into the European mercantilist framework. Albuquerque 09-15 and Almeida 05-09 carry year codes in the handout to tell them apart; in 1503 Albuquerque was not yet Governor. 4.3 · Blue Water Policy and the Cartaz System (Almeida 05-09, 1505-09) Because India's kingdoms had armies and Portugal had ships, the Blue Water Policy followed. Ask: what was a Cartaz, and what did Diu 1509 settle? Blue Water Policy and Cartaz System (Almeida) 1st Governor Francisco de Almeida 05-09 was the 1st Governor of the Portuguese Estado da India (Viceroy in common usage, but the legal title was Governador) Blue Water Policy Emphasis on NAVAL supremacy rather than territorial conquest. Since India had powerful land-based States, the Portuguese chose to dominate oceans and maritime trade routes. The objective: a monopolistic trading regime without extensive territorial expansion Why South India was vulnerable No Mughal Empire yet (1526-1858); South India divided between Vijayanagara (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, with no unified central naval power Their approach Commerce, coercion in trade, and some (boxed) conquest: Goa 1510 Blue Water = oceans and seas. Focus on blue waters was expected: the primary goal of the Age of Discovery (16th c) was trade. Goa 1510 = the exception to the Blue Water policy. Almeida 05-09 = "CEO of the company in India"; from 1510+ the Governor = CEO + CM of Goa. WHY: a better navy; goal = oceanic trade; Indian armies were strong; the south was weak since Talikota 1565 (note partly unclear on the slide). Military: navy versus territorial army Territorial army was strong for Indian kingdoms (some also had a navy). Europe's navy was usually greater than the Indian powers' navy (where the Indian navy was good, e.g. Marathas and Travancore, books talk about it). Land-only states focus on the territorial army; coastal states on the territorial army plus a Navy, in budget and technology (Portugal, Dutch, French, British, Spain). Cartaz: a toll booth on the sea Cartaz = a toll booth on the sea: on land a car on a highway pays at a TOLL booth; in the oceans a ship on a trade route pays Cartaz fees. Cartaz System and the Battle of Diu, 1509 Diu 1509 = not a battle for Diu as a territory, but for the domination of the Arabian Sea. The coalition = "all stakeholders of the old routes": Arabs (Egypt), Indian (Gujarat, Zamorin), military ships from the Ottoman. 1502: Arabs and the Zamorin defeated in India; 1509: top player of the Arabian Sea. Only under Akbar 56-05 was the coastal area added to the Mughal state. Handout: the coalition's scale shows how seriously the Old World trading powers viewed the Portuguese threat; Venice's trade was being destroyed. 4.4 · Afonso de Albuquerque 09-15 (2nd Governor, 1509-15) Albuquerque: 2nd Governor, Goa, Luso-Indian policy Imprisonment and release Albuquerque 09-15 arrived (back in India in 1508) with the King's orders to take over leadership, but Almeida 05-09 did not trust him and arrested him. After the Battle of Diu (1509) a new fleet confirmed the King's orders; he was released and became the 2nd Governor Territorial transformation Turned the Portuguese presence from a purely trading enterprise into a territorial colonial State: annexed Goa (1510) from the Sultan of Bijapur, for better control of the Arabian Sea. Goa 1510 = a notable exception to the Blue Water Policy (a rare land conquest) Luso-Indian policy Encouraged intermarriage between Portuguese settlers and Indian women (mixed ancestry). A substantial share of the women were war widows or captured women, often forced without consent. Greater political stability Administrative and religious Integrated local elites into the administration, attempted to regulate practices such as Sati, and promoted Christianity as a tool of political control [Babur 26-30 not in India] in 1510. Luso-Indian policy: greater political stability via increased numbers (the Portuguese population grows), like the Mughal "more mansabdars" (co-opted). Elites: "co-opted." Two ways to power: (1) fight all, defeat all, remove all; (2) co-opt (e.g. Babur 26-30, Akbar 56-05, H...). Handout: textbooks often call him "Viceroy," but his legal title was Governador, the formal office ruling Portuguese territory in India. The same applies to Almeida 05-09. Religion as soft power Abolition of Sati: two possible intents Religion = Soft Power. Conversion reduces opposition to the political power of the (Christian) Portuguese and gives a narrative of brotherhood: success in social power (conversion) increases political power. Abolition of Sati (or any social reform) can have two intents: (1) Conversion, by weakening the people's bond with their religion (abolishing, making fun of, or targeting the legitimacy of rituals); (2) Noble intent: reform or women's empowerment. 4.5 · Peak under Nuno da Cunha 29-38 (Governor 1529-38) Capital shifted to Goa (1530) Nuno da Cunha 29-38 officially shifted the HQ (capital) from Cochin to Goa in 1530 (Goa annexed 1510). The Portuguese dominated the Indian Ocean trade for nearly a century Western-coast consolidation Acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535) from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, securing strategic ports and trade routes 1613: the EIC's Surat factory, after defeating the Portuguese, ends the "nearly a century" of Portuguese dominance. 4.6 · Religious intolerance: Inquisition and Francis Xavier Because conversion was a political tool, intolerance bred a backlash. Ask: where did Xavier die, and where was he buried? Most aggressive power Among the most religiously aggressive of all European powers in India; Jesuit missionary activity generated widespread resistance Slavery and forced conversions The administration was marked by the slave trade (including the Hughli settlement in Bengal) and forced conversions Goa Inquisition (1560-1812) A brutal colonial church court to investigate and punish heresy (beliefs contradicting church doctrine) and violently enforce Portuguese cultural and religious orthodoxy; deep socio-religious backlash St Francis Xavier In India from 1542, died 1552; spearheaded mass Catholic conversions in coastal India and laid the ideological groundwork for the Goa Inquisition Prelims trap (2021): St Francis Xavier did NOT die in Goa. He died on Shangchuan Island (off China) in 1552 while trying to enter mainland China. His body was later brought to Goa and is preserved in the Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa. The question tested the place of death, not of burial. Xavier "led" to the Goa Inquisition. Breast Ripper: Portuguese Inquisition torture device Slave trade from Africa to the Americas, 1650-1860 Teacher's add-on beside the Portuguese slave trade: about 10 to 15 million enslaved people were taken from western Africa to the Americas (1650-1860), mostly to the West Indies, Central America and South America. Map figures: Brazil 5 million; West Indies 4.5 million; U.S. 0.5 million; Lima and west South America 0.5 million; Europe 0.3 million; Central America 0.2 million. 4.7 · Portuguese contribution: New World crops The Portuguese introduced these New World crops that permanently transformed Indian agriculture and cuisine: tobacco, red chillies, papaya, pineapple, guava. Cocoa and rubber are also New World plants, but reached India only in the British period, not through the Portuguese. The Columbian Exchange (Britannica map) Columbian Exchange map. Americas to the Old World: potatoes, maize, sweet potatoes, pumpkins and squash, cassava, tomatoes, pineapples, avocados, beans, peanuts, cashews, cacao, vanilla, chili peppers, sunflowers, tobacco, quinine, turkeys. Old World to the Americas: pigs, horses, cattle, chickens, sheep, rats, honeybees, grains (wheat, rice, barley, oats, rye), bananas, sugarcane, olives, citrus fruits, coffee, peaches and pears, apples, carrots, grapes, lettuce, cabbage, onions, soybeans, weeds, diseases (bubonic plague, smallpox, typhus, malaria, yellow fever, diphtheria, measles, influenza, whooping cough). The Columbian Exchange: European exploration of the Americas in the 15th and 16th centuries brought the Old and New Worlds into contact. Plants, animals and microbes from Europe, Asia and Africa went to the Americas, and many others went from the Americas to Europe, Asia and Africa. 4.8 · Why did the Portuguese decline? i) Political Strong regional powers rose in Persia, Egypt and North India; especially the rise of the Marathas directly threatened the Portuguese (1739: Marathas defeated the Portuguese); teacher: Konkan coast: Marathas ii) Religious backlash Jesuit activity and the brutality of the Goa Inquisition (1560-1812) produced deep local resistance iii) Economic and administrative decay Corruption, inefficiency, decline in discipline, and employees' piracy and illicit trade (teacher: "personal trade") eroded the institutions iv) External competition The English and Dutch, with superior naval technology, joint-stock finance and more disciplined commercial organisation, displaced them v) Imperial overextension Focus diverted to Brazil (far more lucrative) plus lack of support from Lisbon (the Govt) starved the Estado da India Takeaway: the Portuguese set the stage for all later European expansion in India: colonial administration centred in Goa, armed maritime trade, and religious conversion as a tool of political control became patterns the British would study, adapt and eventually supersede. items.t: 5 · How the Dutch and English broke the Portuguese-Spanish monopoly
items.x: Because the Portuguese-Spanish hold had to break, the 1588 Armada defeat opened the sea. Ask: why did the Dutch and English go to Indonesia first? By the second half of the 16th century two new naval powers had emerged: Britain and the Dutch Republic (Netherlands). Both wanted to break the strict monopoly held by Spain and Portugal over European international trade and to achieve freedom of navigation in the oceans. 1588: the British Navy defeated the Spanish Armada ("Invincible Armada") in the Atlantic, severely weakening Spanish-Portuguese naval supremacy. By 1580 Portugal had entered a political union with Spain, so defeating Spain also opened trade routes Portugal had controlled. With the Armada defeated, British and Dutch ships could travel safely to Asia via the Cape of Good Hope. First priority for both: Indonesia (the spice trade of the East Indies). India came later, for a commercial reason: the people of the spice islands had little interest in English or Dutch goods but readily accepted Indian cotton textiles. To buy spices in Indonesia you first needed cloth from India. The handout's clarification: the Netherlands, Holland and "the Dutch Republic" all refer to the same country. "Dutch" is the adjective; "Holland" is technically a region within the Netherlands but is often used as a general name. The trilateral (triangle) trade: England → India → Indonesia → England. This is the commercial logic that shifted the EIC's focus from Indonesia to the Indian subcontinent. (Compare the triangle in section 1.) Why the monopoly had to be broken: "End the rival's monopoly (e.g. 1502, Da Gama in coastal Malabar) -> a multi-player domain -> establish your own monopoly (requires additional resources), i.e. the Battle of Diu 1509 -> Arabian Sea." Two challenges for the British and the Dutch in trading with the East Indies: (1) How to reach India, China, Indonesia: Spain and Portugal dominate the routes and oceans. (2) How to purchase goods from India: the Portuguese dominate the Indian coastline and the Indian international market. Table: "1588: end of monopoly over routes" (second row left empty). Who dominated world oceanic trade, by period. 1500s: Portugal vs Spain. 1600s: Dutch vs British. 1700s-1815: British vs French, "-> Britain = top naval power." 1870-1945: British + French vs Germany. 1945-91: US vs USSR. 2000s+: US vs China. Freedom of navigation "in oceans and of TRADE." Stressed: Armada ("Naval Fleet"), Atlantic, British and Dutch. Trilateral trade: "England" is replaced by "EIC," so the triangle is EIC -> India -> Indonesia -> EIC. The EIC's triangle: the EIC buys goods from India, sells Indian goods to Indonesia, and buys Indonesian goods. CHARTER = founding document, issued by the State (Monarchy or Parliament), granting special powers and rights to a company. State = an organisation with a territorial (T) motive (defend, annex), so it has a military and may wage war. A State rules a territory, so coins, currency and taxation and the L, E, J powers (legislative, executive, judicial; my reading) are with the State. Company = an organisation with a profit motive for its shareholders, and it requires property. Breaking the monopoly: Diu 1509 and two challenges Who dominated oceanic trade, by period EIC triangle; Charter, State versus Company

Because the VOC had capital and a Charter, it beat the Portuguese in the south. Ask: why is the VOC the first joint-stock company? 1602: the Dutch East India Company (VOC, Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie) was established by a Charter issued by the Dutch Parliament, by merging six smaller Dutch companies that had been competing for eastern trade. Takeaway (handout): the VOC was the world's first multinational company, and the first to issue publicly tradable stocks and shares on a formal exchange: the world's first joint-stock company. An ordinary person could become a part-owner by buying shares, without a say in management: the ancestor of the BSE, NSE, NYSE and the modern shareholder economy. Charter powers: the right to wage war, sign treaties, acquire territory, build forts and mint its own currency: powers that ordinarily belong to a State, showing how European powers saw companies as an extension of State power. The first Dutch expedition (1595) went to the East Indies (Indonesia), not India. Dutch settlements in India: Masulipatnam (Northern Sarkars) 1605 (first factory), Pulicat (Carnatic) 1610, Surat (Gujarat) 1616, Bimilipatam (Golconda) 1641, Karikal (near Pondicherry) 1645, Chinsura (Bengal) 1653, later Kasimbazar, Baranagore, Patna, Balasore, Nagapatnam, Agra, Cochin (where they captured the Portuguese fort in 1663). At its peak in 1669 the VOC was the richest private company in the world: 150 merchant vessels, 40 warships, an army of 10,000 soldiers, 50,000 employees; over its life 5,000 voyages from the Netherlands to the East Indies. 1799: bankrupt and dissolved; possessions taken over by the Dutch government as the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia), a Dutch colony until independence in 1945 after World War II. Prelims 2022 trap: the Gajapati dynasty and the Dutch. The claim that the Dutch received land grants from the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha is INCORRECT. The Gajapatis were a 15th-century dynasty centred in Odisha whose power had declined well before the Dutch arrived. Do not confuse later local rulers of the Odisha coast with the Gajapati dynasty itself. VOC stressed: the VOC's name, six smaller Dutch companies, the first publicly tradable stocks, Charter powers (war, treaties, territory, forts, own currency), Masulipatnam (1605), Chinsura (1653), capture of the Portuguese fort at Cochin in 1663. "CHARTER = founding document." "Much larger capital (Rs) for the company." "Dutch want to be a big buyer of eastern goods ... a big company => deep pockets, i.e. more buying power." To make the VOC big: (1) merger of six companies, (2) joint-stock company (raise Rs from the public). "[* Last time: 1st FACTORY 1500 by the Portuguese]" (the Portuguese Cochin factory, 1500, remains the first European factory). Beside Masulipatnam in Andhra: Northern Sarkars and "5 districts" (the sign between them is unclear; check your notebook). Why the VOC fell: "Bankrupt because of tough competition by the English EIC, plus war defeat during the French Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804) and the Napoleonic War (1804-15)." Table T2 ticks: 1602, 1605, 1653, 1663 and 1741. Colachel (1741): "South Travancore;" Marthanda Varma 29-58 "ended (Dutch) political ambitions" (the next words, about trade conflict, are unclear). 1759, Bedara/Chinsura: "British vs Dutch." Kew Letters: "[SYLLABUS X]" (not in the syllabus). The earlier ruler then wrote letters to different Dutch establishments across the world to give temporary control to the British."
