items.t: 7 · The English EIC and the Royal Charter of 1600
items.x: Because the EIC lived on a licence, its Charter shaped its fate. Ask: who gave the Charter, and what did it give? The English East India Company was formed on 31 December 1600: its founding document was a Royal Charter issued by Queen Elizabeth I 58-03. A Royal Charter is essentially a licence granted by the Monarch. If it was not renewed, the company would legally cease to exist. This shaped the EIC's relationship with the British State for the next two and a half centuries: its survival depended on the goodwill of whoever held power in Britain. The EIC was the 4th joint-stock company in England, formed by pooling money from 215 London merchants ("merchant adventurers") who wanted to challenge Dutch dominance in European trade with the East. The stated goal was trade with the East, not empire-building or colonialism. Britain or England? In 1600 it was England (not Britain) that granted the Charter. England and Scotland united in 1707 to create the Kingdom of Great Britain; in 1801 Ireland was added, creating the United Kingdom. Before 1707 "British" technically means English. What the Royal Charter of 1600 gave the EIC 1. A monopoly over England's trade with the East Indies for 15 years. 2. The right to carry gold (foreign exchange) out of England to purchase eastern goods. 3. Management by a body of private people: a Governor, a Deputy Governor and 24 members, which later evolved into the Board or Court of Directors. The handout's forex aside: for a State, forex is the currency that matters in international trade; domestic currency works only within a country's borders (like a household's internal reward system for children, valid only inside the home). Until 1971, Gold was forex, until the Dollar took over. (Same idea as the section 1 board.) EIC = joint-stock company; special rights and powers via a Charter (31 Dec 1600); Dutch competition. Stressed: founding document, Royal Charter, Elizabeth I 58-03. Why is the VOC (1602) called the first joint-stock company when the English EIC (1600) also was one? "Answer: in 1600 the EIC was not a proper joint-stock company. It operated on a per-VOYAGE system: before each journey to the East Indies the EIC gathered Rs from the public; brought and sold goods in Europe at a profit and shared all the profits; for the next journey, repeated. It is later that the EIC became a proper joint-stock company, i.e. one with permanent capital." A proper joint-stock company "does not usually give back all profits; it gives dividends": profit pie = Retain, Re-invest, assets, Dividends. What the Charter gave: correction. Stressed: England's trade, 15 years, right to carry gold, out of England, private people, Court (of Directors). "WRONG = monopoly over trade with India with the EIC. CORRECT = monopoly over England's (or British) trade with the East Indies, with the EIC." Grant 2 links to "forex is controlled by the State." Grant 3: "BoD/CoD = EIC's top decision-making body = not any government organisation." Why the VOC (1602) is called the first joint-stock company Proper joint-stock company: dividends

items.t: 8 · Charters until 1793: the EIC's changing legal character
items.x: Because the Charter was renewed again and again, the ladder tells the story of its power. Ask: which Charter made it a quasi-State? The EIC's legal existence depended on Charter renewal, and the Charters also tell the shift of power in Britain from the Monarch to Parliament. 1601-03, the first voyage (James Lancaster): the fleet sailed not to India but to Indonesia, consistent with the EIC's original priority of the spice trade. They reached Java and Sumatra, where they set up the very first EIC factory. On the way Lancaster's fleet looted a Portuguese ship, the Sao Tome, in the Strait of Malacca (a cargo of textiles and spices). William Dalrymple and others note that the EIC's first major profit came not from trade but from outright piracy. Shareholders got substantial dividends; the fleet returned in 1603. 1609, James I 03-25: the original 15-year monopoly became a perpetual monopoly. 1657, Cromwell 51-60's Charter: Context: Charles I 25-49 tried to levy taxes without Parliament's consent, which triggered the English Civil War (1642-51). The Parliamentarians (largely Protestant) defeated the Royalists; Charles I 25-49 was beheaded in 1649; England became a Republic under Oliver Cromwell 51-60 (the handout writes his years as 51-60). After Cromwell 51-60's death in 1658 his son briefly took over, but the experiment proved autocratic and unpopular. In 1660 the Monarchy was restored under Charles II 60-85. Cromwell 51-60 issued a new Charter in 1657, declaring the previous Royal Charter invalid, and reorganised the EIC into a permanent joint-stock company. Earlier, money was raised voyage by voyage (pool, voyage, profits, fund dissolved); from 1657 one continuous unified capital fund, giving a stable financial foundation. 1661, Charles II 60-85's Charter (after the Restoration) was arguably the most consequential legally: it turned the EIC from a commercial trading body into a quasi-State power. It gave the right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, and exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over settlements in India. (The right to mint its own money came in 1676.) From 1793 Parliament takes over: the British Parliament begins passing Acts for the renewal of the EIC's Charter, mirroring the democratisation of Britain (power moving from Crown to elected representatives). Indian constitutional history and British political history are inseparable threads. Takeaway (1661): the 1600 EIC was a merchant association with a trade monopoly; the 1661 EIC had the legal powers of a State within its territories. A trading company had, through successive Charters, accumulated the powers of a sovereign. Charter timeline context: "1642-51 English Civil War -> King Charles I 25-49 beheaded. 1651-60 Republic under Cromwell 51-60. 1660 Restoration of the Monarchy under King Charles II 60-85." 1657 box: "per-voyage system ended." 1793 box: "1st time the Charter was issued by P (Parliament)." Priority: 1600 "imp"; 1609 "not imp"; 1657 "not imp"; 1661 "imp" (strongest); 1676 "not imp"; 1793 "imp". Learn 1600, 1661 and 1793 first; 1609, 1657 and 1676 are lower priority. 1661 Charter: "semi" before quasi-State power (semi-State); civil and criminal jurisdiction = "[Ruling Power]." Stressed: forts, troops, war and peace, 1676 (mint), "legal powers of a State." How a company became an empire-builder. "Any company or citizen of a State must follow (a) the law of the home country and (b) the law of the foreign country where it operates. A State's powers: territorial jurisdiction (T) and subject jurisdiction." "The EIC built an empire in India, and the EIC = a Company (empire = 'Company State'). Legally possible because of the 1661 Charter, which gave the EIC State-like powers: war and peace, army, and ..." (the last word is unclear, possibly "over"). After 1793: "WORDS: 'Charter ACT' (ACT) -> tells me it is made by L (Legislature)": an Act of Parliament (not a monarch's charter) renews the EIC. Stressed: Acts, democratisation of Britain. EIC Charter evolution, 1600-1793 How a company became an empire-builder Handout Diagram 2 also marks 1688: Glorious Revolution, William III invited by Parliament (Fort William named after him). EIC's legal character: from merchants to a State within a State 1600 Elizabeth I 58-03: 15-year East Indies monopoly; 215 London merchants; 4th English joint-stock company 1609 James I 03-25: perpetual monopoly 1642-51 English Civil War; Charles I 25-49 beheaded 1649; Cromwell 51-60's Republic 1657 Cromwell 51-60: permanent joint-stock company (one continuous capital fund) 1660 Restoration; Charles II 60-85 on the throne 1661 Charles II 60-85: forts, troops, war and peace, civil and criminal jurisdiction (mint 1676) 1793 onwards: Parliament renews the Charters 8.7 · Why couldn't Indian merchants dominate the new trade routes? Because the Europeans had navies and Indian merchants did not, the new routes went to the Europeans. Ask: what three things did Indian merchants lack? (i) Naval power Indian merchants lacked armed ocean-going fleets to break European domination of the trade routes (ii) Capital VOC (1602) and EIC (1600, by 1657) had moved to permanent joint-stock structures and could pool the huge sums needed for bulk trade (iii) State backing The Mughal State after Akbar 56-05 did not focus on a navy and focused on territorial expansion, investing in the territorial army MILITARY NAVY = armed ocean-going fleets. After (ii): "[Gathering Rupee from masses.]" Stressed: did not focus on a navy; territorial army. Navy = Merchant + Military. "Modern capitalism absent in INDIA. [Why? The State = an organisation with a territorial (T) motive.]" Why Indian merchants could not dominate the new routes

Because the Danes came late and weak, they stayed on the margins. Ask: which post did they use as HQ, and which one became famous? Established 1616, out of envy of Dutch and English profits. Its Charter was issued by King Christian IV 88-48 of Denmark-Norway, granting a 12-year monopoly on trade between Denmark-Norway and the East Indies. The Danes were never in the same league: weaker finance, limited military capacity. The first Danish company ended around 1650; a second Danish EIC was set up in 1670 but wound down gradually, selling all its Indian mainland settlements to the British EIC by 1845. Danish settlements in India 1. 1620: Tranquebar (Tharangambadi), Tamil Nadu: first factory; first fort: Fort Dansborg; official administrative HQ of Danish India from 1620 until 1845. 2. 1624: Pondicherry (brief): under Roland Crappe; a short-lived factory, abandoned for lack of resources, long before the French arrived. 3. 1625: Masulipatnam (Andhra Pradesh); Pipli and Balasore (Odisha). 4. 1755: Serampore (Srirampur / Frederiksnagore), Hooghly district, Bengal: a parwana from Nawab Alivardi Khan 40-56. Tranquebar remained the HQ, but Serampore became the most commercially successful and culturally significant Danish post. Colonial powers in Tranquebar, Serampore and the Nicobar Islands (the Nicobars were sold separately to the British in 1868; today part of India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands UT). 1799-1800: Serampore Mission Press, associated with Baptist missionaries including William Carey: translated the Bible into Indian vernacular languages, ran schools, and made an immense contribution to early printing and education in Bengal. Their architectural legacy at Tranquebar and Serampore and their missionary work (not forced conversions) are the most visible Danish traces. [Denmark], [not Dutch / Holland / Netherlands]. Order of arrival: "Portugal (1500); EIC 1600; VOC 1602; Danish 1616." Stressed: 1616, the Charter of Christian IV 88-48, the 12-year monopoly, 1620-1845 (HQ), Tranquebar (Tharangambadi), Tamil Nadu, Serampore (Frederiksnagore), most commercially successful and culturally significant, William Carey and the Baptist missionaries, early printing and education, "not forced conversions," Serampore Mission Press (1799-1800). Note under Tranquebar: "[* From 1717, ... 17-27, Bengal = successor State]" (one word is unclear; the reign code 17-27 is as written). Table T3 ticks: 1616, 1620, 1755, 1799-1800, and "12-year monopoly." The Danish East India Company

items.t: 10 · How the EIC broke Portuguese dominance: Hawkins, Swally and Surat
items.x: Because the EIC wanted Surat, it first had to beat Portugal. Ask: what is the difference between 1612 and 1613? 1608: the EIC decided to set up a factory at Surat, then the most important port on India's west coast and firmly within Portuguese-dominated territory. It sent Captain William Hawkins to the court of Jahangir 05-27. Jahangir 05-27 first gave Hawkins a Mansab (rank of 400) and a Jagir, but Hawkins was ultimately expelled from the Mughal court due to persistent Portuguese pressure. The lesson: Portugal had to be defeated militarily before the EIC could establish itself on the west coast. 1612, Battle of Swally (Suvali): Captain Thomas Best led a small EIC armed trading fleet to a decisive victory over the Portuguese. The Mughal State had its own reason to welcome this: Mughal ships traded in the Arabian Sea but were perpetually vulnerable to Portuguese piracy, a source of humiliation for a great land power. Impressed by English sea capability, Jahangir 05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613, giving the EIC the legal right to set up a permanent factory at Surat. 1612 versus 1613: 1612 = the Battle of Swally (military victory) and the local Mughal governor's temporary permission/parwana; 1613 = the legally permanent establishment, when Jahangir 05-27 ratified the local agreement with an imperial farman. Breaking Portuguese dominance on the west coast 1608: EIC wants a Surat factory; sends Captain William Hawkins to Jahangir 05-27 Hawkins gets a Mansab (400) and Jagir but is expelled under Portuguese pressure Lesson: defeat Portugal militarily first 1612: Battle of Swally: Captain Thomas Best defeats the Portuguese Mughals welcome it: their ships were vulnerable to Portuguese piracy 1613: Jahangir 05-27's Royal Farman: permanent factory at Surat Jahangir 05-27; "imp" over the 1612 Battle of Swally. Stressed: 1612, Captain Thomas Best, Suvali, rank 400, 1613 Royal Farman. Factory = "Warehouse" + "Home, offices for staff." Lesson box: "Began attacking Mughal ships" (the Portuguese). "ESTADO DA INDIA vs EIC," "FOR TRADE [not the territory (T) of Surat]": the EIC wanted trade rights, not Surat as territory. Why the EIC's army stayed small until Bengal. "A company = an organisation with a PROFIT motive (of the shareholder), e.g. the EIC had an army of about 500-800 men. Spending Rupees on an army would go against that goal. If the army came from its own Rupee, it would be small, to meet the core interests of trade." "1757: free Rupee of Bengal" -> "Large army," "i.e. why Plassey 1757, imp." "Britain's national interest = the EIC's interest." Roe = "a government person working for the EIC's benefit." (1) Britain's trade with the East Indies = the EIC's trade; (2) the EIC has a monopoly over Britain's trade with the East Indies; (3) via the EIC, Britain can dominate WORLD trade. Lesson (imp): "Put companies to act as agents of the State in geopolitics, e.g. the USA's use of companies for implementing sanctions on Russia." How the EIC broke Portuguese dominance: Swally and Surat Why the EIC's army stayed small until Bengal Britain's national interest and the EIC

items.t: 11 · The Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)
items.x: Because one factory was not enough, England sent an ambassador. Ask: what did Roe's Farman of 1618 give? England wanted liberal trading rights across the entire Mughal Empire, so King James I 03-25 sent Thomas Roe as formal ambassador to Jahangir 05-27's court. Roe arrived at Surat in 1615 and stayed until 1619. Jahangir 05-27 refused a formal treaty between equals (a trading company was no sovereign equal). Through sustained diplomacy and personal rapport Roe got a series of privileges and a Royal Farman (1618) allowing the EIC to set up factories throughout the Mughal Empire with liberal trading rights: lower customs duties and ease of doing business. 1616-19: new factories at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach (Bharuch). With Surat they formed the Surat Presidency (1618): the EIC's first administrative Presidency in India, coordinating English trade on the west coast until the later shift to Bombay (1687). Portuguese enraged; naval conflicts continued. 1631-32: Shahjahan 27-58 ordered his Bengal governor Qasim Khan to defeat the Portuguese and eject them from Hugli, because they were misusing their trade privileges with piracy and the slave trade from their Bengal base. Roe's account, The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to the Court of the Great Mogul, is one of the most important primary sources on the Mughal Empire of this period (court administration, wealth, politics, daily life). Roe = "Ambassador, i.e. British Resident in Jahangir 05-27's court" (starred). Stressed: title of Roe's memoir, Royal Farman (1618), right to establish factories across the Empire plus lower duties and ease of business ("= LIBERAL TRADING RIGHTS"), Surat Presidency (1618). Under Surat Presidency: "HQ (e.g. Cochin 1505-1530, HQ of Portugal; Tranquebar, HQ of the Danes 1620)": a Presidency was the EIC's regional HQ. Shah Jahan 27-58; stressed: Hugli action (1631-32) and slave trade.

Because a royal wedding settled a debt of trade and war, Bombay changed hands. Ask: what did England get, and what did it promise? The treaty, signed at Whitehall, London, marked the marriage of King Charles II 60-85 of England and Princess Catherine of Braganza of Portugal. 1. Portugal paid a dowry of 500,000 pounds in cash. 2. England received Bombay and Tangier (Morocco). 3. Trade and military cooperation, with England agreeing to protect Portugal's remaining possessions. Result: a continued Portuguese presence in Goa, Daman and Diu under English protection, lasting until 1961, when independent India took over these territories militarily, after a people's movement. 1668: the British Crown transferred Bombay to the EIC at an annual rent of 10 pounds: the start of Bombay's journey from a Portuguese dowry to the commercial capital of British India. "Restoration of MONARCHY 1660." Stressed: Whitehall, King Charles II 60-85, Princess Catherine of Braganza, dowry and 500,000 pounds in cash, Bombay and Tangier (in Morocco), military cooperation, protect Portugal's remaining possessions. Term 3: "[Goa, Daman and Diu]." Two ways to deal with a rival. (1) "End your rival 100% (destroy)": "Power = 100." (2) (V2) "Thrash the rival and lessen his power permanently; huge anxiety in the rival about survival; instead of (1), convert the rival into your puppet or a junior permanent friend," "non-threatening, never big enough." Result: "Power = 100 + 90" (second number partly unclear). It follows the 1661 treaty; the board does not name the countries. Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661 Two ways to deal with a rival Who beat whom, and why the EIC won. Portuguese beaten by "British vs Portuguese" and "Dutch vs Portuguese"; the two winners meet in "British vs Dutch" -> "By 1650s." MAJOR presence: British in South Asia; Dutch in South East Asia (Indonesia). Minor presence: Dutch in South Asia; British in South East Asia (Singapore, Malaya); this matches the Treaty of Breda terms in section 13. Result: "For INTERNATIONAL TRADE [not T] of India, i.e. who will BUY Indian GOODS." "PRIMARY purpose of empire = TRADE." The rivals fought over who would buy Indian goods, not over land (same idea as the Surat board: "for trade, not the territory of Surat"). Who beat whom: the EIC wins the competition for trade

items.t: 13 · The Dutch: rise, dominance and fall in Asia
items.x: Because the Dutch chased the Portuguese out, they became the richest company, then lost it. Ask: what are the dates that mark the fall? 1623, the Amboyna Massacre: the Dutch killed English traders in the spice islands, a brutal episode that ended English ambitions in Indonesia; the Dutch had effectively removed both the English and the Portuguese from Indonesia. 1658: the Dutch removed the Portuguese from Ceylon. Anglo-Dutch wars 1654-67, settled in the Treaty of Breda (1667): (1) the British leave Indonesia to the Dutch; (2) the Dutch leave the English alone in India; (3) both keep minor presences in each other's primary domains. Cochin: captured from the Portuguese in 1663, held as HQ of Dutch Malabar (not the overall HQ). Dutch zone = Java, Sumatra (Indonesia). 1623 row: "INDONESIAN TRADE" (Amboyna Massacre). Stressed: Indonesia, Anglo-Dutch rivalry, "settled" (Treaty of Breda), Pulicat 1610-1690, Nagapattinam 1690-1795, 1759 Bedara (Chinsura). Marthanda Varma 29-58. Dutch rise, dominance and fall Coast zones (V-shaped peninsula). West side, top to bottom: Gujarat, Konkan, Malabar. East side: Bengal (top), Coromandel. The next board places the Dutch locations on this map. Coast zones: Gujarat, Konkan, Malabar, Bengal, Coromandel Stressed: Masulipatnam, "First Dutch factory," Geldria, "First Dutch fort," "Main HQ" (Pulicat) and Nagapattinam, "Main HQ." The main HQ moved from Pulicat to Nagapattinam (1690). Fort Gustavus (Chinsura) is a lesser mark. Map notes: "N. Sarkars (5 districts) (Andhra)" (number partly legible); "Golconda (1687), annexation by A 58-07" (Aurangzeb 58-07 annexed Golconda in 1687); "1336-1646" (Vijayanagara, whose permission gave Pulicat). Reading: Masulipatnam lay in the Northern Sarkars, under Golconda; Pulicat lay in the Vijayanagara zone. Dutch locations and HQ roles Exam trap: Cochin was NOT the overall Dutch HQ; it was only the Dutch Malabar regional HQ. Overall main HQ: Pulicat (1610-90), then Nagapattinam (1690-1795). (The handout dates Chinsura's Fort Gustavus as 1655-1795, while section 6 and Table T2 list the Chinsura factory as 1653.) HQ example: "e.g. Amazon India: # India HQ: Bengaluru; # Regional HQ: Gurgaon (North)." A company has one main HQ and smaller regional HQs. Pulicat, then Nagapattinam = main HQ (like Bengaluru); Cochin = only the Malabar regional HQ (like Gurgaon for the north). Hence "Cochin = overall HQ" is the trap. Two decisive military defeats 1. 1741, Battle of Colachel: Marthanda Varma 29-58 of Travancore decisively defeated the Dutch, ending their political power in Kerala (see Chapter 7); the Dutch kept Fort Cochin till 1795. 2. 1759, Battle of Bedara (also Battle of Chinsura): the British EIC defeated the Dutch in Bengal, crushing their remaining ambitions in India. Kerala order: Cochin at the top, Travancore along the side, Colachel at the bottom. Marthanda Varma 29-58 of Travancore beat the Dutch at Colachel in the south, while the Dutch still held Cochin in the north of Kerala.

Because France overthrew the Dutch government at home, the Dutch colonies fell to Britain. Ask: what were the Kew Letters? 1795, during the French Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804) leading into the Napoleonic Wars (1804-15): the French army invaded the Netherlands, overthrew the Dutch government and set up a puppet State, the Batavian Republic, controlled by France. Britain declared all Dutch overseas colonies enemy territory. The exiled Dutch leader Prince William V 51-95 had fled to London and issued the "Kew Letters": orders telling Dutch colonial governors to hand over their territories to the British "for safekeeping," so France could not seize them. The British used this as their legal basis to take over the remaining Dutch posts. By 1795 the British occupied the remaining Dutch settlements in South Asia: Cochin (Kerala), Chinsura (Bengal), Pulicat and Tuticorin (Coromandel), and the coastal regions of Ceylon (Trincomalee and Colombo). Kew Letters: "[SYLLABUS X]" = not in the syllabus. Read this section for the story of the Dutch fall, not as an exam topic. "NOT imp FROM exam - FOR UNDERSTANDING" (same call as "SYLLABUS X"): read the Kew Letters for the story, do not memorise them. Inserted "over" so the line reads "hand over their territories." "Kew = place near London."

items.t: 15 · Why Ceylon did not become part of British India: the Crown Colony
items.x: Because Ceylon was too important for a company to run, Britain took it directly. Ask: who ruled India, and who ruled Ceylon? 1795-96: the British captured the Dutch areas of Ceylon and gave administration to the EIC, through the Madras Presidency. Treaty of Amiens, 1802: a peace treaty in Europe between Britain and France along with its Dutch ally, the Batavian Republic. The Dutch formally and permanently ceded the coastal regions of Ceylon to Britain. The British government decided Ceylon was too strategically important to be run by a trading company: it removed the EIC's administration entirely and declared Ceylon a British Crown Colony, ruled directly by an appointed British Governor, separate from the EIC's Indian empire. Takeaway: India was a colony ruled by the EIC (a commercial entity with State-like powers); Ceylon was a Crown Colony where the British State itself governed directly. "Crown Colony": "(not imp) BUT concept," "imp: Meaning." The Ceylon story is not important for the exam, but the meaning of "Crown Colony" is. British Colonies, RULED BY -> "EIC" = Company's Colony; "Br State" = Crown Colony. "Rule = Doing L, E, J on a T": to rule is to do the Legislative, Executive and Judicial work on a Territory (LEJ as in section 4.1). Stressed: "ruled directly," "by the British State." Why Ceylon became a Crown Colony

Because an EIC trade base had to be run, it became a Presidency. Ask: what does a Presidency become after annexations? A Presidency was a regional headquarters of EIC trade. A settlement got Presidency status when it had grown large enough with significant warehouses, offices, residential buildings and a fort. Initially small coastal towns; as the EIC annexed surrounding territories the towns grew into cities and the Presidencies expanded into provinces of British India (governed directly by the British). The Presidencies were named after the major forts built within them. Presidency = HQ, and the years. "Surat 1613 Factory" -> "Br: 1st Presidency = Surat (1618)"; then "shift to Bombay: 1687." "Bombay with EIC: since 1668"; "Bombay = Presidency = HQ = 1687" (Western HQ), "20 yrs" between 1668 and 1687. "Calcutta settlement 1690" -> "Presidency = 1699" (East India). "Madraspatnam (village)" -> "Presidency 1652" (South). Order of the Presidencies: Surat 1618, Madras 1652, Bombay 1687, Calcutta 1699 (west, south, west again after the shift, east). The board gives 1652 (London order; 1653 implemented) and 1699 (1699/1700 in the handout). Learn both years as in the handout. Presidency = HQ: Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta Factory to province. Stressed: factory, fort. Growth: "To Settlement" -> Settlement = Town + Rule/Admin (POLITICAL). "In Beginning, Presidency = BIG TOWN or CITY"; "Madras, Bombay, Calcutta = TRADE HQs (REGIONAL HQs)." Trade HQ -> province of British India through "annexations of Large T" (T = territory). Province box: Bombay  From factory to province The word "investment." For an industrialist it has the usual meaning ("this you know"). For a merchant or trader it means (1) purchased GOODS (PRIMARY) and (2) associated godowns etc. So the EIC's "investment" in India = primarily money spent on buying Indian goods (primary purpose = trade). The word "investment": industrialist versus merchant

items.t: 17 · How each of the three Presidencies came to be
items.x: Because each Presidency grew from a different coastal base, each has its own story. Ask: which came first, and which was named after which fort? 17.1 · Madras Presidency (from 1652/1653) The EIC's first factory in India was a temporary one at Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) in the Northern Sarkars (Andhra Pradesh) in 1611. (Northern Sarkars = the northern coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh, outside Mughal direct control.) 1639: the EIC, led by Francis Day, purchased land at the village of Madraspatanam from Hindu Nayakas (provincial governors of the Vijayanagara Empire, 1336-1646) and built Fort St George (1639-44): the first fort built by the EIC in India and the anchor of the first permanent settlement. 1690: the EIC purchased a fort at Cuddalore (south of Madras) from the Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram 89-00 and named it Fort Saint David. Its history: partly built by the Dutch from 1608; construction halted due to Portuguese pressure on the Vijayanagara Empire; a Hindu merchant eventually completed it. In 1677 Shivaji 74-80 conquered the nearby Jinji fort and region including Cuddalore before it passed to the EIC. The Madras Presidency was formally established as the Presidency of Fort St George in 1652, on the orders of the Court of Directors in London; because of the ship travel time, it was implemented in India in 1653. (Both dates appear in sources: the London order versus the on-ground implementation.) "FACTORY = warehouses + home and office + MAY be a [FORT]" (home and office hard to read): a factory may or may not have a fort. Stressed: 1st EIC factory, temporary, Masulipatnam, 1611, 1639, Madraspatanam, Hindu Nayakas (Vijayanagara governors), Fort St George (1639-1644), Presidency of Fort St George (1652). Vijayanagara: "1336-1646." Fort St David (1690): "After death of Sambhaji 80-89, Rajaram 89-00 left Svarajya, shifted to e.g. Jinji in Carnatic" (the Chhatrapati who sold the fort had moved to Jinji in the Carnatic). "Layered build" (Dutch, Portuguese, Hindu merchant history of the fort): "not imp." "2 FORTS in Madras Presidency: Madras and Cuddalore." How the Madras and Bombay Presidencies came to be Fort St David at Cuddalore 17.2 · Bombay Presidency (1687) From 1613 to 1687 Surat was the EIC's main trade centre on the west coast. The shift happened because of the growing power of the Marathas in Gujarat, making Surat increasingly risky. Bombay, a cluster of seven islands, offered a more defensible location. Charles II 60-85 received Bombay in 1661 as part of the Portuguese dowry and transferred it to the EIC in 1668 at 10 pounds per annum. The Bombay Presidency was established in 1687, replacing Surat as the western HQ. Bombay Castle (Casa da Orta) was originally built by the Portuguese and expanded by the EIC through the 18th century. Bombay: "1st permanent FACTORY = Surat 1613"; "PRESIDENCY 1618" beside "replacing Surat" (last digit slightly unclear; it matches the Surat Presidency of 1618 in Table T5). "1534-1661: Portugal" (Portugal held Bombay from the 1534 Bassein deal to the 1661 dowry). "FORT" = "Bombay Castle (Casa Da Orta)": originally Portuguese. Stressed: Charles II 60-85, Bombay in 1661, dowry, 1668 at 10 pounds per annum rent, Bombay Presidency, in 1687. 17.3 · Calcutta Presidency (from 1699/1700) The EIC's Bengal presence began with a factory at Hugli in 1651, permitted by a nishan from Shah Shuja, the Mughal governor of Bengal and son of Shahjahan 27-58. 1690: the EIC founded a settlement at the village of Sutanuti: the Calcutta establishment. The Calcutta Presidency was formally established in 1699/1700 as the Presidency of Fort William, with its own Governor. Through the 18th century the EIC developed Calcutta Port; Calcutta came to account for 60% of all EIC trade from India. 1800: Fort William College was established by Wellesley 98-05 for training EIC civil servants. 1870: the Calcutta Port Act created the Calcutta Port Commissioners and Port Trust, the first formal legal authority governing the port. Covered later (in the chapter on the Battle of Plassey): Child's War, the 1690 pardon and 1691 Farman, and the 1717 Farman. Calcutta: "27-58" after Shah Jahan. "[3 villages: Sutanuti, Gobindapur, Kolikata]." "famous for Textile" -> "Bengal = 60%": "if EIC bought Rs 100 goods from India, then bought Rs 60 goods from Bengal." Fort William College: "Training of EIC officers"; Wellesley 98-05's years are written out in full. "Presidency = Regional HQ of EIC TRADE"; "Governor = Regional Manager." After "annexations": "Presidency = Province"; "Governor = Ruler / CM / Subadar / Nazim." Before annexations the Governor only managed trade in a region; after, he ruled a province like a Mughal Subadar or Nazim (or a modern Chief Minister). Calcutta Presidency: villages, trade share, Governor's role

items.t: 18 · Chronological reference: EIC factories and permissions (1600-1717)
items.x: Because UPSC likes chronology, the factory dates sit in one table. Ask: what is the first factory in east India, and the first in Bengal? Table T5 stressed: "1613" above "farman" in the Surat row; "First factory in east India" (Balasore and Hariharpur, 1633); "first factory in Bengal" (Hugli, 1651); "Child's War" marked "LATER." Kasimbazar 1658: "Famous on Land [middle word hard to read] TRADING HUB and warehouses of MANY merchants." "LATER" also under "Magna Carta of the Company" (1717). The Child's War and the 1717 farman are taught later (the handout agrees, see 17.3). On the first English factory in India: the handout's text says Masulipatnam (1611) was the first, temporary, factory; the first permanent one was Surat (1613). (Factory map and Table T5 agree.)

items.t: 19 · The French in India and the story of Pondicherry
items.x: Because the French came last, they had Pondicherry rather than a long run. Ask: who was the real founder of French power in India? The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was founded in 1664 by Jean-Baptiste Colbert under King Louis XIV 43-15; great-grandfather of Louis XVI, overthrown in the French Revolution of 1789). It started as a private company but was later nationalised, making it in today's terms a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU). Bengal: Chandernagore. Pondicherry = MAJOR HQ 1674. The French main HQ = Pondicherry (1674); their Bengal base = Chandernagore. Stressed: the 1664 company, King Louis XIV 43-15, "a private company," "later nationalised," Pondicherry (acquired 1674, Sultan of Bijapur), Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General). French East India Company and Pondicherry French settlements in India (handout list) 1. 1668, Surat: first factory, on a farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667. 2. 1669, Masulipatnam: farman from the Sultan of Golconda (1518-1687). 3. 1673, Chandarnagar: permission from Shaista Khan 64-88, Mughal governor of Bengal; financial crunch delayed it: a settlement only in 1690-92. 4. 1674, Pondicherry: acquired from Sikandar Adil Shah (1672-86) of Bijapur and his local governor Sher Khan Lodi. Developed as a city by Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General 1701-06, earlier Governor), the real founder of French power in India: centralised French administration with Pondicherry as capital (1701) and built Fort Louis. 5. 1723, Yanam: permission from Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, also called Asaf Jah I. 6. 1724, Mahe (Malabar coast): acquired from the Nair ruler Vazhunnavar in 1721; trade settlement built 1724-25 after overcoming a rebellion; named after Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46, who came with a fleet from Mauritius. 7. 1739, Karaikal: granted by Pratap Singh 39-63, Maratha ruler of Tanjore, as a reward for French help in a succession dispute. (The Thanjavur Maratha dynasty was founded not by Shivaji 74-80 directly but by his half-brother Venkoji (Ekoji) in 1674, defeating the Nayaka rulers of Madurai.) 8. 1721, Mauritius a French colony, but proper control only by 1735 under Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46 (Governor 1735-46). He came again with a fleet in 1746 and helped Dupleix 42-54 capture Madras in the 1st Carnatic War (1746-48). 9. 1949: a referendum in Chandernagore merged it into India; the rest stayed under French control until 1954. French acquisitions stressed: Surat, "farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667," Chandarnagar, Pondicherry (1674 = the key row), Sultan of Bijapur, "capital 1701," "Fort Louis built," Yanam, "Mahe on the Malabar coast," Karaikal. Mauritius (1721/1735): low priority (no reason is written). "East" for Puducherry, Karaikal and Yanam; Mahe is the odd one out (West coast, Arabian Sea). Pondicherry's occupation history (mnemonic PDa-FDu-BFBF to India). Pondicherry is synonymous with the French, but they were not the first there: Portuguese (16th century) → Danes (briefly in 1624) → French (1674) → Dutch (captured briefly in 1693) → British. The English captured Pondicherry in 1761 and restored it to the French via the Treaty of Paris (1763); the British captured it again (for example in 1793) before finally returning it to the French in 1814. It remained French until transferred to India in 1954.

items.t: 20 · Who came when: a master comparison
items.x: Because two orders of arrival exist, read the question's wording. Ask: founding order or first-factory order? Two orders for "who came first." Company founding: Portugal 1500 -> EIC 1600 -> Dutch 1602 -> Danes 1616 -> French (the EIC's 1600 Charter precedes the VOC's 1602). First factory in India (Tables T1 to T5): Portuguese 1498-1500, Dutch 1605, English 1611, Danish 1620, French 1664/1668. Use the first-factory order unless the question says "company founded"; the French are last either way.

"1750s"; Gunpowder 48-49 PYQ 11, Prelims 2019 Plants domesticated in the New World (a) tobacco, cocoa, rubber "American"; T on (a); F on the rest 50-52 PYQ 12, Prelims 2021 St Francis Xavier (c) 1 and 3 Statement 2 circled, "False"; tick on (c) 53-55 PYQ 14, Prelims 2022 Gajapati / Albuquerque 09-15 / Madras (b) 2 and 3 only "Gajapati" circled; (b) ticked; (a), (c) crossed PYQ 1 · Prelims 1995: Hughly piracy Answer: (a) the Portuguese. They misused their trade privileges from their Bengal base: piracy and the slave trade. This is why Shah Jahan ordered his Bengal governor Qasim Khan to eject them from Hugli in 1631-32 (see section 11). Wrong options: (b) the French at Chandernagore were trading, not pirate dens; (c) the Danish bases (Tranquebar, Serampore) were lawful; (d) the British entered Bengal at Hugli in 1651, after the piracy was suppressed. Answer slide: "Carnatic" over Tranquebar and "Bengal" over Serampore: the two Danish bases are in different regions. PYQ 2 · Prelims 2003: European entry, the NOT-correct statement Answer: (a) is the wrong statement: Albuquerque 09-15 captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510, not 1499. Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 and merely traded. (b), (c), (d) are correct: Masulipatnam (1611); Balasore and Hariharpur, Orissa (1633); Dupleix 42-54 took Madras in 1746 (1st Carnatic War). Question: a true statement (T) after option (d); the question asks for the false one. Answer slide: "09-K" after "1498 and merely traded" (hard to read; probably Albuquerque 09-15's reign). PYQ 3 · Prelims 2005: modern Kochi Answer: (b). The Dutch captured Cochin from the Portuguese in 1663 and held it as their key South-India base. Why the others are wrong: (a) Cochin was under British rule 1795-1947, not Dutch till independence; (c) the order is reversed (Portuguese 1500 first, Dutch 1663 second); (d) Cochin did become part of British India after 1795. (a) "1795 x presence" (no Dutch presence after 1795): F. (b) "built forts," "1663": T. (c) F. (d) F. The Kew Letters (1795, section 14) are why the British, not the Dutch, held Cochin after 1795. PYQ 4 · Prelims 2006: the 1613 factory Answer: (d) Surat. Jahangir 05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613 giving the right to a permanent factory at Surat, after the Battle of Swally (1612). Wrong options: (a) Bangalore came only after the Anglo-Mysore Wars; (b) Madras was acquired in 1639; (c) Masulipatnam had a temporary factory (1611), but the 1613 farman was for Surat. This is the 1612 versus 1613 point in section 10. PYQ 5 · Prelims 2007: the first British fort Answer: (b) Fort St George. Madras, built 1639-44: the first fort built by the EIC in India. Wrong options: (a) Fort William (Calcutta) was built 1696-1700; (c) Fort St David (Cuddalore) was purchased in 1690, not built; (d) Fort St Angelo (Kannur) was built by the Portuguese in 1505. Trap word "constructed" (St David was bought, not built). Side labels: (a) CAL, (b) MAD, (c) MAD, (d) "?"; answer (b). Order of the EIC's main centres: "S, M, B, C" = SURAT, MADRAS, Bo (Bombay), CALCUTTA (matches the Presidency board in section 16). PYQ 5, Prelims 2007: first British fort, board solution PYQ 6 · Prelims 2007: the last Europeans to come Answer: (c) the French. The French EIC was founded in 1664 and set up its first Indian factory at Surat in 1668, the latest of the four. Chronology on the answer slide: Portuguese 1498 -> Dutch 1605 -> English 1611 -> Danish 1620 -> French 1664/1668. Answer: French. Board chain: "PORTUGAL (1500) -> EIC (1600) -> DUTCH 1602 -> Danes 1616 -> Fr" (left unfinished). See the alert at the end of section 20 on the two orders (company founding versus first factory). PYQ 6, Prelims 2007: last Europeans to come PYQ 7 · Prelims 2010: Pondicherry Question: (1) the first European power to occupy it was the Portuguese; (2) the second was the French; (3) the English never occupied it. Options: (a) Only 1; (b) 2 and 3; (c) Only 3; (d) 1, 2 and 3. Answer slide: (a) Only 1. Sequence: Portuguese -> Danes (1624) -> French (1674) -> Dutch (1693) -> English (1761/1793/1814) -> India (1954). Statement 2 is wrong (the second were the Danes; the French were fourth). Statement 3 is wrong (the English captured it several times and restored it by treaty). Board: T for (1), F for (2), T for (3); board picks (d); note: "WORD "occupied" = VERY TEMPORARY OCCUPATION ALSO." A small "L" under (a) is unclear. Board versus answer slide. The board ticks (d) and marks statement 3 true; the answer slide gives (a) Only 1, and the handout's occupation sequence (section 19: Portuguese, Danes, French, Dutch, British) makes statements 2 and 3 false. "Occupied" counts even a very temporary occupation, so the English did occupy it (1761, 1793). Use (a) Only 1; the board tick on (d) is unresolved, check the class recording. PYQ 8 · Prelims 2012: what the English introduced Answer: (d) None of these. (1) Soil-and-crop revenue assessment existed in medieval India (Sher Shah 40-45, Todar Mal); (2) mobile cannons came with Babur 26-30 at Panipat (1526); (3) tobacco and red chillies were introduced by the Portuguese. Trap words: "introduced" ("1st Time" above) and "English": what the English brought for the first time. F marked on the first two statements. Cannons -> "Babur 26-30"; tobacco and red chillies -> "PORTUGAL." Answer (d). PYQ 9 and PYQ 13 · Prelims 2015 and its repeat in Prelims 2021 Question (both years): in the first quarter of the 17th century, EIC factories were at (1) Broach, (2) Chicacole, (3) Trichinopoly. Answer: (a) Only 1. Only Broach (Bharuch) had an EIC factory then: the Roe-era (1616-19) factories were Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach, all in the Mughal Empire. Chicacole (Srikakulam) and Trichinopoly had none; early South-India trade centred on Masulipatnam. "1600-1625"; "ENGLISH" -> "factories"; Broach is the one. Map notes: Gujarat "SURAT 1613," east coast "Masulipatnam 1611" and "MADRAS 1639"; also BROACH and SURAT. By 1625 the EIC was only on the Gujarat side and at Masulipatnam; Madras came in 1639, after the quarter ended. PYQ 13 (Prelims 2021) = same question, same answer: UPSC repeated it. PYQ 9, Prelims 2015: first-quarter 17th-century factories PYQ 15 · Prelims 2023: who surrendered Diu Answer: (c) Bahadur Shah. Under Nuno da Cunha 29-38 the Portuguese acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535) from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat. Wrong options: (a) Ahmad Shah (1411-42, as printed on the slide) did not surrender Diu; (b) Mahmud Begarha resisted the Portuguese; (d) Muhammad Shah 19-48 was a later, minor ruler. "BOMBAY 1534" beside the answer: Bombay passed to the Portuguese with the 1534 Bassein deal (the "1534-1661: Portugal" note in section 17.2). PYQ 16 · Prelims 2025: Portuguese fruits Answer: (c) All the three. The Portuguese brought tobacco, red chillies, papaya, pineapple and guava from the New World (section 4.7). PYQ 10 · Prelims 2018: Bengal exports Answer: (d) cotton, silk, saltpetre and opium: the textile, saltpetre and opium mix that fuelled EIC profits before and after Plassey. "1750s" with "L Textiles." (a) F, "raw": India exported finished goods, not raw cotton. Beside (a): "Before IR (1750-1850)," "FG of India" (reads like "finished goods of India"). On (d): cotton, saltpetre and opium stressed; under saltpetre "L Gunpowder." Answer (d). PYQ 11 · Prelims 2019: New-World plants Answer: (a) tobacco, cocoa and rubber. The Portuguese brought tobacco, red chillies, papaya, pineapple and guava to India; the fuller list is in the Geography notes. "American" above the question; T on (a), F on (b), (c), (d). Cotton in (b) and (c): "Bengal" -> cotton is the Old-World (Bengal) crop, so it cannot be an American plant. Do not mix two lists. This PYQ asks which plants were domesticated in the New World (tobacco, cocoa, rubber qualify). Section 4.7 lists what the Portuguese brought to India: cocoa and rubber are not on that list (they reached India in the British period). The handout and this slide agree; the questions are different. PYQ 12 · Prelims 2021: St Francis Xavier Answer: (c) 1 and 3. Xavier was a founding member of the Jesuit Order (1, true) and the Feast of St Francis Xavier is celebrated in Goa each year (3, true). Statement 2 is the trap: he did not die in Goa; he died on Shangchuan Island (off China) in 1552. His remains were brought to Goa (Basilica of Bom Jesus), but death is not burial. Slide 52 calls it a signature trap: UPSC tested death versus burial. Statement (2) marked "False." F beside (a), (b), (d); (c) is the answer (same point as section 4.6). PYQ 14 · Prelims 2022: Gajapati, Albuquerque 09-15, Madras Question: (1) Dutch factories on lands granted by the Gajapati; (2) Albuquerque 09-15 captured Goa; (3) English factory at Madras leased from Vijayanagara. Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only. Statement 2: Albuquerque 09-15 took Goa from Bijapur in 1510. Statement 3: the EIC got Madraspatanam in 1639 from the Hindu Nayakas (Vijayanagara governors). Statement 1 is the trap: the Dutch did not get land from the Gajapati dynasty, a 15th-century Odisha dynasty that had declined well before the Dutch came (1605 onwards). Do not confuse later Odisha-coast rulers with the Gajapatis themselves. "Gajapati" flagged. "09-15" above Albuquerque 09-15, T, "1510"; "1639" (for Madras); "1336-1646" under Vijayanagara. (a) and (c) rejected, (b) correct. The question says Madras was "leased" from Vijayanagara; the handout says the EIC purchased the land from the Hindu Nayakas (section 17.1). Why Asia? Asia was the economic power of the world: Indonesia gave spices, India textiles, China silk and tea. Arabs and the merchants of Genoa and Venice carried them to a Europe that was not wealthy, and each handoff made huge profit. Da Gama's 1498 cargo sold at 800% profit, and in the 1600s a kilogram of clove cost the equivalent of a kilogram of gold. The road closes. In 1453 the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople and (the teacher corrects it to 'effectively') blockaded the land routes between Europe and Asia. Necessity drove the Age of Discovery, led first by Portugal and Spain. The era gave the astrolabe, the magnetic compass, latitudes and longitudes, geography as a discipline and the caravel, a ship that could sail at an angle against the wind. The line. Pope Alexander VI mediated the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. An imaginary line in the Atlantic, about 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands, gave lands to the east to Portugal and lands to the west to Spain. Brazil's eastern tip fell on the Portuguese side, so Brazil became the only Portuguese colony in the Americas. Calicut and Cochin. Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 and got permission to trade from the Zamorin, but faced Arab opposition and left without a factory. In 1500 Cabral set up the first factory at Calicut, which Arab merchants destroyed, and then the first permanent factory at Cochin under the Raja of Cochin's protection. In 1502 Da Gama bombarded Calicut, and in 1503 Albuquerque built Fort Manuel at Cochin, the first European fort in India. Blue water, then Goa. Almeida 05-09, the first Governor, chose naval supremacy over territory (the Blue Water Policy) and forced every non-Portuguese ship to buy a Cartaz. In 1509 he beat a coalition of Gujarat, Mamluk Egypt and the Zamorin at Diu. Albuquerque 09-15 took Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510, a rare land conquest, and Nuno da Cunha 29-38 moved the HQ to Goa in 1530 and acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535). The fall of the Portuguese. The Goa Inquisition (1560-1812) and forced conversions bred resistance. St Francis Xavier, who spearheaded conversions, died on Shangchuan Island in 1552, not Goa. The causes of decline were political (the Marathas), religious backlash, corruption and personal trade, the English and Dutch, and overextension with Brazil as the priority. The companies arrive. After the English beat the Spanish Armada in 1588, British and Dutch ships could sail to Asia. The VOC was founded in 1602 by merging six companies and was the first joint-stock company with tradable shares. It reached Masulipatnam in 1605 and took Cochin in 1663. It was beaten at Colachel in 1741 by Marthanda Varma 29-58 and at Bedara in 1759, lost its posts through the Kew Letters of 1795 and was dissolved in 1799. A licence that became power. The English EIC began on 31 December 1600 under a Royal Charter of Elizabeth I 58-03, a 15-year monopoly pooled from 215 London merchants. James I 03-25 made it perpetual in 1609 and Cromwell 51-60 made it a permanent joint-stock company in 1657. The 1661 Charter of Charles II 60-85 gave it forts, troops, war and peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction, so it became a quasi-State. Surat, Swally and Roe. In 1608 Hawkins went to Jahangir 05-27's court for a Surat factory but was expelled under Portuguese pressure. The lesson was to defeat Portugal first, and in 1612 Thomas Best won the Battle of Swally. Jahangir then issued a Royal Farman in 1613 for a permanent factory at Surat, and Thomas Roe (1615-19) won the Farman of 1618 for liberal trading rights across the Mughal Empire. Presidencies. In 1661 Catherine of Braganza's dowry gave England Bombay and Tangier and 500,000 pounds, and in 1668 the Crown gave Bombay to the EIC for 10 pounds a year. The EIC's first Presidency was Surat (1618), then Madras (1652/1653), Bombay (1687) and Calcutta (1699/1700), each named after its fort. Each began as a trade HQ and grew into a province of British India. Danes, French and the order. The Danes (company 1616, Tranquebar 1620, Serampore 1755) sold their mainland posts to Britain by 1845. The French company (1664) opened at Surat in 1668 and acquired Pondicherry in 1674, which Francois Martin 01-06 made the capital in 1701. Pondicherry's occupiers ran Portuguese, Danes, French, Dutch, English, then India in 1954, so the order of arrival is a favourite Prelims test.

Prelims 1995 Which pair is correctly matched? (a) Battle of Buxar: Mir Jafar 57-60 vs Clive 57-67; (b) Battle of Wandiwash: French vs East India Company; (c) Battle of Chilianwala: Dalhousie 48-56 vs Marathas; (d) Battle of Kharda: Nizam vs East India Company (b). Wandiwash (1760) = French vs the EIC, the decisive battle of the 3rd Carnatic War; the British under Eyre Coote beat the French under Count de Lally. Traps: Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim 60-63 (with Awadh and Shah Alam II 60-06), not Mir Jafar 57-60; Chilianwala (1849) = EIC under Dalhousie 48-56 vs the Sikhs (2nd Anglo-Sikh War); Kharda (1795) = Nizam vs the Marathas Section 6.2 Prelims 1996 Who were the first European to initiate the policy of taking part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories? (a) Clive 57-67 (b) Dupleix 42-54 (c) Albuquerque 09-15 (d) Warren Hastings 73-85 (b) Dupleix 42-54. He invented the model of empire building in the 2nd Carnatic War (backing Muzaffar Jung 50-51 and Chanda Sahib 49-52). Clive 57-67 and Warren Hastings 73-85 used and refined the model; Albuquerque 09-15 belongs to an earlier era of direct conquest (Goa 1510) Section 5.1 Mains (teacher's board) "Model of empire building (in India) by trading companies was founded by the French and implemented by the British. Analyse." Founded by French = the 2nd Carnatic War (Dupleix 42-54's four steps). Implemented by British = future topics (Plassey, Subsidiary Alliance) Section 5.1 (the model) and Section 6.5

Story so far: one question runs through the chapter: how did a company that existed for profit end up ruling India? Ask: what do the teacher's board codes CW, (T), AWoS and MJ stand for? This chapter asks one question: how did a company that existed for profit end up ruling India? Sections 1 and 2 give the frame (the Charter of 1661, wars for trade versus wars for territory, the Anglo-Mughal War). Sections 3 to 6 are the three Carnatic Wars. The teacher's short codes on the board: CW = Carnatic War (1st, 2nd, 3rd); (T) = territory; AWoS = Austrian War of Succession; Fr eic and Eng eic = the French and English East India Companies; MJ = Muzaffar Jung 50-51; Hyd = Hyderabad. The handout for Chapter 9 ends with an index for the next chapter (Plassey and Buxar). That belongs to Chapter 10. Carnatic Wars in the EIC's conquest of India The Carnatic Wars (1746-63) come first; then the EIC takes the Indian States one by one: Bengal by the Battle of Plassey 1757, Awadh by the Battle of Buxar 1764, Mysore by 4 Anglo-Mysore wars [1766-69, 80-84, 90-92, 99], the Marathas by 3 Anglo-Maratha wars [1775-82, 1803-05, 1817-19], the Sikhs by 2 Anglo-Sikh wars [1844, 1849]. The three classes of regional States (Chapter 3): SS (Successor States): Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad; Rebel States: Marathas, Jats, Sikhs, Farukhabad, Rohilkhand; AAs (Already Autonomous States): Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore. Legend: Diplomacy, then Domination. Apparently Hyderabad, Jats, Farukhabad and Rohilkhand, Rajputs and Travancore came under the EIC through diplomacy, while Bengal, Awadh, Marathas, Sikhs and Mysore are exactly the war list. Board versus notebook. (1) The board writes the Anglo-Mysore wars as [1766-69, 80-84, 90-92, 99]; Chapter 7 gives the first war as 1767-69. (2) Anglo-Sikh wars [1844, 1849] are as on the board; detailed dates come in a later chapter.

items.t: 1 · How did a trading company become a State?
items.x: Chapter 1 of the story: a profit-making firm with State-like powers. Because the 1661 Charter gave forts, troops and courts, the Company could wage war. Ask: under which two conditions did wars for territory happen? How did a trading company become a State? Companies exist to make profit for their shareholders. The EIC was no different. But what the EIC became in India went far beyond a trading enterprise. It became a Company State that, by 1857, controlled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. This chapter deals with Empire Building by the EIC. By 1857 the EIC "RULED" (not merely "controlled") 63% of the territory and 78% of the population. India = British India (63% of territory, 78% of population) + 565 Princely States (37% of territory, 22% of population). 1.1 The 1661 Charter 1661 Charter (Charles II 60-85) The right to build forts  The right to command troops  The right to make war and peace  The right to exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements in India 1676 The right to mint its own money Forts, troops, war, peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction are State-like powers in the hands of a company. The same charter is in the EIC charters table of Chapter 8. 1.2 Two kinds of wars: for trade and for territory The wars the EIC fought in India fall into two broad categories. Wars for trade: fought to protect or expand trade. Wars for territory: fought for empire building. These were different in nature and in motivation. The EIC was not formed for territory (T). Its goal was trade with the East Indies (not just India). Its wars were of two kinds. (1) For trade: defensive, to protect present trade (the Carnatic Wars), or offensive, to expand trade (the Battle of Suvali 1612, Chapter 8). (2) For territory: only in two situations, given below. The Carnatic Wars were wars for trade, though they ended up laying the base for territory. Wars for territory happened under two specific conditions. 1. When the Governor or Governor-General in India was personally ambitious: an empire builder by temperament. Britain was far away. Communication was slow. These men had enough operational freedom to pursue wars that London might not have formally approved. 2. At times the EIC Army put pressure for wars. Any army has a structural interest in war: war brings a bigger defence budget, prestige, promotions and political relevance to the military. Why the EIC fought wars: for trade and for territory The EIC Army was no different. Robert Clive 57-67 Governor of Bengal Presidency, in two stints: 1757-60 and 1765-67 Richard Wellesley 98-05 1798-1805 Francis Hastings 13-23 1813-23 Dalhousie 48-56 1848-56 The EIC Army's self-reinforcing war cycle (condition 2) Overhype threats: the army routinely overhyped threats to the borders; war brings budget, prestige, promotions Pressure to expand: overhyped threats create pressure for territorial expansion New borders: expansion always creates new borders New threats: new borders bring new neighbours, and so new threats, fictional or real Back to the start: the new threats are overhyped again; a self-reinforcing cycle The army's vested interest in wars = three kinds of power: economic power (bigger defence budget, "Def BD"), political power (larger army), social power. Handout parallel: the Pakistan Army today has eaten Pakistan from within by putting its vested interests above the national interest, while the Indian Army has consistently done the opposite.

items.t: 2 · Wars for trade: the Anglo-Mughal War (1686-90)
items.x: Because Aurangzeb 58-07's wars and Bengal's customs disputes hurt trade, the Company picked a fight and lost. Ask: why did Aurangzeb 58-07 not expel it? Wars for trade: Anglo-Mughal War 1686-90 The Anglo-Mughal War of 1686-90 was fought in Bengal and the Arabian Sea. It was the first significant military clash between the EIC and an Indian power. It is also called Child's War, after two men: Josiah Child: Chairman of the Court of Directors of the EIC in London. John Child: Governor of Bombay and the "General" of all EIC forces in India. The reasons were two-fold: Aurangzeb 58-07's constant warfare was disrupting EIC trade (problems in sourcing goods from the hinterland). Ongoing disputes with the Nawab of Bengal over bribes and heavy customs duties levied on the EIC. Child's War, 1686 to 1691 The EIC seizes Hugli It escalates: attacks Mughal ships in the Arabian Sea Aurangzeb 58-07's military crushes the EIC in both Bombay and Bengal By 1690 the Company surrenders February 1690: Aurangzeb 58-07 pardons the EIC in return for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation 1691 Farman: old privileges restored and duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year "1651: the 1st EIC factory in Bengal, in Hughli." That is why the EIC seizes Hugli in this war. 2.1 Why did Aurangzeb 58-07 not abolish the Company and expel the British? Because the EIC was economically useful. Its trade brought forex/gold into India, and Aurangzeb 58-07 needed them for war. With Aurangzeb 58-07's own constant warfare disrupting domestic trade, the EIC's export business was, ironically, even more valuable to the Indian economy. Indian bankers earned interest by lending money to the Company for the purchase of goods. Indian merchants, artisans and ryots all participated in and benefited from this trade ecosystem. 2.2 The 1691 Farman The 1691 Farman was technically a Parwana, because it was issued by the Subahdar of Bengal, not an imperial farman. (For Farman, Parwana and Nishan see Chapter 8.) It was issued under Aurangzeb 58-07's approval. It restored the EIC's old privileges and gave it the right to duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum. Anglo-Mughal War: the 1691 Farman and duty-free trade The Company had been defeated militarily, yet it got this privilege, because of the benefits of European trade with India. Why give duty-free trade to a defeated company? Ryots and artisans sell to the Indian merchant; the Indian merchant sells to the EIC; Indian bankers give loans to the EIC. Everyone in the chain earns. The money the EIC saves on duty is used to buy more Indian goods = more exports. Aside: "TODAY we don't tax exports" (a State gains more from exports than from taxing them).

items.t: 3 · The Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63): why the French, and why three wars
items.x: Because the rival in India was now France, three wars followed. Ask: which two wars were global spillovers, and which one was factionalism? The three Carnatic Wars: frame and results To understand why conquest by the EIC began in Bengal, one must first understand what was happening in South India, and why the French were there. Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54 was the Governor-General of the French EIC from 1742-54. Dupleix 42-54 had personal ambitions of empire building and of dominating the international trade of South India. He would become the template for everything that followed. By 1740, French EIC trade was roughly half the value of British EIC trade. Reason for all three wars: international trade of India, "who will dominate purchase of goods." Main players: British EIC versus French EIC. 1st and 3rd wars = a result or part of some international war (Britain versus France). 2nd war = factionalism in Hyderabad and Carnatic, "R vs R" (rival against rival), the French behind one rival and the British behind the other. Royal armies (British and French) took part in the 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 ONLY. Result: 3/2 = 1.5 each: the French won the 1st war and the 1st phase of the 2nd; the British won the 2nd phase of the 2nd and the 3rd. After 1756-63 the French were limited to Chandernagore and Pondicherry (the five posts are in section 6.4). 3.1 Reasons for the Carnatic Wars The EIC-French contest in India had two overlapping reasons. 1. European rivalry. Two global wars spilled into India. As the two nations fought, their respective companies also entered into hostilities in India. 2. Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad contributed to the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54). The strategy was simple: put your chosen candidates in power to gain strategic influence. 1st Carnatic War 1746-48 The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) spilled into India Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746) Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) French 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54 Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad (factionalism) Ambur (1749); Clive 57-67's Arcot (1751) Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) Phase 1: French. Phase 2: British 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 The Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) spilled into India Battle of Wandiwash (1760) Treaty of Paris (1763) British "42-54, 1742-54: not in 3CW 1756-63." Dupleix 42-54 was recalled in 1754, so he took no part in the 3rd Carnatic War ("Dupleix 42-54 not here", section 6.2). "How a company can build an empire: the first to show it was the French, Dupleix 42-54." The handout heading prints "Carnatic Wars (17456-48, 49-54, 56-63)": a typing slip for 1746-48.

items.t: 4 · The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) and the Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)
items.x: Because the Austrian war reached India, Dupleix 42-54 took Madras and met the Nawab's cavalry. Ask: who sent the 10,000 cavalry, and what did Adyar prove? 4.1 Reason The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) was the Indian chapter of the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48). In that war Britain and France, along with their respective allies, fought each other across Europe, America and India, each wanting its preferred candidate on the Austrian throne. 4.2 Events during the war From Madras to Adyar, 1746 Dupleix 42-54 captures the EIC's Fort St George in Madras; the EIC is defeated The Nawab of Carnatic, Anwaruddin 44-49, intervenes: he expected the French to hand over the fort to the Nawab as promised Dupleix 42-54 refuses Anwaruddin 44-49 sends an army of 10,000 cavalry Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746): about 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers completely destroy the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry The battle was fought on the north bank of the River Adyar. The French force was roughly 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers. It completely destroyed the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. What happened here changed the nature of power in India. Who sent the 10,000 cavalry? The slide's wording ("Dupleix 42-54 refused and sent 10,000 cavalry") misleads. The handout is clear: Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 sent the 10,000 cavalry against the French. The handout's Diagram 1 (section 7) adds a name the text does not give: "La Bourdonnais 35-46 takes Fort St George, Madras." The handout text and the slide credit the capture to Dupleix 42-54 (the Governor-General). La Bourdonnais 35-46 and Madras: Chapter 8. 4.3 Why the French won: three advantages of European warfare The French won due to three critical advantages that would define European military superiority in India across all the wars to come. 1. Superior artillery Light, mobile European cannon that could be repositioned rapidly on the battlefield, against which massed cavalry had no answer (link: like the small bronze cannons of Babur 26-30, spelt Babar 26-30 in this handout) 2. Tactical discipline European-trained infantry fought in coordinated formations, including infantry squares that could hold ground against cavalry charges from any direction 3. Regular cash salaries Unlike Indian armies, where soldiers were often not paid regularly, European-trained sepoys received regular wages. This created a professional, reliable fighting force with no incentive to desert between campaigns French-trained sepoys: the infantry square Key phrases on the three-advantages slide: "light, mobile European cannon", "Babur 26-30", "formations", "infantry squares" and "small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery." "Infantry Square": the men face outward on every side, so a cavalry charge from any direction meets a wall of muskets. Adyar slide, "Turning Point": "Indian kings wanted European help in modernising their military." Takeaway (Adyar 1746): not just a military victory. It was proven conclusively for the first time that a small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery could crush a vastly larger traditional Indian army. The psychological impact was enormous: Europeans gained the confidence to interfere directly in Indian political disputes, which Dupleix 42-54 proceeded to do. Indian royal elites also wanted to use the military service of the Europeans in their internal and external disputes. Wagner Group analogy (handout). The Wagner Group is a company which sells military service to the Russian State. In a way the French were now the Wagner Group of India: a company whose army could be hired by Indian rulers. Developed in section 5.1. 4.4 Consequence: the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) However, in North America, which was more strategically important to France, Britain had won. So in the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748), which ended the War of the Austrian Succession, both sides agreed to return each other's possessions in America and India. Madras went back to the EIC. For Dupleix 42-54 this was deeply frustrating: his victories in India were traded away at a negotiating table in Europe. Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle 1748 But he was not done. His next opportunity came almost immediately, in the form of succession disputes: one in Hyderabad, one in Carnatic. "The French won in India BUT the British won in the Americas." Main interests: Britain = India; France = the Americas, especially North and Central America. So France gave back Madras to recover what it had lost in America. Results: (1) no change in territory; (2) European infantry far greater than Indian cavalry (the Adyar lesson stays though Madras is returned); (3) "Dupleix 42-54 KAT gaya" (Hindi: he was cut out, left empty-handed).

items.t: 5 · The 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54): how Dupleix 42-54 invented the blueprint for empire in India
items.x: Because Aix-La-Chapelle returned Madras, Dupleix 42-54 found new quarrels. Ask: which four claimants, and which side moved first? 5.0 The succession disputes that triggered the war In Carnatic: Anwaruddin 44-49 had been appointed Nawab of Carnatic by the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1744. (The slide adds: he then became autonomous of the Nizam.) On his death a succession dispute began between: his son Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah (Md Ali 52-95), and; Chanda Sahib 49-52, the son-in-law of the earlier Nawab Dost Ali Khan 32-40 (1732-40). In Hyderabad: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 died in 1748. The rivals for the throne were: his son Nasir Jung 48-50, and; his grandson Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (the slide adds: grandson from a daughter). 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54: factionalism and rival claimants Dupleix 42-54 backed Muzaffar Jung 50-51 in Hyderabad and Chanda Sahib 49-52 in Carnatic. He wanted his chosen candidates in power for economic/trade and political influence. An anxious EIC backed the opposing sides: Nasir Jung 48-50 in Hyderabad and Md Ali 52-95 in Carnatic. Carnatic Chanda Sahib 49-52 (son-in-law of Dost Ali Khan 32-40) Md Ali 52-95 (son of Anwaruddin 44-49) Hyderabad Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (grandson of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48) Nasir Jung 48-50 (son of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48) Mnemonics (handout and board). French side: "MuzaFFrance" = Muzaffar Jung 50-51; Chanda Sahib 49-52: "Paris and the moon (Chanda) are symbols of romance." British side: "Nasir Hussain: England captain, cricket" = Nasir Jung 48-50; "Jinnah, pro-British" = Md Ali 52-95 (the same first names as Jinnah's). Order (1) French EIC, (2) English EIC: the French interfered first, the EIC only reacted. Why did the EIC react at all? "Fear of the British = if the French EIC is able to put its favourite in power, then loss of trade for the EIC." Dupleix 42-54 wanted (a) empire building and (b) a monopoly of the international trade of South India. Anwaruddin 44-49 wanted his son Md Ali 52-95 to be Nawab. Carnatic map: Arcot, Madras, Wandiwash, Pondicherry Map code "MWP": on the coast from north to south Madras (HQ of the EIC), Wandiwash (battle of the 3rd Carnatic War), Pondicherry (HQ of the French EIC). Arcot, inland, is the capital of Carnatic. Hyderabad lies north of the River Krishna; the Northern Sarkars run along the coast further up. 2nd Carnatic War: "all gathered in Carnatic" (Nasir Jung 48-50 and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 arrived in Carnatic too). Two phases: French EIC ahead in the 1st phase (till 1751); English EIC ahead in the 2nd. 5.1 Phase 1: French victory (1749-51) Phase 1 of the 2nd Carnatic War Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 is killed Chanda Sahib 49-52 is declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot By December 1750: Nasir Jung 48-50 is also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is declared Nizam Muzaffar Jung 50-51 marches toward Hyderabad, accompanied by Bussy's army February 1751, Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass: Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is killed by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool; the Nawab of Kurnool is also killed Bussy reaches Hyderabad and installs Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 was killed. Chanda Sahib 49-52 was declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot. (The slide notes: Ambur is 190 km west of Chennai; the teacher added "towards Bengaluru.") By December 1750, Nasir Jung 48-50 was also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 was declared Nizam. Bussy was the junior of Dupleix 42-54. Accompanied by Bussy's army, Muzaffar Jung 50-51 began marching toward Hyderabad. But he was killed in February 1751 at the Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool, who felt cheated as he was not given the territory promised to him for his support. The Nawab of Kurnool was also killed. (The slide's aside on the pass: "unlucky lol.") Bussy now reached Hyderabad and installed Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam. He was a son of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 and an uncle of the recently killed Muzaffar Jung 50-51. "Asaf Jahi dynasty, by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 [Asaf Jah I]." All the Hyderabad claimants (Nasir Jung 48-50, Muzaffar Jung 50-51, Salabat Jung 51-62) belong to this one family (Chapter 3). Wagner Group analogy: the French EIC as hired army Wagner Group = a company that sells a service for money; the service is military service. Muzaffar Jung 50-51 ("MJ") and Chanda Sahib 49-52 hired the French EIC, like a Wagner Group, to become rulers. Death of MJ = a blot on the military reputation of the French EIC: a firm that sells protection cannot let its client be killed. So Bussy created terror on the way to Hyderabad as a general message, "don't mess with the French EIC," and made Salabat Jung 51-62 the Nizam. The gains from Phase 1 Dupleix 42-54's gains from Phase 1 Hyderabad: the resident Bussy was made the French resident and agent at the Nizam's court, wielding real political influence Hyderabad: the army A French army was stationed for the Nizam's protection, and Hyderabad was to pay for it Hyderabad: the payment The payment was the Northern Sarkars region (present-day Andhra Pradesh): Bussy administered it on behalf of the Nizam and kept its revenues as payment for the French army Hyderabad: cash 2,00,000 pounds for the French EIC from the Nizam Hyderabad: personal Bussy extracted personal jagirs in Masulipatnam and Yanam Carnatic: title Dupleix 42-54 declared himself Nawab of all lands between the River Krishna and Cape Comorin (= Carnatic), with Chanda Sahib 49-52 as his Deputy Nawab of Arcot Carnatic: personal Dupleix 42-54 extracted a personal jagir of Rs 1 lakh per annum in Villianallur near Pondicherry In the Northern Sarkars Bussy's methods were brutal: terror and massacre of civilians for land revenue extraction. In Andhra folklore this terror is preserved in the word "boochi" (meaning ghost, or the feared), derived from Bussy's name. Gains of the French EIC (not only Dupleix 42-54's). (1) "Hyderabad under French military domination" (army stationed there). (2) "THINK: the French are selling a military service" (Hyderabad pays for the army; the Wagner idea again). (3) "In a way Salabat Jung 51-62 = puppet of the French EIC." (4) "The French can counter any anti-French decision via supervision" (the purpose of a resident in the court). Geography: Carnatic = the land from the River Krishna (top) down to Kanya Kumari or Cape Comorin (tip). The notebook page adds: (1) Dupleix 42-54 got 80 villages as the Jagirdari of Villianallur, worth Rs 1 lakh. (2) "Today, for inflation, = 3 crore rupees per annum" (how large a personal income this was). Yanam and Masulipatnam are Bussy's personal jagirs. Notebook page versus handout. (1) The page dates the 2nd Carnatic War "1750-54"; the handout and every slide give 1749-54 (use this). (2) The page writes "x 300%", but Rs 1 lakh becomes Rs 3 crore only at 300 times; take the point (a very large income), not the arithmetic. Why Company employees build empires THINK: why do Company men build empires? An employee of the French EIC gets only a salary. BUT empire building brings him personal jagirs plus cash. The personal interest of these empire-builder employees drives the wars, in every company: the French EIC, the English EIC, the Estado da India and the Dutch VOC. (Condition 1 of section 1.2: the personally ambitious Governor.) Takeaway: Dupleix 42-54 invented the model of empire building in India: put your candidate in power, station your army at his expense, extract territory as payment, and sit in the court as the real power behind the throne. The British EIC refined this model and used it with devastating effect for the next century. (Handout aside: "Thanks, Dupleix 42-54" would be the EIC's thought.) Dupleix 42-54's model of empire building (later copied and refined by the EIC) 1. Succession dispute = opportunity: interfere and bring your favourite claimant into power 2. Extract gains, military domination: station your army in the Indian State and make the State pay for this army 3. Extract gains, territory as payment: take land as payment for the army 4. Puppet State: station your Resident in the Indian King's court, who establishes his indirect rule Model slide. Step 1: "FACTIONALISM (R vs R)": the opening is always a quarrel between two rivals. Step 2: "Free of cost domination": the Indian State itself pays for the army that dominates it. Step 4: "Resident in the Indian King's court" and "Indirect Rule." Mains question: model of empire building, French and British Mains question: "Model of empire building (in India) by trading companies was founded by the French and implemented by the British. Analyse." "Founded by French" = the 2nd Carnatic War (the four steps above, with Hyderabad and Carnatic as examples). "Implemented by British" = future topics (Plassey and Buxar in Chapter 10, the Subsidiary Alliance in Chapter 11). Prelims 1996: the first European to take part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories = (b) Dupleix 42-54. He invented the model: back a candidate, station your army at his expense, take territory as payment, sit in court as the real power. It was first used in the 2nd Carnatic War (backing Muzaffar Jung 50-51 and Chanda Sahib 49-52). Clive 57-67 came later: he used and refined the model in Bengal (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764) but did not invent it. Albuquerque 09-15 was a 16th-century Portuguese conqueror (took Goa 1510): an earlier era of direct conquest, not the "back-a-claimant" model. Warren Hastings 73-85 was a later EIC Governor-General: a refiner, not the originator. 5.2 Phase 2: the EIC bounces back The EIC decided to fight back by supporting Md Ali 52-95 (Carnatic), who was holding out in Trichinopoly. Dupleix 42-54 got obsessed with eliminating any future challenge to his power. Hence he made the critical mistake of leaving the capital Arcot unguarded and focusing on Trichinopoly. Robert Clive 57-67, operating from Madras with a small force of roughly 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys, took over Arcot (the slide dates it: Arcot 1751). He then defended it against a massive counter-siege for 53 days. The capital was now with the British! Clive 57-67 became a celebrated figure back in Britain. The French government in Paris, anxious to honour the 1748 treaty and preserve its more lucrative American possessions, refused to help Dupleix 42-54. By 1754 the French had lost the 2nd Carnatic War. Phase 2: how the capital was lost Md Ali 52-95 holds out in Trichinopoly, backed by the EIC Dupleix 42-54's critical mistake: he focuses on Trichinopoly and leaves the capital Arcot unguarded Clive 57-67 takes Arcot (1751) from Madras with about 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys He defends it through a 53-day counter-siege Paris refuses to help Dupleix 42-54: it wants to honour the 1748 treaty and keep its American possessions By 1754 the French have lost the 2nd Carnatic War Key phrases: "1748 treaty" and "refused to help Dupleix 42-54." The real reason for the defeat: France chose America over India again, exactly as in 1748. 5.3 The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) Dupleix 42-54 was recalled to France, replaced by Godeheu, on account of the high war expenditure. He died in poverty in France in 1763, abandoned by the State he had served. The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) was a middle path: 1. Hyderabad French influence remained in Hyderabad: (1) Bussy as agent, (2) the French army in Hyderabad, (3) the Northern Sarkars with the French French 2. Factories French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic were retained  3. Carnatic Md Ali 52-95 became Nawab of Carnatic: hence EIC influence in Carnatic British Chanda Sahib 49-52, having escaped to Tanjore (present-day Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu), was beheaded by Pratap Singh 39-63, the Maratha Raja of Thanjavur: an old rival. Maratha rule in Tanjore had begun in 1674 when Venkoji (also known as Ekoji), half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80, conquered the region. Why was a winning Governor-General recalled? "Company = an organisation with a profit motive." High war expenditure eats profit, so the company removes the man who causes it. "Factory = warehouses + homes + offices + maybe a fort" (Chapter 8). The treaty is a split: the French gain in Hyderabad, the British in Carnatic. How wars end: war aims and power differential Theory of treaties ("imp factors").
