War is expensive for both, the losing and the victorious party, so both want it to end. The victor ends the war if it has achieved its war aims, the core goal of the war. For the EIC the core motive was trade, so it could settle once its trade was safe (Hyderabad and Carnatic, each a gain). When a treaty is negotiated, the important factors are the power differential between the two sides and their ability, economic and military. Apply to all three treaties: 1748 (Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 and 1st Carnatic War 1746-48), 1754 and 1763.

Because royal armies now joined the Companies, the contest turned decisive. Ask: why did France lose, and why did the EIC win all three wars? 6.1 Reason The 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63) was once again a European conflict brought to Indian shores: the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63), fought across Europe, the Americas, Africa and India. French side: Count de Lally (of the French State, not the French EIC) arrived from France with the Royal military and led the French alongside Bussy of the French EIC. British side: Eyre Coote (of the British State, not the EIC) arrived from Britain with the Royal military and led the British alongside Robert Clive 57-67 of the EIC. Recap before the 3rd war. Of the three Carnatic Wars (1746-63), wars 1 and 3 come from "IR" (international relations: Britain against France), war 2 from factionalism. New in war 3: the Royal militaries (French and British) joined the armies of the French EIC and the English EIC: [EIC + Britain] versus [French EIC + France]. Typed slide: "had impacts" above "a European conflict on Indian shores"; key names Count de Lally, Eyre Coote and royal military on both sides. Three Carnatic Wars: causes and royal armies 6.2 Why did France lose the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63)? Handout map: Coromandel Coast, Madras to Pondicherry The most decisive battle was the Battle of Wandiwash (1760). (The handout's memory line: "where the French were washed away.") After that the French lost everywhere, including Pondicherry itself, their headquarters officially since 1701, with Fort Louis. The chain slides add: Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760, and the Siege of Pondicherry came in 1761. Map pointers = the board's "MWP": Madras (the British base), Wandiwash (between the two) and Pondicherry (the French base). Wandiwash lies between the two headquarters, which is why the decisive battle was there. Prelims 1995: UPSC asked "match the battle to who fought it" by jumbling correct pairs. The correct pairs are: Battle of Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim 60-63 (with Awadh and Shah Alam II 60-06); Battle of Chilianwala (1849) = EIC under Dalhousie 48-56 vs the Sikhs (2nd Anglo-Sikh War); Battle of Kharda (1795) = Nizam of Hyderabad vs the Marathas; Battle of Wandiwash (1760) = French vs the East India Company. The answer was (b). The trap in (a): Mir Jafar 57-60 was the EIC's man at Plassey 1757, not its enemy at Buxar. France lost for four reasons. Wandiwash 1760: why France lost, tactics and leadership 1. Tactical mistake Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic. Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Bengal and took over the Northern Sarkars in 1759 2. Poor leadership Lally was despised by his own officers and sepoys for his rude conduct, which demoralised the army 3. Financial weakness French soldiers went unpaid for months. The French EIC had spent heavily in the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) and the first two Carnatic Wars without commensurate gains. In contrast, Britain had been profiting from eastern trade since 1600. British capitalism was mature; feudalism in France ended only after the French Revolution of 1789, while the Industrial Revolution had begun in Britain (1750-1850) 4. Superior British navy This gave Britain decisive advantages in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic. Britain's navy was able to dominate the Coromandel coast Tactical mistake in two steps. (1) Bussy leaves the Northern Sarkars and goes down to Carnatic to help Lally. (2) From Bengal, Clive 57-67 comes down into the unguarded Northern Sarkars (1759). Poor leadership: "Dupleix 42-54 not here": the one able French leader had been recalled in 1754, so France fought this war with Lally. Financial weakness. The "earlier wars" that drained the French EIC: Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 [1st Carnatic War 1746-48] and the 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54. On the second: "Hyderabad gains, BUT STILL higher war expenditure" (even the winning phase cost more than it earned). Navy: Carnatic lies along the Coromandel Coast, so whoever commands the sea commands the war there. British capitalism versus French feudalism What "British capitalism was mature" means. To see capitalism in a society, wake up at 4 am and sit in a balcony facing a main road: people are already at work. At mass level people believe they can become rich by working hard. Bombay never sleeps: the city provides opportunities to earn 24x7. The French Revolution of 1789 ended feudalism, and only then did capitalism come to France (but merchants existed in France before 1789). Britain had this money-making society earlier, so it could pay for its wars. 6.3 Why did the EIC win the Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63)? 1. France starved Dupleix 42-54 of reinforcements To preserve its gains from the 1748 Treaty (Aix-La-Chapelle) 2. Leadership French: the recall of Dupleix 42-54 after the 2nd Carnatic War hurt the chances of French victory; Lally displayed poor leadership in the 3rd Carnatic War. British: Robert Clive 57-67 and Eyre Coote displayed good leadership 3. Superior British navy British naval dominance of the coast 4. Finances The EIC was a private joint-stock firm with deep capital; it had accumulated wealth, along with huge monetary gains after Plassey 1757. The French EIC was a State PSU with weak finances. The French economy was weak compared to Britain, which was the world's top economy of the time. Past war expenditure without any formidable gains hurt French capabilities, e.g. Lally's troops went unpaid (the slide adds: unpaid for months, so low morale) 5. Tactical mistakes Leaving Arcot (the capital of Carnatic) unguarded in the 2nd Carnatic War and leaving the Northern Sarkars unguarded in the 3rd Carnatic War Title note "all (3)": this table answers "Why the EIC won all 3 Carnatic Wars," while section 6.2 answers only the 3rd war. For a Mains answer, use 6.3 for the whole contest and 6.2 for Wandiwash. The handout numbers these factors 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 (2 is printed twice). There are five factors; renumbered 1 to 5 here. 6.4 The Treaty of Paris (1763) Under the Treaty of Paris (1763): France lost all gains made in India since 1749 and was restricted to its pre-1749 position. France retained only five small trading posts: Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam and Chandernagore. France was barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases. P Pondicherry East coast M Mahe West coast (teacher: Malabar) K Karaikal East coast Y Yanam East coast C Chandernagore East (teacher: Bengal) Mnemonic "PM KYC (Yojana)": Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, Chandernagore. Only Mahe is on the west coast (Malabar); Chandernagore is in Bengal. "Trading posts" becomes "trading CENTRES." Three treaties to learn in order: 1748 Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle, 1754 Treaty of Pondicherry, 1763 Treaty of Paris. In 1769 the French EIC was abolished by France. This signifies that the French government had given up on its ambitions of dominating the international trade of India. The abolition of the French EIC does not mean other French traders could not trade in India, just that the French State was not interested in running a government company for it. After successfully countering the Portuguese by 1612, the Dutch by the 1650s and the French by 1763, the British EIC now had a monopoly over India's international trade. "NOT (T)": in 1763 the EIC has a monopoly over trade, not territory. What was decided was only "who will buy Indian goods, who will dominate exports from India." The Carnatic Wars were wars for trade (section 1.2). 6.5 Link with Plassey, and what came later Takeaway: link with the Battle of Plassey (1757). The 3rd Carnatic War brought large numbers of British Royal military troops to India; this strength and Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy made Plassey possible. Without Carnatic there may not have been a Plassey, which led to Empire Building by the EIC. From a global war to Plassey (teacher's flow) Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) 3rd Carnatic War British Royal military in India Confidence of Clive 57-67 for accepting Jafar's offer: Plassey 1757 Carnatic Wars: legacy and link with Plassey Later: In the Treaty of Hyderabad (1766), Hyderabad formally ceded the Northern Sarkars to the EIC in exchange for Rs 7 lakh annually and protection against the Marathas and Mysore. Hyderabad became the 1st Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC, in 1798. Mysore signed in 1799 and Travancore in 1805, while Carnatic was annexed in 1801. Thus the Carnatic Wars, though fought for the international trade of India, laid the foundation of British domination of South India. "3rd CW + 3.5 decades": from the end of the 3rd Carnatic War (1763), about three and a half decades to the first Subsidiary Alliance (Hyderabad, 1798). The row: Hyderabad 1798, Mysore 1799, Travancore 1805, Carnatic annexed 1801. "Jafar's offer" = Mir Jafar 57-60's deal with Clive 57-67 (Chapter 10).

items.t: 7 · Diagram 1: the Carnatic Wars in one chain
items.x: Last scene: the whole chain on one page. Ask: can you retell it from the Austrian war of 1740 to the Treaty of Paris in 1763? Reading Diagram 1. In the printed figure the middle-row arrows run from the Treaty of Pondicherry box to Arcot and then to the 2nd Carnatic War box, the reverse of time order. Read the middle row left to right: 2nd Carnatic War (Ambur 1749), Arcot 1751, Treaty of Pondicherry 1754. The slides show the chain in the correct order, as below. The Carnatic Wars: the chain, 1740 to 1763 Austrian War of Succession (1740-48): Anglo-French rivalry in Europe spills into India 1st Carnatic War (1746-48): Battle of Adyar/St Thome 1746; the French crush the Nawab's cavalry Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748): ends the Austrian War; Madras returned to the EIC 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54): Ambur 1749; Chanda Sahib 49-52 and Salabat Jung 51-62 installed; Dupleix 42-54 invents the empire model Clive 57-67's Arcot (1751): 53-day defence; Md Ali 52-95 (Wallajah) prevails Treaty of Pondicherry (1754): Dupleix 42-54 recalled, replaced by Godeheu; French momentum broken 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63): Seven Years' Global War; de Lally versus Eyre Coote Wandiwash (22 January 1760): decisive EIC victory over the French Siege of Pondicherry (1761), then Treaty of Paris (1763): French power in India permanently broken

1600 Britain profiting from eastern trade since this year 1612 Portuguese countered by the EIC (Battle of Suvali: an offensive war for trade) 1650s Dutch countered by the EIC 1651 First EIC factory in Bengal, at Hugli (teacher's note) 1661 Charter: right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, civil and criminal jurisdiction ★ 1674 Maratha rule in Tanjore begins under Venkoji (Ekoji), half-brother of Shivaji 74-80 1676 EIC gets the right to mint its own money 1686 Anglo-Mughal War (Child's War) begins, to 1690 ★ 1690 February: Aurangzeb 58-07 pardons the EIC for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation 1691 Farman (technically a Parwana): duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year ★ 1701 Pondicherry the French headquarters officially, with Fort Louis 1732 Dost Ali Khan 32-40 Nawab of Carnatic (to 1740) 1740 War of the Austrian Succession (to 1748); French EIC trade about half of British EIC trade 1742 Dupleix 42-54 becomes Governor-General of the French EIC (to 1754) ★ 1744 Anwaruddin 44-49 appointed Nawab of Carnatic by the Nizam of Hyderabad 1746 1st Carnatic War (to 1748); Fort St George captured; Battle of Adyar/St Thome ★ 1748 Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle: Madras returned to the EIC; Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 dies ★ 1749 2nd Carnatic War (to 1754); Battle of Ambur: Anwaruddin 44-49 killed, Chanda Sahib 49-52 Nawab ★ 1750 December: Nasir Jung 48-50 killed; Muzaffar Jung 50-51 declared Nizam 1751 February: Muzaffar Jung 50-51 killed at Lakkireddipalli Pass; Salabat Jung 51-62 installed; Clive 57-67 takes Arcot (53-day defence) ★ 1754 Treaty of Pondicherry; Dupleix 42-54 recalled, replaced by Godeheu ★ 1756 3rd Carnatic War and the Seven Years' Global War (both to 1763) ★ 1757 Battle of Plassey, made possible by the Royal troops of the 3rd Carnatic War 1759 Clive 57-67 takes the Northern Sarkars after Bussy leaves them 1760 22 January: Battle of Wandiwash, Eyre Coote defeats Lally ★ 1761 Siege of Pondicherry 1763 Treaty of Paris: France back to its pre-1749 position, five posts only; Dupleix 42-54 dies in poverty ★ 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: Northern Sarkars ceded to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year 1769 French EIC abolished by France 1798 Hyderabad: first Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance ★ 1799 Mysore signs the Subsidiary Alliance 1801 Carnatic annexed 1805 Travancore signs the Subsidiary Alliance 1857 EIC controls 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population

A shop that became a State. Companies exist for profit, and the EIC was no different, yet by 1857 it ruled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. The 1661 Charter had given it forts, troops, war and peace and courts, and 1676 its own mint. Its wars were for trade (defensive, like the Carnatic Wars) or for territory, when a Governor was personally ambitious or the EIC Army pushed for war. Child's War (1686-90). Aurangzeb 58-07's wars and quarrels over bribes and customs in Bengal pushed the EIC to seize Hugli and attack Mughal ships. Aurangzeb 58-07 crushed it in Bombay and Bengal, the Company surrendered by 1690, and in February 1690 he pardoned it for Rs 1.5 lakh. The 1691 Farman, technically a Parwana, gave duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year, because the EIC brought forex and gold and fed bankers, merchants, artisans and ryots. Enter Dupleix. Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54 is Governor-General of the French EIC from 1742 to 1754, with personal ambitions of empire and of dominating South India's trade; by 1740 French trade is about half of the British. The three Carnatic Wars are 1746-48, 1749-54 and 1756-63: the 1st and 3rd are global wars spilling into India, and the 2nd is factionalism, R versus R. Adyar, 1746. The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) reaches India, and Dupleix 42-54 captures the EIC's Fort St George at Madras. Anwaruddin 44-49, Nawab of Carnatic, expected the fort and, when Dupleix 42-54 refused, sent 10,000 cavalry; at Adyar about 700 French-trained sepoys and 300 French soldiers destroyed them with light cannon, infantry squares and regular pay. It was a turning point: Indian kings now wanted European help to modernise their armies. Aix-La-Chapelle, 1748. The treaty ended the Austrian war and returned possessions in America and India, so Madras went back to the EIC. The French had won in India but the British in the Americas, and Britain's main interest was India while France's was the Americas. Nothing changed in territory, European infantry stayed far greater than Indian cavalry, and Dupleix 42-54 was left empty-handed. Two quarrels, four claimants. In Carnatic, Md Ali 52-95 (son of Anwaruddin 44-49) faces Chanda Sahib 49-52 (son-in-law of Dost Ali Khan 32-40). In Hyderabad, after Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 dies in 1748, his son Nasir Jung 48-50 faces his grandson Muzaffar Jung 50-51. The French move first for Chanda Sahib 49-52 and Muzaffar Jung 50-51, and the anxious EIC reacts for Md Ali 52-95 and Nasir Jung 48-50, fearing lost trade. Phase 1: the French kingmaker. At Ambur in 1749 Anwaruddin 44-49 dies and Chanda Sahib 49-52 is made Nawab; by December 1750 Nasir Jung 48-50 is dead and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is Nizam. Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is killed in February 1751 at Lakkireddipalli Pass, so Bussy installs Salabat Jung 51-62. The French gain a resident and an army at Hyderabad, paid for with the Northern Sarkars, 2,00,000 pounds and jagirs, and Dupleix 42-54 styles himself Nawab from the Krishna to Cape Comorin. His four steps are a model: a succession dispute, an army at the State's cost, territory as payment, a Resident. Phase 2: Arcot, 1751. Dupleix 42-54 fixes on Trichinopoly, where Md Ali 52-95 holds out, and leaves Arcot unguarded, so Clive 57-67 takes it from Madras with about 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys and holds it for 53 days. Paris, wanting to honour the 1748 treaty and keep America, refuses to help. By the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) Dupleix 42-54 is recalled, Godeheu replaces him, the French keep Hyderabad influence and Md Ali 52-95 becomes Nawab of Carnatic; Chanda Sahib 49-52 is beheaded at Tanjore by Pratap Singh 39-63. The 3rd war and Wandiwash. The Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) brings royal armies for the first time: Count de Lally with Bussy for France, Eyre Coote with Clive 57-67 for Britain. Bussy leaves the Northern Sarkars to help Lally, so Clive 57-67 takes them in 1759, and Lally's rude conduct and unpaid soldiers weaken the French, who also face a superior British navy. Eyre Coote wins the decisive battle of Wandiwash on 22 January 1760 and Pondicherry falls in 1761. Paris, 1763. France loses all gains since 1749, keeps five posts (Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, Chandernagore) and may not keep a strong army or fortify its bases; in 1769 the French EIC is abolished. Having countered the Portuguese by 1612 and the Dutch by the 1650s, the British EIC now has a monopoly over India's international trade. It won all three wars because France starved Dupleix 42-54, had weaker leadership and a weaker navy, and could not match a private joint-stock firm with deep capital. From Carnatic to Plassey. The 3rd war brought large royal military forces to India, and that strength plus Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy made Plassey 1757 possible. In 1766 Hyderabad ceded the Northern Sarkars to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year; Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, Mysore in 1799, Travancore in 1805, and Carnatic was annexed in 1801. The French founded the model of empire building and the British implemented it.

Prelims 2004 Three statements: (1) in the Third Battle of Panipat, Ahmed Shah Abdali defeated Ibrahim Lodi; (2) Tipu 82-99 Sultan was killed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War; (3) Mir Jafar 57-60 entered into a conspiracy with the English for the defeat of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 in the Battle of Plassey. Which is/are correct? Options: (a) 1, 2 and 3 (b) Only 3 (c) 2 and 3 (d) None of these (b) Only 3. Statement 1 is false: in the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) Abdali defeated the Marathas; Ibrahim Lodi lost the First Panipat (1526) to Babur 26-30. Statement 2 is false: Tipu 82-99 Sultan was killed in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1798-99) at Srirangapatna, not the Third (1789-92). Board solution: [1st BoP 1526] F; [4th 1799] F; statement 3 T; (b). Only statement 3 is from this chapter, but the answer can still be reached from it Section 5 (the conspiracy and the battle) Prelims 2005 The correct chronological order of the battles fought in India in the 18th century: (a) Wandiwash, Buxar, Ambur, Plassey (b) Ambur, Plassey, Wandiwash, Buxar (c) Wandiwash, Plassey, Ambur, Buxar (d) Ambur, Buxar, Wandiwash, Plassey (b): Ambur (1749), Plassey (1757), Wandiwash (1760), Buxar (1764). Method: write the year over each battle of option (a) (1760, 1764, 1749, 1757) to reach (b). (a) puts Wandiwash and Buxar before Ambur; (c) puts Wandiwash before Plassey; (d) puts Buxar before Wandiwash. Ambur and Wandiwash are Carnatic Wars battles (Chapter 9) Section 9 (chronology box) Mains (year not given) Why were there recurrent famines in British-ruled India? One paragraph of that answer comes from this topic: the Great Bengal Famine 1770 under the Dual Government (high revenue demand, harsh collection, hoarding unchecked, nobody responsible for relief) and the "Famine = Nature factor AND Human factor" board Section 8.2.2 (Indirect Rule, the 1770 famine and Direct Rule)

Plassey 1757 = conquest by the EIC, not rule. "x Rule of EIC": rule = L, E, J on T (legislative, executive and judicial power over a territory, Chapter 8). Plassey gave: (1) conquest by the EIC, a transformation from TRADER to STATE-like BEHAVIOUR; (2) DRAIN of wealth; (3) change in TRADE STRUCTURE. Buxar 1764 leads to ToA 1765 (Treaty of Allahabad), which gave two things: Rule in Bengal [the EIC becomes the FM, the finance minister, of Bengal] and military domination of Awadh. Company State: definition and phases Chapter 10 on one board: Plassey, Buxar and ToA 1765 Company State = the EIC's empire in India = British India = British "Ruled" India; "ruled" = L, E, J by the British. By 1857 it covered 63% of the territory and 78% of the population. British India has two phases: Company State [1765-1858], beginning with ToA 1765, and Crown Colony [1858 to 26 January 1950 OR 15 August 1947]. Company = organisation with a money (profit) motive. State = organisation with a territory motive. Company State = a State set up by a Company. It took territory from the Indian Regional States (three kinds, Chapter 3: successor, rebel, already autonomous) by Diplomacy and War. Course chain: Decline of the Mughal State, Rise of Regional States, Advent of Europeans, Establishment of the Company State.

items.t: 1 · Plassey marks the beginning of conquest
items.x: Story so far: the EIC is a trader. Plassey is where it first acts like a conqueror. Keep the spine in mind: abuse, conquest, plunder, legalise. Plassey marks the beginning of conquest Plassey marks the beginning of the transformation of the EIC into a Company State. Conquest means military domination and political supremacy. It began here, in Bengal. But the EIC did not legally take over sovereign functions in Bengal after the Battle of Plassey 1757. It focused on military control and on extracting wealth. Takeaway: Rule did not begin in 1757. Conquest and the Drain of Wealth from India, however, did. Extracting wealth = PLUNDER = ATTACK + LOOT. Plassey Plunder [1757-65] = illegal. 1765: the EIC became FM (finance minister, that is the Diwan) of Bengal and got the LEGAL RIGHT to use Bengal's wealth: the loot was legalised. This ties Plassey to Buxar.

items.t: 2 · The Royal Farman of 1717: the seed of conflict
items.x: Chapter 1 of the story: a doctor's cure buys the trader a golden ticket, and the Nawab hands it over with conditions. 2.1 The four Farmans that strengthened the EIC 1613 Jahangir 05-27 The right to establish a factory in Surat, after the EIC defeated the Portuguese in the Battle of Suvali 1612 1618 Jahangir 05-27 The right to establish factories in the whole of the Mughal empire and liberal trading rights, due to lobbying by Thomas Roe (British Resident 1615-19) 1691 The Subahdar of Bengal, with Aurangzeb 58-07's approval The right to Duty-Free Trade (DFT) in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum. The EIC's trade was economically beneficial and brought forex into India 1717 Imperial (Royal) Farman Farrukhsiyar 13-19 Often called the "Magna Carta of the Company". It was the result of medical diplomacy: Dr William Hamilton, an English surgeon with the EIC, successfully treated Farrukhsiyar 13-19 for a serious illness Liberal trading rights (1618) = lower export duties, less paperwork, use of more ports. Board heading: the Farmans as the economic strengthening of the EIC ("Eco ... of EIC"). 2.2 What the 1717 Farman gave, and what the Nawab refused The 1717 Imperial (Royal) Farman gave the EIC three rights: The right to Duty-Free Trade (DFT) in Deccan, Gujarat and Bengal. For Bengal this was a Royal Farman reiterating a pre-existing privilege, granted under the sign and seal of the Subahdar in 1691 (the slide calls the 1691 grant a provincial privilege or Parwana). The right to use the Royal Mint. 1717 Imperial Farman: source of conflict with the Nawab of Bengal The EIC could mint Indian coins and so save the cost of converting gold into Indian currency (sikkas) for purchasing Indian goods. The right to rent 38 villages around Calcutta for expanding its trading settlement. Why the mint mattered. Within Indian territory only Indian sikkas can be used. The EIC took gold and silver to the Royal Mint and got sikkas back; the Royal Mint earned a commission. Minting its own coins would save the EIC this cost and take the commission from the government. Years noted under the settlement clause: [1690] and [Presidency 1699] (read as the Calcutta settlement and its becoming a Presidency, Chapter 8). The 1717 Farman became a source of conflict between the EIC and the Nawab of Bengal. Bengal by 1717 was a successor State. Recall: successor means uttaradhikari, one who comes from within the family. Here the family is the political family of the Mughal State (the Mughal Emperor and his Mansabdars). So certain powerful Mansabdars established their rule in certain provinces and took away the real powers of the Emperor, making him a symbolic authority. They were MQK 17-27, Sadat Khan 22-39 and Nizam 24-48 in Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad respectively (Chapter 3). Nawab Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) dealt with the three rights like this: Duty-free trade Allowed duty-free trade by the EIC, but refused to let EIC officials misuse Dastaks for their own private trade The privilege was for the Company's goods, not for the officials' personal goods Use of the Royal Mint Refused It hurt sovereign authority and government revenue (the government earned commission on the conversion of gold into Indian sikkas) 38 villages around Calcutta Allowed renting but NOT purchase Stressed on the board: "NOT purchase" The slide table for the Nawabs says MQK 17-27 "won the 1717 Farman"; the handout's figure says he "accepted the 1717 Farman, resisted Dastak abuse". The Farman was issued to the EIC by Farrukhsiyar 13-19; MQK 17-27 accepted it in part and resisted the rest. Read the slide's phrase in that sense.

Because the Nawab set conditions, officers found loopholes: the Dastak. Ask 'whose law is broken?' for each villain (intruder, friend, cheat). 3.1 Private trade and what a Dastak was Private trade (PVT TRADE) = EIC officers buying Indian goods for trade in their personal capacity, apart from buying for the EIC. Reason: greed; corruption; a "stab in the back" of the EIC by its own employees. It violates the Royal Charter (monopoly over British trade in the East Indies): an employee should not become a competitor to his own company. Dastak = document issued by EIC officers; it "operationalised" duty-free trade. Sample: "It is certified that these 100 goods are of the EIC. Please allow DFT exit from port. (Signed)", shown to the Indian customs officer, who lets the container leave India without duty payment. Misuse = using a Dastak for private trade by MISDECLARING the goods as the EIC's; result: loss of duty [tax revenue] for the Indian State. What a Dastak is A permit issued by EIC officials certifying that goods belonged to the EIC, and hence exempt from export duty Misuse In practice EIC officials also used these permits for their own private trade, claiming goods bought in a personal capacity as company goods. They also sold Dastaks to other exporters Scale (by 1750) Private trade by EIC officials was worth 1,00,000 pounds per annum, roughly fifty times their annual salaries Why the EIC could not control it Even its own top officials in India engaged in private trade Effect Tax (duty) evasion and loss of revenue for the Bengal Suba Who curbed it later Cornwallis 86-93 curbed private trade: an honest Governor General of that era Private trade and the Dastak "therefore primary motive is not salary BUT PVT TRADE": private trade was worth 50 times the salary, so an officer came to India for private trade, not salary. Cornwallis 86-93 [increased salary]: that is how private trade was curbed. 3.2 Who was violating whose law? It is worth understanding exactly what was illegal, and for whom. Trade in the East Indies by any British entity other than the EIC violated the Royal Charter issued by the British Crown: that was British law. Interlopers Non-EIC British merchants who traded with India (the teacher: Britishers, either traders or other companies) They violated the Royal Charter (British law), leading to court cases back in Britain Free merchants Non-EIC British merchants stationed in India who agreed to sell Indian goods to the EIC in India itself rather than exporting independently (the teacher: an "ex-interloper") None: their trade became artificially legal in the eyes of British law Dastak misuse by EIC officials EIC officials passing private goods as Company goods NOT British law but Indian law: specifically customs duty evasion (the slide adds: under Bengal's framework) Interlopers against free merchants The teacher's board: how an interloper became a free merchant Earlier: ryots and artisans sell to the Indian merchant, who sells to the EIC, which exports Interloper: buys from Indian merchants and exports on his own; say his profit is Rs 100, which is a loss of Rs 100 to the EIC The EIC is unable to stop it: the Charter is broken, and there are court cases in Britain Free merchant: the same man now sells to the EIC inside India and does not export himself; the Rs 100 is shared No Charter is broken: the EIC earns some share, and the free merchant gains because there is no court case in Britain

items.t: 4 · Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 and the road to Plassey (1757)
items.x: Because the cheating hurt Bengal's revenue, a young Nawab finally tries to stop it. Watch who tolerated it and who did not. Siraj-ud-Daula and the road to Plassey (1757) 4.1 Why Alivardi Khan 40-56 tolerated the EIC's provocations Afraid of the French, the EIC began adding fortifications in Calcutta, that is strengthening Fort William (thickening walls, filling gaps, raising the height), from 1755, without the permission of Alivardi Khan 40-56. A fort is a military structure. Building or expanding one on another sovereign's territory without permission is a challenge to that sovereign's authority. However, Alivardi Khan 40-56 was pragmatic and followed the path of diplomacy rather than military confrontation, since the EIC's trade was economically beneficial to Bengal. He must also have noticed the Battle of Adyar 1746, which proved the military capabilities of European infantry. Why the EIC was fortifying. 1756: the Seven Years' Global War made the EIC anxious. 60% of the EIC's trade was Bengal. EIC's reasoning: "We need to be ATMANIRBHAR (self-reliant), because Adyar 1746 tells us that the Nawab won't be able to help us" against the French. Fort = military structure; fortification = building a fort or strengthening one: fill gaps in the walls, increase height, increase thickness. Adyar 1746 (Carnatic Wars, dated 1746-63 on the board) explains both sides: it made Alivardi Khan 40-56 cautious and the EIC self-reliant (Chapter 9). 4.2 Why Siraj 56-57 did not tolerate them Siraj 56-57 was the precious grandson of Alivardi Khan 40-56 through his daughter, as Alivardi Khan 40-56 had no sons and Siraj 56-57 was the only grandson. Siraj 56-57 was disliked in the Bengal court. He had disrespected senior Mansabdars and had at one point imprisoned Jagat Seth, the powerful banker, for extortion. He was young, impulsive, surrounded by enemies. When he came to power he stopped all Dastak misuse, hurting the private trade fortunes of EIC officials. The British then gave asylum to Krishna Ballabh (for money), a fugitive from Siraj 56-57's court, charged with fraud, and added new fortifications to Calcutta. Siraj 56-57 first seized the EIC factory at Kasimbazar and then captured Calcutta. He renamed Calcutta Alinagar. The road to Plassey 1717 Farman: duty-free trade; Dastaks misused for private trade; the Bengal Suba loses revenue From 1755: the EIC fortifies Fort William without permission; Alivardi Khan 40-56 chooses diplomacy Siraj 56-57 becomes Nawab: he stops all Dastak misuse; EIC officials' private fortunes are hurt The British shelter Krishna Ballabh (for money) and add new fortifications Siraj 56-57 seizes Kasimbazar and captures Calcutta (Alinagar): the Black Hole Tragedy Clive 57-67 arrives from Madras, recaptures Calcutta; Treaty of Alinagar; the French are neutralised Conspiracy with Mir Jafar 57-60: Plassey, 23 June 1757 4.3 The Black Hole Tragedy (1756): fact versus propaganda What happened During the capture of Calcutta, British prisoners were locked overnight in a small, airless guardroom in Fort William The colonial account Written by J.Z. Holwell, a survivor and briefly Governor of Bengal. It claimed that 146 were locked in and 123 died of suffocation Modern historians The actual number of dead was approximately 30 to 40 Why it mattered It became a powerful propaganda tool to justify the EIC's military response against Siraj 56-57 and to demonise Indian rulers in the British public imagination 1760 Holwell built a monument in memory of the Black Hole Tragedy 1821 It had fallen into ruin and was demolished 1901 Viceroy Curzon 99-05 (1899-1905) built a marble replica at the same spot 1940 Netaji Bose led a big agitation to remove it, calling it colonial propaganda to tarnish Siraj 56-57's image, and used the campaign to build Hindu-Muslim unity Result The monument was not demolished but shifted from the public square to the graveyard of St. John's Church, Calcutta, where it stands today The slide puts the 1940 result a little more sharply than the handout: Netaji Bose's agitation for demolition "forced the British to shift it" to the graveyard of St. John's Church. Both agree it was shifted, not demolished.

items.t: 5 · Robert Clive 57-67, the conspiracy and the battle
items.x: Because Siraj dared to act, the EIC sends Clive. Notice how he wins: by a deal, not by force. Was the Battle of Plassey (23rd June 1757) really a battle? 5.1 Clive 57-67 recaptures Calcutta and neutralises the French Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Madras with Royal military forces and recaptured Calcutta. The Treaty of Alinagar (Alinagar was the name Siraj 56-57 had given to Calcutta) restored all EIC privileges. Clive 57-67 destroyed Hugli port, which was being used by the French, and defeated the French at Chandarnagar (the slide adds: a French settlement since 1690). The reason: the Anglo-French conflict was live as part of the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63). Clive recaptures Calcutta; the French are neutralised The French threat in Bengal was neutralised. Plassey field: the Bengal Army with Siraj 56-57 on higher ground, rain falling on it; below, advancing upward, Clive 57-67 + EIC army + British Royal military. The Company's army and the Royal (King's) military are different forces (matters for the plunder figures in section 6). Clive 57-67 was Governor of the Bengal Presidency of the EIC in two terms, 1757-60 and 1765-67. 5.2 Plassey, 23 June 1757: conspiracy, not a battle What happened next was not war: it was conspiracy. Mir Jafar 57-60 was the commander of Bengal's army. That is what the books say. Technically the Subahdar was the commander of the army. Mir Jafar 57-60 was the Bakshi (Bakhshi) at the province level, that is the war paymaster and head of military intelligence. Since Siraj 56-57 was young and inexperienced, in practice Mir Jafar 57-60 was the real commander. He approached Clive 57-67 and made a deal with the EIC to remove Siraj 56-57. At the Battle of Plassey (1757), Mir Jafar 57-60 ensured that the bulk of the Bengal army did not fight and turned back. Siraj 56-57 was easily defeated and fled. He was later captured and beheaded on the orders of Miran, Mir Jafar 57-60's son. Mir Jafar 57-60 became Subahdar (he was again Subahdar from 1763 to 1765). But he was now the EIC's puppet, as the EIC did not withdraw from the military domination established after the defeat of Siraj 56-57. The political supremacy of the EIC in India had begun. Takeaway: Plassey was no real battle. The EIC's victory in Bengal came from court conspiracy. The first real military victory for the EIC comes seven years later, at Buxar (1764). Exam points of the Plassey slide: "made a deal with EIC", "Bengal army did not fight", "Mir Jafar 57-60", "EIC's puppet", "EIC's political supremacy in India had begun". This is exactly statement 3 of Prelims 2004. Prelims 2004: answer (b) Only 3. Statement 1: Ibrahim Lodi lost the First Panipat (1526) to Babur 26-30; in the Third Panipat (1761) Abdali defeated the Marathas. Statement 2: Tipu 82-99 Sultan was killed in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1798-99, Srirangapatna), not the Third (1789-92); board: [4th 1799]. Statement 3 is correct: Mir Jafar 57-60, the Bakhshi and de facto commander (Siraj 56-57 was young), conspired with Clive 57-67 and kept the bulk of the Bengal army out of Plassey (1757).

Because the victory was a bought one, the EIC collects the payment. Follow the money: cash, then trade, then gold, then army, then a new puppet. What did the EIC extract from Bengal after Plassey? Remember that companies are organisations with a profit motive, and the EIC was a company even if it had started behaving as a State. The immediate financial settlement after Plassey was staggering. 6.1 The cash The Royal British military 2,75,000 pounds, for distribution to soldiers (not the EIC army, which was different) Immediately after the Battle of Plassey 1757 Clive 57-67 personally 2,34,000 pounds, plus a personal jagir of 35,000 pounds per annum Immediately after the Battle of Plassey 1757 The EIC Rs 2.25 crore Immediately after the Battle of Plassey 1757 The EIC, as "political gifts" from Bengal A further 2.5 million pounds Between 1757 and 1765 Plunder table grouping: first three rows = "immediately after BoPlassey 1757"; last row = "1757-65". Stressed: "personal jagir" and "2.5 million pounds extracted as political gifts". Scale of 2.5 million pounds (handout): multiply by 250 for inflation alone (Retail Price Index). Or: Britain's GDP in 1760 was 70 million pounds, so 2.5 million = 3.5% of GDP; 2026 UK GDP is 2.27 trillion pounds; 3.5% of that = 80 billion pounds or 108.5 billion USD; multiplier approximately x32,000. 6.2 Beyond the cash: Bengal's economy and polity, the EIC's trade structure and the EIC army Private domestic trade via Gomastas; Bengal treasury money and the Drain 1. Private trade, international and now domestic too After Plassey there was rampant misuse of Dastaks. EIC officials made large fortunes not just from private international trade but also from private domestic trade. This domestic trade was conducted through Indian agents called Gomastas, who procured goods directly from peasants and artisans, cutting out Indian merchants and traders. They also did not pay domestic taxes on this trade, which hurt further the Indian merchants competing against them. Before: ryots and artisans sold to the Indian merchant, who sold to the EIC. Now the Indian merchant is cut out and goods go "via Gomastas [Indian agents of the EIC]" straight to EIC officers. Stressed: "Private trade", "Domestic trade", "paid no domestic tax". 2. The structure of the EIC's international trade changed: the Drain of Wealth begins Before Plassey, gold had to be shipped from Britain to buy Indian goods. After Plassey, Bengal's own Diwani revenues funded the purchase of not just Indian but also Chinese goods: tea, silk, porcelain. Further, gold from the Bengal treasury was also shipped to Britain. Thus, from gold inflow before 1757, there was now gold outflow from India. Hence began the Drain of Wealth. "The EIC took money from the Bengal treasury" and used it to: buy Indian goods and export them; buy Chinese goods and sell them in Europe; take gold to Britain; build a large army. Earlier: gold INFLOW to India. Now: gold OUTFLOW from India = DRAIN. Wording. The handout and slide say that after Plassey "Bengal's own Diwani revenues" funded purchases, but the Diwani was legally received only in 1765 (section 8.2). The board says "money from the Bengal treasury" and calls the 1757-65 extraction illegal plunder, legalised in 1765. In an answer write "Bengal's revenues" or "Bengal treasury" for 1757-65 and "Diwani revenues" from 1765. 3. A large standing army The EIC also used the Plassey Plunder to build its own large standing army. For a trading company, maintaining a large army made no economic sense (it hurt dividends to shareholders). But now it could be funded from Bengal's extracted wealth rather than from company profits. Thus Robert Clive 57-67 laid the foundation of the real military strength of the EIC and of Empire Building by the EIC. 4. A change of puppet When Mir Jafar 57-60 could no longer meet the EIC's growing financial demands, the EIC replaced him with his son-in-law, Mir Qasim 60-63, an efficient administrator (the slide says "a brilliant administrator"). Hence the EIC was the real political power in Bengal after 1757. How Plassey changed the trade structure (the Drain) Before 1757: gold is shipped from Britain to buy Indian goods: gold inflow to India Plassey 1757: military domination; a puppet Subahdar Bengal's own revenue now pays for Indian goods (exported) and Chinese goods (tea, silk, porcelain, sold in Europe) Gold from the Bengal treasury is shipped to Britain, and the plunder pays for a large standing army After 1757: gold outflow from India = the Drain of Wealth 6.3 The Nawabs of Bengal: the succession Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) The Nawab of the 1717 Farman: accepted it in part, resisted Dastak abuse and the Royal Mint Shuja-ud-din 27-39 Continuity Nawab: a low-drama interim Sarfaraz Khan (1739-40) Added on the board between Shuja-ud-din 27-39 and Alivardi Khan 40-56 (the 1739-40 gap) Alivardi Khan 40-56 Pragmatic; tolerated the EIC's provocations and warned Siraj 56-57 on his deathbed Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 Precious grandson; stopped Dastak abuse; Black Hole; defeated at Plassey on 23 June 1757, then beheaded Mir Jafar 57-60 The EIC's puppet after Plassey (ruled 1757-60, then 1763-65) Mir Qasim 60-63 Son-in-law of Mir Jafar 57-60; shifted the capital to Patna (Bihar); militarised; ended Dastak abuse; then rebelled Najm-ud-Daula (1765) The Nizamat reduced to a puppet role: the Dual Government (1765-72) begins Reign-year code for Mir Jafar 57-60. The handout text writes Mir Jafar 57-60 (again Subahdar 1763-65); the slide table and the handout flow chart write Mir Jafar 57-65; the board writes "Jafar 57-60, 63-65". All mean two terms: 1757-60 and 1763-65, with Mir Qasim 60-63 in between. This notebook keeps 57-60.

items.t: 7 · Battle of Buxar (1764): the EIC gets the right to rule
items.x: Because the new puppet refuses to obey, a real war follows. Ask: who is on each side, and who really fought? 7.1 Why did Mir Qasim 60-63 rebel? Mir Qasim 60-63 was an able man and had no intention of remaining a puppet. To escape the EIC's constant supervision, he shifted his base from the capital Murshidabad to Bihar, where he could gather resources and build an army quietly. (The slide table and the handout's flow chart say he shifted the capital to Patna, which is in Bihar.) To gather money for the army he punished zamindars who underreported their land revenue. Battle of Buxar (1764): why Mir Qasim rebelled For the support of Indian merchants he abolished all internal duties on domestic trade (like GST today; the slide says "think 0 GST"). This brought a level playing field between Indian merchants and the EIC officials who had been doing untaxed domestic trade via their Gomastas since 1757. This autonomous behaviour was intolerable to the EIC. A battle was fought in Bihar; Mir Qasim 60-63 was defeated, and the EIC brought back Mir Jafar 57-60 as puppet Nawab of Bengal (1763-65). Mir Qasim 60-63 escaped westward to Awadh (the slide: with money) and forged an alliance with Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 of Awadh and Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06. Shuja 54-75 agreed on the promise of 3 crore rupees, the territory of Bihar and its treasury, after victory. Board: Murshidabad to Bihar: Mir Qasim 60-63 moves west, away from the EIC's eyes. Awadh | "Bi Be" (Bihar, Bengal): after defeat he crosses west out of the Bengal Suba into Awadh. Stressed: "Punished zamindars", "support of Indian merchants", "Shah Alam II 60-06", "Shuja 54-75 joined", "3 crore rupees + Bihar and its treasury", and "EIC brought Mir Jafar 57-60 back as puppet Nawab (1763-65)". 7.2 Why Shah Alam II 60-06 was in Awadh Danger at Delhi Shah Alam II 60-06 had left Delhi, frustrated with court factionalism and fearing for his life after the murders and brutalities inflicted on his predecessors by Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk (also known as Gaddar-ul-Mulk) Two Emperors destroyed by their own Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk blinded Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur 48-54 in 1754 and murdered Emperor Alamgir II 54-59 in 1759 His own kingdom So Shah Alam II 60-06 left Delhi to establish his own kingdom in Bengal, which had stopped paying tribute since 1751 1761 He attacked Bengal in 1761 but was defeated by the EIC. The EIC still respected him, since he was Emperor of Hindustan In Awadh Since then he was in Awadh and had chosen Shuja 54-75 as his Wazir 7.3 The battle and after The Battle of Buxar (1764) was fought in Bihar. All preparations had been made for a defensive strategy: laying siege to the fort where the EIC army was stationed. But Shuja 54-75 lost patience. Against the explicit advice of Mir Qasim 60-63, he switched to an offensive strategy and ordered a direct attack on the fort, handing the advantage to the EIC. The battle was closely fought, and at one point the Indian side appeared to be winning. Battle of Buxar 1764: Awadh side against EIC + Bengal Then the EIC commander Hector Munroe launched a final charge and turned the tables. Clive 57-67 was in London at the time. Mir Qasim 60-63 Escaped and died somewhere later Shuja 54-75 Was surprised to find himself not beheaded Shah Alam II 60-06 Was treated with respect, as in him resided the symbolic sovereignty of the Mughal State. With him as an ally, the foreigner EIC's legal right as a political power in India would be stronger Who really fought at Buxar. Indian side: only Awadh was a State; the Mughal Emperor was there "practically as an individual" and Mir Qasim 60-63 "as an individual" (no State behind either). Other side: EIC + Bengal (puppet Mir Jafar 57-60, 1763-65 term). A very closely fought battle, so the judgement: in 1764, AT BEST, EIC military power = one of the multiple Indian kingdoms. Not yet a superpower. 7.4 The teacher's question: why was the EIC able to build an empire? Why was the EIC able to build an empire? imp Reason: Indian territory had multiple States and not one State ruling the whole of India. The States were not united: each had a territory motive and each kingdom wanted to be an empire = rivalry, which "is very natural". Therefore resources were not united: economic and military. So a power that was "at best one of the multiple Indian kingdoms" in 1764 could defeat or ally with them one at a time. Warning: "Please don't use it to bash India, bash Indians and lament Indian unity." Correct statement: Indian KINGS were not united, not "Indians were not united". Starred comparison: Why was China not politically conquered? It was weak, but it was ONE State: the Manchu dynasty, till 1911.

Because the EIC has now won both ways, it writes the peace. Remember the three counterparties: Paper (Emperor), Power (Bengal), Pay (Awadh). Why is the Treaty of Allahabad of 1765 so important, and what exactly did it decide? Why was the EIC able to build an empire? Treaty of Allahabad 1765: three signatories, three sets of clauses Clive 57-67 was sent back to India from London after the Buxar victory to negotiate the settlement. The Treaty of Allahabad (ToA 1765) was signed by Clive 57-67 on behalf of the EIC, and by Shah Alam II 60-06 and Shuja 54-75 on the Indian side. It is one of the most consequential treaties in Indian history, because it laid the legal and structural foundation of the British Empire (the Company State) in India. Clive 57-67 did insider trading on EIC shares. He asked his broker in London to buy EIC shares before the terms of ToA 1765 became public. This made Clive 57-67 one of the wealthiest men in Europe. ToA 1765 can be understood by breaking it into three components: @ Emperor, @ Bengal, @ Awadh. Robert Clive 57-67 Signed for the EIC Shah Alam II 60-06 Mughal Emperor: the Indian side Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 Nawab of Awadh: the Indian side Signatories: stress on "after Buxar". Clive 57-67 = Governor of the Bengal Presidency of the EIC, 1757-60 and 1765-67; the treaty belongs to his second term. Insider trading: Clive 57-67 bought EIC shares before ToA 1765 became public and became the "richest man of Europe". 8.1 @ The Emperor ToA 1765, @ The Emperor: tribute, Delhi, Allahabad and Kora Annual tribute The EIC promised to pay Shah Alam II 60-06 an annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees Not paid Recapture Delhi The EIC promised to militarily help him recapture Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans (who had held it since 1761) No army was supplied Allahabad and Kora Given to him (taken from Awadh) so that the Emperor maintains his status His seat This was deliberate and clever. The EIC was absorbing itself into the existing legal-political structure of the Mughal State, positioning itself as a Mansabdar (who maintains an army for the Emperor and pays tribute), and Bengal became, in legal terms, the EIC's Watan Jagir. Recall: this is exactly how Rebel States got absorbed into the Mughal Empire instead of declaring independence (Chapter 3). In practice the EIC paid neither the Rs 26 lakh nor did it supply an army to recapture Delhi. It was all legal formality. The EIC is trying to become part of the Indian political-legal structure, that is, a Mansabdar. Mapping: (1) mansab = post: the finance ministership [Diwani] of Bengal; (2) a Mansabdar maintains an army for the king = helping the king militarily: the promise of help to recapture Delhi; (3) a Vatan Jagir holder pays tribute to the Emperor: the Rs 26 lakh. So "Bengal is LIKE a Vatan Jagir of the EIC" and the EIC is the FM of Bengal. LIKE = a legal dress, not a real one. The handout spells it Watan Jagir; the board (and Chapter 7) writes Vatan Jagir. Same term. The handout diagram adds that the country stayed "technically Mughal till 1858". 8.2 @ Bengal 8.2.1 Dual Government (1765-72) First, the background: who did what in a Mughal Suba. Suba system under Akbar 56-05: Nazim, Diwan, Bakshi Nazim / Subadar Military commander + law and order The centre (the King) Diwan "CM + FM": civil administration and the finance of the Suba The centre (the Wazir's line), not the Nazim Bakshi Military intelligence + war paymaster The centre (the Mir Bakshi's line), not the Nazim Deputies Naib Nazims, Naib Diwans, Naib Bakshis Their own heads Under Akbar 56-05 the three provincial officers did not report to each other: checks and balances. By 1717 in Bengal the system was diluted and checks and balances ended: the Subadar / Nawab became "like a King" and all reported to him at the Suba level. Hence Mir Jafar 57-60, the Bakshi (war paymaster and head of military intelligence), mattered at Plassey. Chain of reporting in 1717 and in 1765 1717: the link between Delhi and the Subadar is cut; the Bakshi, the Diwan and other Mansabdars all report to the Subadar. 1765: two separate heads under Delhi again: the Subadar, holding the Nizamat "minus military", and the Diwan, now the EIC, holding the Diwani. The EIC as Diwan does not report to the Nawab. Dual Government (1765-72): the structure Dual Government 1765-72: Diwani, Nizamat and Md Reza Khan Diwani meant revenue administration, control of the revenue (treasury), civil administration and civil justice. The EIC received the Diwani of Bengal Suba, that is Bengal, Orissa and Bihar. This was the first time the EIC formally received a sovereign function, for example the power to tax. Before Buxar the EIC had only trade income (since 31st December 1600). From 1765 it had two incomes: trade income and tax revenue from the richest province of India. The Nizamat remained with the Nawab legally: law and order and criminal justice. The military, in practice, was with the EIC. This arrangement was the Dual Government (1765-72). Diwani The EIC Revenue administration, the treasury, civil administration and civil justice (Civil Courts) over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa Nizamat The Nawab Law and order, police, criminal justice (the military was in practice with the EIC, the teacher adds "since 1757") In practice the EIC appointed a Deputy Nawab (Naib Nazim), Md Reza Khan, as its Diwan. Indian civil servants continued to run the administration, reporting to the EIC on Diwani matters and to the Nawab on Nizamat matters. The Dual Government meant, in effect, that sovereign functions had been split into two and two separate top authorities installed over each. Dual Government = "2 TOP AUTHORITIES": two bosses, BUT one administration. The Nizamat "stayed with" the Nawab, except the military, with the EIC since 1757. Drawn as a Y: Nawab [Nizamat] and EIC [Diwani] at the top, both meeting at the Deputy Nawab (Naib Nazim), then one long line of officials: "Admin = Indians". The men on the ground were the same Indian officials; only the top was split. Diwani notes: "PLUNDER (1757-65) now LEGAL"; "Two incomes now: OLD = TRADE, NEW = revenue of Bengal". Listing differences. Handout text: Diwani = revenue administration, treasury, civil administration, civil justice. Handout treaty diagram: "(NOT health/education)" and Nizamat = "law and order + domestic governance". Slide: Nizamat = law and order + police + criminal justice. For the exam: Diwani = revenue + civil justice; Nizamat = law and order (police) + criminal justice. Why did the EIC not annex Bengal outright? The EIC was a company, and companies work for profit, not for ruling. When the opportunity existed to annex Bengal outright, it chose not to, because annexation would bring administrative costs and responsibilities. Military domination after Plassey 1757 meant the company was not threatened militarily. After Buxar 1764 it secured only the legal right over the finances of Bengal. So now the drain of Bengal's wealth was not illegal plunder but a legal right of the EIC. More reasons for not annexing: "RULING is a tension OR a responsibility" and "lack of experience of ruling". So the EIC took the money (Diwani) and left the headache (Nizamat) with the Nawab. 8.2.2 Policy of Indirect Rule, the 1770 famine and Direct Rule The Policy of Indirect Rule was now formally installed in Bengal's Nizamat. The three elements of Indirect Rule are: The three elements of Indirect Rule (PoIR) The King or Nawab is a puppet. A British Resident is stationed in court. The Resident controls the puppet and thus governs indirectly. All three were now in place. Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR): the 3-step process The EIC also obtained the legal right to appoint the Deputy Nawab. This meant that if the Deputy Subahdar refused to follow informal EIC instructions in Nizamat matters, he could be removed by the EIC. By 1772 the British Resident had established complete indirect control over the Nizamat. PoIR is a "3 step PROCESS" and a process "can take years": (a) the Nawab is a puppet; (b) a British Resident is stationed in court "to play the Nawab as a puppet"; (c) the Resident controls him. Board: "Policy implementation takes time"; "Began in Bengal, ToA 1765". Hence "installed" in 1765 but "complete" only by 1772. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (GBF 1770) and the end of the Dual Government In 1772 the Dual Government was formally ended. The Nizamat was taken over legally from the Nawab, and the EIC replaced Indian administrators with its own officers, establishing Direct Rule. Thus the Company State was properly established in Bengal. The reason was the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (GBF 1770). The famine killed one crore people, an estimated one-third of Bengal's population. High land revenue demand and harsh tax collection methods continued even as crops failed and people starved. Grain hoarding by speculators went unchecked, because neither the EIC nor the Nawab took responsibility for famine relief. The EIC claimed that famine relief was the Nawab's domain, and the Nawab lacked the resources for it. Due to the famine, land revenue collection and law and order collapsed, forcing the EIC to establish its own Direct Rule. From 1772 the Nawab of Bengal became as powerless a figurehead as the Chhatrapati of the Marathas had become after the Treaty of Sangola 1750 (Chapter 4). GBF 1770 led to the collapse of L and O (law and order, the Nizamat side) and of LR (land revenue, the Diwani side): both halves of the Dual Government failed together. Direct Rule came under W. Hastings 73-85. PYQ (Mains): "Why were there recurrent famines in British-ruled India?" One paragraph of that answer comes from this topic. Concept of famine: nature factor and human factor Famine = a function of [NATURE factor AND HUMAN factor]. Nature factor: drought or floods reduce the supply of food, so the price of food rises; that alone is not yet a famine. Human factor: prosperous people with good savings can still buy (food can be imported); a caring, welfare State maintains a buffer and imports food. A famine happens when nature fails and the human side fails. In Bengal 1770 the human side failed completely: high revenue demand, hoarding unchecked, nobody in charge of relief. This is the paragraph for the Mains question. Concept of bankruptcy: liabilities and leverage The EIC went bankrupt (1772): two incomes Bankruptcy = being unable to meet liabilities (loan repayment, employees' salaries, price of goods and services bought). In capitalism companies run on LEVERAGE: a 1 crore company takes a 0.4 crore loan; 10 crore takes 4; 100 crore takes 40; 1,000 crore takes 400; and so on. A bank lends when confident of the EMI; an income shock means no EMI, and the company is "Bank-RUPT". "The EIC went BANKRUPT (1772)": it had two incomes, trade and LR (land revenue). Since 1757 it did not bring gold from Britain to buy goods but used Indian (Bengal) money, the money in the Bengal treasury, which was LR paid by the people. When GBF 1770 hit LR, trade income fell with it: both incomes collapsed together = the income shock. This is the money side of why the Dual Government ended in 1772. From the Dual Government to Direct Rule 1765: Diwani to the EIC, Nizamat with the Nawab: power without responsibility at the top, one Indian bureaucracy below High revenue demand and harsh collection continue 1770 Great Bengal Famine: about 1 crore dead (one-third of Bengal); hoarding unchecked; neither the EIC nor the Nawab takes charge of relief Land revenue (Diwani side) and law and order (Nizamat side) collapse; the EIC's two incomes fall; the teacher: the EIC went bankrupt (1772) 1772: the EIC takes the Nizamat legally, replaces Indian administrators with its own officers Direct Rule (W. Hastings 73-85): the Company State is properly established in Bengal 8.3 @ Awadh Compensation Shuja 54-75 was made to pay 50 lakh rupees to the EIC as compensation Benaras Benaras was separated from Awadh (the EIC formally annexed it in 1775) Kora and Allahabad Went to the Emperor Duty-free trade The EIC was granted duty-free trade in Awadh, and Dastak misuse began there too Policy of Ring Fence Initiated with Awadh (see below) Mini Subsidiary Alliance Awadh partially outsourced its military to the EIC (see below) The Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF) The Policy of Ring Fence was initiated with Awadh. It is mainly associated with Warren Hastings 73-85, but Clive 57-67 planted its seed here. It meant creating a military buffer around the EIC's core territory by signing military alliances with neighbouring States. Under this military alliance with Awadh, if anyone attacked the EIC in Bengal, Awadh was treaty-bound to help. Think of it like the US using NATO during the Cold War: a buffer of allied Western Europe protected the core, that is the USA, from the USSR. Prelims match-the-following (forecast). PoRF = Warren Hastings 73-85, even though Clive 57-67 planted the seed with Awadh in 1765. Do not pick Clive 57-67. Ring Fence concept: build a buffer around the core Ring Fence at Bengal: Awadh as buffer Ring Fence analogy. Urban home: a lower-middle-class house puts broken glass on the boundary wall; a rich house puts coils of barbed wire. Rural: a farmer rings his field with a thorny hedge so that cattle do not destroy the crop. The home or field is the CORE interest; the glass, wire or hedge is the Ring Fence. Common idea: BUILD A BUFFER AROUND THE CORE. Applied to 1765: Bengal is the core interest of the EIC; Awadh is the buffer. An enemy of the EIC coming from the west must first pass through Awadh. The fence is "via military alliance". Simple definition: PoRF = military alliance with neighbours. Target diagram: British India = inner circle, allied neighbours = ring, enemies outside. The mini Subsidiary Alliance A mini Subsidiary Alliance was signed. Awadh was forced to partially outsource a core sovereign function, its own military, to the EIC. The size of the Awadh army was reduced, and an EIC army was permanently stationed in Awadh and paid for by Awadh via an annual subsidy. (The handout's joke: the EIC saying "haha, thank you Dupleix 42-54 for the 1751 idea at Hyderabad".) Thus the EIC now partially controlled the military resources of Awadh. Combined with the military alliance, it meant that these resources could be used directly by the EIC itself (under its command) for protecting Bengal. The clauses relating to Awadh are a prelude to the full Subsidiary Alliance that Wellesley 98-05 would formalise three decades later (Chapter 11). A formal and proper Subsidiary Alliance was signed with Awadh in 1801, when Awadh's own army was disbanded and its foreign policy was also taken over by the EIC. But the architecture was drawn here in 1765. Mini Subsidiary Alliance (1765) against the formal one (1801) British Resident Yes (tick) Yes Military alliance Yes (tick) Yes EIC army stationed Yes (tick) Yes Subsidy paid by Awadh Yes (tick) Yes Awadh's own army Size reduced BUT not disbanded (cross) Disbanded (tick, 1801) External sovereign functions ("D, L, FA taken") Legally not taken (cross) Taken (tick, 1801): the handout says its foreign policy was also taken over Two traps. (1) "Awadh was the first to sign a Subsidiary Alliance" is FALSE: the first was Hyderabad 1798. Awadh's 1765 arrangement was only a mini Subsidiary Alliance; the formal one came in 1801. 8.4 Clive 57-67's empire toolkit: born in one treaty Policy of Indirect Rule Puppet Nawab + British Resident + control through the Resident: installed in Bengal's Nizamat Policy of Ring Fence A buffer of allied neighbouring States around the EIC's core: seeded with Awadh Mini Subsidiary Alliance Outsourcing a State's military to the EIC, stationed and subsidised: drawn with Awadh Takeaway: Clive 57-67 was the father of the strategic policy toolkit that the EIC used for empire building. The Policy of Indirect Rule, the Policy of Ring Fence and the mini Subsidiary Alliance were all either invented or operationalised by Clive 57-67 in this single treaty. Thus the foundations of Empire were laid by Clive 57-67 in ToA 1765, and men like Wellesley 98-05 later built upon it. ToA 1765 is the source of all three instruments. Learn them as a set with their places: Indirect Rule in Bengal's Nizamat; Ring Fence and mini Subsidiary Alliance with Awadh.

Last scene: line up the 18th-century battles. Two French battles frame two English ones. 18th-century battles: chronology The four empire-shaping battles fought in 18th-century India: 1 1749 Ambur Dupleix 42-54 (French) defeats Anwaruddin; opens the 2nd Carnatic War 2 1757 Plassey EIC (Clive 57-67) + Mir Jafar 57-60's conspiracy defeats Siraj 56-57 3 1760 Wandiwash EIC (Eyre Coote) crushes the French (Lally); ends the 3rd Carnatic War 4 1764 Buxar EIC (Hector Munroe) defeats Mir Qasim 60-63 + Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 + Shah Alam II 60-06 Prelims 2005: order Ambur (1749), Plassey (1757), Wandiwash (1760), Buxar (1764): option (b). Handout line: two French battles frame two English ones: French high at Ambur, French out at Wandiwash; EIC political breakthrough at Plassey, EIC sovereign breakthrough at Buxar. Fifth battle added in front: Battle of Adyar 1746, 1st Carnatic War (1746-48), Carnatic versus French ("Carnatic vs Fr. and EIC"). Full order: Adyar 1746, Ambur 1749, Plassey 1757, Wandiwash 1760, Buxar 1764. PYQ method: write the year over each battle in option (a): 1760, 1764, 1749, 1757, then pick (b). Do the same in the exam hall. The handout chronology row for Plassey has a printing slip ("Siraj56-5756-57"); read Siraj 56-57. The handout page also ends with the index of the next chapter (Subsidiary Alliance of Wellesley 98-05), which belongs to Chapter 11. From Plassey to the Company State Plassey 1757: conspiracy with Mir Jafar 57-60; conquest (military domination and political supremacy) without rule Plassey Plunder 1757-65: cash, political gifts, Gomasta trade, gold outflow: the Drain begins; a standing army is built Mir Qasim 60-63 resists: moves to Bihar, punishes zamindars, abolishes internal duties; defeated 1763 Buxar 1764: Awadh, the Emperor and Mir Qasim 60-63 lose a closely fought battle to Hector Munroe ToA 1765: the EIC becomes Diwan of Bengal Suba: the plunder becomes a legal right; Awadh becomes a buffer Dual Government 1765-72: two top authorities, nobody responsible; Great Bengal Famine 1770 1772: Nizamat taken over; Direct Rule; the Company State is properly established Nature No real battle: court conspiracy The EIC's first real military victory; closely fought EIC commander Robert Clive 57-67 Hector Munroe (Clive 57-67 was in London) Indian side Siraj 56-57; the bulk of his army did not fight (Mir Jafar 57-60) Mir Qasim 60-63 + Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 + Shah Alam II 60-06 What the EIC got Military domination and political supremacy; a puppet Subahdar; the Plassey Plunder The Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa through ToA 1765: a legal sovereign function The handout's phrase The EIC's political breakthrough The EIC's sovereign breakthrough Wealth Illegal plunder (1757-65) The drain becomes a legal right (from 1765)

The Doctor's gift (1717). The EIC is just a trader with a few Farmans: 1613 a factory at Surat, 1618 factories across the empire (Thomas Roe), 1691 duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year. Then the EIC surgeon Dr William Hamilton cures Emperor Farrukhsiyar 13-19, and the reward is the 1717 Farman, the Magna Carta of the Company: duty-free trade, the Royal Mint, and rent of 38 villages around Calcutta. The Nawab says yes, but. MQK 17-27 allows duty-free trade but no Dastak misuse; refuses the Royal Mint (it hurts sovereignty and his commission); allows renting villages but not buying them. The cheating begins. Officers use the Dastak, a duty-free pass meant for EIC goods, to do private trade. By 1750 private trade is 1,00,000 pounds a year, about 50 times their salaries, and Bengal loses duty revenue. Interlopers break the Royal Charter; free merchants sell to the EIC in India; Dastak misuse breaks Indian law. A young Nawab says enough (1756-57). Alivardi Khan 40-56 had tolerated the EIC (he was pragmatic, and Adyar 1746 had shown the strength of European infantry). His grandson Siraj 56-57, young and disliked at court, stops the Dastak misuse. The EIC shelters Krishna Ballabh and adds fortifications, so Siraj seizes Kasimbazar and then Calcutta, which he renames Alinagar. The Black Hole story is born (146 locked in and 123 dead in Holwell's account; modern estimate 30 to 40). Clive returns. Clive 57-67 arrives from Madras with the Royal military, recaptures Calcutta, signs the Treaty of Alinagar (all EIC privileges restored), destroys Hugli and beats the French at Chandarnagar (the Seven Years' War is on). Plassey, 23 June 1757: the conspiracy. Mir Jafar 57-60, Siraj's Bakshi (bag = war paymaster, binoculars = head of military intelligence), makes a deal with Clive. At Plassey the bulk of the army does not fight; Siraj flees and is beheaded on the orders of Miran, Mir Jafar's son. The EIC has conquest, not rule. The loot. Plunder 1757-65: 2,75,000 pounds to the Royal military, 2,34,000 pounds plus a jagir of 35,000 a year to Clive 57-67, Rs 2.25 crore to the EIC, and 2.5 million pounds of political gifts. Gomastas run untaxed private trade; Bengal's treasury buys Indian and Chinese goods and sends gold to Britain: the Drain begins; a large army is built. When Mir Jafar 57-60 cannot pay more, Mir Qasim 60-63 replaces him. The puppet rebels. Mir Qasim 60-63 shifts his base to Bihar, punishes zamindars who underreported revenue, abolishes all internal duties. He is defeated in 1763, escapes to Awadh, and forms a league with Shuja 54-75 and Shah Alam II 60-06 (who is in Awadh because he left Delhi fearing Imad-ul-Mulk). Buxar, 1764: the real battle. Seven years after Plassey a closely fought battle is won by Hector Munroe (Clive 57-67 is in London). Shuja 54-75 had attacked the fort against Mir Qasim's advice. This is the EIC's first real military victory. Allahabad, 1765: Paper, Power, Pay. Paper: the Emperor gets promises (Rs 26 lakh tribute, help to retake Delhi) that are never kept, plus Allahabad and Kora. Power: the EIC gets the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (Nizamat stays with the Nawab): the Dual Government, with Md Reza Khan. Pay: Awadh pays Rs 50 lakh, loses Benaras, and becomes the buffer (Ring Fence, mini Subsidiary Alliance). Indirect Rule, Ring Fence and the mini SA are Clive 57-67's toolkit. The bill comes due (1770-73). The Great Bengal Famine 1770 kills about one-third of the population while neither the EIC nor the Nawab takes charge. Land revenue and law and order collapse and the EIC goes bankrupt (1772). The EIC takes over the Nizamat; W. Hastings 73-85 carries Direct Rule: the Company State stands.
