Chapter 12 title: Anglo-Mysore Wars (1766-99) + Travancore + Carnatic The board answers the one Mains question wanted from this chapter: "Why Indian States lost?" (1) Why multiple States? Each State's motive was T (territory), and territory means rivalry; rivals do not form a stable alliance of Indians (sad face). (2) Why did States lose territory and sign the SA? Three branches: Factionalism (Indians split); War defeats (and fear of neighbours: Hyderabad joined the EIC for protection, Chapter 11); Internal revolts (Travancore). (3) The EIC's opportunity: (B) Better leadership and Better army. Unreadable marks: the last line "(4)# (circled sign)" and the circled "2" in "alliance (2) of Indians". The circled T is read as territory, as in Chapter 10. Timeline of the EIC's key wars: Plassey to the Sikh Wars The EIC's wars in course order: Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764 (Chapter 10); 1st Anglo-Mysore 1767 to the 4th (1799) (this chapter); 1st Anglo-Maratha 1775 to the 3rd (1817-19) (Chapter 13); 1st Anglo-Sikh 1844-45 to the 2nd (1849). Hold these as the skeleton of the whole EIC conquest. The four Anglo-Mysore Wars on one line: Won, Tie, Lost, Lost 1st 1767-69 Won by Mysore Madras 1769 No loss of territory for Mysore 2nd 1780-84 Tie (the handout: stalemate); reason: the French factor Mangalore 1784 No loss of territory for Mysore 3rd 1790-92 Lost Seringapatam 1792 Huge territory loss for Mysore: gains for the EIC's Madras Presidency, the Marathas and Hyderabad 4th 1799 Lost; reason: the French factor Mysore reorganised under an SA (1799) Huge territory loss for Mysore Two groupings: the first two wars cost Mysore no territory; the last two cost it huge territory, shared by the EIC's Madras Presidency, the Marathas and Hyderabad. 2nd and 4th wars: "Reason: Fr FACTOR": the 2nd began when the EIC seized the French port of Mahe (1779), the 4th when Tipu 82-99's talks with Napoleon gave Wellesley 98-05 his pretext.

items.t: 1 · Why was Mysore such a serious threat?
items.x: Because Mysore built a war machine and a trading State, it frightened the EIC and every neighbour. Ask: what is the goal and what is the tool of Military Fiscalism? Why Mysore was a serious threat: Military Fiscalism Hyder Ali 61-82 and then Tipu 82-99 made Mysore more than a State trying to survive: it tried to dominate the trade, the coastline and the politics of South India. That made it a threat to every neighbouring power, and to the EIC in two special ways. 1.1 Military Fiscalism Mysore followed Military Fiscalism: the primary goal of maximising State revenue was to fund an ever-stronger military. (The EIC had followed the same model since 1765 to build its own strong military.) Under Hyder Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99, Mysore built a centralised State with a modern military and a navy, with French assistance. France gave arms and technical support in exchange for trade concessions, to counter EIC trade. The French connection made both the EIC and the neighbouring Indian States even more anxious. Military Fiscalism: Military = GOAL, Fiscalism = TOOL. Frame for the chapter: each player has goals (TRADE + T for territory) and efficient tools to achieve them. Mysore's goal is military strength; its tool is revenue maximisation. Under all three: "Anxiety/RIVALRY @ Ma, Hyd, Tr, Ca" (Marathas, Hyderabad, Travancore, Carnatic), the four neighbours who feared Mysore. 1.2 Mercantilist trading State Tipu 82-99 set up a State-owned trading company that entered international trade directly. Mysore was acting as a rival Mercantilist State, exactly as the EIC did. Two mercantilist powers competing over the same trade routes and coastal markets cannot coexist easily. In the late 1780s he put a trade embargo on exports of pepper, cardamom and sandalwood from ports under Mysore's control, and barred local merchants from dealing with British traders entirely. Malabar was a critical source of pepper for the EIC and had been under Mysore's control since 1766. He brought in his own Mauludi calendar: a new lunisolar calendar based on the Prophet's birth era, introduced to replace the Islamic Hijri calendar. He sent delegations to France, Turkey (the Ottoman Empire) and Egypt to seek anti-British alliances. Takeaway: the EIC-Mysore rivalry was not just a military conflict. It was a clash between two entities following the same model (Military Fiscalism plus Mercantilism) in the same geography. Only one could win. The EIC's diplomatic advantage: Mysore's ambitions also threatened every neighbouring State, so coalitions against Mysore were easy to build. "Trade embargo" (late 1780s) is the economic background that leads to the 3rd A-My 1790-92. France (the delegations, under "Other aspects") is a Prelims hook; see Prelims 2001 below. Prelims 2001: answer (d) Tipu 82-99 Sultan 82-99. Reign codes beside the options place each ruler: Haider Ali 61-82 (built the French-model army but set up no modern embassies), Mir Qasim 60-63 (Nawab of Bengal, Buxar 1764), Shah Alam II 60-06 (the Mughal Emperor). Tipu 82-99's delegations to France, Turkey and Egypt are the "embassies on modern lines." Map of South India: territories gained and lost in the Mysore Wars Working map for the chapter. Guntur sits inside the Northern Sarkars: under the 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad, Hyderabad gave the Northern Sarkars to the EIC (4 of the 5 districts; Guntur was not given) and the EIC promised 7 lakh rupees a year plus military help to Hyderabad against Mysore (and, as written, against the Marathas "Ma" in future if needed). Lost in the 3rd war: Malabar, Bara Mahal (Baramahal), Dindigul. Lost in the 4th: Kanara, Coimbatore. Seringapatam is Mysore's capital; Mangalore its coastal port; Coorg lies between them (section 8).

Because the threat was real, the EIC and Hyderabad moved in 1766 and Hyder broke the coalition. Ask: who was paid how much? 1st Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69): the reason 2.1 Reason Even before Hyder Ali 61-82 came to power, he had begun modernising his army with French help (the French were present in Mahe). In 1755 he set up a modern arsenal (arms factory) at Dindigul Fort. This continued friendship threatened the EIC. 1766: Hyder Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar (the slide adds Calicut), important for the spice trade. The same year, the EIC promised to help Hyderabad invade Mysore, so that the EIC would get the Northern Sarkars (important to connect Bengal with Madras). (Recall: in 1766 Hyderabad gave the EIC the Northern Sarkars in return for protection against Mysore and the Marathas.) The Marathas also saw Mysore as a rival and joined. So the EIC crafted a triple alliance of EIC, Hyderabad and Marathas against Mysore. (It was formed twice; the 2nd time in 1790.) "[not Part of Travancore]" beside Malabar and Calicut: the 1766 annexation took Malabar and Calicut, not Travancore (Chapter 7). Map line Madras through Andhra to Bengal: the EIC wanted the Northern Sarkars as a land link between its two Presidencies. "+ 7 lakh Rs p.a. to HYD": what the EIC promised Hyderabad for the Sarkars. "3rd A-My [1790-92]" marks the second formation of the triple alliance. 2.2 Events Hyder Ali 61-82 broke the coalition through skilled diplomacy: 1767: he paid the Marathas Rs 35 lakh to exit the war. Then he allied with Hyderabad: he gave the Nizam Rs 20 lakh, promised to make the Nizam's son Nawab of Carnatic, and agreed to a joint future attack on Carnatic (it was under Md Ali 52-95, an ally of the EIC). 1768: Hyderabad feared a counter-invasion of Hyderabad itself by the EIC and exited by making peace with the EIC. 1769: Hyder Ali 61-82 had outmanoeuvred the EIC forces and marched to the gates of Madras. Meanwhile the EIC navy from Bombay captured coastal areas of Mysore, e.g. Mangalore. "IR: No permanent friends or enemies in foreign policy": the Marathas and Hyderabad were EIC allies in 1766 and Hyder 61-82's partners (or paid-off neutrals) in 1767-68. "BY eic" under "made peace" (a caret mark, hard to read: check your notebook): the Hyderabad peace seems to be one made with the EIC's initiative. Stressed: Madras, "EIC's Bombay" navy and Mangalore: a land front at Madras and a sea front on the west coast. 2.3 Result: the Treaty of Madras (1769) The EIC, fearing the destruction of Madras, was forced to sign the Treaty of Madras (1769). Both sides returned conquered territories and agreed to a defensive military alliance: each promised to help the other if attacked by a third party. This was a PoRF arrangement only on paper (PoRF = Policy of Ring Fence, Chapter 10): a fake alliance in practice, as the very next war showed. Military alliances: offensive versus defensive Why "military alliance" is taught here: the 1769 treaty was a defensive alliance. Offensive alliance: valid even when one member is the aggressor (Pact of Steel 1939, Germany and Italy). Defensive alliance: valid only when a member is the victim of aggression (NATO 1949, SEATO 1954, Baghdad Pact 1955, later CENTO 1958). Example: Pakistan was a member of these defensive blocs, but in the 1965 and 1971 wars Pakistan was the aggressor, so the pacts did not bind the others. Rule: a defensive clause is only as good as the question "who attacked whom".

items.t: 3 · 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84): how the EIC broke the Mysore-Marathas-Hyderabad alliance
items.x: Because the 1769 alliance was empty and Mahe was seized, Hyder struck again and a Confederacy formed. Ask: how did Hastings split it? 3.1 Reason for war 1771: the Marathas attacked Mysore, and the EIC refused to honour its 1769 treaty obligation to come to Mysore's defence. The final trigger: France entered the American War of Independence (1776-83) against Britain in 1778, and the EIC seized the French port of Mahe in Malabar in 1779. Mahe was under Mysore's military protection, and through it Hyder Ali 61-82 was importing French arms and ammunition. Mahe as the supply route: France to Mahe to Mysore. Seizing Mahe cut the arms line, so Hyder 61-82 attacked. World frame: the American Revolution runs 1765-83 in two phases, violent protest 1765-76 and the American War of Independence 1776-83. France joined in 1778: a war in America opens a war in India (the 2nd war is tagged "Fr FACTOR"). 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84): the reason, French Mahe 3.2 Events Hyder Ali 61-82 invaded Carnatic (an EIC ally) and captured Arcot (the capital). He then inflicted one of the worst defeats ever suffered by a European army in India at the Battle of Pollilur (September 1780): Colonel Baillie's disciplined infantry formations were annihilated, Hyder Ali 61-82's troops using iron-cased rockets to devastating effect. Pollilur was a shock to the EIC. Battle of Pollilur (September 1780) has been tested in UPSC Prelims (the rocket-warfare innovation of Mysore). Keep the four tags: Sep 1780, Colonel Baillie, iron-cased rockets, Hyder Ali 61-82. 2nd Anglo-Mysore War: Pollilur and the Triple Confederacy The Triple Confederacy (1780-82): an alliance of Marathas, Mysore and Hyderabad against the EIC, established by Nana Fadnis, the de-facto ruler and most important minister in the Peshwa's council. Nana Fadnis (Fadnavis) was the first Indian statesman to understand that the EIC was in India not just for trade but had ambitions of empire building. Hyderabad joined because the EIC had illegally occupied Guntur (one of the 5 districts of the Northern Sarkars, not handed over in 1766) and had stopped paying the annual 7 lakh rupees agreed for ceding the Northern Sarkars. "PRE" beside Nana Fadnis, "1st Indian" stressed: a Prelims line. Board: the three members (My, Ma, Hyd), 1780-82; an arrow from the Marathas to the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) (the Marathas were already at war with the EIC); "Guntur taken by EIC" under Hyderabad (their grievance). A confederacy is an alliance against the EIC: the reverse of the triple alliance of 1766 and 1790. 3.3 How the EIC broke it, and the result Warren Hastings 73-85 broke the coalition through careful diplomacy: He returned Guntur to Hyderabad, removing their grievance. He signed the Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas, which ended the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). The Marathas and Hyderabad withdrew their support, leaving Mysore isolated to fight the EIC alone. Nana Fadnis ensured the Marathas did not send an army in favour of the British (the handout's note: Chanakya Neeti, let both rivals destroy each other). Hyder Ali 61-82 died of cancer in December 1782. Tipu 82-99 took over and continued the war. Result: the Treaty of Mangalore (1784). The war ended in a stalemate. Both sides returned each other's territories; the status quo was maintained. Both of Hastings 73-85's moves are stressed; the war is tagged "(Tie)". Each partner's gain: Hyderabad = Guntur back; the Marathas = the Treaty of Salbai (which also closed their own war with the EIC). The coalition collapsed because each partner's grievance was settled separately. Maps: Anglo-Mysore Wars I and II; Third War territories

items.t: 4 · 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92): when the tide turned
items.x: Because the 2nd war ended in a tie, the EIC waited for a pretext and rebuilt its alliance. Ask: what did Tipu lose in 1792? 4.1 Reason and events Tipu 82-99 attacked Travancore, a formal ally of the EIC. This gave Cornwallis 86-93 the justification to declare war. The EIC formed a Triple Alliance with the Marathas and Hyderabad in 1790 (in 1782-84 the Marathas did not fight Mysore). The combined forces of EIC, Marathas and Hyderabad put Mysore under severe military pressure from multiple directions. Tipu 82-99 fought hard but could not hold against a coordinated three-front campaign. (The handout's Travancore section dates Tipu 82-99's attack on Travancore to 1789 and calls it the pretext for this war: see section 10.1.) Key words: "attacked Travancore", "Cornwallis 86-93", "Triple Alliance". Story: a trigger (Travancore), a Governor General who uses it (Cornwallis 86-93), and the coalition Mysore had broken in 1767 and 1782 now rebuilt against it. The triple alliance of 1766-67 was formed twice, the second time in 1790 (3rd A-My). 4.2 Result: the Treaty of Seringapatam / Srirangapatnam (1792) Territory Mysore lost half its Kingdom, including the rich Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal War fine 3 crore rupees Hostages Two of Tipu 82-99's own sons surrendered to guarantee compliance Every term is stressed: half its Kingdom, 3 crore rupees, Two of Tipu 82-99's own sons, hostages. Map: Malabar [important for spices], Baramahal and Dindigul are the hatched British areas, with small arrows to the Peshwa's and the Nizam's shares, and "Notice: encirclement by EIC": the EIC now held land on Mysore's west (Malabar), south-east (Baramahal) and far south (Dindigul), with allies to its north. Source mismatch on the war's dates. The title and the teacher's board say the 3rd war is 1790-92. The handout text in section 6 writes "1789-92" (counting from Tipu 82-99's attack on Travancore in 1789) and the handout's flow chart (section 5) writes "1789-92" too. Use 1790-92 for the war; 1789 is the Travancore attack. Marked map of South India: Peshwa, Nizam and Tippoo dominions The same historical map is shown twice (before the 3rd war and after the 4th). Use it as a locating tool: Mahe and Calicut (the French and Malabar spice coast), Pondicherry and Karikal (the French towns on the east coast), Guntur (the Northern Sarkars) and the three dominions that divided Mysore. It adds no date.

items.t: 5 · 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): how Mysore finally fell
items.x: Because Tipu looked to Napoleon, Wellesley found his excuse. Ask: why did Hyderabad have no choice? 5.1 Reason Tipu 82-99's ongoing negotiations with Napoleon gave Wellesley 98-05 his political pretext in London. Britain was already at war with France. Wellesley 98-05, an empire builder by nature, used Tipu 82-99's secret letters to the French as proof of a threat and got British approval for war. "(* Recall PIA 1784)": Pitt's India Act 1784 banned offensive wars without the Court's command, so Wellesley 98-05 needed an excuse; the Napoleon letters were it (Chapter 11: the threat was there but not real). The war is tagged "Reason: Fr FACTOR". 5.2 Events and result The EIC and Hyderabad fought Mysore (Hyderabad had to, because of the SA of 1798). Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18 did not send an army, on the advice of Nana Fadnis, despite EIC requests. Arthur Wellesley, commanding his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces, was among the key military commanders in the Siege of Srirangapatnam. Tipu 82-99 died defending his capital. "D, C, FA of HYD with EIC: military alliance, therefore no choice." Since the 1798 SA, Hyderabad's Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs were in the EIC's hands (Chapter 11), so Hyderabad could not refuse to fight. "Arthur Wellesley" and "Royal regiment" are stressed: he was a Royal Army officer, not an EIC officer, commanding his regiment alongside the EIC forces (no reign code: only Richard Wellesley 98-05, the Governor General, is Wellesley 98-05). Result: The best parts of Mysore's remaining territory (Kanara, Coimbatore and others) were divided between the EIC and Hyderabad. The central core of Mysore went back to the old Wodeyar dynasty, with five-year-old Krishnaraja III placed on the throne under a Subsidiary Alliance (1799). The last major military threat to the EIC in the south was over. Some territory was offered to the Peshwa on condition of signing an SA; the Marathas refused, on Nana Fadnis's advice. Key words: Kanara, Coimbatore, Wodeyar dynasty, five-year-old Krishnaraja III, Subsidiary Alliance (1799). Map: Kanara (west coast near Mangalore) and Coimbatore (south-east of Mysore) are the 4th war's gains to the EIC. The 1792 gains were Malabar, Dindigul, Baramahal; the 1799 gains were Kanara, Coimbatore. Do not mix the two lists. Map: Anglo-Mysore War IV (1799), Kanara and Coimbatore Prelims 2004: answer (b) Only 3. For this chapter, carry "Tipu 82-99 died in the 4th war (1799), at Seringapatam, not in the 3rd." The board's side list Abdali, Farrukhabad, Rohilkhand, Awadh against Ma (Marathas) names the Third Panipat sides (Chapter 4); do not add to it from outside the board. Slide and handout agree; no conflict. The handout's flow chart differs from its text in four places. Use the text, the slides and the board. (1) Chart: Hyder 61-82 paid the Marathas "Rs 30 lakh"; text and slide: 35 lakh. (2) Chart: 1792 fine "3.3 crore"; text and slides (stressed on the board): 3 crore. (3) Chart: 3rd war "1789-92"; board: 1790-92 (alert in section 4). (4) Chart lists Malabar among the 1799 gains; text and slide: Malabar was lost in 1792; the 1799 gains were Kanara and Coimbatore. Details only in the chart: Sir Eyre Coote at Porto Novo (1781); "Congreve rockets and French Risalas" at Pollilur (text and slide say iron-cased rockets: use that); a Treaty of Bidanur beside Mangalore; General Meadows in the 3rd war; the siege date 4 May 1799; "zones to Hyderabad" in 1799 and an "honour-share to Marathas" (the text says territory offered to the Peshwa on condition of an SA was refused).

Because the fourth war ended Mysore, ask why. Four reasons, and then the teacher's wider question. 1 No stable alliance Mysore's aggressive expansion and the EIC's diplomacy prevented stable alliances "External ally weak and could not help"; "Domestic - Rivalry" (Indian neighbours were rivals) 2 French naval gap Mysore depended on French arms and ammunition. France was busy with the American War of Independence (1776-83) and then the Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804), and its navy was no match for Britain's. A French fleet able to resupply Mysore at scale never reached the Indian coast Underlined 3 Military Fiscalism over-extension Revenue-maximisation funded a strong army, but war fines (3 crore rupees after the 3rd war) drained the treasury needed for a long campaign; the EIC was relatively rich Circled "BUT" (the strength became the weakness); underlined 3 crore rupees 4 Seringapatam open to siege A three-way coalition (EIC + Marathas + Hyderabad) could surround Mysore from many directions, as in 1789-92 and 1799; the capital's geography became a vulnerability, not a stronghold none Beside reason 1: an external ally (France) was weak and could not help, and the domestic Indian neighbours were rivals (the "multiple States, motive T, rivalry" logic of the title board). Reason 3, circled "BUT": the same Military Fiscalism that made Mysore strong also emptied its treasury: strength and weakness from one source. Verdict: Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 concluded that Mysore was too strong and too ambitious for Indirect Rule to work: it had to be defeated militarily and then subordinated. Mysore fought well and modernised seriously. It lost because it fought largely alone. How the teacher's "Why Indian States lost" skeleton uses this chapter (150 or 250 words): Intro (about 25 words): Indian States lost to the EIC because they were many, not one: each pursued territory, so they were rivals and could not form a stable alliance; the EIC had better leadership and a better army and used diplomacy and war. Body (three branches from the title board): (1) Factionalism: Mysore's expansion made Marathas, Hyderabad, Travancore and Carnatic anxious, so the EIC built the triple alliances of 1766-67 and 1790; Hastings 73-85 broke the Triple Confederacy (1780-82) by settling each partner separately (Guntur to Hyderabad, Salbai with the Marathas). (2) War defeats and fear of neighbours: Mysore lost Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal in 1792 and Kanara and Coimbatore in 1799; Hyderabad, fearing neighbours, signed the first SA (1798) and had no choice but to fight Mysore. (3) Internal revolts: Travancore signed the SA in 1805 to crush a Nair mutiny, and the Kundara Proclamation of 1809 followed; demobilised Mysore soldiers fed Dhondia Wagh (1799-1800). Closing: Mysore fought well and modernised, but fought largely alone; by 1809 the EIC was paramount from the Krishna to Kanyakumari. For a 250-word version, add the Carnatic (Carnatic Debts, annexation 1801) and the Military Fiscalism "BUT" point; for 150 words, keep intro plus the three branches in one or two sentences each. The last board line "(4)# (circled sign)" is unreadable:  for what it adds.

Because the SA disbanded Mysore's army, the jobless soldiers found a leader. Ask: who put him down? After Seringapatam (1799), a former prisoner of Tipu 82-99 named Dhondia Wagh escaped and raised a mounted force from demobilised Mysore soldiers (the SA disbanded the army), raiding the Mysore-Maratha borderlands in 1799-1800. He styled himself "King of Two Worlds" and threatened EIC supply lines. Colonel Arthur Wellesley was sent; Dhondia was killed in action in 1800, with which the EIC was formally supreme in southern India by 1801. Stressed: "SA disbanded the army". A consequence of the SA (Chapter 11): disbanded soldiers had no job and became raiders. Also: "prisoner of Tipu 82-99" (he knew Mysore's army) and "threatened EIC supply lines."

items.t: 8 · A note on Tipu 82-99's religious policy
items.x: A side note on Tipu's religious policy; the slides carry no ink. Ask: what is the handout's conclusion on his secularism? Tipu 82-99's religious approach was syncretic yet contradictory, often a source of confusion. 8.1 Patronage in the Mysore heartland He patronised the Sringeri Sharada Math, wrote letters to its Shankaracharya seeking blessings, got yajnas conducted before wars and made generous grants to several Hindu temples in Mysore 8.2 Coercion in conquered Malabar and Coorg Forced conversions of Nairs and Christians in Malabar; destroyed churches and temples during his campaigns there. The same brutalities in 1785 in Coorg against the Kodavas (the handout's note: mountain warriors who still do not need a licence for certain arms; earlier under the Hindu Nayakas) who were resisting occupation by Mysore Geography North to south: Mysore, Coorg (in the Western Ghats), Malabar. Coorg connected the capital (Seringapatam) to the wealthy coastal ports of Malabar Conclusion Secularism was not a value for Tipu 82-99 but a tactic for domestic stability of his Kingdom, since values (as per the discipline of Psychology) are hardest to change in one's personality Note The King of Coorg allied with the EIC in 1790 and helped Cornwallis 86-93's army navigate the mountains in the 3rd war (1790-92)

Because the Carnatic was a debtor to EIC officials, annexation was the end of a long squeeze. Ask: what were the two charges? The EIC had influence over Carnatic indirectly since the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54), keeping its ally Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah 52-95 on the throne. Its grip tightened after establishing domination over South India's trade after the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63). Six years after Md Ali 52-95's death in 1795, the EIC annexed Carnatic in 1801. (Wars and treaties: Chapter 9.) 9.1 The Carnatic Debts Even before formal annexation, much of Carnatic's wealth had been quietly extracted through the Carnatic Debts. Successive Nawabs borrowed massive sums from private EIC officials at high interest rates, using the Jagirs of Carnatic as collateral. EIC officials collected land revenue from those fertile lands directly as payment of interest. 9.2 Carnatic Treaty (1801): annexation under Wellesley 98-05 Wellesley 98-05 used two justifications: 1. Maladministration by the Nawab (the board adds "Financial": financial maladministration). 2. The accusation that the Nawab had been secretly communicating with Tipu 82-99. Wellesley 98-05 held that a Nawab so financially compromised was not worth preserving even as a puppet. Two small additions carry the point. "Financial" before "Maladministration": the charge was about money (the Carnatic Debts), not law and order. "secretly communicating with Tipu 82-99" is stressed: the same Tipu 82-99 who had been the 4th war's target was the second excuse. Carnatic was annexed outright: direct EIC territory, not an SA State (contrast Mysore, Hyderabad, Travancore).

items.t: 10 · Travancore: what happens when the SA breaks its own promises?
items.x: Because Travancore hedged with the EIC against Mysore, it paid later. Ask: what did the EIC get for crushing a mutiny? 10.1 Travancore before the SA Travancore's modern State was built in the 18th century by Marthanda Varma 29-58, who decisively defeated the Dutch at the Battle of Colachel (1741) and reorganised the kingdom into a centralised revenue-based State. His successor Rama Varma 58-98 maintained the EIC alliance as a hedge against Mysore, relevant during Tipu 82-99's late-1780s expansion and embargo on Travancore's pepper exports (section 1). Rama Varma 58-98's EIC alliance was the trigger for Tipu 82-99's attack on Travancore in 1789, which Cornwallis 86-93 used as the pretext for the 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (section 4). After Rama Varma 58-98's death in 1798, the kingdom entered fiscal and political strain. 10.2 British Resident stationed (1800), Subsidiary Alliance signed (1805) Travancore signed a "Treaty of Perpetual Friendship" with the EIC in 1795 (in Rama Varma 58-98's reign): they agreed to pay for a British force to protect against Tipu 82-99. In 1800 a British Resident was stationed in Travancore's court (the handout's note: can you see the imprint of ToA 1765, Chapter 10?). In 1805 Travancore signed a proper Subsidiary Alliance with Wellesley 98-05. The EIC extracted it in exchange for helping the king crush a revolt by his own Nair troops, who had mutinied over non-payment of salary. The State lost sovereignty on the standard SA template (see the SA terms in Chapter 11). Takeaway: Travancore is the chapter's clearest worked example of how the SA gets extracted: not at sword-point, but in exchange for internal-security help that the EIC Resident has often had a hand in destabilising in the first place. The Nair troops' salary mutiny gave the king an immediate problem; Wellesley 98-05 priced the help at full sovereign concession. Within four years the consequences exploded in the Velu Thampi Dalawa revolt and the Kundara Proclamation (1809). Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 cover the same State from other angles. Chapter 7 gives Marthanda Varma 29-58's trade monopoly and the Colachel victory and tells the Malabar 1766 story; Chapter 11 lists Travancore as the 8th SA signatory (1805), the last under Wellesley 98-05 before his recall. This chapter adds the 1795 Treaty, the 1800 Resident, the mechanism of extraction and the 1809 revolt (Chapter 7, Chapter 11).

items.t: 11 · Velu Thampi Dalawa and the Kundara Proclamation (1809)
items.x: Because the SA's costs were unbearable, Travancore rose. Ask: when and where was the proclamation issued? By 1809 the SA's consequences were unbearable. Velu Thampi Dalawa, Prime Minister of Travancore (1802-09), led a major armed revolt against the EIC, supported by soldiers and peasants angered by heavy subsidy demands and constant British interference in internal affairs, a direct breach of the SA treaty's own promise of non-interference. In January 1809, from the town of Kundara, he issued the Kundara Proclamation (1809): a public call to all Travancoreans to rise against British paramountcy. The revolt was crushed within months. Velu Thampi died later the same year. Travancore was reduced to a subservient SA State. (The handout's note: every consequence of the SA from Chapter 11 (loss of military jobs, high taxes from subsidy pressure, PoIR creeping in illegally) played out here within four years of signing.) The Kundara Proclamation (January 1809) is one of the most significant early revolts against the British in South India. Use that wording. (The handout's flow chart in section 12 says "first organised revolt in south India"; the text and slide say "one of the most significant early revolts": the safer claim in an answer.)

Last scene: the south is closed. Ask: which State was handled how, in which year? The four Mysore wars ended the last big southern rival of the EIC. The Carnatic annexation of 1801, the Travancore SA of 1805 and the SA of 1809 with Cochin completed the southern consolidation. By 1809, with Kundara suppressed, the EIC was paramount from the Krishna to Kanyakumari, setting the stage for the 2nd and 3rd Anglo-Maratha Wars (1803-05, 1817-19) in the north-west and the Deccan (see Chapter 13). Southern consolidation, 1799 to 1809 1799: Mysore falls; the Wodeyars return under an SA 1801: Carnatic annexed outright; direct EIC territory (the EIC formally supreme in the south) 1805: Travancore SA (for crushing the Nair mutiny) 1809: Kundara Proclamation crushed; Cochin SA By 1809: the EIC is paramount from the Krishna to Kanyakumari Figure-only details in this chart (not in the handout text): the ceded zones named as Bellary, Cuddapah and Anantapur (to the Nizam), the "honour-share to Marathas" (the text says the Peshwa was offered territory on condition of signing an SA and refused), Malabar listed with the 1799 gains (it was lost in 1792) and "first organised revolt in south India" for Kundara. Where chart and text differ, use the text and the slide. The handout page for this chapter ends with the index of the next chapter (Why did the Deccan matter, the three Anglo-Maratha Wars, the Pindaris and Francis Hastings 13-23, why the Marathas lost). That belongs to Chapter 13.

Travancore's Treaty of Perpetual Friendship with the EIC 1798 Rama Varma 58-98 dies; Hyderabad signs the first Subsidiary Alliance 1799 4th Anglo-Mysore War: Siege of Seringapatam, Tipu 82-99 dies; Wodeyars restored (Krishnaraja III, age 5) under an SA; Kanara and Coimbatore to the EIC and Hyderabad ★ 1799-1800 Dhondia Wagh raids the Mysore-Maratha borderlands 1800 Dhondia Wagh killed by Colonel Arthur Wellesley; a British Resident is stationed in Travancore 1801 Carnatic annexed by Wellesley 98-05 (Carnatic Debts); the EIC formally supreme in the south ★ 1802 Velu Thampi Dalawa becomes Prime Minister of Travancore (to 1809) 1805 Travancore signs the Subsidiary Alliance (price of crushing the Nair mutiny) ★ 1809 January: Kundara Proclamation of Velu Thampi Dalawa, crushed within months; SA with Cochin; the EIC paramount from the Krishna to Kanyakumari ★

A State that frightened everyone. Hyder Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99 followed Military Fiscalism: the goal was a stronger military and the tool was maximising revenue. France gave arms and support in exchange for trade concessions, and Tipu ran a State-owned trading company and put an embargo on pepper, cardamom and sandalwood. The teacher's four anxious neighbours were the Marathas, Hyderabad, Travancore and the Carnatic. 1766: the first alliance. Hyder Ali 61-82 had a modern arsenal at Dindigul Fort (1755) and in 1766 annexed Malabar and Calicut. The same year, under the Treaty of Hyderabad, the EIC promised to help Hyderabad invade Mysore and received the Northern Sarkars (4 of 5 districts, Guntur kept) for Rs 7 lakh a year. The Marathas joined, giving the triple alliance of EIC, Hyderabad and Marathas. The bribe and the gates of Madras. In 1767 Hyder paid the Marathas Rs 35 lakh to exit, and gave the Nizam Rs 20 lakh plus a promise of the Carnatic Nawabi for his son. Hyderabad made peace with the EIC in 1768. In 1769 Hyder reached the gates of Madras while the Bombay navy took coastal Mysore (Mangalore). The EIC signed the Treaty of Madras: territories returned and a defensive alliance. The teacher marks the 1st war as won by Mysore. A promise broken. In 1771 the Marathas attacked Mysore and the EIC refused its 1769 duty, so the alliance was a paper one. France then joined the American War (1778) and in 1779 the EIC seized the French port of Mahe, under Mysore's protection and Hyder's arms route. Pollilur and the Confederacy. Hyder invaded the Carnatic and took Arcot. At Pollilur (September 1780) his iron-cased rockets annihilated Colonel Baillie's infantry, one of the worst defeats ever suffered by a European army in India. Nana Fadnis, the first Indian statesman to grasp the EIC's empire ambitions, built the Triple Confederacy of Marathas, Mysore and Hyderabad (1780-82); Hyderabad joined over Guntur and the unpaid 7 lakh. Hastings splits the coalition. Warren Hastings 73-85 returned Guntur to Hyderabad and signed the Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas, ending the 1st Anglo-Maratha War. Mysore was left isolated. Hyder died of cancer in December 1782 and Tipu 82-99 continued, until the Treaty of Mangalore (1784): a stalemate, territories returned. The Travancore trigger, 1790-92. Tipu 82-99 attacked Travancore, a formal EIC ally (1789), and Cornwallis 86-93 used it to declare war. The EIC formed a Triple Alliance with the Marathas and Hyderabad in 1790, and Mysore faced a three-front campaign. By the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) Tipu lost half his Kingdom (Malabar, Dindigul, Baramahal), paid 3 crore and gave two sons as hostages. The teacher: notice the encirclement by the EIC. Napoleon and the fall, 1799. Tipu 82-99's talks with Napoleon gave Wellesley 98-05 his pretext in London. Hyderabad had to fight because of its SA of 1798, the Peshwa sent no army on Nana Fadnis's advice, and Arthur Wellesley, with his Royal regiment, was among the key commanders at the siege. Tipu died defending Seringapatam. Kanara and Coimbatore went to the EIC and Hyderabad, and the Wodeyars returned under an SA with five-year-old Krishnaraja III. Four reasons and one answer. Mysore had no stable alliance (its external ally was weak and its Indian neighbours were rivals), a French naval gap (France was busy in 1776-83 and 1792-1804 and its navy could not match Britain's), Military Fiscalism over-extension (the war fine drained the treasury: the teacher's BUT), and a Seringapatam that three coalition armies could surround. Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 judged it too strong for Indirect Rule: it fought well but largely alone. The teacher's Mains skeleton generalises this to why Indian States lost: factionalism, war defeats and fear of neighbours, internal revolts. Clean-up in the south. Dhondia Wagh, a former prisoner of Tipu 82-99, raised a mounted force from soldiers disbanded under the SA, raided the Mysore-Maratha borderlands (1799-1800) as 'King of Two Worlds', and was killed in 1800 by Colonel Arthur Wellesley. In 1801 Wellesley 98-05 annexed the Carnatic, whose Nawabs had borrowed from private EIC officials against their Jagirs (the Carnatic Debts), citing financial maladministration and secret contact with Tipu. It became direct EIC territory, not an SA State. Travancore pays for help. Marthanda Varma 29-58 had built the State and beaten the Dutch at Colachel (1741), and Rama Varma 58-98 kept the EIC alliance as a hedge against Mysore, which triggered Tipu's 1789 attack. Travancore signed a Treaty of Perpetual Friendship in 1795, took a British Resident in 1800, and in 1805 signed a proper SA with Wellesley 98-05, extracted in exchange for crushing a revolt by its own Nair troops over unpaid salary. Kundara, 1809. Velu Thampi Dalawa, Prime Minister 1802-09, led an armed revolt against heavy subsidy demands and constant interference, and in January 1809 issued the Kundara Proclamation calling all Travancoreans to rise. It was crushed within months and he died that year. With the Cochin SA of 1809, the EIC was paramount from the Krishna to Kanyakumari, setting up the 2nd and 3rd Anglo-Maratha Wars.

Prelims 1999 Match years (A. 1775, B. 1780, C. 1824, D. 1838) with events (1. First Anglo-Burmese War, 2. First Anglo-Afghan War, 3. First Anglo-Maratha War, 4. Second Anglo-Mysore War) (c) A-3 B-4 C-1 D-2. Use the year the war broke out, not the year it ended. Write the full range beside each war: 1824-26, 1838-42, 1775-82, 1780-84 Section 2 (1775) and Section 9 (Burma, Afghanistan); the Mysore war is in [[12 Chapter 12]] Prelims 2004 Which pairs are correctly matched: A. AD 1767-69 First Anglo-Maratha War, B. AD 1790-92 Third Mysore War, C. AD 1824-26 First Anglo-Burmese War, D. AD 1845-46 Second Sikh War? Options: (a) 2 and 4 (b) 3 and 4 (c) 1 and 2 (d) 2 and 3 (d) 2 and 3. B and C are right. A is wrong: 1767-69 is the First Anglo-Mysore War (the First Anglo-Maratha War began 1775). D is wrong: 1845-46 is the First Anglo-Sikh War (the Second was 1848-49). Section 2 and Section 9 Prelims 2010 The immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 to invade India and fight the Third Battle of Panipat (a) He wanted to avenge the Marathas' expulsion of his Viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore. (b) is wrong: Adina Beg Khan invited the Marathas, not Abdali. The topic belongs to [[4 Chapter 4]] Section 10 Prelims (year not given) The handout says the Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817) has been tested in UPSC Prelims Two points to carry: (i) Appa Sahib signed the Subsidiary Alliance in 1816 and still fought in 1817: the SA did not prevent the war, its terms caused it. (ii) The "disbanded army" clause was bypassed with Arab and Rohilla mercenaries hired as internal-security retainers Section 6 Mains No Mains PYQ is shown on the slides and the bank has none for this chapter Two book practice Mains questions are in the bank (why the Marathas lost; Subsidiary Alliance against Paramountcy). Skeletons are written below from the notes only The end of this block

Story so far: the Mughals are gone from the stage and the EIC faces the Marathas. Before the details, learn the three wars as one board: reason, result, treaty. Ask: which war was won, and which two lost? The three Anglo-Maratha Wars: reason, result, treaty 1st war (1775-82): reason = factionalism; began at Surat 1775; EIC won; ended at Salbai 1782 with a military alliance (EIC + Marathas). 2nd war (1803-05): reason = factionalism; began with Bassein 1802, an SA by the Swarajya (the Peshwa signing for the Maratha State); Marathas lost; "SA: Scindhia". Gaikwad and Peshwa had already signed SA in 1802 and did not fight, so the fighters were Bhonsle + Scindhia + Holkar. Between the 2nd and 3rd wars: 1816 SA - Bhonsle (Treaty of Nagpur). 3rd war (1817-19): reason = breach of SA by the EIC, i.e. the Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR) as part of the Policy of Paramountcy (PoP); Marathas lost: Holkar signed SA, Swarajya annexed. Bhonsle and the Peshwa had no proper army (the SA had disbanded it); Holkar had one. Read the board with care. (1) The year after "SALBAI" on the 1st war looks like "1789"; the typed slide and the handout say 1782. Use 1782. (2) Reason of the 3rd war: the board says "breach of SA by the EIC" (Residents turned Indirect Rule into puppetry), while a handout bracket calls the 1817 revolt "a violation of SA treaties" (the rulers' revolt). Use the teacher's line for "reason".

items.t: 1 · Why did the Deccan matter so much to the EIC?
items.x: Because the EIC needed coast, cotton and the Malabar side, the Marathas and Mysore stood in its way. Ask: which three reasons did the teacher underline? Why the Deccan mattered to the EIC The Deccan and the Konkan coast were commercially critical to the EIC: a large coastline, a significant cotton trade from Gujarat with China, and Maratha control over parts of the Malabar coast. The Maratha Confederacy along with Mysore were the last major Indian powers able to check EIC expansion across the subcontinent. Three Anglo-Maratha Wars and four Anglo-Mysore Wars (the previous chapter, Chapter 12) decided the outcome. Two commercial reasons: large coastline and cotton; the third is Maratha control of parts of the Malabar coast. The Deccan is drawn as an inverted triangle (inner lines). The small years on the map (1802 along the Peshwa's territory, 1804 along Sindhia, 1805 along Gaikwar, 1803 near Agra and Surat) are not explained in the handout text. The Gaikwar "1805" does not match the text (Gaikwad signed June 1802, Treaty of Cambay). Use the map for where, the text for the years.

Because a Peshwa was thrown out by his own ministers, he sold land to the EIC for help. Ask: why is Purandhar an example of factionalism within the EIC? 2.1 What triggered the war? The cause was factionalism within the Maratha Confederacy itself, a pattern that repeats across all three wars. In 1773 Raghunath Rao 73-74 became Peshwa after the murder of his nephew Narayan Rao 72-73. In the Baarbhai Conspiracy (1774), Nana Fadnis and eleven other ministers of the Peshwa's council removed Raghunath Rao 73-74 from power. Raghunath Rao 73-74 then approached the EIC's Governor of Bombay, William Hornby, and signed the Treaty of Surat (1775). Under it the EIC agreed to help him regain the Peshwaship in return for Salsette and Bassein (Vasai, near Mumbai) along with some revenue from Bharuch and Surat. Factionalism is the root cause. Learn the Peshwas' names and years, the Baarbhai Conspiracy 1774, the Bombay Governor William Hornby, and the deal: "EIC to help him" in return for Salsette and Bassein plus revenue. The deal = help for land and money. The pattern (handout): exactly what happened in the Carnatic and Hyderabad during the Carnatic Wars: a succession dispute, a losing claimant, and Europeans offering military help for territory and influence. Factionalism of Indian States was the Europeans' most reliable ally. See Chapter 9. How the 1st Anglo-Maratha War began 1773: Narayan Rao 72-73 is murdered; Raghunath Rao 73-74 becomes Peshwa 1774, Baarbhai Conspiracy: Nana Fadnis + 11 ministers remove Raghunath Rao 73-74 Raghunath Rao 73-74 goes to the EIC's Governor of Bombay, William Hornby 1775, Treaty of Surat: EIC help for him in return for Salsette, Bassein and revenue from Bharuch, Surat 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) begins 2.2 Warren Hastings 73-85 overturns Surat: the Treaty of Purandhar (1776) Warren Hastings 73-85, the Governor General in Calcutta, overturned the Treaty of Surat to avoid expensive war expenditure. He negotiated the Treaty of Purandhar (1776) with Nana Fadnis: 1 The EIC would recognise Madhav Rao II 74-95 as the legitimate Peshwa, and Raghunath Rao 73-74 would be pensioned off 2 The EIC would receive Salsette and Bharuch 3 The Marathas would not allow any French presence in their domain Treaty of Purandhar 1776: terms and negotiators [1665: To PURANDHAR]: do not confuse the two Purandhars; the first was in 1665 (Chapter 4). Board note: GBF 1770 → 1772 → Loan by BANKRUPTCY (one word is). Read with Chapter 10: the Great Bengal Famine 1770 led to the EIC's bankruptcy in 1772, the money trouble behind Warren Hastings 73-85's wish to avoid war expenditure. The handout adds: this fits the Policy of Relative Isolation (later chapter). However, the EIC in Bombay continued sheltering Raghunath Rao 73-74. Nana Fadnis retaliated by offering a port to the French. Talks collapsed and war resumed. "eg of FACTIONALISM within EIC": the Bombay EIC and the Calcutta EIC (Warren Hastings 73-85) pulled in two directions. Factionalism was not only a Maratha disease. 2.3 Events and the Treaty of Salbai (1782) In 1779, at the Battle of Wadgaon (near Pune), Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia and Tukoji Rao Holkar defeated the EIC and Raghunath Rao 73-74. But the war continued inconclusively. By 1782 the EIC was in a difficult position, but so were the Marathas, who were also engaged in the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). Treaty of Salbai 1782: terms The Treaty of Salbai (1782) was negotiated and signed at Gwalior by Mahadji Scindhia on behalf of the Marathas. It ended the war. Its terms: 1 Military alliance between the EIC and the Marathas. The Marathas broke their anti-British alliance (the Triple Confederacy) and agreed to fight on the side of the EIC if Hyder Ali 61-82 did not restore the territories he had taken from the British and the Nawab of Arcot. (The handout: PoRF established by the EIC with the Marathas.) 2 The EIC got Salsette and Bharuch 3 No French settlements in Maratha domain 4 The EIC returned all Maratha territory it had captured, recognised Madhav Rao II 74-95 as Peshwa and pensioned off Raghunath Rao 73-74 "alliance WITH neighbours" = Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF): a buffer of allied neighbours around the EIC (Chapter 10). Triple Confederacy = alliance of Marathas (Ma), Mysore (My) and Hyderabad (HYD), 1780-82; it led to the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). Stressed: military alliance, Salsette and Bharuch, no French settlements, Madhav Rao II 74-95 recognised, Raghunath Rao 73-74 pensioned off. Why pension a rival? Handout: pensions were deliberate EIC diplomatic practice; the EIC could use this person in future succession disputes. The same device returns in 1818 with Bajirao II 96-18 at Bithur (Section 7). The handout figure is a one-page summary of the story; it dates the Peshwa's pension to 1819 and the text dates Bajirao II 96-18's surrender to June 1818 (Section 6). Both belong to the same settlement (3rd war 1817-19).

Because Salbai bought peace, the Marathas had 21 years to repair themselves. Ask: why did they decline instead? The 21-year gap between the Treaty of Salbai (1782) and the Treaty of Bassein (1802) was not a period of Maratha strength: it was a period of Maratha decline. 1794 Mahadji Scindhia, who had dominated Maratha politics, dies 1795 Madhav Rao II 74-95 commits suicide 1796 Bajirao II 96-18 becomes Peshwa (the handout: Peshwa from 1796, formally tenured 1796-1818) 1800 Nana Fadnis dies: the one man who had consistently held the Confederacy together for two decades; factionalism accelerates sharply The Maratha capital, Shaniwar Wada at Pune, and the whole Confederacy were engulfed in factionalism. The empire-builder Wellesley 98-05 was waiting for exactly this opportunity.

Because a Holkar was executed, a Peshwa fled to the EIC and signed away his army. Ask: why did the SA unite the old rivals? 4.1 The trigger: Bassein (December 1802) In 1801 Vithoji Rao Holkar had been plundering the Peshwa's territories. He was captured and brutally executed on the orders of Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18. To avenge the death of his stepbrother, Yashwantrao Holkar attacked and defeated both the Peshwa and Daulat Rao Scindhia (who had supported the Peshwa) in October 1802. Bajirao II 96-18 fled and signed the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802): he agreed to a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC in exchange for EIC help to regain the Peshwaship. The great army of Svarajya was to be disbanded once the EIC put its now-puppet Bajirao II 96-18 back as Peshwa. The Treaty of Bassein also triggered the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Ironically, it made Scindhia, Holkar and Bhonsle, who had been rivals, unite against the EIC. The Gaikwad had already signed an SA in June 1802 (Treaty of Cambay) to get EIC help in a succession dispute. Stressed: Yashwantrao Holkar attacked and defeated the Peshwa and Scindhia, Treaty of Bassein (Dec 1802), Bajirao II 96-18 fled, Subsidiary Alliance, 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05), Gaikwad. SA order matters for the exam (section 4.3): Gaikwad (June 1802) came before the Peshwa (December 1802). 4.2 The battlefield: Assaye (1803) The EIC deployed significant military force. Arthur Wellesley, commanding his Royal regiment alongside the EIC army, fought key engagements, including the Battle of Assaye (1803) against the Marathas. He later described it as the toughest fight of his entire military career, harder, in his view, than anything he faced against Napoleon in Europe. Stressed: Assaye, Arthur Wellesley, Royal regiment, alongside the EIC army. Two forces again: the Royal regiment (the King's army) fought alongside the EIC army (the Company's army), as at Plassey (Chapter 10). Arthur Wellesley is not the Governor General: the Governor General is Wellesley 98-05 (Chapter 11 on the Wellesley brothers). 4.3 Consequences The war was lost by the Marathas. The consequences were far-reaching: 1. Bajirao II 96-18 regained the Peshwaship but was now a puppet of the EIC. 2. Scindhia lost all territory north of the River Yamuna, including Delhi and Agra, and all his territory in Gujarat. He was forced to sign a Subsidiary Alliance. In Delhi a British Resident was stationed, who established the Policy of Indirect Rule: the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06 was now effectively under the EIC's indirect control. 3. Bhonsle of Nagpur lost Orissa but stubbornly refused to accept the Subsidiary Alliance. He was forced to sign a mini alliance (similar in structure to the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 with Awadh): he ceded territory and accepted an EIC army to be paid for by Bhonsle, but not yet the full Subsidiary Alliance. Recall (handout bracket): Bhonsle raided the Bengal Suba in 1745-51 and extracted the Chauth of Bengal and Bihar and control of Orissa from Alivardi Khan 40-56. Orissa now returns to the EIC, the inheritor of Bengal (Chapter 10). The handout prints the Awadh treaty year as "17765"; it is 1765. The Emperor's masters, in order (handout bracket): Zulfikar Khan, the Sayyid Brothers, the Irani and Turani group, Safdar Jung 39-54, the Marathas, and now the EIC. See Chapter 2. 2nd War consequences contd.: Jats, Rajputs, Wellesley recalled, Non-Intervention 4. The Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas, who had earlier paid Chauth and Sardeshmukhi tributes to the Marathas, were now forced to sign an SA with the EIC, as the EIC replaced the Marathas as the dominant regional power of north and central India. 5. Wellesley 98-05 was recalled to London because of the high war expenditure in his tenure. Cornwallis 86-93 was despatched with clear orders to follow a policy of non-interference (he arrived in July 1805 and died in October 1805). Order of the Subsidiary Alliances: 1802 Gaikwad, 1802 Peshwa, 1803/04 Scindhia (1816 Bhonsle and 1818 Holkar follow, Section 7). Stressed: "high war expenditure" and "policy of non-interference". The Policy of Non-Intervention was meant to prevent war expenditure, but it gave Bhonsle and Holkar time to rebuild their military strength and confidence. Cornwallis 86-93: the code belongs to the man, not to the 1805 episode (a later, very short visit, July to October 1805, ending in his death); it is kept as written. 4.4 The Vellore Mutiny (1806) The handout's bracketed note on the Vellore Mutiny (1806), during George Barlow (Acting GG, 1805-07). Cause: new dress codes forbade sepoys from wearing religious marks (tilaks and turbans) and mandated leather cockades (ribbons shaped like a Christian cross on the hat, made of cow or pig skin). Result: an uprising in the Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu). It is often called the "Prelude to 1857." Four exam handles: new dress codes, leather cockades, cow or pig skin, Vellore Fort (north Tamil Nadu).

items.t: 5 · The Pindaris, Francis Hastings 13-23 and the Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58)
items.x: Because Wellesley 98-05 spent too much, the EIC paused, and the pause let Pindaris and loopholes grow. Ask: what is Paramountcy, and what did the 1816 loophole allow? After Wellesley 98-05 the EIC followed a Policy of Non-Intervention to prevent war expenditure. This gave Bhonsle and Holkar time to rebuild their military strength and confidence. Meanwhile the Pindaris, disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar, began raiding EIC territory in the Northern Sarkars and parts of the Madras Presidency. They were defeated by the next empire-builder, Governor General Francis Hastings 13-23, whose Policy of Paramountcy (PoP, 1813-58) re-initiated imperial expansion. Under PoP the EIC was to be the paramount or supreme power in India and it would do anything, even annexation, if needed to protect its interests. Pindaris: disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar who raided EIC territory (the who and the what). Two Hastings in this chapter: Warren Hastings 73-85 (1st war: Surat, Purandhar, Salbai) and Francis Hastings 13-23 (3rd war: Pindaris, Paramountcy). Do not mix them up. The Hastings trap. "Lord Hastings" or "Hastings" alone can mean either. Fix it by the war: 1775-82 = Warren Hastings 73-85; 1817-19 = Francis Hastings 13-23. The codes are the quickest tell: 73-85 against 13-23. The British Resident began treating Bajirao II 96-18 as a puppet, in a way that left him with no real authority. In Nagpur, Appa Sahib signed an SA under the Treaty of Nagpur (1816) for EIC help in a factionalism dispute over who would be regent of the Bhonsle of Nagpur (Maharaja Parsoji Bhonsle suffered from paralysis and was unable to rule). The treaty required disbanding the official state army, but rulers were allowed to keep retainers and police for internal security. Appa Sahib exploited this loophole by secretly recruiting fierce Arab and Rohilla mercenaries. Once his power was secure, and having Parsoji secretly murdered to become the actual Maharaja, Appa Sahib now wanted to rule independently and not as a puppet of the British Resident. PoP = 1813-58. The 3rd war's reason on the overview board is "PoIR as part of PoP": the Policy of Indirect Rule (Residents controlling puppets) now ran inside the Policy of Paramountcy. Stressed: "signed SA", the succession dispute over the regent, secretly recruiting fierce Arab and Rohilla mercenaries, British Resident, "as a puppet" (for both Appa Sahib and Bajirao II 96-18). Same pattern as Surat 1775 and Bassein 1802: a succession or power dispute, the ruler asks the EIC for help, the EIC takes control. The loophole is the SA template's weak point and the reason the 3rd war broke out.

items.t: 6 · Third Anglo-Maratha War and the Pindari War (1817-19)
items.x: Because the rulers rebelled against being puppets, the largest EIC force ever marched. Ask: why does Sitabuldi show the SA caused the war? 6.1 The Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817) In late 1817 Bajirao II 96-18, Appa Sahib (regent of the Bhonsle of Nagpur) and Yashwantrao Holkar united in revolt, determined to end the EIC's political domination. (The handout's bracket: this is a violation of SA treaties.) This led to the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19). Bajirao II 96-18 had signed a Subsidiary Alliance under which the EIC army had replaced the Svarajya's own army, so technically he had no State army. He fought with men he personally recruited outside the EIC's supervision. Appa Sahib acted as Senapati (Commander-in-Chief). He used his Arab mercenaries to launch a surprise, close-quarters attack directly on the British Residency and the adjacent Sitabuldi hills. Despite heavily outnumbering the garrison, his forces were defeated at the Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817). Tested in Prelims (handout), Sitabuldi: (i) Appa Sahib signed the SA in 1816 but fought in 1817: the SA did not prevent the war, its terms caused it. (ii) The "disbanded army" requirement was bypassed through Arab and Rohilla mercenaries hired as "internal security retainers": the SA template's loophole. Naming slip. The handout and typed slide name "Yashwantrao Holkar" among the rebels of 1817, while the board and later battle slides write only "Holkar". Learn "Holkar of Indore" for the 3rd war and "Yashwantrao Holkar" for the 1802 revenge on the Peshwa; if a question gives a first name for 1817, follow the handout. 6.2 Battles and surrender Force size The EIC deployed its largest military force ever in India: about 1.2 lakh troops Battle of Sitabuldi (Nov 1817) Appa Sahib defeated (Section 6.1) Battle of Mahidpur (Dec 1817) Holkar decisively defeated Battle of Koregaon (1 Jan 1818) A small EIC force of Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army. Later commemorated as the Bhima-Koregaon Victory Pillar Surrender (June 1818) Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 surrendered Three battles, three opponents: Sitabuldi = Appa Sahib (Bhonsle), Mahidpur = Holkar, Koregaon = Peshwa. Also stressed: Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army; the Bhima-Koregaon Victory Pillar. 1.2 lakh = 1,20,000 troops (handout). The question bank's explanation writes "1.2 lakh (110,000)"; the numbers disagree. Use about 1.2 lakh.

items.t: 7 · Consequences of the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19)
items.x: Because the war was lost, the Peshwaship ended and the last throne was spared only for a while. Ask: what were the five results, and why was the Chhatrapati kept? 1. The Peshwaship was abolished. Bajirao II 96-18 was pensioned off to Bithur, near Kanpur. (His adopted son was Nana Sahib, who would later lead the Kanpur revolt in 1857.) 2. Svarajya was annexed into the Bombay Presidency. The original Maratha homeland became a province of the Company State; the regional headquarters of EIC trade evolved into a province of British India. 3. Appa Sahib was deposed and replaced by a puppet. Bhonsle lost huge territory. 3rd War consequences contd.: Holkar, Satara and Kolhapur 4. Holkar's Subsidiary Alliance via the Treaty of Mandsaur (1818). Holkar of Indore was forced to sign after being decisively defeated at Mahidpur. 5. Satara and Kolhapur were not annexed. The EIC maintained the Chhatrapati's line as a symbolic gesture. Why keep the Chhatrapati? Handout: a powerless figurehead since the 1750s anyway; keeping him cost nothing and avoided the optics of destroying a revered institution. Satara was annexed in 1848 under Dalhousie 48-56's Doctrine of Lapse (Chapter 14). Family tree behind the two spared thrones: Shivaji 74-80 had two sons, Sambhaji 80-89 and Rajaram 89-00. Sambhaji 80-89's line: Shahu 19-49 (Satara), then Ram Raja (1749-77) ("To SANGOLA"). Rajaram 89-00's line: Tarabai [and Shivaji II]; his second wife Rajasbai's son Sambhaji II (1714) got Kolhapur by the Treaty of Warna, 1731. So Satara and Kolhapur are two branches of one family (Chapter 4). The date beside "Sangola" on the board reads like "1758"; Chapter 4 gives the Treaty of Sangola in 1750. Learn Sangola 1750 (Chapter 4). The last digit of "Shahu 19-49" on the board is also unclear; use Shahu 19-49. Two additions in the handout figure not in the handout text: the 1803 battles of Deogaon and Surji-Arjangaon (Scindhia and Bhonsle subdued) and the Holkar rise after 1800. They sit beside the map crosses at Assaye, Argaon and Gawilgarh (Section 1). Learn Assaye first; the others are extras. Bhonsle's treaty status: three readings. Text: after the 2nd war Bhonsle refused the full SA and signed a mini alliance (territory ceded, an EIC army he paid for). Board: "1816: SA - BHONSLE" (Treaty of Nagpur) = full SA. Handout figure: Scindhia and Bhonsle "reduced to Subsidiary-Alliance rulers" after the 3rd war. They fit: mini alliance 1803-05, full SA 1816, complete reduction by 1818.

Because the pattern repeated in three wars, the teacher distilled four reasons. Ask: which two are internal and which two external? Four structural reasons explain the Maratha defeat: 1. Factionalism. 2. Absence of unified command. Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle and the Gaikwad of Baroda never coordinated effectively. 3. The EIC's superior finances. 4. Naval and logistics advantage. The Konkan coast could be blockaded by EIC ships; the EIC could move troops faster across India via sea and better road infrastructure than the Marathas. Takeaway: the Confederacy fell less from EIC military superiority than from its own structure: factionalism and no unified command, against the EIC's deeper finances and naval-logistics reach. A divided Maratha house was the EIC's most reliable ally. Stressed: Factionalism (the first and repeating cause), unified command, Naval & logistics advantage. Overview-board lesson: factionalism is the reason in two wars out of three, and a disbanded army is the weak point in the third. The four reasons: the first two are internal (the Marathas' own structure), the last two external (the EIC's edge).

items.t: 9 · Wars due to the EIC army over-hyping the threat to borders
items.x: Because the EIC had won in the Deccan, its army looked to the borders. Ask: what are the two kinds of EIC wars, and what is a protectorate? Wars by the EIC: for trade or for territory Wars by the EIC are of two kinds: for trade, and for T (territory). Wars for territory have two drivers: (1) empire-builder Governor Generals, and (2) the vested interest of the EIC army, which benefits from a big threat and overhypes the threat to the borders. The wars in this section are the second kind. Protectorate: symbolic sovereignty not taken Protectorate: symbolic sovereignty is not taken. Of the two kinds of sovereign function, external (EXT) goes to Britain (Br); domestic (Dom) is not taken. Like a Subsidiary Alliance: the State loses external sovereign functions but keeps symbolic sovereignty and domestic functions. 9.1 Nepal, Burma and Coorg Anglo-Nepal 1814-16 Francis Hastings 13-23 Treaty of Sugauli (1816): Nepal became a British Protectorate; it lost Kumaon, Garhwal and the Terai to British India 1st Anglo-Burmese 1824-26 Amherst 23-28 Burma was expanding territory, giving the EIC the chance to overhype the threat to borders. Treaty of Yandabo (1826) annexed Assam, Nagaland and parts of lower Burma (Arakan and Tenasserim); Cachar annexed in 1830. The Ahom Kingdom of Assam had supported the EIC: in a stab in the back it was annexed too Coorg War 1834 William Bentinck 28-35 On grounds of maladministration by Vira Raja. Massive coffee plantations were set up after annexation "misc": the miscellaneous part of the chapter, a short list to memorise, not a full story. Burmese row: "= THREAT TO Assam" - the threat the EIC army overhyped was to Assam, the Ahom kingdom that had backed the EIC and was then annexed. Stressed: Sugauli (1816), British Protectorate, Kumaon-Garhwal-Terai, Yandabo (1826), Assam-Nagaland, lower Burma, Cachar 1830, maladministration by Vira Raja. 9.2 Afghanistan and Sindh 1st Anglo-Afghan War (1838-42), under Auckland 36-42: Part of the Great Game between Britain and Russia (the teacher: "over Central Asia"). Under Auckland 36-42's Forward Policy (the teacher: "Aggressive foreign policy"), the EIC tried to install Shah Shuja in Kabul against the actual ruler, Dost Mohammed. Disaster: 20,000 British and Indian soldiers dead, expenditure of Rs 1.5 crore, and the famous retreat from Kabul (only one European survivor reached British India). Auckland 36-42 was recalled. Ellenborough 42-44 ended the war. Dost Mohammed recaptured power but maintained good relations with the stronger power, the British. Annexation of Sindh (1843), under Ellenborough 42-44: Taken from the "Char Yaar" (four Baloch chiefs of the Talpur dynasty) without any justification. The military commander was Sir Charles Napier. 1st and 2nd Anglo-Sikh Wars 1845-46, 1848-49 Hardinge 44-48 and Dalhousie 48-56 Led to the annexation of Punjab in 1849 (later chapter, [[14 Chapter 14]]) 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 Dalhousie 48-56 Pegu (lower Burma) annexed (later chapter) Peccavi: after conquering Sindh, Napier sent his superiors a one-word Latin dispatch: "Peccavi," meaning "I have sinned." The pun is "I have Sindh," capturing the brazenness of the annexation. Stressed: the Great Game, Auckland 36-42's Forward Policy, Auckland 36-42 recalled, Ellenborough 42-44 ended it, Dost Mohammed; Sindh: Ellenborough 42-44, "Char Yaar", Sir Charles Napier; last slide: 2nd Anglo-Burmese War, Dalhousie 48-56, Pegu. The tags "over Central Asia" and "aggressive foreign policy" are the why of the Afghan war.

The whole story on one board. The teacher puts the three wars on one line. The 1st war (1775-82): reason factionalism, it began at Surat 1775, the EIC 'won' and it ended at Salbai 1782 with a military alliance. The 2nd (1803-05): reason factionalism, it began with Bassein 1802, an SA signed for the Svarajya, and the Marathas lost. The 3rd (1817-19): reason a breach of the SA by the EIC, and the Marathas lost, with the Swarajya annexed. Why the Deccan mattered. The Deccan and the Konkan coast were commercially critical to the EIC: a large coastline, a major cotton trade from Gujarat to China, and Maratha control over parts of the Malabar coast. The Maratha Confederacy and Mysore were the last major powers able to check the EIC. Three Anglo-Maratha Wars and four Anglo-Mysore Wars decided the outcome. A claimant and a treaty at Surat. In 1773 Raghunath Rao 73-74 became Peshwa after the murder of his nephew Narayan Rao 72-73. In 1774, in the Baarbhai Conspiracy, Nana Fadnis and eleven other ministers removed him. He went to the EIC's Governor of Bombay, William Hornby, and in 1775 signed the Treaty of Surat: EIC help in return for Salsette, Bassein and some revenue from Bharuch and Surat. Warren Hastings cancels, then Purandhar collapses. Warren Hastings 73-85, the Governor General in Calcutta, overturned Surat to avoid expensive war expenditure and negotiated the Treaty of Purandhar (1776) with Nana Fadnis. Madhav Rao II 74-95 was recognised, Raghunath Rao 73-74 pensioned, Salsette and Bharuch went to the EIC, and no French presence was allowed. But Bombay kept sheltering Raghunath, Nana Fadnis offered the French a port, and the war resumed. Wadgaon and the peace of Salbai. At Wadgaon (1779), near Pune, Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia and Tukoji Rao Holkar defeated the EIC and Raghunath Rao 73-74. The war then stalled, with both sides in difficulty, the Marathas also being tied to the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). In 1782 Mahadji Scindhia signed the Treaty of Salbai at Gwalior: a military alliance against Hyder Ali 61-82's retention of territories, Salsette and Bharuch to the EIC, no French, territory returned, Madhav Rao II 74-95 recognised and Raghunath pensioned. Twenty-one years of decline. Between Salbai (1782) and Bassein (1802) the Marathas declined. Mahadji Scindhia died in 1794, Madhav Rao II 74-95 committed suicide in 1795, Bajirao II 96-18 became Peshwa in 1796, and Nana Fadnis, the one man who held the Confederacy together for two decades, died in 1800. Wellesley 98-05, the empire-builder, was waiting for exactly this opportunity. Bassein: the Peshwa signs an SA. In 1801 Vithoji Rao Holkar was captured and executed on the orders of Bajirao II 96-18. To avenge his stepbrother, Yashwantrao Holkar defeated the Peshwa and Daulat Rao Scindhia in October 1802. Bajirao fled and signed the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802), an SA in which the army of the Svarajya was to be disbanded once the EIC restored its puppet Peshwa. The Gaikwad had already signed the Treaty of Cambay in June 1802. Assaye and a lost war. Scindhia, Holkar and Bhonsle united against the EIC. Arthur Wellesley fought them at Assaye (1803), which he called the toughest fight of his career, harder than anything against Napoleon. The Marathas lost: the Peshwa was a puppet; Scindhia lost all north of the Yamuna (Delhi, Agra) and all of Gujarat and signed an SA, with a British Resident in Delhi putting Shah Alam II 60-06 effectively under EIC indirect control; Bhonsle lost Orissa and signed only a mini alliance. Wellesley 98-05 was recalled for the war's cost, and Cornwallis 86-93 arrived in July 1805 and died in October. Pindaris, Paramountcy and a loophole. After Wellesley 98-05 the EIC followed non-intervention, giving Bhonsle and Holkar time to rebuild. Pindaris, disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar, raided the Northern Sarkars and Madras. Francis Hastings 13-23 crushed them and launched the Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58): the EIC was to be supreme and could even annex. Residents treated Bajirao II 96-18 as a puppet. In Nagpur Appa Sahib signed an SA in 1816 but, using the loophole that retainers were allowed, secretly recruited Arab and Rohilla mercenaries and had Parsoji murdered. The third war: Sitabuldi, Mahidpur, Koregaon. In late 1817 Bajirao II 96-18, Appa Sahib and Yashwantrao Holkar rose together. Appa Sahib, as Senapati, used his Arab mercenaries at Sitabuldi (November 1817) but was defeated. Holkar fell at Mahidpur (December 1817). At Koregaon (1 January 1818) a small EIC force of Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army. The EIC used its largest force ever, about 1.2 lakh, and Bajirao surrendered in June 1818. The settlement of 1818. The Peshwaship was abolished and Bajirao II 96-18 pensioned to Bithur near Kanpur, where his adopted son Nana Sahib would later lead the Kanpur revolt of 1857. Svarajya was annexed into the Bombay Presidency. Appa Sahib was deposed, and Bhonsle lost huge territory. Holkar signed an SA at Mandsaur (1818). Satara and Kolhapur were spared as the Chhatrapati's symbolic line; Satara was annexed in 1848 under Dalhousie 48-56's Doctrine of Lapse. Why they lost, and the next wars. The Marathas lost for four reasons: factionalism, no unified command (Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaikwad), the EIC's finances, and its naval and logistics advantage. The EIC's army, with a vested interest in big threats, then overhyped border dangers: Nepal 1814-16 (Sugauli, a protectorate), Burma 1824-26 (Yandabo), Coorg 1834, Afghanistan 1838-42 (20,000 dead), Sindh 1843 (Napier's Peccavi), the Sikh wars and Burma II 1852-53.
