Dutt Body 3: social and ideological Russian Revolution 1917 (peasant-worker mobilisation model, anti-imperial vocabulary); self-determination (Wilson's Fourteen Points 1918) and rising anti-racism Body 4: the carriers Gandhi from South Africa (1893-1915 diaspora struggles); Nehru from Cambridge (western liberal-democratic theory) Closing The ideas arrived through people; the empire's own moral claim became its weak point The question bank holds 14 Prelims PYQs, 1 Mains PYQ, 15 practice Prelims and 2 practice Mains questions (use the Question bank button). Several of the 14 are cross-listed (education chronology, Charter Act 1833, Press Regulation 1799, Factory Act, economic critics of colonialism) and belong mainly to other chapters.

Story so far: one roof, four columns. Keep the board in mind: 1765 Orientalism, 1786-93 Authoritarianism, from 1813 three reform ideas, from 1858 Racism. Ask: what was the teacher's one-line summary of each? Chapter 15 title: British Imperial Ideology Master board: four phases of imperial ideology under White Man's Burden Whole chapter on one board: 1765 Orientalism; 1786-93 Cornwallis 86-93's Authoritarianism; from 1813 Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism; from 1858 Racism + Authoritarianism; all under the roof "White Man's Burden". The one-liners are the exam answers. Orientalism = "Rule India the India Way" (Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages, Indian syllabus). Authoritarianism = "My way or highway" (Indians removed from all senior positions). Liberalism = "give the best ideas of our time to India, but best = west." Utilitarianism = "civil servant mind" (effectiveness, max results, implementable, practical): good laws and a strong State. Evangelicalism = "Christianize India to modernize India." After 1857: "Indians are beyond reform... Dogs and Indians not allowed... more Authoritarianism plus more Racism." Board versus handout on dates. Board: Authoritarianism 1786-93 (Cornwallis 86-93), boundaries 1813 and 1858 (Queen Victoria's Proclamation, Section 7.1). Handout summary table (Section 13): 1786-1805 (Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05) plus Conservatism 1801-27, which the board omits. Use the board for the sequence, the table for champions.

Because every ideology was both belief and cover story, policy followed ideas. Ask: what are the two layers, and why show both in Mains? British Imperial Ideologies are the ideas that shaped colonial policy. They were not one fixed set. They changed over time and sometimes competed. They shared one function: they gave the British a way to tell themselves and the world that what they were doing in India was not just profitable but morally right. Every ideology was both a genuine belief held by some Englishmen and a convenient narrative to make imperialism look ethical. Both layers operate at once. For Mains: always show both layers. Sincere belief and convenient cover story together. Many Englishmen were sincere (Section 5.5), and the ideas still served British power.

Because the British were sure of themselves, they felt a duty to civilise. Ask: which five roots of confidence, and which four counter-currents did WMB create? No class notes beyond the board below; the typed slides repeat the handout. White Man's Burden: why Britain felt superior All other ideologies rested on one belief: Western European civilisation was superior, so the British had a responsibility to civilise the rest of the world. This is the White Man's Burden (WMB). WMB = "Civilize the rest of the world" and "We are superior". Reasons for the confidence: Industrial Revolution 1750-1850: first; Seven Years' Global War 1756-63: won; earliest of democracies; empire. (The list trails off; the handout carries the rest.) 2.1 The roots of British civilisational confidence The British had genuine reasons to believe in their superiority: 1. World's first modern democracy: the English Civil War + Glorious Revolution (17th century). 2. Birthplace of the Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850). 3. Won the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63): the top global power. 4. Financially backed the coalition that defeated Napoleon at Leipzig (1813); led the allied armies to final victory with Prussia at Waterloo (1815). 5. Capitalism and science transforming British society at an unprecedented pace. A nation that achieves all this within 150 years can convince itself that it is destined to lead the world. Every major imperial power had its own version of WMB. 2.2 WMB as roof, and the counter-ideologies as reaction WMB was the roof over everything else. The specific ideologies below were different answers to the same question: how exactly should we civilise India? WMB also generated its opposite: powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies worldwide: 1. American Revolution: a political movement from 1765, War of Independence 1776-83. 2. French Revolution (1789): liberty, equality, fraternity. 3. European revolutions of 1830 and 1848. 4. Irish Home Rule movement (1870-1914) and the Irish armed struggle for independence (1916-21). These challenged imperial-superiority assumptions and inspired colonised peoples, including Indian nationalists. (Section 12 develops this: Mains 2014.) The typed slide shows only two of the four counter-ideologies (American Revolution, Irish struggle). Use the handout's four (repeated in Section 12).

items.t: 3 · Orientalism (1765-1813): Rule India, the India Way
items.x: Because the EIC was scared and some wanted to spare India, it chose to rule the India way. Ask: which four things, which four institutions, and which one is the Prelims 2020 answer? 3.1 Orientalism defined In the 18th century the British used language and literature as the measure of civilisation. Scholars like William Jones studied Sanskrit and found it older and grammatically more sophisticated than ancient Greek and Latin. The conclusion: India had been a great ancient civilisation, and European and Indian languages belonged to the same family (today's Indo-European family: genuine scholarship, not propaganda). So Orientalism said: India's ancient past was glorious even if its present was degenerate, so the British should study Indian tradition and rule India by its own customs and laws. In short: Rule India, the India Way. Date slip in the typed slide: William Jones is dated "(late 19th c)"; the handout places this scholarship in the 18th century (Asiatic Society 1784). Use the handout. "Oriental" = related to east. "Rule India the INDIA WAY" = four things: Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages, Indian syllabus in schools and colleges. 3.2 Why the EIC adopted Orientalism Two practical reasons: 1. The EIC was militarily not yet confident before 1813. Victory in the Carnatic, Mysore and Maratha Wars was never guaranteed, and one badly handled cultural insult could trigger mass resistance. Ruling through Indian customs reduced that risk. 2. Some Englishmen believed India was not ready for British modernity. Imposing alien systems would do more damage than good. Warren Hastings 73-85 was Orientalism's most prominent champion. He argued that the more the British understood Indian traditions, the lighter the chains of colonialism would feel. 3.2.1 The four Orientalist institutions 1 1781 Calcutta Madrasa Warren Hastings 73-85, as Governor-General of Bengal; mainly for the study of Islamic law and customs 2 1784 Asiatic Society of Bengal Sir William Jones, as Puisne Judge of the Supreme Court at Calcutta; to study Asian history, antiquities and culture 3 1791 Sanskrit College, Banaras Jonathan Duncan, as British Resident at Benares; for the study of Hindu law and philosophy 4 1800 Fort William College, Calcutta Wellesley 98-05, as Governor-General of Bengal; to train newly recruited EIC civil servants in Indian languages and administration Figure-only names: Colebrooke, Wilson and Prinsep (Brahmi decipherment) and the ASI founded 1861 by Alexander Cunningham. The summary table (Section 13) also lists Colebrooke and Wilson as Orientalism champions. Learn them lightly. Wellesley 98-05's second motive for Fort William College: to keep French republican ideas away from his officers. The French Revolution 1789 had overthrown the monarchy by 1792, and Wellesley 98-05 did not want anti-monarchy ideas infecting his men. 3.3 Orientalism's political angle The British supported the Aryan Invasion Theory: ancient India's cultural greatness was actually brought by Europeans who migrated to India in ancient times. Even while praising India, the British claimed credit. The argument of kinship: Europeans and Indians were separated kin connected through language. It was used to reduce Indian opposition: "we are not foreigners, we are cousins who have come home." This was a rhetoric of love to disguise the reality of exploitation. Prelims 2020 trap: (d) train British civilians. (a) Board of Directors asked: wrong, it was Wellesley 98-05's own initiative. (b) revive oriental learning: wrong, that was the Asiatic Society 1784 and Sanskrit College 1791. (c) employment for William Carey: wrong, Carey was an employee, not the founding purpose.

Because critics said the past was dead, Cornwallis 86-93 imposed the English way. Ask: which four steps, and what did Munro's formula add? 4.1 The Cornwallis 86-93 shift Orientalism had critics from the beginning. The study of ancient India had only confirmed that India's past was glorious and its present degenerate. That made restoring the past pointless and called for imposing the British system instead. Cornwallis 86-93 was the first Governor-General to implement this vision systematically. He ruled India, the English Way. Four specific measures: 1. All-British senior administration. He replaced all Indians in senior administrative positions with British officials. His argument: Indian administrators were corrupt and incompetent; only British authority could deliver rule of law. (Deeper argument: only by removing Indians from power can the British civilise India. This "corrupt-native-needs-the-honest-foreigner" story was used through 1947 to justify exclusion.) 2. Rule of Law through codification. The Charter Act 1793, influenced by Cornwallis 86-93, established civil law and protection of individual rights and private property. It reintroduced separation of powers at the district level: the District Collector would no longer also be the District Judge. 3. Permanent Settlement (1793) in Bengal, converting zamindars into large landlords on the English model. (Full treatment in the Land Revenue Systems chapter, Chapter 16.) 4. Aloof Elite. EIC officials were discouraged from mixing with Indians. Indian wives were discouraged. Eurasians were barred from EIC service. Officials having Indian wives were barred from purchasing land in India. Authoritarianism = "MY WAY OR HIGHWAY": "Removed Indians from all senior positions." "PS 1793 based on English way of agriculture = OUTLIER to Orientalism." Orientalism meant ruling the Indian way; the Permanent Settlement copied the English landlord model, so it breaks that pattern and belongs with Authoritarianism. 4.2 The Aloof-Elite doctrine Cornwallis 86-93 had personally commanded the British army's defeat in the American War of Independence (1776-83). He had watched British settlers in the 13 American colonies develop deep roots (family, property, identity) and then fight for independence as their homeland. He was determined not to let the same happen in India. The rule: keep the rulers separate from the ruled. Never let India become home. Wellesley 98-05 shared this authoritarian instinct. Both administrations were control-oriented, centralised and mistrustful of Indian agency. 4.3 Conservatism: Munro, Malcolm, Elphinstone, Metcalfe Thomas Munro (Governor of Madras 1820-27) was a hybrid of Orientalism and Authoritarianism. India should be governed through its own traditions, but the British would govern, with no leadership role for Indians. Total power centralised in EIC hands, but exercised through Indian forms (Indian laws and customs). His Ryotwari Settlement (1801-07, 1820+) in the Madras Presidency was inspired by the ancient Indian model of the State collecting revenue directly from the peasant, without intermediaries. But all collection was done by EIC officials, with no Indians in senior roles. The formula: Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance. Mountstuart Elphinstone, John Malcolm and Charles Metcalfe followed the same school. Elphinstone, a disciple of Munro, later implemented the Ryotwari Settlement in Bombay. No class notes for Conservatism beyond the typed slide; the master board has no column for it.

items.t: 5 · Three new ideologies (post 1813): Liberalism, Utilitarianism, Evangelicalism
items.x: Because the EIC was confident by 1813, three reform ideas took over. Ask: what did each want, and who was the champion of each? 5.1 The post-1813 sharp turn By 1813 the landscape had changed dramatically: 1. The EIC had defeated all major Indian powers; only Holkar, Bhonsle and the Sikh State remained as potential rivals. 2. The Company's army had grown huge. 3. Britain had defeated Napoleon. 4. The Industrial Revolution was in full swing. The EIC was now confident enough to rule India the British way: openly, aggressively, without apology. There was also a new economic motive: an India with western tastes and western education would become a market for British manufactured goods. Three ideologies filled the space Orientalism had occupied: Liberalism, Utilitarianism, Evangelicalism. 5.2 Liberalism Liberals argued that the EIC had governed India badly under Orientalism. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (one crore Indians perished while the EIC doubled land revenue) was cited as proof. India needed to be modernised through the best ideas of the age (best meaning western). Goal: liberate India from feudalism: feudal polity (no democracy), feudal economy (agrarian, closed, unequal), feudal society (birth-based discrimination, no women's rights), and replace it with modern British institutions. Thomas Macaulay, legal member of the GG's council under the Charter Act 1833, was the most prominent Liberal. His three signature interventions: 1. Law Commission (1834): codified western-style laws for British India by 1837. 2. Minute on Indian Education (1835): proposed western education in English to create Brown Sahibs (brown on the outside, British on the inside): a class of Indians as cultural intermediaries between British rulers and the Indian masses. 3. Charter Act 1813 (a Liberal-influenced reform): ended the EIC's monopoly over Indian trade and let non-EIC British businesses enter India freely. This was economic liberalism for British businesses, not for Indian ones. Social reform followed too: Bentinck 28-35 brought the Sati Abolition Act 1829 under Liberal influence (full treatment in Chapter 19). Date wrinkle. The slide and handout list the Charter Act 1813 among Macaulay's "interventions", yet his council seat came under the Charter Act 1833. The handout calls the 1813 Act a "Liberal-influenced reform": read it as a Liberal-era measure that opened trade, not Macaulay's own act. His own: Law Commission 1834, Minute 1835. 5.3 Utilitarianism Associated with Jeremy Bentham and James Mill. India needed not culture change but good policy and a strong rule of law. The State's job: design laws that maximise benefit for the largest number of people. James Mill's History of British India (1818) declared India's great past a myth and argued India needed an effective schoolmaster: someone to impose good governance from above. Mill joined the Court of Directors of the EIC in London and pushed for the Law Commission in 1834 under Macaulay. Utilitarianism contains an inherent authoritarian streak. Utilitarianism = "civil servant mind": effectiveness, max results, implementable, practical. "Bring good laws and a strong State for rule of law." A utilitarian cares what works, not what is traditional or Christian, hence laws and a strong State. 5.4 Evangelicalism Evangelists argued India's fundamental problem was its religion, which promoted superstition, ignorance, idolatry and tyranny of priests and blocked scientific thinking. Religion shapes values; values shape society. Change the religion, change everything. Their model was Protestant Christianity in western Europe, where Protestant ethics supported the rise of capitalism and modernity. Charles Grant, a member of the Court of Directors and later an MP, influenced the Charter Act 1813 to legalise the entry of Christian missionaries into India. The Lex Loci Act / Removal of Religious-Caste Disabilities Act (1850) allowed a convert to retain inheritance rights in family property, removing one practical obstacle to conversion (full treatment in Chapter 19). "Evangelicalism: CHRISTIANIZE India to MODERNIZE India." Charter Act 1813 appears under two ideologies. Liberal side: ended the EIC's trade monopoly (section 5.2). Evangelical side: allowed missionaries (this section). Both are in the handout. Keep the two effects apart. 5.5 Common ground across the three All three pushed for reform of the colonial State and together built the narrative of Benevolent Colonialism: "we are here to help you." Many Englishmen who believed in these ideologies were sincere. And yet all three together contributed to the conditions that produced the Revolt of 1857: cultural, economic and political resistance to a colonial project that had touched almost every aspect of Indian life.

Because Liberal confidence peaked in 1828-35, four interventions followed. Ask: which four, and what is the Charter Act 1833 trap? The short window from Bentinck 28-35 through the Charter Act 1833 to Macaulay's 1835 Minute is the high-water mark of Liberal confidence in India. Four headline interventions: 1. Sati Abolition Act 1829: criminalised widow-burning (full treatment in Chapter 19). 2. Thuggee Suppression (1830s-40s): under Captain William Sleeman; restored police order on the Grand Trunk roads (Section 8; Prelims 1997). 3. Macaulay's Education Minute 1835: made English the medium of higher instruction, displacing Persian. 4. Cornwallis 86-93 Code progressively revised into a uniform criminal procedure: the foundation Macaulay's 1834 Law Commission would build on. Charter Act 1833 trap: it did NOT provide for an Indian to be appointed law member in the GG's council (Prelims 2003, answer (d) in the bank). Macaulay, the law member, was a Briton.

Because 1857 shocked the British, reform retreated and race hardened. Ask: which six fronts, and which two architects? The Revolt of 1857 shook the British not just militarily but psychologically. The scale of Indian violence against British rule (soldiers, civilians, women, children) broke the paternalistic narrative. The British had told themselves they were trustees and reformers. 1857 told them that a very large number of Indians did not see it that way. Board column 4: "1857 Revolt = SHOCK for British." "Indians are beyond Reform." "Ideology = DOGS & Indians not allowed." "Up-up Authoritarianism (+) up-up RACISM." 7.1 The six-front sharp shift after 1857 1. Reformist impulse retreated sharply. Liberalism, Utilitarianism and Evangelicalism (Section 5) collapsed. Many concluded that Indians were beyond redemption through reform. 2. Racial sciences shift. European racial classification in the second half of the 19th century shifted from language (the Orientalist criterion) to physical features. Indians were now classed as an inferior and fundamentally different race: not separated kin (Section 3) but a lower order of humanity. 3. Aryan Invasion Theory kept but twisted. Europeans had founded the Vedic civilisation, but by intermarrying with indigenous Indians over millennia they lost their racial superiority and degraded. Even India's ancient greatness was now used as evidence of Indian inferiority. 4. "Dogs and Indians not allowed": seen on signs at clubs and parks in colonial India; it captures the spirit of post-1857 attitudes. 5. Authoritarianism increased. The British became distrustful of sharing power with Indians in any meaningful way. 6. Social reforms slowed sharply. Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 explicitly promised religious tolerance and non-interference in Indian customs: a direct acknowledgement that missionary and reformer interference had been a major grievance of 1857. From here, social and political reforms came mainly in response to pressure from Indian leaders, not British initiative. The table below contrasts the two uses of the Aryan idea and of race. Criterion of race Language Physical features Indians seen as Separated kin, cousins Inferior, different race, a lower order Aryan Invasion Theory Europeans brought India's greatness: "cousins come home" Europeans founded Vedic civilisation but intermarried and degraded Policy mood Rule India the India Way Reform retreated; more Authoritarianism 7.2 Post-1857 architects: Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05 The architects of this harder imperialism were Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05: men for whom empire was a project of prestige, paramountcy and racial hierarchy. 1. Lytton 76-80: the Vernacular Press Act 1878 and Arms Act 1878 reinstated racial privilege (VPA in Chapter 19). 2. Curzon 99-05: the Partition of Bengal (1905) was the same mindset applied administratively (in Chapter 29).

items.t: 8 · Law and order paternalism: Sleeman and the Thugs
items.x: Because the roads were unsafe, a parallel track of law-and-order paternalism ran. Ask: whose department, which three tools, and which distractors in Prelims 1997? Between Orientalism and Liberalism the EIC also ran a parallel track of law-and-order paternalism: reclaiming the roads, the courts and rural policing in the name of the peasant's physical safety. The flagship was the Thuggee and Dacoity Suppression campaign of the 1830s-40s, built around Captain (later Major-General Sir) William Sleeman, under Bentinck 28-35. His Thuggee and Dacoity Department (set up 1835) used three tools: 1. Informant networks infiltrating Thug bands. 2. Approver testimony: captured Thugs gave evidence against their associates in exchange for lighter sentences. 3. Swift judicial commissions: dedicated tribunals delivering rapid trials. Together these dismantled organised highway murder cults that had made long-distance trade on the Grand Trunk Road a life-and-death gamble. Over 3,000 Thugs were convicted between 1831 and 1841. Prelims 1997 trap: answer (b) Captain Sleeman. Prendergast = Upper Burma 1885-86 (Section 10). Burnes = Afghan frontier, killed in the 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1841 (Section 9). Pemberton = Assam/Burma frontier officer.

items.t: 9 · The Forward Policy in Afghanistan: from Auckland 36-42 to Lytton 76-80
items.x: Because Russia was feared, the frontier was pushed into Afghanistan. Ask: which four Governors-General, and what did Gandamak 1879 give? The Forward Policy was the militarised face of post-1840s British imperialism on the north-west frontier: Britain should actively push its effective frontier into Afghanistan to pre-empt Tsarist Russian influence, rather than defend a fixed line at the Indus. Its arc ran through multiple Governors-General and is a classic PYQ trap: 1. Auckland 36-42 launched the disastrous 1st Anglo-Afghan War (1839-42) to reinstall Shah Shuja against Dost Mohammad. The retreat from Kabul (January 1842) wiped out almost an entire British-Indian army. 2. Ellenborough 42-44 initiated what later came to be called the Forward Policy: a punitive return to Kabul in 1842 to restore British prestige, followed by a doctrine of pushing the frontier outward. 3. Lytton 76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy and launched the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War (1878-80), forcing the Treaty of Gandamak 1879. The war continued into its 2nd phase after the massacre of British Resident Louis Cavagnari at Kabul. 4. Ripon 80-84 reversed the Forward Policy and withdrew British forces from Afghanistan: the pendulum swing that Liberal governments in London demanded. Slide versus handout on Ellenborough 42-44. Handout: he initiated the Forward Policy (punitive return to Kabul 1842 to restore prestige, then the frontier-outward doctrine; its flow chart agrees). Slide: he "Ended Forward Policy (*Correct this in notes)", so the slide is flagged for correction by its own author. This notebook follows the handout. The safe core is the same either way: Auckland 36-42 = 1st war 1839-42; Lytton 76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy (2nd war 1878-80); Ripon 80-84 reversed it. The slide also spells "Aukland". 9.1 The Treaty of Gandamak 1879 The handout calls Gandamak 1879 a mini subsidiary alliance, with five terms: British Resident stationed At the Amir's court Army stationed British forces Foreign policy taken By the British Territory Khyber Pass and some other lands to the British In return The British pay 6 lakh annually to the Amir Prelims 1999 trap: (d) Lytton 76-80. (a) Minto (Minto II 1905-10) is after Curzon 99-05. (b) Dufferin 84-88 is famous for Upper Burma 1886, not Afghanistan. (c) Elgin (I 1862-63 or II 1894-99) is a different era. The answer slide says Lytton 76-80 carried forward the policy "initiated by Ellenborough 42-44", which supports the handout over the Ellenborough slide. 9.2 Revision: Russophobia and the Great Game Russophobia: the British fear that Czarist Russia, expanding through Central Asia, would one day reach the north-west land approach to India. The Great Game: this Anglo-Russian rivalry over Central Asia. It shaped British frontier and foreign policy far more than trade. Offensive answer: the Forward Policy, pushing the effective frontier outward through the two Anglo-Afghan Wars (1839-42 and 1878-80). Defensive twin: the Policy of Ring Fence: keeping strong, friendly border States as a buffer around British India, with Afghanistan and Punjab as the buffer in the north-west. The 1838 Tripartite Treaty (Sikh State, EIC and Shah Shuja) was built on this buffer logic (see Chapter 6, Chapter 14). The Persian flank: the same logic produced the Anglo-Persian War 1856-57 and finally the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907, which split Iran into three: a Russian sphere in the north, a neutral buffer in the middle and a British sphere in the south (see Chapter 14). Revision box. Belongs with the policies chapter: the Ring Fence idea began with Clive 57-67 in 1765 (Chapter 10); the Five-Policy Arc is in Chapter 14.

Because the land-grab ended in Burma, one year matters. Ask: which Viceroy, which year, and what is the slide's nuance? The last major territorial extension of British India was Upper Burma, annexed in January 1886 after the 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885-86. The Viceroy was Dufferin 84-88. King Thibaw was deposed and exiled to Ratnagiri. The field commander was General Henry Prendergast, the same man who appeared as a distractor in the Prelims 1997 Thuggee question. Upper Burma was merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852) and governed as a province of British India until the 1937 separation. "Lower Burma, British from 1852" is the 2nd Anglo-Burmese War (1852-53) of Dalhousie 48-56 (Chapter 14). The handout's Ch 14 section on it is the home for that war. Prelims 2000: (a) Dufferin 84-88, with a nuance. Handout: Dufferin 84-88 added Upper Burma in January 1886. Traps: Dalhousie 48-56 (Punjab 1849, Awadh 1856, Doctrine of Lapse) was the big annexation GG, but his last major extension was Awadh 1856; Lytton 76-80 made no territorial extension (he tightened Paramountcy-era instruments, such as the Treaty of Jacobabad 1876, without annexing); Curzon 99-05's Partition of Bengal 1905 was administrative. Nuance: Burma was not traditionally part of India, so the "famous" answer, and possibly the official key, is Dalhousie 48-56; but the question says "British Indian territory", so (a) Dufferin 84-88 is legally correct. Use (a), as the handout and bank do, and keep Dalhousie 48-56 in mind.

Because trade was bent to the empire, tariffs favoured Britain. Ask: what is the key word, and where was it formalised? "Imperial Preference" was a commercial tariff arrangement: the constituent units of the British Empire (Britain, the Dominions and India) granted one another preferential (lower) tariff rates denied to non-Empire competitors. Formalised at the Ottawa Conference of 1932, locking India's trade into an Empire-first structure that subordinated Indian industrial interests to British manufacturing needs. (Full treatment in the Drain Theory chapter, Chapter 27.) Effect on India: British goods entered Indian ports at a lower tariff than German, Japanese or American competitors. India's tariff regime systematically advantaged the very British manufacturing economy that Indian industries were trying to compete with. Prelims 1999 trap: answer (a) special privileges on British imports in India. (b) racial discrimination is a different phenomenon (Section 7). (c) subordination of Indian interest is too vague, a general description of colonialism and not the specific definition. (d) preference to British political agents over Princes is Political Department protocol. The key word is tariff. 11.1 The stray table of five antiquarians (Prelims 2023) 1 Alexander Rea Excavated at Amaravati and Bhattiprolu 2 A.H. Longhurst Excavated at Nagarjunakonda and Hampi 3 Robert Sewell Wrote "A Forgotten Empire" (Vijayanagara) 4 James Burgess First Director of the Archaeological Survey of Western and Southern India 5 Walter Elliot Of the Madras Civil Service; catalogued Andhra Buddhist sites and coins Stray table. It sits between Imperial Preference and the foreign ideologies with no heading or link to the ideology story; it answers Prelims 2023: all five = archaeological excavations (a). The handout's flow chart ties it to Orientalist scholarship through the ASI (founded 1861, Alexander Cunningham) (Section 3.2.1). The full ASI story is not in this chapter. Names only in the figure: Wilkins (Orientalism) and Trevelyan (Liberal-era) are not in the handout text. Use the figure as a picture of the sequence, and the text for facts.

items.t: 12 · Foreign ideologies motivating India's anti-colonial struggle
items.x: Because the burden produced its opposite, world events fed Indian nationalism. Ask: which three buckets and which two carriers answer Mains 2014? Numbering glitch. The handout numbers these points 13.1 to 13.3 (under "Sec. 13"); here they are 12.1 to 12.3. WMB (Section 2) produced its opposite: powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies across the globe that travelled back into India through newspapers, returning students and political exiles. 12.1 Pre-1900 political and ideological currents 1. American Revolution (1765-83): political movement from 1765, War of Independence 1776-83. 2. French Revolution of 1789: liberty, equality, fraternity. 3. European revolutions of 1830 and 1848: democratic uprisings across the continent. 4. Irish Home Rule (1870-1914) and Irish armed struggle (1916-21) against Britain: direct anti-British inspiration. All challenged imperial superiority and inspired colonised peoples worldwide. 12.2 Three 20th-century shocks that radicalised Indian nationalism 1. Industrial Revolution's destructive impact on Indian handloom: deindustrialisation fed the Drain Theory of Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt. 2. Russian Revolution of 1917: gave the Indian left a peasant-worker mobilisation model and an anti-imperial vocabulary. 3. Post-WWI principle of self-determination (Wilson's Fourteen Points, 1918) and rising anti-racism: made continued British rule increasingly indefensible in international forums. 12.3 Returning Indian leaders brought these currents home The world-developments travelled through people, not ideas alone: 1. Gandhi from South Africa: anti-colonial training from Indian-diaspora struggles in South Africa (1893-1915). 2. Nehru from Cambridge: Western liberal-democratic political theory absorbed during his Cambridge studies, applied in Indian Congress politics. Mains 2014 (10M, 150 words): "What were the major political, economic and social developments in the world which motivated the anti-colonial struggle in India?" Handout's three-bucket answer: Enlightenment + American + French + Irish revolutions (political and ideological); Industrial Revolution deindustrialisation (economic); Russian Revolution 1917 + Wilson's self-determination + anti-racism (social and ideological); then returning leaders (Gandhi from South Africa, Nehru from Cambridge). The companion Appendix FYQ_Mains with the five-part treatment is not in this notebook. Skeleton: see the Exam lens.

Last scene: the eight ideologies with champions and measures. Ask: which champion goes with which ideology, and which three share 1813? The handout's summary table printed badly; it is rebuilt here from the clean typed slides. 1 White Man's Burden Foundation (throughout) All Englishmen Civilising-mission rhetoric 2 Orientalism 1765-1813 Warren Hastings 73-85, William Jones, Colebrooke, Wilson Calcutta Madrasa 1781; Asiatic Society 1784; Sanskrit College 1791; Fort William College 1800 3 Authoritarianism 1786-1805 Cornwallis 86-93, Wellesley 98-05 Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793; Permanent Settlement 1793; Aloof Elite 4 Conservatism 1801-27 Munro, Malcolm, Elphinstone, Metcalfe Ryotwari Settlement; political agencies 5 Liberalism 1813-57 T.B. Macaulay, Bentinck 28-35 Sati Abolition 1829; Minute on Education 1835; Law Commission 1834 6 Utilitarianism 1813-57 Bentham, James Mill, JS Mill Law Commission 1834; codification; IPC 1860 7 Evangelicalism 1813-57 Charles Grant, Wilberforce, Zachary Macaulay Charter Act 1813 (missionaries); Lex Loci Act 1850 8 Racism / Crown Paramountcy Post 1857 Lytton 76-80, Curzon 99-05, Dufferin 84-88 Queen's Proclamation 1858; Vernacular Press Act 1878; Upper Burma 1886; Imperial Preference (Ottawa 1932) Items only in the summary table: Colebrooke, Wilson (Orientalism champions); Wilberforce, Zachary Macaulay (Evangelicalism); JS Mill (Utilitarianism); IPC 1860 (Utilitarianism's codification). They are not explained in the handout text; learn them as names to match.

1765 Orientalism begins (the board's start year) 1776 American War of Independence begins (to 1783) 1781 Calcutta Madrasa founded by Warren Hastings 73-85 ★ 1784 Asiatic Society of Bengal founded by Sir William Jones ★ 1786 Cornwallis 86-93's Authoritarianism begins 1789 French Revolution 1791 Sanskrit College, Banaras (Jonathan Duncan) ★ 1793 Charter Act 1793 and the Permanent Settlement ★ 1800 Fort William College (Wellesley 98-05) ★ 1813 Leipzig; Charter Act 1813; the post-1813 sharp turn ★ 1815 Waterloo 1818 James Mill's History of British India 1829 Sati Abolition Act (Bentinck 28-35) 1833 Charter Act 1833 (Macaulay as legal member) 1834 Law Commission ★ 1835 Macaulay's Minute on Education; Thuggee and Dacoity Department set up ★ 1838 Tripartite Treaty (Sikh State, EIC, Shah Shuja) 1839 1st Anglo-Afghan War begins (to 1842) ★ 1842 Retreat from Kabul (January); punitive return to Kabul 1850 Lex Loci Act 1852 Lower Burma British 1856 Anglo-Persian War begins (to 1857) 1857 Revolt of 1857 ★ 1858 Queen Victoria's Proclamation ★ 1878 2nd Anglo-Afghan War begins (to 1880); Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act ★ 1879 Treaty of Gandamak ★ 1886 Upper Burma annexed (January); Thibaw to Ratnagiri ★ 1905 Partition of Bengal (Curzon 99-05) 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention: Iran split in three 1917 Russian Revolution 1932 Ottawa Conference: Imperial Preference ★ 1937 Burma separated from British India

A nation sure of itself. Britain had reasons for pride: the first modern democracy, the Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850), victory in the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63), Napoleon beaten (Leipzig 1813, Waterloo 1815) and the rise of capitalism and science. Within 150 years it could convince itself it was destined to lead, and that it owed the world its civilisation. This is the White Man's Burden. Scared, so Orientalist. Before 1813 the EIC was not militarily confident, and one badly handled insult could trigger mass resistance. Scholars like William Jones found Sanskrit older and more sophisticated than Greek and Latin. So Orientalism said: rule India the India way, with Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages and an Indian syllabus. Warren Hastings 73-85 was its champion. Four Orientalist institutions. The Calcutta Madrasa came in 1781 (Warren Hastings 73-85), the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784 (Sir William Jones), the Sanskrit College at Banaras in 1791 (Jonathan Duncan) and Fort William College in 1800 (Wellesley 98-05) to train British civilians. The Aryan Invasion Theory and kinship through language added a rhetoric of love: we are cousins who have come home. My way or highway. The critics said the study of India showed a glorious past and a degenerate present, so restoring the past was pointless. Cornwallis 86-93 ruled India the English way: all-British senior posts, rule of law with the Collector no longer also Judge (Charter Act 1793), the Permanent Settlement 1793 and an Aloof Elite. He had lost America and did not want settlers putting down roots. Indian coat, British hand. Thomas Munro, Governor of Madras 1820-27, governed through Indian forms but kept all power with the EIC: Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance. His Ryotwari Settlement copied the ancient State-peasant model but all collection was by EIC officials. Elphinstone, Malcolm and Metcalfe followed him. 1813: confidence, then three ideas. Indian powers had been beaten except Holkar, Bhonsle and the Sikh State, the army was huge, Napoleon was beaten and the Industrial Revolution was in full swing, with a market for British goods to win. Liberalism (Macaulay: Law Commission 1834, Minute on Education 1835, Brown Sahibs), Utilitarianism (Bentham and James Mill: good laws, a strong State, the schoolmaster) and Evangelicalism (Charles Grant, Charter Act 1813, Lex Loci Act 1850) filled the space. The Liberal window, 1828-35. From Bentinck 28-35 through the Charter Act 1833 to Macaulay's Minute 1835, Liberal confidence peaked: the Sati Abolition Act 1829, Thuggee suppression under Captain Sleeman (three tools: informants, approvers, swift commissions; over 3,000 Thugs convicted 1831-41), English replacing Persian in higher instruction, and Cornwallis 86-93's Code revised into uniform criminal procedure. The shock of 1857. The Revolt shook the British psychologically and broke the paternalistic narrative. Six fronts shifted: reform retreated, race was read by physical features, the Aryan theory was twisted, Dogs and Indians not allowed, Authoritarianism rose and social reforms slowed after Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858. Lytton 76-80 (Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act 1878) and Curzon 99-05 (Partition of Bengal 1905) were its architects. The Forward Policy and the Great Game. Fearing Tsarist Russia, the British pushed the frontier into Afghanistan: Auckland 36-42's 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1839-42, Ellenborough 42-44's punitive return to Kabul, Lytton 76-80's 2nd war 1878-80 and the Treaty of Gandamak 1879, then Ripon 80-84's reversal. The defensive twin was the Ring Fence, and the Persian flank ended with the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907. Upper Burma and Imperial Preference. Dufferin 84-88 annexed Upper Burma in January 1886, the last major extension, deposing King Thibaw. Trade was also bent to the empire: Imperial Preference, formalised at Ottawa in 1932, let British goods enter Indian ports at lower tariffs than German, Japanese or American goods. The ideas come home. The White Man's Burden produced its opposite: the American Revolution, the French Revolution 1789, the European revolutions of 1830 and 1848 and the Irish struggle. Later shocks added deindustrialisation and the Drain Theory, the Russian Revolution 1917, Wilson's self-determination and anti-racism. They travelled through people: Gandhi from South Africa (1893-1915) and Nehru from Cambridge.
