Story so far: the EIC holds the territory; now it must run it. The teacher's four verdicts set the weight of this chapter. Ask: why does he call the whole thing PubAd in British India? Chapter 18 title slide: EIC administration Four verdicts: no Qs in Mains, few rare Qs in Prelims, troubles aspirants in every book, best version in this handout. Subject = history of Public Administration (PubAd) in British India: how a Company State built its working machinery, not a list of Acts. Administration: machinery of the State, three pillars

items.t: 1 · Administration as the machinery of the State
items.x: Because the State needs machinery to work, the EIC had to build or borrow it. Ask: which three pillars carry the chapter, and what are 'T' and 'Ppl'? Administration is the machinery of the State: how the State implements its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC changed from a trading company into a Company State (the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function; the slide dates the Company State 1765-1858), it had to build this machinery from scratch. More accurately, it had to decide how much of the existing Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. The chapter covers three pillars: Judiciary, Civil Services and Police. ORG (the State) = its three machines. "WORK = RULE": rule over T (territory) and Ppl (people). Administration is the daily work of ruling them. Links to the L, E, J shorthand (Chapter 8, Chapter 10): the Company State had taken the territory; this chapter is how it handled the people. Mains warning (handout). UPSC Mains PYQs mapped to administration mostly ask about the economic impact of British rule: Drain of Wealth, de-industrialisation, the Sepoy Army as an imperial tool. They need other chapters: Drain of Wealth in Moderates / Drain Theory; de-industrialisation in British Imperial Ideology and Land Revenue Systems; Sepoy Army in the 1857 Revolt. This chapter is the administrative skeleton; those supply the economic and military flesh.

Because law was sensitive, the EIC began with Mughal courts and changed them only step by step. Ask: which six questions did every reform have to answer? 2.1 Why judicial reform was so complicated The EIC was not walking into a blank slate. It entered a society with established legal traditions, different religious communities and a functioning (though imperfect) court system. It had to answer six questions: 1 Which law should apply: Hindu, Islamic or British? Personal laws kept; Anglo-Muhammadan law; Supreme Court on British law 2 Should laws be written down or left to the judges' discretion? Codification: Gentoo Code, Hedaya, Code of 1781, Cornwallis 86-93 Code 3 What hierarchy of courts? 1772, 1773, 1793, Bentinck 28-35 4 Should lawyers be allowed to represent parties? Yes, from 1793 5 Should judges be Indians or British? All senior posts European under Cornwallis 86-93; lower posts opened from 1833 6 In which language should courts function? Persian replaced in 1835 Each question carried political, social and financial implications, and the answers changed as British confidence, ambition and administrative needs evolved. 2.2 The Mughal judicial system in Bengal (before 1772) The Mughal system in Bengal had two separate hierarchies, one for civil and one for criminal matters. Civil matters (Diwani = finance, land revenue and civil justice): Courts ran from the local level up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA) at the suba (provincial) level. In inter-personal matters (marriage, inheritance) the personal laws of Hindus and Muslims applied. Mughal judicial system in the provinces: civil and criminal Pandits judged Hindu cases and Maulvis judged Muslim cases. At the top the Diwan served as Chief Justice of the SDA. For land revenue and non-personal civil disputes, the original jurisdiction lay with the Zamindar at the local level, in his revenue court, the Kachari. Appeals went up: Zamindar, then Amil (the provincial revenue officer at district level), then the SDA at the provincial capital (Murshidabad), presided over by the Diwan or Naib Diwan. Around this time Muhammad Reza Khan, the Naib Nazim, held the posts of Chief Justice of both the SDA and the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Amil versus Amalguzar. The handout uses Amil for the mutated 18th-century Bengal system; the canonical Mughal term is Amalguzar (revenue officer at district level). Same post. Criminal matters: Nizamat Adalats (commonly called Faujdari Adalats) sat at the district level, with the Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA) at the top. The Mughal State was an Islamic state, so Islamic law governed criminal proceedings, applied uniformly regardless of religion. At the village level the Zamindar held petty criminal jurisdiction alongside his police duties. Major crimes bypassed the Zamindar and went straight to the district Faujdari Adalat. Strict division of labour: the Kazis were the actual judges who pronounced verdicts (the board calls it a "2 People Bench," Kazi with Mufti), the Muftis gave expert interpretation of Islamic law, and the district Faujdar (executive police chief) secured the accused and physically executed the sentence. The Naib Nazim headed the SNA. Civil courts were religion-specific (judge depended on faith); criminal courts were State-uniform (ruling State's law for everyone). Civil has two tracks under the SDA: personal law (Diwani Adalat, Pandits and Maulvis) and LR / non-personal (Amalguzar, then Zamindar's Kachari). Criminal has one track: "Law = Islamic Law." 18th-century Bengal courts at suba level Who is Chief Justice of the SNA? General Mughal board: SNA [CJ = Nazim / Subadar]. 18th-century Bengal boards and the handout: CJ = Naib Nazim. By the 18th century the Subadar was distant and Naib Nazim Muhammad Reza Khan ran the courts. For Bengal before 1772 use Naib Nazim for the SNA and Diwan for the SDA; Reza Khan held both chief justiceships, having been made the EIC's Diwan in 1765. Personal matters in civil and criminal law, 18th-century Bengal Remember this pair: standard books stop at personal law in civil matters and criminal law in criminal matters. Civil = Hindu law for Hindus, Muslim law for Muslims. Criminal = Islamic law for everyone. Faujdar: like the SP at district Faujdar = like today's SP (Superintendent of Police) at the district. Two jobs: LEO (as the board writes it; the handout calls him the executive police chief who secured the accused) and executing the judgement of the Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat. He does not judge; the Kazi does. Judicial structure before 1772 Suba (province) Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA), CJ the Diwan (Reza Khan held both chief justiceships) Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA), headed by the Naib Nazim District Diwani Adalat: Pandits (Hindu cases) and Maulvis (Muslim cases); revenue side: Amil (Amalguzar) Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat: Kazi judges, Mufti interprets, Faujdar executes Local Zamindar's Kachari: land revenue and non-personal disputes Zamindar: petty crimes only; major crimes go straight to the district court Law applied Personal law (Hindu law, Muslim law) Islamic law for all 2.3 The Dual Government period (1765-1772) After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC gained the Diwani rights over Bengal: revenue administration, Treasury and control of property / civil courts. (Modern welfare duties such as health and education were not included: they were traditionally handled by private or religious patronage, not by the Mughal government.) The Nawab retained the Nizamat (law and order). This created the Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism ("rule India the Indian way"), the EIC did not rush to impose its own system. Muhammad Reza Khan continued to head both the Diwani (on the EIC's behalf) and the Nizamat (on the Nawab's behalf). Indian officials remained the effective decision-makers on the ground. The EIC was mainly concerned with collecting land revenue. Outcome: revenue collection was poor; law and order deteriorated, made catastrophic by the Great Bengal Famine of 1770, which killed roughly one-third of Bengal's population. Board outcome row: "Poverty leads to Crimes". Hunger pushed people into crime, so law and order failed because of the famine, which a hands-off administration worsened. (Dual Government, Diwani versus Nizamat and Reza Khan as the EIC's Diwan: Chapter 10.) 2.4 Direct Government (1772) and the judicial plan of Hastings 73-85 In 1772 Hastings 73-85 (Governor from 1772, GG of Bengal 1773-1785) ended the Dual Government and took direct administration of both the Diwani and the Nizamat. Rationale: EIC administration, based on rule of law and equality before law, would be fairer and more efficient and would firmly establish British authority. (The ideology shifts slightly from pure Orientalism to a hybrid: rule more directly, but still use Indian legal frameworks.) Diwani (civil) courts at the district The British DC is the judge, assisted by Pandits and Maulvis Personal laws continued in marriage and inheritance Nizamat (criminal) courts at the district Kazis and Muftis continue as judges, now supervised by the European DC The British thought law and order too sensitive to replace fully Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat Headed by the Governor (from 1773, the GG of Bengal) and his Council members The top of both ladders passes to the Company 1772 changes: courts under Hastings Muhammad Reza Khan (Naib Nazim) was imprisoned without trial from 1772 to 1774, accused of corruption and poor law-and-order maintenance. Conditions did not improve, so he was released in 1774 and reinstated as head of the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Why Kazis and Muftis stayed in criminal courts: "Law and order (L and O) = sensitive, therefore the British continue with K and M as J." Civil: the DC sits as judge. Criminal: the DC only supervises (taking over was too risky). 2.4.1 The changes of 1773 Two further adjustments: 1. A proper attempt at separation of revenue and judicial powers: an officer serving as DC was not to serve as judge too. In practice the overlap remained, but the principle was established. 2. To bring justice physically closer to the people, the district-level Diwani Adalats were replaced by 18 Mofussil courts, each headed by a European judge. 1773 Act: Mofussil courts and Supreme Court (Mofussil = rural areas and countryside districts below the district headquarters.) "PROPER SoP @ DC by CW 86-93." The handout calls 1773 a "proper attempt" at separation; the real Separation of Powers at the DC level was done by Cornwallis 86-93 in 1793. 1773 only set the principle. Exam links the DC's loss of judicial power to 1793 and Cornwallis 86-93 (Prelims 2010). 1773 versus 1793. 1773 (Hastings 73-85): separation attempted, overlap remained, 18 Mofussil courts. 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): DC stripped of all judicial powers, the 18 Mofussil courts abolished, district Diwani Adalats back ("Mofussil courts ended, DA back"). 2.4.2 The Supreme Court (1774) The Regulating Act 1773 led to a Supreme Court in Calcutta in 1774, specifically to hear cases involving British subjects in Bengal, under British law. (British people, British judges, British law: a completely separate judicial track.) Supreme Courts followed in Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823). The Supreme Court was entirely separate from the Indian court hierarchy. 1774: Indian court ladder and the Supreme Court 1774 on one board: SDA headed by the GG; SNA headed by Naib Nazim Md Reza Khan (reinstated 1774); Mofussil courts with a European judge assisted by Pandits and Maulvis; Nizamat courts with Kazi and Mufti under the European DC's supervision. The Supreme Court sits outside this ladder, only for Britishers. 2.4.3 Codification of laws 1775: a committee of 11 Pandits compiled Hindu law into a single coherent code so courts could interpret it uniformly. The English translation was published as the Gentoo Code (1776). ("Gentoo" comes from the Portuguese "Gentios," a derogatory term for Hindus, used because Hindus worshipped multiple Gods unlike monotheistic Christians.) 1778: a similar effort for Islamic law. Because of Mughal rule, Islamic law was already well organised, so the EIC simply translated the most authoritative existing Arabic legal manual, the Al-Hidayah, first into Persian by Indian scholars and then into English as The Hedaya (1791). The Code of 1781 made written orders compulsory and prescribed rules for court functioning. "WRITTEN LAW" answers question 2 (written or discretion?). "ENGLISH WRITTEN": the Gentoo Code and the Hedaya are the English written versions of Indian law, usable by British judges. Code of 1781 = "in Bengal" only (see Section 2.5.2). 2.5 The Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (judiciary) Cornwallis 86-93 (GG 1786-1793) introduced the most systematic judicial reform of the early period. He is rightly called the father of civil services, but his influence on the judiciary was equally significant. 2.5.1 Why did Cornwallis 86-93 reform the judiciary? He had just introduced the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (PS1793), creating a new class of large zamindars as private property owners. For this to work, zamindars needed secure property rights: courts they could trust, and revenue officials who could not harass them. An officer who collected your tax should not also be the judge hearing your appeal against his own actions. So Cornwallis 86-93 properly implemented Separation of Powers at the level of the DC: the District Collector was stripped of all judicial powers and confined to revenue collection and administration. Why Cornwallis separated powers "Imagine": PS1793 has a sunset clause (applied, the zamindar's estate goes up for auction). If the DC applies it on a zamindar (Z) and the zamindar files a case in the Diwani Adalat, what if the judge is the same DC? Conflict of interest, so security of property falls for the zamindar. Hence the DC could no longer be a judge. Also: Cornwallis 86-93 = AUTHORITARIAN, therefore he removed Indians from all senior positions (other side of the same reform). Prelims 2010 trap (handout, Section 2.5). "By a regulation in 1793, the DC was deprived of his judicial powers and made the collecting agent only. Why?" Correct: (c) absolute power in one person was undesirable (separation of powers; the post-PS1793 zamindar class needed independent courts). (a) efficiency of revenue collection is a partial truth, not the principal motivation. (b) "judicial power must be European-only, revenue can be Indian" is wrong: Cornwallis 86-93 in fact removed Indians from all senior positions, including revenue. (d) "judicial work demanded deep India knowledge" is a partial truth, not the principal motivation. Cornwallis Code 1793: courts of appeal and circuit 2.5.2 In civil matters The 18 Mofussil courts were replaced by Diwani Adalats at the district level and City Courts for urban areas. Bengal was divided into four divisions: Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta and Dacca, and a Provincial Court of Appeal was set up in each. Appeals: district Diwani Adalats and City Courts, then the Provincial Court of Appeal, then the Sadar Diwani Adalat, shifted from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Personal laws of Hindus and Muslims continued in civil matters. PS1793 governed land revenue disputes. Per Charter Act 1793, all regulations for governing Bengal were codified, written orders made compulsory and laws printed in the vernaculars so people could know their rights. Code of 1781 versus Code of 1793: the difference is the ISSUING AUTHORITY. The 1781 code (Hastings, Bengal only) was issued by the GG (in Bengal), so a future GG could change it. The 1793 Code came through the Charter Act 1793, "By Br (P)": the British Parliament, so it carries more weight. The board writes "HASTINGS 78-85" (last digits, look like 78); typed slides and handout write Hastings 73-85. This notebook keeps 73-85. Check your own notes. 2.5.3 In criminal matters Faujdari / Nizamat Adalats at the district level were abolished. Four Provincial Courts of Circuit were set up in the four divisions. A Court of Circuit is a court that physically moves around its division, hearing cases in different areas in rotation. This eliminated the need for a district-level criminal court. Appeals from the Courts of Circuit went to the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Islamic law continued in criminal matters, but with British legal modifications. This hybrid was Anglo-Muhammadan law. For about 70 years, until the Indian Penal Code 1860, courts applied it. Court of Circuit = travelling bench: week 1 in district 1, week 2 in district 2, week 3 in district 3, week 4 in district 4, then back to week 1; no district needs its own criminal court. Stressed: Anglo-Muhammadan law and IPC 1860, with the three codes CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861 (Section 2.7). 2.5.4 Anglo-Muhammadan law in practice: three examples (handout only, no class notes) Handout only. Class notes stop at the name "Anglo-Muhammadan law"; the three examples below come from the handout alone. A: weapon rule replaced by intent rule Whether a killing was capital murder depended on the weapon used: a sharp iron instrument (sword) meant murder; strangling, drowning or a heavy stone was often a lesser crime (the instrument was not "designed" to draw blood) He abolished this loophole: the intent of the accused decides, not the instrument. This matches the modern principle of mens rea B: the end of "blood money" (Diyat) Murder was largely a private dispute between families: the victim's heirs could pardon the killer for financial compensation (blood money, Diyat) Relatives could no longer pardon a murderer. This set the principle that a major crime is an offence against the State, not just a private injury C: abolition of mutilation The standard punishment for serious theft or dacoity was amputation of a hand or foot The EIC completely outlawed mutilation and replaced it with hard labour and rigorous imprisonment, typically 7 to 14 years 2.5.5 Personnel and a new profession: lawyers Cornwallis 86-93 was authoritarian. He removed Indians from all senior positions. All courts were headed by European officials. Kazis and Muftis were retained only as assistants, not judges. The office of Naib Nazim was abolished. Cornwallis 1793: personnel and a new profession One progressive change: lawyers were now permitted to appear in courts. This created a new professional class, the Indian lawyer, and, along with PS1793 (which made land a tradeable commodity), also a class of property dealers. "[NA ABOLISHED]": the district Nizamat Adalat is gone. "Cornwallis 86-93, father of: CS (civil services), property dealers, lawyer." A short word under the fork reads like "SHO" (station house officer, the police Daroga of Section 4.3):. 2.5.6 Why the new system increased litigation (class slide only, not in the handout) Class slide only; the handout does not carry this table. It gives three reasons litigation rose after PS1793. 1. Separation of Powers (key reason) The DC lost all judicial and magisterial powers. Earlier the Collector could resolve revenue disputes swiftly and informally on the spot; after 1793 every such dispute had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats 2. Abolition of court fees Cornwallis 86-93 initially abolished court fees to make justice "accessible," which instantly flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits. Fees were reimposed just 2 years later, in 1795 3. A legal profession Formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) and a rigid hierarchy of appeals: cases were deliberately prolonged and appealed 2.6 Judicial system in Ryotwari areas The Bengal model of separated judicial and revenue functions worked in a zamindari system. In Ryotwari areas, where the ryot is recognised as the direct landowner, conditions were very different: A very large number of small landowners meant a very large number of land-related disputes. District courts were physically distant for poor ryots in villages. Judicial system in Ryotwari areas Madras, 1814: the Bengal system was replaced on Munro's advice. Separation of judicial and revenue powers was ended. The European DC and his subordinates were given judicial powers so disputes could be resolved at the ground level. (Less paperwork, less travel, faster justice, at least in theory.) This led to greater Indianisation at the lower judiciary, because the DC's subordinates included Indian officials. The downside: enormous concentration of power in one official. The DC now collected taxes, maintained order and judged disputes, including disputes arising from his own tax collection decisions. Bombay, 1819: the same Ryotwari system was applied by Elphinstone, a follower of Munro's philosophy. Why Bengal separated and Madras merged: "WHR (where) the number of landowners is LESS" = zamindari: few big landowners, few disputes, a distant court is workable. Ryotwari: many landowners, so courts must come to the village. Downside row: "+ his juniors" (the DC's subordinates, including Indians, also gain judicial powers). Result of concentrated power: Madras Torture Commission Report 1855, "oppression by Mirasidars revealed." Beside INDIANS: a scale of 300, 200, 100, seemingly pay or rank scales for Indians below a DC above 300. Madras Torture Commission 1855, two homes. Handout: police section (4.3.2), exposing atrocities of revenue officials after the Daroga system failed in Madras. Class: Ryotwari judicial system (a DC with all powers, plus juniors), with Mirasidars (Madras village landholders). Learn the fact once, 1855, Madras Torture Commission, oppression exposed, and use it in either answer. 2.7 Charter Act 1833 (judicial impact) The Charter Act of 1833 made the GG of India the single central legislative authority for all of British India, and the laws passed were to apply equally to Indians and Britishers alike. (A major shift: one law for everyone, regardless of race.) One Law Member was added to the GG's Council: Thomas Macaulay was appointed, and a Law Commission (1834) was set up under him to codify all laws systematically. Codification was substantially complete by 1837, but full implementation came after 1857: Civil Procedure Code (CPC) 1859 Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860 Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) 1861 Subordinate judicial positions below the rank of District Judge were opened to Indians. Impact on the common Indian: justice became psychologically distant (new laws were western, complex and unfamiliar), physically distant for rural areas and financially distant (legal fees few could afford). The system was more systematic, but it served the educated and propertied far better than the poor. "Personal laws continued in personal matters": despite the IPC, CPC and CrPC, marriage and inheritance stayed under Hindu and Muslim personal law. "Indianisation of the lower J": posts below District Judge opened to Indians (follows the 1814 Madras Indianisation, Section 2.6). "Western Edu 1835": western, English-language law goes with western education from 1835 (Chapter 19: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture); the English-educated class could use the new courts. 2.8 Reforms by Bentinck 28-35 (GG 1828-33; GG of India 1833-35) Concept versus reality. Concept: polity = three equal organs, L, E, J. Reality: E is the top prestige; DC and senior civil servants want E, and an inefficient officer is posted as a punishment to the Divisional Court. J was the dumping ground, hence Bentinck 28-35 abolished those courts. Bentinck 28-35: shorter court ladders Bentinck 28-35: concept versus reality of L, E, J Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts: both the Provincial Courts of Appeal (civil) and the Courts of Circuit (criminal) that Cornwallis 86-93 had created. Why: these courts had become parking grounds for inefficient officers (punishment postings for non-performers), which contributed to high pendency. High-ranking officers also meant high State expenditure, so the courts were ended as a fiscal-prudence measure. Transfer: judicial powers and pending cases went to District Judges. After Bentinck 28-35 the ladders are shorter. Civil: District Diwani Adalat + City Courts go straight up to the SDA (4 Provincial Courts of Appeal gone). Criminal: Nizamat Adalat goes straight up to the SNA (4 Courts of Circuit gone). Stressed: "high State expenditure"; the courts removed were Cornwallis 86-93's ("86-93" noted beside "Cornwallis"). Reforms by William Bentinck 28-35 1835, language of the courts: Persian was replaced: vernaculars in the lower courts and English in the higher courts. Legal backing: Act XXIX of 1837. The removal caused anxiety among Muslim elites, because Persian education had been an important pathway to administrative careers. Courts for the Northwest Provinces: he created a Sadar Diwani Adalat and a Sadar Nizamat Adalat in the Northwest Provinces (the portion of Awadh annexed in 1801, given full province status in 1836), so people from this region did not have to travel to Bengal to file appeals. NWP circle: 1801 (Awadh portion annexed), then NWP 1836 (full province status); the other oval is the Bengal Presidency; between them: "Distance." Appeals to Calcutta meant a long journey, so the NWP got its own two Sadar courts. Context on Persian. Persian was introduced under the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th century. It got a major boost when Humayun 30-40, to win military support from Persia's Safavid dynasty to reclaim his throne from the Suri Dynasty (1540-55), accepted the condition of promoting Persian. Akbar 56-05, with finance minister Todar Mal, made Persian compulsory for all administrative records. 2.9 Indian High Courts Act 1861 and 2.10 the Federal Court (GOI Act 1935) The Indian High Courts Act 1861 led to High Courts in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta in 1862. The Calcutta High Court was created by merging three existing courts: the Sadar Diwani Adalat, the Sadar Nizamat Adalat and the Supreme Court at Calcutta. This finally ended the dual-track system of separate courts for Indians and the British. The GOI Act 1935, implemented from 1937, established a Federal Court, the direct ancestor of today's Supreme Court of India. It dealt with inter-governmental disputes (Centre versus Province, Province versus Province) and heard appeals from High Courts. Today's Supreme Court, set up under the Constitution of India 1950, continues this role with expanded jurisdiction. The judiciary: from Mughal courts to the Federal Court Before 1772: two ladders (civil: Diwan, Pandits and Maulvis, Zamindar's Kachari; criminal: Naib Nazim, Kazi, Mufti, Faujdar); personal law in civil, Islamic law in criminal Dual Government 1765-72: Reza Khan heads both Diwani and Nizamat; revenue poor; law and order falls; famine 1770 1772 (Hastings 73-85): DC as civil judge; Kazi and Mufti kept under DC supervision; Governor and Council head the two Sadar Adalats 1773-74: 18 Mofussil courts; Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), later Madras 1800 and Bombay 1823; Gentoo Code 1776, Hedaya 1791, Code of 1781 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): DC loses judicial power; four divisions with Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit; Anglo-Muhammadan law; Indians out of senior posts; lawyers in 1814 and 1819: Madras and Bombay merge the DC's roles in Ryotwari areas 1833-37 (Bentinck 28-35 and Macaulay): divisional courts abolished; Persian replaced 1835; NWP Adalats; Law Commission 1834 1859-62: CPC, IPC, CrPC; High Courts 1862 end the dual track 1937: Federal Court, ancestor of the Supreme Court of India (1950)

Because courts and revenue need officers, the question became who gets hired and how. Ask: what separates a service from mere employment, and what did Cornwallis 86-93 NOT introduce? 3.1 Issues in civil services, and what a "service" means Seven design questions for any civil service: (1) nomination or examination? (2) if exam, a specialised body like the UPSC or not? (3) syllabus: Indian or Western? (4) exam location: London, or India and London? (5) age limit: low or high? (6) organisation of services (today IAS, IPS, IFS, IRS and more): common exam or a separate exam per service? (7) training: on the job or in a training institute? The chapter reads as the EIC's answers to these seven, in order. In any organisation officials may be simply employed, or organised into a service. A service means a pre-defined career path, fixed rules for pay, promotion and removal, and a clear structure of seniority and accountability: the difference between being an employee and being a member of a cadre. The history of the EIC's civil services is a move from a chaotic, patronage-based system to a structured, merit-based administrative cadre, with an extra tension: how many Indians would be allowed in? Issues in civil services Without a service: "No career ladder" = "Total discretion" in employment and promotion. The boss alone decides who is hired and promoted; a service replaces discretion with rules. 3.2 Recruitment: from patronage to examination Initially EIC officials were recruited by nomination, not merit. Posts were either purchased or handed out through patronage. EIC Directors actively lobbied British Parliamentarians with offers of jobs for their sons. This bred corruption and incompetence. 3.3 Training Until 1800 Essentially on the job 1800-1806 Fort William College, Calcutta, set up by Wellesley 98-05 for training in Indian laws, customs and languages 1806-1858 Haileybury College, London (East India College) 1858 onwards British universities 3.4 Cornwallis 86-93: founder of civil services Cornwallis 86-93 brought the first proper structure to the civil services. He organised ("ORGanised") EIC employees into two tiers: Today's parallel Like today's Group A Like today's Group B Who Senior officers who signed a formal legal contract, a "covenant," with the EIC's Court of Directors in London before sailing to India Junior officers hired locally in India by the GG or provincial governors Pay and path High defined pay, clear career path Lower pay, less formal Access Under Cornwallis 86-93 reserved strictly for Europeans The space where Indians were allowed to serve: at first very low-level clerical roles, then Deputy Collectors and Deputy Magistrates by the 1830s-40s as the empire grew and needed cheaper local administrators "ORGanised employees into..." = what "service" means (Section 3.1): a pool of employees becomes ranked cadres. CCS access: Europeans-only = "Authoritarian" (the same Cornwallis 86-93 who removed Indians from senior judicial posts). UCS: "Indians + British": not Indians-only, but the space where Indians could enter. DID Two tiers CCS plus UCS: the first proper structure DID Strict seniority for promotions London bosses could no longer push underqualified relatives over experienced officers (the slide calls it "Merit @ Promotions") DID Massively higher salaries To reduce the incentive to be corrupt DID Curbed private trade by EIC officials (see the Dastak and private trade story in [[10 Chapter 10]]) DID Separation of Powers DC stripped of judicial powers in 1793 DID NOT Merit-based selection for entry Entry stayed patronage-based: nomination by the EIC's Court of Directors in London, right until the Charter Act 1853 This is why he is called the founder of civil services in India: he converted a corrupt, patronage-ridden set of employees into a structured, professionalised service. Prelims 2010 trap (handout, Section 3.4). "Who among the following GGs created the Covenanted Civil Service, which later became the Indian Civil Service?" Correct: (c) Cornwallis 86-93. (a) Hastings 73-85 is wrong: first GG of Bengal under the Regulating Act 1773, introduced a judicial plan but not the CCS structure. (b) Wellesley 98-05 is wrong: set up Fort William College 1800 for CCS training but did not create the service structure. (d) Bentinck 28-35 is wrong: opened the UCS to Indians under the Charter Act 1833 and encouraged some senior Indian recruitment, but did not create the CCS. Also: the CCS was later renamed ICS in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94, per the Aitchison Commission 1887, NOT by the Indian Councils Act 1892. 3.5 Charter Act 1833 and Bentinck 28-35 The Charter Act of 1833 opened the Uncovenanted Civil Services to Indians, primarily to reduce administration cost by using cheaper Indian labour in junior roles. Bentinck 28-35 went slightly further and encouraged recruitment of Indians to some senior positions. 3.6 Charter Act 1853: the exam opened to Indians The Charter Act of 1853 was a landmark: it mandated a Civil Service Examination for the CS and Indians were eligible to appear. 1854: a Select Committee of Parliament under Macaulay recommended replacing patronage-based recruitment with exam-based recruitment for a permanent civil service. This led to the Civil Services Commission (1854) in London, which held its first examination in 1855. Eligibility on paper did not mean access in practice: Age limit The maximum age ranged from 18 to 23, kept deliberately low. 1859: the Crown cut the maximum entry age to 23. Then 22 in 1860, 21 in 1866, and 19 in 1876 (implemented 1878 so as not to hit aspirants already preparing) Syllabus Dominated by English Literature, designed to produce what Macaulay called "Brown Sahibs": Indians educated in English culture and values, culturally loyal to Britain Venue Held only in London For an Indian candidate Cost of travel to England; inferior preparation compared with British candidates; a syllabus that rewarded English cultural knowledge over Indian First Indians through 1864: Satyendranath Tagore (brother of Rabindranath Tagore) was the first Indian to clear the CCS exam. 1867: four more Indians cleared it Low age, English Literature, London exam: "To prevent entry of Indians into CS." The age ladder is "not imp" (do not memorise every step). "Literature = source of values": English Literature carried English values, which is how the Brown Sahib is made. The exam tested "culture's knowledge", and western education in Britain was better than in India, so a Briton had the advantage. 3.7 The fight for Indianisation (1860 onwards) From 1860 the western-educated Indian middle class (WEMC), the very product of British educational policy, began demanding Indianisation of the civil services. Two core demands: Simultaneous examination in India (not just London). A higher maximum age limit. The British response was hostile. Post-1857 British administrators were insecure about Indian assertion and determined to keep Indians out of senior positions. WEMC = Western Educated Middle Class [1835+]: the date is the western education of 1835 (see "Western Edu 1835", Section 2.7); the class demanding entry is the one the British made. Gap: promised by the 1919 Act, repeated by Lee 1923-24, set up in 1926. 3.11 GOI Act 1935 Context: Hindustan Republican Army (1924), CPI (1925), HSRA (1928), Anti-Simon agitations (1928), Lahore Conspiracy Case (1928), Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34), Chittagong Armoury Raid (1930-33), the martyrdom of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru, Bhagwati Charan Vohra and Chandrashekhar Azad (1931). The Act made the federal distribution of subjects between Centre and Provinces a formal constitutional structure. It mandated a Federal Public Service Commission (set up in 1937, replacing the 1926 PSC, the direct predecessor of today's UPSC) and Provincial Public Service Commissions for each Province or group of Provinces. By 1947 more than 50% of civil service positions had been Indianised. On 26 January 1950 the Federal PSC became the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) under Article 378 of the Constitution. (Article 378 is a transition provision: it ensures membership of the British-era UPSC and State PSCs continued seamlessly. Articles 315 and 316 govern the UPSC and State PSCs. Article 312 governs All India Services.) "GOI 1935 = Last COI by Bn (P)": the last of the constitutions given by the British Parliament. Context items to know: Hindustan Republican Army, CPI, HSRA, Anti-Simon, Lahore Conspiracy Case, Civil Disobedience, Chittagong Armoury Raid, the 1931 martyrdoms. Federal distribution of subjects: "TODAY'S 7th Schedule", i.e. the 1935 Centre-Province division is today's Seventh Schedule of the Constitution (the sources say nothing more about it). The civil services: from patronage to the UPSC Early EIC: nomination, purchase and patronage; Directors lobby Parliamentarians for sons' jobs 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): CCS plus UCS, higher pay, private trade curbed, seniority for promotion; entry still by nomination Training: on the job until 1800; Fort William College 1800-06; Haileybury 1806-58; universities from 1858 1833: UCS opened to Indians (cheaper junior labour); Bentinck 28-35 encourages some senior posts 1853-55: exam mandated, London-only; first exam 1855; Satyendranath Tagore 1864; four more 1867 1860 onwards: Indians demand a simultaneous exam and a higher age; British hostile; Lytton 76-80 offers lateral entry (Statutory CS 1878-79) 1887-92: Aitchison; ICS, PCS, Subordinate by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94 1912-17: Islington: 25% Indians, no simultaneous exam 1919-26: GOI Act 1919: exam in India 1922, PSC 1926, 33% 1923-24: Lee: 20-40-40, 50:50 in 15 years 1935-50: Federal PSC 1937; over 50% Indianised by 1947; UPSC under Article 378 on 26 January 1950 3.12 The civil services on one board Twelve-box chain, board additions: 73-85 over the Hastings era (ad hoc patronage); 86-93 beside Cornwallis; "based promotions (= MERIT)" under Cornwallis's seniority: promotion by seniority is the merit he brought, while entry stayed patronage until 1853 ("Merit @ Promotions", Section 3.4). Satyendranath over 1864 Tagore (first Indian, not Rabindranath). "ISLINGTON 1917: 25% Indians in ICS Report" inserted between the 1887 and 1919 boxes (Section 3.8). The board is a snake: the middle row reads right to left (1833, 1853, 1864, 1879), then drops to 1887. The board agrees with the handout and Lecture 20 on every date except the Statutory CS (1879 on the slide, 1878 in the handout; alert in Section 3.7.1). It shows the 1892 order inside the 1887 Aitchison box, so the "1887 report, 1892 order" pairing is on the board itself.

Because the third pillar was the most sensitive, the Mughal chain was kept for the longest time. Ask: why did the Daroga system fail, and why was Napier's Sindh model chosen? Police and the summary come from Lecture 21 only (Lecture 20 has no police slides). The title-slide verdict (few and rare Prelims questions) still applies. 4.1 The inherited system (pre-1781) Civil services evolution, 1773 to 1947 Police: the inherited system before 1781 The EIC treated law and order as extremely sensitive, so the Mughal system of policing was left untouched for the longest time. Under it in Bengal: Overall head Naib Nazim (Deputy Subadar) Rural districts (Sarkars) Faujdars (Sarkar here means a sub-divisional unit, not government; the meaning differs by region) Towns and urban areas Kotwals Villages Zamindars held police duties and paid Village Watchmen from their own resources Naib Nazim = Md Reza Khan @ SUBA; Faujdars @ DISTRICT; Kotwals @ TOWNS; Zamindars below, who PAID the Village Chowkidars, one in each village. The same Reza Khan who headed the Diwani and the Nizamat (Sections 2.2, 2.3) is police head at the suba. Village Watchmen = Village Chowkidars (same post). 4.2 Warren Hastings 73-85's reforms of 1781 The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 had led to a sharp increase in crime. Hastings 73-85 replaced Faujdars with English Magistrates (DC/DM) in rural districts. Zamindars kept their police duties under the DM's supervision. The problem: very few DMs, and poor supervision of zamindars, who continued to oppress the masses freely. Warren Hastings 73-85: police reforms of 1781 73-85, chain: GG (Be) -> DC/DM -> Zamindars -> VW (village watchmen). Against Section 4.1: the Faujdar rung is gone and an English magistrate sits there, but the zamindar is still between the magistrate and the village, hence poor supervision. 4.3 The Daroga system of Cornwallis 86-93 (1793) Daroga system of Cornwallis 86-93, 1793 Daroga system: chain of command Ended the police powers of zamindars: under PS1793 zamindars were to be agrarian capitalists, not local police authorities. Divided each district into thanas of 30 square miles each. Each thana was under a new officer, the Daroga (Indian), appointed and supervised by the DM. The English District Magistrate (DM) was made the absolute, supreme head of law and order within his district. Rather than an intermediary like an English Naib Nazim or an Inspector General, Cornwallis 86-93 centralised ultimate oversight of criminal and police administration in the GG and his Council. Chain of command: Darogas, then DM, then the central government. "[PS1793, Cornwallis Code 1793]": the Daroga system belongs with the Permanent Settlement and the Cornwallis 86-93 Code, one package (Sections 2.5.1, 2.5.2). "(AGRARIAN capitalist)": under PS1793 the zamindar is a landowning businessman, so he cannot also be the local police. Structure: many DC/DMs under one GG; many Darogas in thanas under each DM; no IG or Naib Nazim in between ("No intermediary"). 1 mile = 1.6 km, so a thana of 30 square miles is about 30 x 2.56 = 77 sq km (arithmetic from this conversion). 4.3.1 DC and DM: two roles, usually one person In most of British India (and in India today) the District Collector and District Magistrate are the same person holding two roles. Cornwallis 86-93 separated the judicial function from this officer (the DC/DM lost the power to be a judge), but the revenue and law-and-order functions stayed combined: DC (revenue) Collects land revenue, manages government land, maintains land records, collects various taxes The Mughal Diwani / Amalguzar function DM (law and order) Heads the district's criminal administration; coordinates with the SP to keep peace, prevent riots and issue executive orders such as Section 144 of the CrPC The Mughal Nizamat / Faujdari function DC hat: land revenue, government land, land records, taxes. DM hat: criminal administration, Faujdari. Stressing Faujdari (not Nizamat) makes the DM heir of the Mughal Faujdari function (district law and order) and the DC heir of the Diwani / Amalguzar function: the Section 2.2 ladder carried into today's district. Faujdar = SP, or DM = heir of Faujdari? Lecture 20 says "Faujdar = like SP at DISTRICT" (Section 2.2); Lecture 21 says the DM descends from the Nizamat / Faujdari function. Reading: the function (district law and order) passes to the DM as head, while the SP is the Faujdar's day-to-day counterpart. Answer: "the DM inherits the Faujdari function; the Faujdar was like today's SP"; do not claim the DM is the Faujdar. 4.3.2 Result: the Daroga-Zamindar nexus A Daroga-Zamindar nexus quickly developed: zamindars bribed Darogas and kept private armed men (lathiyals). The nexus became the primary instrument of oppression of the rural poor in the early 1800s. The British blamed "Indian corruption" rather than the structural weaknesses of the system. 1799: Wellesley 98-05 restored police powers to zamindars, in effect admitting the Daroga system had not worked. 1802: the Daroga system was extended to Madras but was later abolished there too because of its failures. The resulting atrocities of revenue officials were exposed by the Madras Torture Commission report of 1855, which led to corrective measures. "Next: Gave Police Powers To DC's Juniors in MADRAS" (between the 1802 and 1855 rows): the Daroga system was dropped in Madras, police powers went to the DC's juniors (revenue officials), and the atrocities of revenue officials were exposed in 1855 by the Madras Torture Commission. Same "DC + his juniors" pattern as the Ryotwari judiciary (Section 2.6): in Madras the Collector's office held revenue, police and judicial power at once. 4.4 The Police Act 1861 The Daroga system had failed. The British looked for a proven alternative and found it in the Irish Constabulary model: a centralised, hierarchical, quasi-military police force, effective in Ireland since 1787, designed as much for suppressing political agitation as for preventing ordinary crime. (The British were not primarily building a crime-prevention force; they were building a political control mechanism.) 4.4.1 Province-by-province road-test (pre-1861) Police Act 1861 and the Irish Constabulary model Sindh 1843 (annexed) Charles Napier, the military general who conquered Sindh, set up the Sindh Police on the Irish Constabulary model immediately after conquest Punjab 1849 Post-annexation Bombay 1853  Madras 1859  The 1st Police Commission (1860) was set up by Canning 56-62 under M.H. Court. It simply formalised what had already proved effective on the ground and borrowed heavily from the Sindh model when drafting the 1861 Police Act. A common UPSC trap: Charles Napier did NOT head the 1860 commission (many guidebooks wrongly say he did). Napier gave the blueprint (Sindh); M.H. Court's commission drew the national map using it. "EACH Province" = "Concept of Provincial Police": the Act's novelty is a police force for every province. Chart: IG answerable (a/c, dotted) to the Governor / LG; SP to the DM; dotted arrows = political accountability to civilian authority ("overall a/c"). Solid arrows SI -> SP -> IG = operational chain. The line SI to DM is crossed out: the Sub-Inspector no longer reports to the DC / DM as the Daroga did. Exam points: Irish Constabulary model, 1st Police Commission (1860), M.H. Court, Sindh model (Napier trap in the alert above). 4.4.2 The Police Act 1861 The Police Act, 1861 was passed in March 1861 by the GG's Council (as last restructured by the Charter Act 1853). (The Indian Councils Act 1861 came in August 1861 and created the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC); do not mix them.) It created the provincial police structure across all provinces: each Province to have its own police organisation, with a clear hierarchy: Inspector General (IG) The provincial police The Governor / Lieutenant Governor (LG) Superintendent of Police (SP) The district police The DC / DM Sub-Inspector (SI) The thana The SP (not to the DC as earlier) Police Act 1861: provisions and hierarchy Operational accountability ran upward through the police chain: SI, SP, IG. Political accountability ran to civilian authority: SP to DC/DM, IG to LG / Governor. This was only the organisational chart. In 1861 the British simply posted military officers or nominated European men into the senior posts: no formal cadre, no competitive exam, no unified service, just employees of provincial governments. The posts existed; the service did not yet. From 1857 onwards a "Police Raj" was created: Indians were excluded from all senior positions, and the emphasis was on effective policing, intelligence collection and political surveillance. "(not BY Bn P)": the Police Act 1861 was passed by the GG's Council, not the British Parliament (contrast with the Charter Act 1793, the 1919 Act and the 1935 Act). "Own" police organisation = own Resources and HR. "Specialist": before 1861 police work was done by non-specialists, the zamindar and the DC; now a specialist ladder (IG, SP, SI). "(not to DC as earlier)": the SI reports to the SP. Bracket "e.g. Financial Control" by the Accountability row (reading: an example of civilian political control;). "(IPS not created yet)": the missing cadre is the future IPS (Section 4.4.3). "Police Raj" = "overuse of police"; emphasis: "ensure no repeat of 1857" (intelligence and surveillance meant to stop another revolt). 4.4.3 Formalisation into a structured cadre Formalisation into a cadre, 1893 to 1905 1893 First open competitive exam for senior police posts, held in London; top candidates became probationary Assistant Superintendents of Police under the Secretary of State for India 1902-03 Curzon 99-05 set up the 2nd Police Commission under Sir Andrew Fraser; report 1903. It organised superior police officers into one unified all-India cadre, the Imperial Police (IP) (informally the Indian Police); scheme implemented from about 1905 (Fraser's package) Provincial Police Service (PPS) created, with a new rank Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP) that accommodated Indians at officer level, always junior to the British IP. CID set up in every province, plus a central intelligence bureau, the Department of Criminal Intelligence (1903), forerunner of today's IB. But the IP itself stayed closed to Indians: Fraser did NOT recommend appointing Indians to it 1920 Direct entry into the IP officially opened to Indians (simultaneous exams in England and India from 1921), largely a result of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (GOI Act 1919) By 1931 Only 20% of SPs were Indians From 1939 More Indians posted as SP because British candidates were unavailable (recruited for World War II, 1939-45) 1948 The IP was administratively replaced by the Indian Police Service (IPS) by a Home Ministry resolution; statutory backing came from the All India Services Act, 1951 1861 built the structure, 1902-03 built the service, 1948-51 built the IPS. (Today's IPS is an All India Service under Article 312, with State police under State governments, directly inheriting the 1861 framework.) Fraser package: the door opened only at the junior end. Keywords: Fraser, 2nd Police Commission, Imperial Police (IP), Provincial Police Service, DySP "but always junior to the British IP"; Fraser did "NOT recommend" Indians to the IP: Indians got a lower rank (PPS, DySP), the top cadre stayed closed, "preserving racial superiority at the top". The Imperial Police of 1902-03 is the ancestor of today's IPS. Diagram (IB) DCI over CID1, CID2, CIDn: the central Department of Criminal Intelligence (1903), forerunner of the IB, above a CID in every province. 1920 to 1951 keywords: simultaneous exams, India from 1921, 20% of SPs were Indians, More Indians posted as SP, IPS via a Home Ministry resolution, All India Services Act 1951; "(* ICS exam in India: 1922)": the police exam in India began in 1921, the ICS exam in India in 1922.

items.t: 5 · The three-pillar administrative legacy (handout and Lecture 21 slides 19 to 21)
items.x: Because each pillar moved only when pushed, the handout ends with one pattern. Ask: which two triggers drove reform, and what three legacies were left? The EIC's administrative evolution across judiciary, civil services and police shows a consistent pattern: structural improvement followed political convenience, not principle. Each major reform was triggered by a crisis (the Great Bengal Famine 1770, the 1857 revolt) or was a concession wrested by the Indian National Movement after sustained pressure. The British never voluntarily Indianised their administration beyond what was economically necessary (to reduce costs) or politically unavoidable (to manage nationalist pressure). They left behind, however inadvertently, a set of institutions that independent India would inherit, adapt and build upon: codified law, an organised civil service, a hierarchical police. Judiciary Diwani Adalats (civil; Pandits and Maulvis) plus Nizamat Adalats (criminal; Kazis, Muftis, Faujdars) Hastings 73-85's 1772 plan; 1774 Supreme Court at Calcutta; Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793 with Anglo-Muhammadan law Charter Act 1833 (Macaulay, Law Commission 1834) leading to CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861; High Courts Act 1861 (High Courts at Madras, Bombay, Calcutta 1862) GOI Act 1935: Federal Court (1937), then Supreme Court of India 1950; CPC, IPC and CrPC replaced in 2024 by BNS, BNSS and BSA Civil services Mansabdari nobility under Mughal patronage Cornwallis 86-93 (1793): founder of CCS plus UCS; salaries raised; seniority for promotion Charter 1853: exam mandated, Indians eligible (London only); ICS renamed by executive order 1892 (Lansdowne 88-94, per Aitchison 1887, NOT by ICA 1892) Lee Commission 1923 leading to PSC 1926; GOI 1935 Federal PSC (1937) then UPSC 1950 (Article 378); AIS under Article 312 Police Naib Nazim to Faujdars (rural) and Kotwals (towns), plus Zamindars (villages) Hastings 73-85's 1781 reforms; Cornwallis 86-93's Daroga System 1793 (failed through the Daroga-Zamindar nexus) Irish Constabulary road-test (Sindh 1843 Napier, Punjab 1849, Bombay 1853, Madras 1859); 1st Police Commission 1860 (M.H. Court) leading to the Police Act 1861 (March 1861) 2nd Police Commission 1902-03 (Fraser) leading to the Imperial Police (IP) cadre; 1948 Home Ministry resolution leading to the IPS; AIS Act 1951 plus Article 312 The handout's summary table is scrambled in the PDF (words split across cells); the table above is rebuilt from the readable pieces. The judiciary "modern legacy" cell reads "CPC/IPC/CrPC replaced 2024 by BNS/BNSS/BS" and is cut off after "BS" in the handout; the class matrix prints BNS/BNSS/BSA, so the table uses BSA. The 2024 replacement appears only in this table and the class matrix. The class summary slides carry the typed pattern (reform followed political convenience, never voluntary Indianisation beyond cost or politics, the inherited institutions) and the matrix above in clean form, to check the scrambled handout table against.

items.t: 6 · The class PYQs and the Governor-General board
items.x: Because the teacher then tested the chapter on real papers, the answers sit on the slides. Ask: why is Banerji the only one dismissed, why is Cornwallis 86-93 wrong for Ryotwari, and where do the reign-year codes come from? Four PYQs, each with a question slide and typed answer slides, then a board of Governor-General and Viceroy tenures. 6.1 Prelims 2010: why the DC lost his judicial powers The answer is (c), exactly as in the alert in Section 2.5.1. Hook: "Tax-man can't be judge of his own tax: PS1793 zamindars needed clean courts, so Cornwallis split the hat," and why the others fail: (a) revenue efficiency was a side-benefit, not the principal motive; (b) wrong on facts, because Cornwallis 86-93 removed Indians from all senior positions; (d) "the DC lacked law training" is at best a partial truth, because the trigger was the conflict of interest after PS1793. 6.2 Prelims 2010: who created the CCS "1892" beside the question: the CCS was renamed ICS in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94 (Aitchison 1887), not ICA 1892; it was created in 1793 by Cornwallis 86-93. Keep the two dates apart and the options sort themselves. Reasons: (a) Hastings 73-85 ended the Dual Government and built the judicial plan of 1772-74 but did not create the CCS; (b) Wellesley 98-05 set up Fort William College (1800-1806) for training, and "the cadre structure pre-dated him by 7 years" (1793 to 1800); (d) Bentinck 28-35 opened the UCS to Indians under the Charter Act 1833, 40 years after Cornwallis 86-93. Hook: "Cornwallis = Covenant: sign the contract in London, sail to India, draw senior pay." 6.3 Prelims 1999: the Indian leader dismissed from the ICS Answer (b) Surendranath Banerji; Tagore, Dutt and Bose false. Tagore (1864, first Indian to clear the exam, Section 3.6) had a full ICS career. R.C. Dutt (cleared 1869) retired honourably as a Divisional Commissioner. S.C. Bose cleared in 1920 and resigned in 1921 in protest; resignation is not dismissal. Banerji was among the four who cleared in 1867 and was dismissed in 1874 on a technical, age-related ground, a politically motivated removal that made him one of the earliest militant Moderates. Wider context (post-1857 insecurity, Indians kept out of senior posts): Section 3.7. Class only (not in the handout): the handout says only "1867: four more Indians cleared it". Banerji, Dutt and Bose, with 1874, 1869, 1920 and 1921, come from the class slides alone; use them for this question and do not mix them with the handout's table. 6.4 Prelims 2017: who introduced Ryotwari Three tags on three names. Cornwallis "86-93" = the Permanent Settlement 1793 in Bengal, the opposite (zamindari) system, so every option containing 1 is wrong. Alexander Read "1792 - Baramahal" = the early experiment. Munro "G (Ma) 1820-27" (read as Governor of Madras) = delivered the mature Ryotwari from 1820. Answer (c) 2 and 3 only. Hook: "Ryotwari = Read drafted, Munro delivered: Madras 1820. Cornwallis stayed in Bengal with zamindars." Munro 1814 versus 1820: two different things. In Section 2.6 the Bengal judicial model was replaced in Madras in 1814 on Munro's advice (the DC regained judicial powers), and Bombay followed in 1819 under Elphinstone, "a follower of Munro's philosophy". The 1820 on this PYQ is the formal rollout of the Ryotwari revenue settlement in Madras. Do not swap them; the settlement itself belongs to Chapter 16: Land Revenue Systems. 6.5 The Governor-General and Viceroy board Source of the reign-year codes used in this notebook: the board has no chapter content, only the list below. Every code the chapter uses for a Governor-General or Viceroy matches it: Hastings 73-85, Cornwallis 86-93, Wellesley 98-05, Bentinck 28-35, Canning 56-62, Dufferin 84-88, Lansdowne 88-94, Curzon 99-05, Chelmsford 16-21. (Lytton 76-80 and Ripon 80-84 are not on the board.) W. HASTINGS 73-85 MINTO 05-10 CORNWALLIS 86-93 HARDINGE 10-16 SHORE 94-98 CHELMSFORD 16-21 WELLESLEY 98-05 READING 21-26 CORNWALLIS 86-93 (months) IRWIN 26-31 F. HASTINGS 13-23 WELLINGDON 31-36 BENTINCK 28-35 LINLITHGOW 36-43 DALHOUSIE 48-56 WAVELL 43-47 CANNING 56-62 (MAYO 69-72 written to its left) MTB 1947-48 DUFFERIN 84-88  LANSDOWNE 88-94  CURZON 99-05  Governor-General and Viceroy tenures board Two Hastings, one code each. W. HASTINGS 73-85 (Warren, the Hastings of this chapter) and F. HASTINGS 13-23 (Francis). Never put 73-85 on the other. Oddities on the board: Cornwallis 86-93 appears a second time with "(months)" after Wellesley 98-05 (as written;); MAYO 69-72 is joined to Canning's row by a line though he comes after Canning 56-62; the right column spells WELLINGDON (31-36) and abbreviates Mountbatten as MTB 1947-48.

A trading company must run a state. Administration is the machinery by which a State carries out its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC turned from a trading company into a Company State (1765-1858; the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function) it had to decide how much Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. Three pillars carry the story: judiciary, civil services and police. The teacher calls the whole chapter the history of Public Administration in British India. The Mughal ladders of Bengal. Before 1772 Bengal had two separate hierarchies. In civil matters (Diwani) courts ran up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat, with Pandits and Maulvis judging personal law and the Zamindar's Kachari handling land revenue disputes. In criminal matters (Nizamat) Islamic law applied to everyone: the Kazi judged, the Mufti interpreted and the Faujdar, like today's SP, caught the accused and carried out the sentence. One man, two hats. After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC held the Diwani and the Nawab kept the Nizamat: a Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism, the EIC let Muhammad Reza Khan head both and cared mainly about revenue. Revenue fell, law and order broke down, and the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed about one-third of Bengal. Hastings 73-85 steps in. In 1772 Hastings 73-85 ended the Dual Government. The British DC sat as judge in the civil courts, while in criminal courts the Kazi and Mufti stayed as judges under the DC's watch, because law and order was too sensitive to replace. The Regulating Act 1773 led to the Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774 for British subjects under British law, with Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823) to follow. Laws were written down too: the Gentoo Code (1776), the Hedaya (1791) and the Code of 1781. Cornwallis 86-93's Code of 1793. With the Permanent Settlement of 1793, zamindars became property owners and needed courts they could trust: if the DC auctioned an estate and then judged the owner's appeal, there was a conflict of interest. Cornwallis 86-93 stripped the DC of all judicial power (the Prelims 2010 answer), divided Bengal into four divisions with Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit, created Anglo-Muhammadan law, removed Indians from all senior posts and permitted lawyers. Ryotwari, Bentinck 28-35 and the codes. Courts clogged after 1793: the DC could no longer settle disputes on the spot, court fees were abolished (back in 1795), and lawyers prolonged cases. In Ryotwari areas, with many small landowners, Madras (1814, on Munro's advice) and Bombay (1819, Elphinstone) merged the DC's roles again. Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts, replaced Persian in 1835, and the Charter Act 1833's Law Commission under Macaulay led to the CPC 1859, IPC 1860 and CrPC 1861. High Courts came in 1862 and the Federal Court in 1937. From patronage to a service. A service means a career ladder with rules, not total discretion. Early EIC officials came by nomination and patronage, and Directors lobbied Parliamentarians with jobs for their sons. Cornwallis 86-93 organised them into the Covenanted Civil Service (senior, signed a covenant in London, Europeans only, like Group A) and the Uncovenanted (junior, hired locally, where Indians served, like Group B), with higher pay, curbed private trade and strict seniority; but entry stayed by nomination until the Charter Act 1853. The exam and its three locks. The Charter Act 1853 mandated an exam for the CCS and the first exam was held in London in 1855. Indians were eligible on paper, but the age limit was kept low, the syllabus was dominated by English Literature (to produce Macaulay's Brown Sahibs) and the venue was London. Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to clear it in 1864 and four more followed in 1867. The long fight for Indianisation. From 1860 the WEMC demanded a simultaneous exam in India and a higher age limit. The British answered with Lytton 76-80's lateral entry for loyal elite Indians (a Statutory Civil Services Act the teacher calls unimportant). Aitchison 1887 led to the three tiers ICS, PCS and Subordinate in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94; Islington (1912, report 1917) offered 25% yet refused a simultaneous exam, which the teacher marks as a CONTRADICTION; the GOI Act 1919 brought the exam to India in 1922, the PSC in 1926 and a 33% target; Lee (1923-24) set 20-40-40 and the PSC came in October 1926 with Ross Barker as first Chairman; the GOI Act 1935 gave the Federal PSC (1937), over 50% were Indianised by 1947, and Article 378 made it the UPSC in 1950. From Faujdar to Daroga. Under the Mughals the chain ran Naib Nazim, Faujdar, Kotwal, Zamindar. After the 1770 famine raised crime, Hastings 73-85 put English Magistrates in place of the Faujdars in 1781. Cornwallis 86-93 ended the zamindars' police powers in 1793: thanas of 30 square miles under an Indian Daroga, the DM supreme in his district. But a Daroga-Zamindar nexus of bribes and lathiyals oppressed the rural poor; Wellesley 98-05 restored the zamindars' powers in 1799, and the Madras trial of 1802 ended in the Torture Commission report of 1855. The Police Act 1861. The British turned to the Irish Constabulary model, a centralised, quasi-military force built as much for political control as for crime. It was road-tested in Sindh (1843, Charles Napier), Punjab (1849), Bombay (1853) and Madras (1859); M.H. Court's 1st Police Commission (1860), set up by Canning 56-62, borrowed from Sindh, and Napier did not head it. The Police Act (March 1861), passed by the GG's Council, set up the IG, SP and SI hierarchy (the SI reports to the SP, not the DC) but only posts, not a service. Fraser's commission (1902-03) created the Imperial Police cadre, closed to Indians; direct entry opened to Indians in 1920, yet only 20% of SPs were Indians by 1931; the IPS came in 1948 and the AIS Act in 1951. Crisis or pressure. Each major reform followed a crisis (the 1770 famine, the 1857 revolt) or a concession won by the Indian National Movement. The British Indianised only as far as cost or politics demanded. What they left behind, however inadvertently, was codified law, an organised civil service and a hierarchical police, which independent India inherited and adapted.

2025, 15 marks, 250 words: Phule's writings and efforts of social reform touched issues of almost all subaltern classes. Discuss Intro: Phule was the first reformer to attack caste, gender, class and economic exploitation together. Body: education (girls' school Pune 1848 with Savitribai; Hunter Commission 1882 memorandum); women (widow remarriage, against child marriage, infanticide prevention centre 1863); Dalits (Gulamgiri 1873, Satyashodhak Samaj 1873, Din Bandhu 1877); peasants (Cultivator's Whipcord 1881, night schools); workers (Bombay Millhands Association 1890 with Narayan Lokhande). Close: he spoke for the oppressed and organised them, bottom-up, unlike top-down upper-caste reformers 2021, 10 marks, 150 words: Trace the rise and growth of socio-religious reform movements with special reference to Young Bengal and Brahmo Samaj Intro: the shift from Orientalism after 1813, cultural nationalism and the Doctrine of Reason. Body: Young Bengal (Derozio, pure rationality, Society for Acquisition of General Knowledge 1838, failed for lack of faith engagement); Brahmo Samaj 1828 (monotheism, anti-Sati 1829, splits 1866 and 1878). Close: both stayed elite and urban; reason plus scripture worked better than reason alone 2019, 10 marks, 150 words: Examine the linkages between the 19th century "Indian Renaissance" and the emergence of national identity Intro: Europe's Renaissance chain and Bengal's parallel. Body: cultural nationalism (mild before 1857, strong after), the Doctrine of Reason turned on social practice and then on British rule, the Western Educated Middle Class. Close: from that class came the leaders of the Indian National Movement; Netaji called Vivekananda the spiritual father of the movement in Bengal 2017, 15 marks, 250 words: The women's question as part of 19th-century social reform: major issues and debates Intro: the British used women's status as the yardstick of civilisation, so reformers worked on women's issues. Body: Sati 1829, child marriage (IPC 1860, Age of Consent 1891, Rakhmabai), widows (1856 Act and its catch), infanticide (1870), polygamy, female education (Bethune 1849, Phule 1848, Vidyasagar's schools); debates: scripture versus logic, Tilak against Bhandarkar. Close: laws were top-down and the problem lay in society, so most reforms failed at scale

Story so far: the whole chapter is seven questions, from Renaissance to success and failure. Ask: where does each later section answer one of the seven? Chapter outline: seven questions on reform Seven questions. (1) Was there a Renaissance? (2) Why Bengal? (3) Why the 19th century? (4) What were the social issues? (5) Methods: Press, People's movement, Laws (for laws, reformers "went to the British"). (6) The famous reformers. (7) Success or failure, and why? The chapter follows this order.

Because Europe's rebirth by reason changed religion, society, economy and polity, the Bengal reformers borrowed the same method. Ask: what did the reformers take from the past, and what did they use to fix it? The word Renaissance first named Western Europe's 14th-century intellectual rebirth: a conscious recovery of ancient learning, driven by reason and aimed at human welfare. 19th-century Bengal looked strikingly similar: the same problems: an oppressive priestly establishment misusing social power, no modern education, birth-based privilege and deep poverty; the same response: reformers reached back into ancient Indian scriptures to restore what was great, and used reason and rationality to remove what was not. The chain of consequences. The European Renaissance triggered a cascade: Reformation in religion, end of Feudalism in society, Capitalism in economy, Enlightenment in polity, and the Scientific and Industrial Revolutions. The Bengal Renaissance had a similar cascading effect: it fed a modern Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC), and from that class came the leaders of the Indian National Movement. Renaissance = re-birth of society; mother of Capitalism, Enlightenment and the Humanities. Before it, Europe in the Dark Ages: education was theology; the Church taught "we are born to suffer", no happiness on earth; wealth concentrated, no scope of being rich; no democracy. Then Venice and Genoa earned cash from trade, new towns in port areas grew, and cash became a source of power (against land). The theme turned to "Happiness of the Human", changing each field: art (portrait painting), economy (capitalism: security of property, equality of opportunity, "right to be rich"), society (inter-personal relations, rights and obligations in marriage, hence social reforms), polity (fundamental rights, democracy, Enlightenment 17th-18th c), technology (medicine, machines, Industrial Revolution 1750-1850, voyages of discovery 16th c) and psychology/philosophy. The "method of R" = reason. Method of the Renaissance: learn from the past, then reason Renaissance method, "like a UPSC aspirant". Step 1: go back to the golden past (ancient Greek and Roman scriptures), copy-paste it to today's times, realise it will not work. Step 2: reason, logic, rationality. So: learn from the past, then new solutions via the Doctrine of Logic/Reason/Rationality (DoL/R/R). Link: Constitution 1950: Scientific Temperament = Fundamental Duty. Why "socio-religious reform" and not simply "social reform"? In India religion did not merely coexist with social practice, it determined it. Sati, child marriage, caste hierarchy, widow remarriage and polygamy were all justified by selective interpretations of religious texts. You could not touch the social practice without confronting the religious sanction behind it. Socio-religious reform versus social reform Socio-religious reformers use Logic AND Religion; pure social reformers use only Logic. The masses are deeply religious, so a practice rooted in religion changes only by reforming or re-interpreting the religion. Derozians = social reformers, not socio-religious: only logic to convince people and Government. Hence their failure (Section 7).

Because reformers had a method, they listed the evils it must tackle. Ask: which of these were never evil in themselves, only distorted? Reformers identified these major social ills: education, idolatry, priestcraft, child marriage, widow remarriage, female infanticide, polygamy, polytheism and casteism. A small mismatch. The handout lists nine ills; the board draws ten, adding child sacrifice (Sagar Island 1803, Section 6). Learn ten. Not every item is evil in itself. Idol worship helps a worshipper concentrate spiritual energy; not all priests are negative: Ramakrishna Paramhansa himself was a temple priest. Polytheism is inherently pluralistic and so secular in character. Social ills arise when there is no genuine spirituality, when social power is misused, and when society is fragmented by divisions. The problem was never the practice itself but its distortion.

items.t: 3 · Why social reform began in the 19th century, and why in Bengal
items.x: Because the evils were old, something new must have started the reform. Ask: what did the British (Liberals, Evangelists, cultural nationalism) and Western education add? 3.1 The role of the British After 1813 the British moved away from Orientalism (which treated Indian culture and learning as worthy of respect and study) towards a new coalition of Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists, who actively supported Western education and social reform. The Evangelists also promoted conversion to Christianity, which created fear among Indians for the survival of their religion and pressure to reform from within. Why the government mattered: it has L (legislative) and E (executive) power, finance and military resources (MR); so if the Government wants, social reform becomes possible. 1813: British criticism of Indian civilisation (Chapter 15), answered by cultural nationalism. 1857: British ideology = "Dogs and Indians not allowed". 3.2 Cultural nationalism as a response As the British moved away from Orientalism they argued that the greatness of ancient India was a myth. Indian reformers pushed back with cultural pride: "we will prove you wrong by cleaning up what has gone wrong and recovering what was great." This cultural nationalism ran through all 19th-century reform: mild before 1857, far stronger after. Colonialism has three faces: political, economic, cultural; each calls up a nationalism. Cultural nationalism: "by studying scripture we will prove that our ancient civilisation [Vedas, Shastras] does not support social ills and supports reason"; the ancient past was great; in the present, social reform makes Indian society great. Socio-religious reformers: searching for modernity in scriptures The "Ctrl+F" method. Step 1: identify the logical, ideal practice. Step 2: open the scriptures (like a PDF), Ctrl+F "LOGIC", get "50 results". Step 3: go to the people with those 50 results. The target population is deeply religious, so this has better chances than a pure social reformer. Same for Roy on Sati: "choose logic, then Ctrl+F logic in scripture". 3.3 Western education (1835 onwards) Reformers educated in Western thought met the Doctrine of Reason: no practice, however old or sacred-seeming, is beyond rational scrutiny. It became their primary tool against irrational and inhumane practices. Logic chain (board: "UPSC syllabus minus anything which glorifies India"): Orientalism → Liberalism (1813+), so the government took up social reform for the White Man's Burden (WMB). Western education (1835) → a WEMC motivated by Reason (R) → social reform was the first step → the WEMC became the leaders of social reform. 3.4 Why in Bengal Why Bengal? It was the political headquarters (the Governor General sat here), so Western education progressed most here. Education growth of the three presidency cities: Section 24.

items.t: 4 · Who led the reforms, over time
items.x: Because the government held the legislative and executive power, the early reformers asked for its help. Ask: why did British interest fall after 1857? First half of the 19th century (pre-1857) Western-educated men from upper castes, willing to seek the colonial government's help to pass reform laws Willing to assist: it fitted the White Man's Burden (WMB), the colonial belief that it was the "civilised" Englishman's duty to uplift "backward" peoples Second half (post-1857) More culturally nationalistic leaders, some without Western education at all (the teacher's examples: Dayanand and Vivekananda, who focused on the masses) Far less interested in reform and far more overtly racist about Indian civilisation. The 1857 Revolt shook British confidence and bred contempt Pre-1857 reformers: WEMC, gradualists, wanted British support (L and E), tool = press, no mass movement, top-down reforms, at first neglected sensitive issues (women, caste). Post-1857: British ideology = "very up racism and authoritarianism". Why British interest in social reform fell after 1857 Why British interest fell after 1857. The EIC's business function ended in 1833, leaving only the State's (territory, T) motive. Social reform = secondary motive; primary motive = empire + Drain (political and economic colonialism), not sacrificed for a secondary one. The Revolt came from fear for religion and customs, so the British gave up the secondary motive. Ideology after 1857: more racism and authoritarianism, "Indians are beyond reform".

Because the reformers differed, the teacher sorts them by method, belief and goal. Ask: where does each man sit on the gradual or radical line? Three axes: method, beliefs, goals. (Add the first teacher cut: social versus socio-religious reformers, Section 1.) Classifying the reformers: method and beliefs, with dates 5.1 By method No mass movement attempted: Ram Mohan Roy (the teacher: he spoke complex Sanskritised Bangla prose, so he did not even try). Built mass movements: Keshab Chandra Sen (1860s), Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1870s), Swami Vivekananda (1880s). Pure rationality: Derozio and Young Bengal. They failed to create a mass movement because their target people were religious and pure reason without faith did not move them. Rationality plus scripture was more successful: Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Dayanand, Vivekananda. Mass-movement builders use the press AND go to the people (they change hearts, values, attitudes); usually radical. Press-only elite workers are "armchair intellectuals", usually gradualist. Separate axis: who wants British help (L and E authority) and who does not. 5.2 By beliefs Logic and rationality are the final authority (if reason and scripture conflict, choose reason): pre-1857 reformers, Roy and his contemporaries, with milder cultural nationalism and ease with Western frameworks. The Vedas are infallible: Dayanand, Ramakrishna, Vivekananda, the post-1857 camp, with stronger cultural nationalism. Their answer was to recover the pure original Vedic teaching. "Upanishads = main" (Ramakrishna); "Rig = main Veda"; "Vedas have test of rational thought" (Dayanand's claim that the Vedas stand the test of reason). 5.3 By goals Gradual reform: Roy, Debendranath Tagore, the Brahmo Samaj, the Prarthana Samaj. They avoided sensitive issues such as caste and marriage practices for fear of alienating the masses they wanted to uplift. Radical, immediate reform: Derozio's Young Bengal, Keshab Chandra Sen, Dayanand, Vivekananda, Vidyasagar, who took up even the most sensitive issues and wanted fast change. Gradualists do "holey-holey" (slow) reform, are not full-time reformers, do "easy first, tough reform later", and argue "society is not ready yet". Radicals work in mission mode, can be full-time reformers, and do "all together, tough first". Types of reformers: gradualists versus radicals Overlaps are normal. The same man sits in several boxes: Roy is no-mass-movement, rationality-plus-scripture, reason-as-final-authority and gradualist; Keshab is a radical mass-movement builder; Vidyasagar is radical and rationality-plus-scripture but not a mass-movement builder. Build the table yourself from the teacher's rule "10 basic Qs on XYZ".

Because the State held executive power, it could ban one cruel practice early. Ask: was this a social reform or an early executive act? In 1803, Wellesley 98-05 banned child sacrifice at Sagar Island (Sagar Dwip, where the Ganga meets the Bay of Bengal, a major Hindu pilgrimage site) in Bengal. An early sign that the colonial government would use executive power against specific social practices. Concept for the next section (Derozio was a Eurasian). Before the 1911 census: mixed parentage = "Eurasian"; a European living in India = "Anglo-Indian" (Anglo living in India). From the 1911 census: mixed parentage = Anglo-Indian; Europeans = "Europeans in India".

items.t: 7 · Henry Vivian Derozio and Young Bengal (late 1820s to 1831)
items.x: Because logic alone was the first experiment, Young Bengal tried it. Ask: why did total faith in reason, with no religion, fail with a religious people? 7.1 Derozio Henry Vivian Derozio was a Eurasian teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta. He died suddenly in December 1831. In his active years (late 1820s to 1831) his followers were not called "Young Bengal": they were "Derozians", "Ultra-Reformers" or "the radicals". "Young Bengal" came later. (The label echoes Mazzini's "Young Italy", educated youth breaking from a tradition-bound older generation.) His method was "question everything": he pushed students to challenge orthodoxy (blind following of old practice) with reason, Western sciences and sometimes outright atheism. Formula: only logic + negating religion + radical reform = "viral" and "infamous".
