Story so far: the chapter has two halves, the Moderates' positives and the Drain. Ask: which of the three positives on the board comes first? The chapter on one board: Moderates and Drain Two halves: (I) the Moderates, (II) the Drain. (I) Moderates. GOAL = LTD SG, not Purna Swaraj (limited self-government; "x" over Purna Swaraj; SG = the power to do L, E, J on our sovereign functions). Methods = Gradualism, "3Ps," Constitutional methods. (II) Drain = wealth moving from India to Britain ("Home"). Starred warning: "wealth is not always equal to rupees." Answer frame: positives of the Moderates Answer frame for "positives of the Moderates": (1) Non-Drain Theory: the project of national building and the culture of parliamentary politics (INC session functioned like a Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha session), linked to ICA 1892 (Chapter 28; the reason is not written: check your notebook). (2) Drain Theory: the WEMC (Western Educated Middle Class) Moderates defeated the narrative of WMB (the White Man's Burden) through press, speeches and books. The rest of the chapter follows this structure.

Because India had no single political community, unity came before rights. Ask: how did the 1886 rule, the 1888 veto and the 1889 clause each serve unity? What was the first goal the INC declared? At the very first INC session in 1885 in Bombay, the Congress declared its goal as "building national unity." This was not an accident. India in 1885 was a land of regions, languages, castes and religions, with no pre-existing sense of a single Indian political community. The Moderates understood that building such a community was the first task, even before demanding rights from the British. So they made a deliberate choice to focus only on issues common to all Indians. In 1886, Dadabhai Naoroji laid down an informal INC rule: the Congress would take up only political questions, not social or class questions, because social issues could divide Indians against each other. Key phrases: "building national unity" and "common to all Indians." Naoroji's rule (1886) is the method that delivers the goal. Also: "only political questions, not social or class questions" and "Congress = a platform against colonial rule." The handout's bracket explains the rule: only issues where it was Indians against the British, and not Religion Hindu vs Muslim Caste Upper Caste vs Lower Caste Gender Men vs Women Class Working Class vs Capitalist Class Land Ryots vs Landlords The Congress was to be a platform against colonial rule, not a forum for internal Indian disputes. For Hindu-Muslim unity the INC took two concrete steps: 1888 INC decision (the communal veto): no resolution would be passed by the INC if the majority of Hindu or Muslim members disagreed with it. 1889 Minority Clause: the INC demanded that the British government reserve seats in the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) and the Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) for religious minorities, in proportion to their share of the population. Both show the Moderates tried to build a Congress that worked for all Indians. The 1889 clause is notable: it was the INC itself, not the Muslim League, that first formally demanded minority representation in legislative councils. "No INC resolution would pass" (the veto). Margin: "Br have ML1906 veto power on constitutional progress -> Partition of India = appeasement." [Cramped; read as: the British gave the Muslim League (1906) a veto over constitutional progress, which led to the Partition of India, called appeasement. Check your notebook.] Communal veto and trust in the INC A communal veto normally leads to trouble: "Communal VETO -> ML 1906 -> Pakistan." The INC's veto was different: anyone who is a member of the INC has agreed to its ideology, Secularism and National Unity. So there was trust that the veto would not be misused for dividing India or for divisive politics. Linked point: in the Constituent Assembly, reservation on the basis of religion was ruled out. Why? Answer: Pakistan. Rotating sessions, non-host President Each session was held in a different part of the country, and the President was specifically not from the host region. The logic: a Bengali leader presiding in Calcutta builds nothing new. A Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta, speaking to Bengali concerns, builds an all-India leadership and creates inter-regional bonds that would not exist otherwise. The handout's picture: a Bengali delegate or newspaper reader sees a Marathi president describe the problems of Bengal's peasants, and begins to see him as his national leader too; the Marathi leader, by visiting Bengal, becomes aware of Bengal's issues. This is nation building through simple structural design. Prelims 2013, the Naoroji trap. Statement 3 ("stressed the need for eradication of all social evils before anything else") is false: Naoroji's 1886 rule kept social questions out of the INC. Only statement 1 (exposed the economic exploitation of India) is right: answer (a). (The same PYQ is tagged again in section 3.2.)

items.t: 2 · Building a culture of parliamentary politics
items.x: Because unity needed a shared habit, INC sessions copied parliament. Ask: which parts of a Lok Sabha sitting did a session reproduce? How did INC sessions contribute beyond passing resolutions? The INC sessions were consciously modelled on parliamentary practice. A President functioned like a Speaker. Members spoke, debated and voted on resolutions. For India, this was new. Watch a Lok Sabha session today: the procedures, the order of speaking, the formal adoption of resolutions all have roots in the culture built by INC sessions from 1885 onwards. That is why it can be said that the modern political era in India, in a true sense, began with the INC. "In a true sense, India's modern political era began with the INC." Same idea as "INC session functioned like LS/RS session," linked to ICA 1892 (Chapter 28).

items.t: 3.1 · The case for supporting Indian capitalists
items.x: Because the Moderates wanted a modern economy, they backed capitalists. Ask: why was this pro-industrialisation and not anti-poor? Why did the Moderates support Indian businessmen? The question causes confusion: supporting capitalists sounds against workers and the poor. But the Moderates' position was not anti-poor: it was pro-industrialisation. Industrialise like the West India needs to industrialise like the West. 19th-century industrialisation ran on capitalism. Every major industrialised country (Britain, the US, Germany, Japan) industrialised on the backs of its capitalist class No communist model yet Communist-led industrialisation (Soviet Russia) was born only in 1917 and showed results only after 1929. In the 1880s and 1890s that model did not exist. The Moderates worked with the tools available Indian capitalists were struggling They were not powerful monopolists. They were under severe competitive pressure from British imports flooding Indian markets and from British businesses operating inside India with the government's backing. An Indian capitalist in 1890 needed support, not criticism

Because the ICA 1892 disappointed them, the Moderates built their sharpest idea. Ask: why is wealth not always equal to rupees? What is the most important intellectual contribution of the Moderates? Without question it is the Drain Theory: the systematic, evidence-based argument that British rule was economically exploiting India, not developing it, and that the entire claim of the White Man's Burden (WMB) was false. The theory gained particular prominence after the bitter disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892), which failed to deliver any meaningful reform (see Chapter 28). Core idea: the British were using their political control over the Indian State to extract economic benefits for Britain. This was not charity or development: it was exploitation. The Moderates proved it with data and argument, building an economic critique of colonialism that was sharp, factual and difficult to counter. Ahead of its time: Lenin and Lala Lajpat Rai would later argue along similar lines, that colonialism is the product of British capitalism needing new markets and raw materials. The Moderates reached this conclusion through an economic lens well before it became a standard argument in global socialist circles. Key phrases: "evidence-based," "White Man's Burden was false," "disappointment with the ICA 1892", "Britain used its political control over the Indian State to extract economic benefits for Britain," "colonialism as the product of British capitalism." Drain Theory = "WEMC Moderates defeated the narrative of WMB" through press, speeches and books. The architects Romesh Chandra Dutt (R.C. Dutt) Former ICS officer turned economic historian. Wrote The Economic History of British India (Vol. I, 1902) and India in the Victorian Age (Vol. II, 1904). A data-driven account of how British land revenue policy, trade regulation and fiscal management impoverished India. Gave the theory its historical depth and empirical backbone Dadabhai Naoroji Poverty & Un-British Rule in India (1901): the most systematic presentation of the theory and a landmark text in the economic history of colonialism globally MG Ranade Often called the father of Indian economics Book-and-date matches: the two Dutt titles with their years, the Naoroji title with 1901, and "father of Indian economics" (Ranade). The handout figure adds facts not in the running text (a flow chart placed near the Drain Theory material). It is the source for the Prelims 2015 match (Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer, R.C. Dutt are all economic critics) and Prelims 1997 (Gokhale). The flow order is a layout, not a time sequence. This second figure summarises the Moderates' contribution: the Drain Theory is the world's first economic critique of colonialism, "before Hobson, Lenin." (The running text says Lenin and Lajpat Rai argued similarly later.) "British Committee 1889" and "India journal" are not explained in this chapter. Prelims 1996 (answer d), Prelims 2008 and Prelims 2013: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan is the one who did not believe in Naoroji's Drain Theory (1996). 'Un-british' (as in Un-British Rule) is Dadabhai Naoroji (2008). The most effective contribution of Naoroji is exposing economic exploitation (2013: only statement 1). Prelims 2015: Naoroji, G. Subramaniam Iyer and R.C. Dutt were all economic critics: answer (d) 1, 2 and 3. PYQ Prelims 1996: who did not believe in the Drain Theory PYQ 1 (Prelims 1996): "did not believe" asks for the odd one out. Sorted into camps: Tilak = "extremist," and Dutt and Ranade together as "Drain Theory" (its architects). Answer (d) Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, loyal to the British and opposed to the INC's politics of self-rule; Tilak stood inside the nationalist camp that embraced the economic critique. [Why Tilak is labelled "extremist" is not written; read as a different political camp, not a rejecter of the Drain Theory.] PYQ 8 (Prelims 2013): "T" beside statement 1 (exposed the economic exploitation of India), none beside 2 or 3; answer (a) Only 1. PYQ 9 (Prelims 2015): "T" beside 1 (Naoroji) and 3 (R.C. Dutt); nothing beside 2 (G. Subramaniam Iyer). The typed answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3, the same as the key. [Why 2 is unmarked is not written: check your notebook.] Typed answers add the wrong-option facts. For "Un-british" (Prelims 2008): Anandamohan Bose = Bengal Moderate organiser, Badruddin Tyabji = first Muslim INC President (1887), Pherozeshah Mehta = Bombay INC founder-figure; the phrase is Naoroji's (Poverty & Un-British Rule in India, 1901). Two concepts the teacher builds before the mechanisms Rupees are not wealth. One keyboard sells for Rs 100. If the RBI prints Rs 20 more, it sells for Rs 120: inflation, but the value is the same (one keyboard). If a country exports minerals, rupees and forex come in, but wealth goes out (e.g. a poor African country selling minerals to the outside world). Middle East (crude oil, natural gas): to prevent the ill-effects of this drain, it is trying to use forex for diversifying and developing its economy. Hence the first board: "wealth is not always equal to rupees." [The slide's "Rs" is the rupee sign.] How Drain and Swaraj are connected Concept: rupees versus value How are Drain and Swaraj connected? Britain misused its control over our sovereignty (sovereign functions) to ensure the drain of wealth from India. Why a drain? Because we did not have SG (self-government), the power to do L, E, J (legislative, executive, judicial functions) on our own sovereign functions. Same L, E, J shorthand as Chapter 8 and Chapter 10. Drain Theory in one line: "The misuse of political power over the State of the Colony for the economic benefit of the Colonial Power." Handout's closing note: the economic critique was inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj: without self-rule, the drain could never be stopped. If a question is on the Drain of wealth "If a question is on the Drain of wealth": split into Pre-IR in Britain (1757-1813) and Post-IR in Britain (1813-1947). Pre-IR: Plassey Plunder (1757-65) and Land Revenue (LR) from 1765. Post-IR: the later mechanisms. "If the question is on the Drain THEORY given by the MODERATES, write the post-1813 drain." Why: the Industrial Revolution in Britain ran 1750-1850; the EIC was a trader; in 1813 the EIC's monopoly on British business with India ended, and industrialised Britain got access to the Indian economy. Pre-1800s or pre-1813? The handout and slide title the periods "Pre-19th Century (pre-1800s)" and "19th Century (1813 onwards)"; the board splits at 1813 (pre-IR 1757-1813, post-IR 1813-1947). Use 1757-1813; "pre-1800s" is the slide's shorthand.

items.t: 3.3 · Impact of British industrialisation on India
items.x: Because Britain industrialised, India was reshaped as raw-material source and market. Ask: where did the artisans go when no factory opened? What exactly did British industrialisation do to India? How British industrialisation changed India Before British IR: India = net exporter of finished goods (textiles, handicrafts) British industrial capitalism: India = (1) a raw-material source + (2) an export market for British factories Commercialisation of agriculture: cotton, indigo, jute (and opium) grown for British factories, not for food Handicrafts destroyed: artisans lose domestic and export markets; no Indian factories to absorb them Forced into agriculture: disguised unemployment; agriculture overburdened British industrial capitalism converted India into a source of raw materials and an export market for British factories. Before British industrial dominance, India was a net exporter of finished goods (textiles, handicrafts, processed goods). After, India became a net exporter of raw materials, while finished goods flooded back in as imports. This process is the commercialisation of agriculture: Indian agriculture was reoriented away from food crops and towards cash crops and raw materials for export to British factories. The peasants no longer grew what they ate; they grew what Britain's mills needed: cotton, indigo, jute, opium (Prelims 2018). The handout's analogy: an African country that exports crude oil and imports refined products and machinery: the raw material goes out cheap, the finished product comes back expensive. "Br sells FGs (finished goods) to India, therefore India = [an export market] for Britain." Key phrases: "(1) raw-material source," "(2) export market," "Britain commercialised Indian agriculture," "(cotton, indigo, jute)," "Opium," "Handicrafts destroyed." Crops: food versus cash crops Crops = Food crops and Cash crops. Cash crops (jute, sugar, tea, cotton) are inputs (raw material) for the industrial sector. Commercialisation of agriculture (cash crops, "B") pushed out food crops ("A"), leading to FOOD INSECURITY [FAMINES]. Why machine-made goods beat handicrafts Machine-made British goods beat Indian handicrafts: cheaper and better in quality. Cheaper through mass production: the factory setup is a one-time cost (100 crore); the first Bisleri bottle costs 100 crore, but rapid mass production has a low additional cost, so the Nth bottle's average cost is Rs 1. Artisan = skill, hands and tools make crafts (goods); worker = physical labour on machines makes manufactured goods. The Indian handicrafts sector was destroyed. Indian artisans lost both domestic and export markets. Since there was no industrialisation of India (no Indian factories came up to replace the handicrafts), the artisans had nowhere to go. They could not become factory workers and were forced back onto agriculture. The handout's contrast: an artisan uses skill and hands; a factory worker uses labour and machines. The two are decentralised and rural versus centralised and urban. When the artisan is pushed off his trade but no factory exists, he falls back on the land. The result is disguised unemployment in agriculture: too many people on too little land, each doing far less productive work than they could. This is why the agriculture sector became overburdened. The handout: in a modern economy the worker works in machine-based factories and agriculture employs a small fraction. Britain achieved this transition. India was denied it. Industrial GDP, agrarian employment Two circles: in GDP terms the economy can be mostly industrial (agriculture a small wedge), yet in employment terms agriculture can still be the big circle: "Even in an industrialised GDP, agriculture can be over-burdened." (The point behind disguised unemployment.) Bracket: "Link: effect of AI" [no more is written; check your notebook]. Prelims 1999, 2018 and 2020 land here. 1999: no independent development of industries because of the absence of heavy industries (a) (not scarcity of capital or resources, not the rich preferring land). 2018: the economic result of British rule in the 19th century was commercialisation of agriculture (c) (not export of handicrafts, not growth of Indian factories, not urban growth). 2020: the first-half-of-19th-century impact of the Industrial Revolution was that Indian handicrafts were ruined (a) (no machines, no railways, no heavy duties on British imports). PYQ Prelims 2018: economic result of British rule PYQ Prelims 2020: impact of the Industrial Revolution PYQ 4 (Prelims 1999): "F" beside (b) scarcity of foreign capital and (c) scarcity of natural resources. Answer (a) absence of heavy industries. Reasoning: the drain shipped India's own surplus out, so capital was not scarce; India was the raw-material source, so resources were not scarce; the rich drifting back to land was a consequence of having no factories, not the cause. PYQ 11 (Prelims 2020): "1800-1850" splits into "Till 1813" and "1813-1857" (the post-1813 frame). (a) "T" (handicrafts ruined). (b) "F", trap word "large" (no machine age came to India then). (c) "F", "1853 = 1st" (the first railway line is 1853, so not "many parts" in the first half). (d) "F", "1st WWI": the first protective tariffs came in World War I (section 3.4.2). Side note: "PRO-Lancashire = Br Textile industry" (British policy favoured the British textile industry). A wordless sketch of an arrow "Br" entering a circle through a gap [read as India an open door for British goods; check your notebook]. The transport revolution Transport revolution = part of the Industrial Revolution; it contributed to the Drain. Steam engine (1769) later led to (1) machines, (2) ships and boats, (3) railways. Suez Canal (1859-69) reduced the distance to the Arabian Sea by 4,500 miles (board note: 9,000 km); route from Britain round Africa against the shorter route via Suez. Impact on India: "LOOT escalated." Verdict: "Awesome stuff for the colonisers = hell for the people of the colonies." Miles against kilometres. Handout and slide: Suez cut the India-Britain sea distance by 4,500 miles. The board writes "4500 miles (9000 Km)"; 4,500 miles is nearer 7,200 km, so the 9,000 km does not match. Hold 4,500 miles. The revolution in transport made the drain worse, not better. Steam-powered railways, steam-fitted ships, paved roads, modern ports and the Suez Canal (built 1859-1869) made it cheaper and faster to extract raw materials from India and ship finished goods back. Transport revolution and the Drain "Paved roads" = "Pakka roads." "State": an organisation that rules (T) and (ppl): territory and people [T read as territory]. So "State of the Colony" = the organisation that rules the colony's territory and people, which Britain controlled and misused for its own economic benefit. Rail-road-port system: raw materials out, goods in Rail-road-port system = a one-way pump. In India (circle 1): raw materials (1.1) go by rail and road to the port (1.2); by sea to Britain (1.3), the British port (1.4), then by rail to the factory, e.g. Lancashire (1.5). Finished goods (1.6) leave the factory, cross the sea (1.7), return to the Indian port, then by rail and road to the urban areas = the market (1.8). Demand comes from the rich with buying power; Indian factories are at an infant stage (crossed out). Legend: "Rail-Road infra in India [1850s] by Dalhousie 48-56 for faster movement of the army." [Code smudged, read as "48-56"; matches the handout.]

Because the drain had to run through some channel, the notes list the mechanisms before and after 1813. Ask: which mechanism needed no army, only a policy? How exactly did the money leave India? What were the specific mechanisms? The notes distinguish two periods. 3.4.1 · Pre-19th century (pre-1800s) Misuse of the Dastaks Duty-free trade passes originally granted only for the EIC's own goods, but misused by Company servants for private trade (the teacher: "Loss of TAX revenue for India") Plassey plunder + Land Revenue (LR) The Plassey plunder of 1757-65, plus LR extraction from British India beginning 1765. The LR of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar formally began with the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 (see [[10 Chapter 10]]) Result: the gold flow reversed Earlier, gold flowed into India as payment for Indian goods. After Plassey and the acquisition of LR rights, gold flowed out of India "PRELIMS" above the title; the period line is marked. Key phrases: "misused by Company servants for private trade" and "Loss of TAX Revenue for India." (Dastak and Plassey Plunder: Chapter 10.) 3.4.2 · From the 19th century (1813 onwards) The modern colonial relationship developed: colony = source of raw materials and export market. The 19th-century mechanisms, as the teacher numbers them (1) The colony's new role: a source of raw materials plus an export market for British factories (2) Absence of protective tariffs: no import duty on British goods until World War I (1914-19) (3) Exchange rate manipulation: the rupee-to-pound rate managed to benefit British businesses (4) Council Bills (post-1833): tax-financed trade; India got no forex for its exports Components of the Drain: 19th century (1813 onwards) Also: the EIC's own forex earnings (for example opium exported to China) taken to London "PRELIMS" above the title. Mechanisms numbered (2) tariffs, (3) exchange rate, (4) Council Bills (CBs), with the colony's new role as the first (section 3.3). "World War I (1914-19), when protective tariffs were applied for the first time." Margin: "(1858) Council = India Council; Bill = like (Cheque)" [last word partly unclear: check your notebook]. (2) Absence of protective tariffs How a tariff protects. A British finished good costs Rs 100; an Indian one costs Rs 110. (a) India independent: 20% import duty at the economic frontier, so the British good costs Rs 120 against the Indian Rs 110: the Indian good wins. (b) India a colony of Britain: 0% customs duty, so Rs 100 against Rs 110: the British good wins. The "economic frontier" is guarded by the customs service (IRS Customs under the Ministry of Finance). Case (a) = post-1947 import substitution. Bottom sketch: goods go in and out of a country; forex moves the other way. No import duty was imposed on British goods entering India to protect Indian manufacturers. This policy lasted until World War I (1914-19), when protective tariffs were applied for the first time. The result: British goods flooded Indian markets and Indian manufacturers could not compete. Absence of protective tariffs: the numbers (3) Exchange rate manipulation A weak currency boosts exports. An Indian manufacturer exporter, X, sells at $1 in the international market. Case A: $1 = Rs 50, X earns Rs 50. Case B: $1 = Rs 100 (weaker rupee), X earns Rs 100: Rs 50 extra, which buys one more factory and more workers, so more goods: GDP and exports rise. "This was done by China 1978 onwards." Colonial side: "British kept the rupee STRONG, or the pound weaker than ideal" [my reading: Indian exporters were denied this boost and British exports stayed competitive in India; the board states only the two lines]. Exchange rate manipulation: the rupee-to-pound rate was managed in a way that benefitted British businesses (the slide: keeping British exports competitive in India). The handout's analogy: China has at times been accused of keeping its currency artificially undervalued to make Chinese exports cheaper; the British did something similar in reverse, managing the exchange rate to keep British exports competitive in India. Monetary and fiscal policy interplay Exchange rate manipulation: weak currency, more exports Interplay of monetary and fiscal policy: the exchange rate is a monetary tool; corporate taxes are a fiscal tool. Step 1: a weak rupee raises GDP and makes the industrialist richer. Step 2, after some years, corporate taxes are raised: the stimulus is taken back. [A side example of the two policies working together; not about the British.] (4) Council Bills (post-1833): tax-financed trade Council Bills are the most complex mechanism: "CBs, next slides." Council Bills mechanism Council Bill mechanism. A British importer who wants Indian goods gives forex to the Secretary of State (SoS) for India in London and gets a CB (Council Bill). He comes to India with the CBs; the Government of India (GOI) takes them and gives him rupees: "Indian taxpayer rupees." He buys Indian goods and leaves. Ideally India gets (1) forex in and sends (2) goods out. Here India gets CBs in (not forex) and sends goods out. Council Bills: tax-financed trade (post-1833) A foreign importer wants Indian goods: instead of paying forex to India directly... He buys Council Bills in London: pays the India Council in forex, which STAYS in London He uses the Bills in India: presents the Council Bills to purchase Indian goods The GOI pays him in rupees: from Indian taxpayer money Net result: India got NO forex for its exports; the Indian taxpayer financed the trade The Secretary of State (SoS) for India held India's foreign exchange in London. When a foreign importer wanted Indian goods, instead of paying forex directly, he bought Council Bills (CBs), promissory notes issued by the India Council in London. He paid for them with his forex, which stayed in London. He then used the CBs in India to purchase Indian goods, and the GOI accepted the CBs and gave Indian rupees to the importer. The handout's picture: a foreign buyer gives dollars not to India but to a London office and gets a voucher; he uses the voucher in India to buy goods and gets rupees. India got rupees (its own currency) but never the forex for its exports. And the rupees to pay the importer came from Indian taxpayers. So India did not get forex for its exports; Indian taxpayer money financed this trade. Council Bills: the four arrows Council Bills in four numbers. (1) Forex from the British importer to India: crossed out (X X X X X); it never goes to India. (2) Forex goes up to the SoS for India (London): ticked. (3) The SoS gives the importer a CB. (4) The importer takes the CB ("*Cheque") to India; the GOI takes it and gives Indian rupees to the British importer, who buys goods and leaves. The forex stays in London; the rupees come from India. The EIC's own forex earnings The EIC earned forex by exporting Indian goods, for example opium exported to China. This forex too was taken to London and did not return to India. 3.4.3 · Home Charges "imp for Prelims." The Drain splits into two heads: (1) Home Charges, (2) not Home Charges. The next board defines Home Charges. Home Charges: think like a British nationalist Drain splits into Home Charges and not-HC "Home" in Home Charges means Britain, not India. Think like a British nationalist: you go to a cafe; the cafe provides goods and services and charges you rupees; money moved from your pocket to the cafe's because the cafe provided goods and services and charged for it. Cafe = Britain, you = India: India pays forex to Britain and gets goods and services (G&S) back. So Home Charges = what India was made to pay Britain for goods and services Britain claimed to provide. [The circled word before "Charges for it" is unclear, probably "so".] Lecture 30 carries the list. The teacher numbers seven items (interest on EIC loans and on foreign debt share item 3); the table below and the mnemonic split it into eight. Home Charges, billed to India (1/2) "Think like a British nationalist." Key phrases: "Britain, not India," "goods and services," and "Secretary of State" = Br (the Secretary of State is Britain). Top right: "Governance + Security of (T) of India = Services" (T = territory): the "services" are governing and defending the territory of India. Justification: "It is expenditure incurred by Britain on behalf of India" (India -> Rs -> Britain). Row 1: "Br CS, MS live in Britain, therefore" the rupees go to Britain [CS, MS read as civil and military services; check your notebook]. Row 2: dividends were paid from trade and LR income (1765-1833) plus LR alone (1833-58). Big bracket: had the civil and military services been Indianised, the drain would have fallen; so the demand for Indianisation was not just the selfish interest of the WEMC but the national interest (Chapter 26). [The abbreviation "IoCd" and the lone "1784" under the table are unclear.] Home Charges, billed to India (2/2) Each item is dressed as goods or a service. Stores = "Goods." War Office = "Service = Stability / Law of India" [last word read as "Law"]. FDI interest = "this way, a development service to India," and the territory was kept "not under threat" [the word "WHR" is as written]. Rupees India pays Britain are forex leaving India (Rs -> Britain, "= FOREX"). Not a Home Charge: "Where Rs goes from India to Britain BUT India is providing service to Britain": rupees leave India in both cases, but for the army abroad India gives the service, so it is a drain but not an HC. Tree: Drain = HC + not-HC; the army abroad is the not-HC head. The handout's definition. "Home" here means Britain, not India. Home Charges were charges that India was made to pay for goods and services supposedly provided to India by Britain or the Secretary of State. Each item carries the British justification of the day. Salaries, pensions and training costs of British officials and soldiers They gave their careers to the service of India Dividends to EIC shareholders The EIC gave governance service to India by running the Company State Interest on loans taken by the EIC Loans taken to meet expenses of the GOI Interest on foreign debt Debt incurred for India's administration and development Expenses of the Secretary of State for India and the India Council in London (earlier the Board of Control) (no justification written) Purchase of stores and goods for India by the SoS (stationery, steel and other supplies) (no justification written) Payments to the British War Office for weapons purchased for India's defence, and for use of the Royal Military in crises such as 1857 (no justification written) Interest on FDI, paid to British businesses that invested in India To attract FDI for India's development The army abroad. The handout adds: the use of the British Indian Army abroad (campaigns in Afghanistan, Africa, China) was not technically a Home Charge, because India was not receiving a service: it was giving one to the Empire. Those war expenses were charged directly to the Indian budget as military expenditure, a separate and equally egregious drain that falls outside the category of Home Charges. Seven or eight Home Charges? Lecture 30 slides 1 and 2 number seven items, with "Interest on EIC loans + foreign debt" as one item (3). The table above and the FLOW DIPS mnemonic list eight by splitting item 3 into loans interest and foreign-debt interest. The content is the same; hold the heads, not the count. Prelims 2011: the handout contradicts itself on statement 3. The PYQ's key is (d) 1, 2 and 3: statement 1 (support for the Indian office in London), statement 2 (salaries and pensions of British personnel engaged in India) and statement 3 (funds for waging wars outside India by the British). But the handout's note above says the army's use abroad is technically not a Home Charge. For the exam, answer (d), as the key and the handout's own alert say; keep the note as the conceptual distinction (payments for services Britain claimed to give India are Home Charges; imperial campaigns charged to the military budget are a separate drain). The Home Charges section has no class notes beyond the "Home = Britain" café board, so the teacher's view on statement 3 comes from Lecture 30 (slides 25 to 27): see the next blocks. PYQ Prelims 2011: Home Charges PYQ 7 (Prelims 2011): "HC" beside statements 1 and 2, nothing beside 3. (b) 1 and 2 preferred: "I would have marked this even if the answer key in the market says (d)"; (d) is circled too, so he knows the key. Tree: wars are "FOR" either the "protection of the territory (T) of India" or "for the British empire" [branch word "UR" is as written]. Reasoning: only what Britain bills India as a service is a Home Charge; war for the British empire (statement 3) is the army abroad, not an HC. PYQ Prelims 2011: typed note on Home Charges Drain = HC + not-HC. Typed rule: an expense was not a Home Charge merely because it was paid from Indian revenues; it also had to be a payment or a liability in Britain. Every Home Charge was part of the drain, but not every military expense, and not every expense India paid, was an HC. UPSC accepted statement 3 "but it is loosely worded: a war abroad became a Home Charge only for payments made in Britain. Strict academic answer = (b); answer to mark = (d)". For the record: wars waged in defence of India were put under Home Charges, and the suppression of the 1857 Revolt itself was charged to them. Prelims 2011: key (d) against the teacher's (b). The UPSC key is (d) 1, 2 and 3 (handout alert and typed slide: "answer to mark = (d)"). His marking is (b) 1 and 2, treating the army abroad as not an HC. The slide's own line: (b) is the strict academic answer, (d) the answer to mark against the key. [Which to mark in your own test is your decision; check your notebook.] The net effect: double drain through asymmetric trade (i) Net exporter of raw materials. India shipped out more raw material (cotton, jute, indigo, tea, opium) than it imported, on paper a "positive" trade balance. But the forex India earned was also drained through Council Bills, Home Charges and guaranteed FDI interest. So India shipped out wealth (raw material) and its export earnings too: a double drain. (ii) Asymmetric trade. India did not receive an equivalent value of finished goods back: British finished goods (cotton textiles, machine-made products) flooded India tariff-favoured, but their total value was less than the raw material India shipped out. The net effect: double drain through asymmetric trade "What we earned in forex goes out in HC." Insertions: "Br Businesses" after "favoured" (tariffs favoured British businesses) and "of imports of India" (finished goods' total value was less than the raw materials shipped out, measured as India's imports). Diagrams: India sells to Britain = Ex(Rs); Britain sells to India = Im(Rs), each with a rupee arrow back (payment). Ex[Rs] > Im[Rs], i.e. India = net exporter = TRADE SURPLUS / WEALTH DEFICIT: rupees say surplus, wealth says deficit ("wealth is not always equal to rupees"). Bottom: a country that primarily earns forex by selling raw materials to the world and not finished goods is "selling Home's land" [read as selling its own land's produce; check your notebook]. "Guaranteed FDI interest" is explained in section 3.5 under Railways (a guaranteed 5% a year in London). The handout does not give a separate number for the drain here.

items.t: 3.5 · Did British rule modernise India? The debate
items.x: Because the British claimed benefits, the Moderates answered each; the teacher marks the whole debate mmp. Ask: what did each answer count that the British claim left out? Were there any genuine modernising benefits that justify the drain? This debate was structured by the Moderates themselves: the British made certain arguments in their favour, and the Moderates (and later historians) developed counter-arguments. A calibration before the debate. A 2022 estimate by Utsa Patnaik puts the total value of the drain at $45 trillion at 2022 prices. Whatever modernisation happened, it happened as an unintended by-product. No part of it was done for India. The facts below are the handout's, confirmed against the typed slides (the "central claim" slide is typed). The only board marker in the debate is "mmp" (see the exam lens). "mmp" on the debate title, Railways 1/2, the 5% Guaranteed-Interest Trap and Canals; "MMP" (capitals) on the "2% Drain" rejoinder; "mml" as written on Railways 2/2. The whole debate is marked, every sub-topic. Railways Railways linked India internally and to the world economy through rail-to-port infrastructure Purpose: Dalhousie 48-56 introduced railways in 1853 primarily for faster movement of the British army: military control was the original purpose, not economic development  Direction: railways connected Indian markets and sources of raw materials to ports, and through ports to British manufacturers. They did not connect Indian markets to Indian manufacturers  Technology: very limited transfer, and only in low-technology areas like bridge-building and tunnelling  Real goal: to create investment opportunities for British railway companies  Guarantee: British capitalists got a guaranteed 5% annual interest on their invested capital, paid in pound sterling in London Railways: "mmp" on Railways 1/2 (military first; ports, not Indian mills); "mml" [as written] on Railways 2/2 (little technology transfer; the real byproduct: 78% by 1947, feeder roads, national unity); "mmp" on "The 5% Guaranteed-Interest Trap" (paid from day one; the GOI covers any shortfall; buy-back guarantee; FDI became FD). The board explanation of the trap follows. The 5% started the moment the FDI was made, so investors earned 5% even in the years the railway was under construction and earning nothing. Once the railway ran, if it failed to earn 5% in any year, the GOI made up the deficit. At any point, the investors had the right to sell the railway back to the GOI at a price equal to the exact total FDI. So if FDI was 100 pounds, they got at least 5 pounds a year from the day of investment, and if they wrapped up before 99 years, they also got 100 pounds back. FDI became an FD (fixed deposit with simple interest paid every year). That led to wasteful construction: profits were private, losses were public. The same money could have been invested in irrigation for India's food security. FDI became FD "FDI became FD" = number (1) under Home Charges (interest on FDI), explained on the railways. (1) British railway manufacturers bring FDI to India. (2) The British-run GOI acquires land and gives it on a 99-year lease to British businesses for free; "forex which could have come to India is not coming to India." (3) Any time before 99 years, if the British business finds the project not profitable "or whatever reason," it can sell to the GOI at the boxed price "FDI + 5% interest p.a." Starred consequences: wasteful construction as there was no fear of loss; this is how the railways became government owned; losses borne by the Indian taxpayer; profits of the British [last line cut off]. Buy-back price: board against handout. The handout and typed slide say investors could sell back at a price equal to the exact total FDI, with 5% paid every year. The boxed board writes "Price = FDI + 5% interest p.a." Read together: the full FDI back, with the guaranteed 5% a year on top, as a fixed deposit pays. Hold: full FDI back plus 5% a year; [if the exact wording is asked, check your notebook]. The by-product was real: by 1947 railways covered 78% of India. Feeder roads from Indian factory hubs to the railway lines let Indian businesses eventually use the network. Railways also increased people-to-people contact across regions, strengthening national unity and the inter-regional bonds the Indian National Movement would depend on. Railway date. The handout says Dalhousie 48-56 introduced railways in 1853; the board says the rail-road infra came "in India 1850s by Dalhousie 48-56 for faster movement of the army." They agree: 1853 falls in the 1850s, and the purpose is the army. (Chapter 14.) Canals British-built canals became a role model for Asia and helped develop irrigation infrastructure and food security Quantity: by 1947 only 25% of cultivated area was under public irrigation  Geography: canals were built only in non-Permanent Settlement 1793 areas (Punjab, western UP, coastal Madras), where land revenue could still be increased. Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, locked under the Permanent Settlement of 1793, saw little canal investment  Access: canal water was not free; only rich farmers could afford it  Result: recurring famines in the 1860s and 1870s, and as late as the Bengal Famine of 1943, are proof there was no genuine food security Canals: "mmp" on the title. The British response to famine was a series of Famine Commissions: the Strachey Commission (1880), the Lyall Commission (1897) and the MacDonnell Commission (1900), but their recommendations were rarely implemented with seriousness. The famines kept recurring because the structural problem was never addressed: extractive land revenue, export-oriented agriculture and inadequate irrigation. The British rejoinder: "the drain was only 2%" The drain was only 2% of India's export value in the early 1900s. This small amount paid for real development: it attracted FDI into railways, roadways and irrigation Quantity: GDP growth was not substantial  Quality: growth was regionally uneven, and investment in irrigation, health and education remained low  Neither the quantity nor the quality of development justified what India paid as the drain  Naoroji's argument: even if 2% sounds small, it was surplus capital. Invested in India instead of drained to Britain, it would have compounded over decades and generated significant GDP growth. It is not the absolute percentage that matters: it is what it could have become The "2% drain" rejoinder: "MMP" in capitals, the heaviest marking of the debate. Naoroji's clincher: even 2% was surplus capital that would have compounded. The handout's savings-account picture: 2% of your income seems small, but invested and compounded over 50 years, it becomes substantial wealth. The drain robbed India of that compounding effect, year after year. Drain Theory's central claim is structural: a colonial power using political control to redirect economic surplus. This made the economic critique inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj: without self-rule, the drain could never be stopped. The last PYQ alerts of the handout Prelims 1997 (answer b). M.C. Setalvad, B.N. Rau and Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer were members of the All India National Liberal Federation (AINLF). The handout: the AINLF was founded in 1918, the Moderate splinter from the INC under leaders like Surendranath Banerjea and Tej Bahadur Sapru (the handout words this as "after the Surat Split aftermath when Moderates left INC"; hold the date 1918). Setalvad = eminent jurist, later the 1st Attorney General of India; B.N. Rau = Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly; Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer = member of the Constituent Assembly's Drafting Committee. The wrong options: Swaraj Party, Madras Labour Union, Servants of India Society. Prelims 2008 (answer c). Gokhale is the one who rejected the title of Knighthood and refused a position in the Council of the Secretary of State for India (not Motilal Nehru, Ranade or Tilak). Handout figure: Gokhale 1866-1915, Gandhi's political master, Servants of India Society 1905 Poona. A land with no single people. In 1885 the first INC session at Bombay declared its goal as building national unity. India was a land of regions, languages, castes and religions with no pre-existing single political community, so the Moderates decided that building one came before demanding rights from the British. One versus only. In 1886 Naoroji laid down the informal rule that the INC takes only political questions, not social or class ones, so the fight is Indians against British and not Hindu against Muslim, upper against lower caste, men against women, worker against capitalist or ryot against landlord. In 1888 the INC added a veto (no resolution if the majority of Hindu or Muslim members disagree) and in 1889 the Minority Clause, the INC's own demand for reserved seats in the ILC and PLCs. The host never presides. Each session was held in a different part of the country and the President was never from the host region. A Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta and speaking to Bengali concerns builds an all-India leadership and inter-regional bonds, nation building by simple design. A parliament before a parliament. The President functioned like a Speaker and members spoke, debated and voted on resolutions, which was new for India. Today's Lok Sabha procedures have their roots in the culture of INC sessions, so the modern political era began with the INC. Why back the capitalists? The Moderates were not anti-poor, they were pro-industrialisation: every industrialised country had risen on its capitalist class, communist industrialisation was born only in 1917 and showed results after 1929, and Indian capitalists were struggling against British imports and British firms in India. The Drain Theory. After the disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 the Moderates built the Drain Theory: an evidence-based argument that Britain used its political control over the Indian State for its own economic benefit, so the White Man's Burden was false. Naoroji (Poverty & Un-British Rule in India, 1901), R.C. Dutt (1902 and 1904) and Ranade (father of Indian economics) made it, spread by press, speeches and books. How British factories rebuilt India. Before British industrialisation India was a net exporter of finished goods. Afterwards it was a raw-material source and an export market: farms grew cotton, indigo, jute and opium for British mills, handicrafts were destroyed, and artisans with no Indian factories to join were forced into an overburdened agriculture. Steam, rail and the Suez shortcut. The steam engine (1769) later brought machines, ships and railways, and the Suez Canal (1859-69) cut the sea distance by 4,500 miles. The teacher's board shows the rail-road-port loop carrying raw materials out and finished goods in, with railways built under Dalhousie 48-56 for the army, and he writes that the loot escalated. Plunder first, policy later. Before 1813 the drain was Dastak misuse, the Plassey plunder of 1757-65 and land revenue from 1765. After 1813 it was policy: no protective tariff until World War I, a managed exchange rate that favoured British business, and Council Bills in which the importer's forex stayed in London and the GOI paid rupees from taxpayers. The cafe bill and the double drain. Home Charges are what India paid Britain for goods and services Britain said it gave, Home meaning Britain; the teacher says to think like a British nationalist, since the bill reads as services (governance and security of the territory), goods (stores), stability (War Office) and development (FDI interest). The eight heads include salaries and pensions, EIC dividends, loan and foreign-debt interest, India Office costs, stores, War Office payments and FDI interest. The army abroad is a drain but not an HC, because India gave that service. India sold more than it bought in rupees (Ex > Im) yet lost the forex it earned, a trade surplus but a wealth deficit, the double drain. Railways, canals and only 2 per cent. The teacher marks this whole debate 'mmp'. The British pointed to railways (but with a guaranteed 5% in London, army purpose, 78% coverage by 1947; on his board FDI became FD: free land on a 99-year lease, buy-back, losses on the Indian taxpayer), canals (but only 25% irrigated, outside Permanent Settlement areas, water not free) and said the drain was only 2%. Naoroji replied that 2% was surplus capital that would have compounded, and the chapter closes that the critique was inseparable from the demand for Swaraj.

Story so far: the whole chapter is one question. What did the Moderates' politeness buy in 1892? Ask: for each section, is it a gain, a trick or a refusal? ICA 1892 = the second of the three Indian Councils Acts (1861, 1892, 1909); in each, split the Viceroy's Council in your mind into two boxes (Box A, the Executive Council; Box B, the Legislative Council). Secretary of State: Lord Cross. Viceroy: Lansdowne 88-94 (1888 to 1894). The Act is therefore also called the Lord Cross Act. The Act is about what the councils looked like (size, membership, powers) and the one small federal step. Everything else was unchanged. The handout begins at "Sec. 2" (there is no Sec. 1 in this chapter's handout pages), and the index printed at the end of the handout pages belongs to Chapter 29, not to this chapter.

Because the Moderates had spent seven years on 3P, 1892 is their moment of truth. Ask: why is the Act both a result and a proof of failure? ICA 1892: significance and key names The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was simultaneously a result of the Moderates' struggle and proof of its failure. The Moderates (from 1885 to 1892) had spent years petitioning, writing memorials and presenting carefully reasoned arguments for constitutional reform. This is the Method = 3P = Prayer, Protest in Press, Petitions. What they got was an Act that gave just enough to show the British had listened, and little enough to show they had no intention of actually conceding power. "3P" = Prayer, Protest in Press, Petitions. "PROOF of failure of Moderate Methods/Politics" = "Did NOT bring Ltd SG": the 3P method did not bring even Limited Self-Government. Keep for Mains: the Act is evidence that the method failed, and the failure pushes the Moderates to upgrade their demand (Chapter 26: Moderates' demands and weaknesses). Viceroys before Lansdowne 88-94: Lytton 76-80, Ripon 80-84, Dufferin 84-88. Three four-year terms in a row, then Lansdowne 88-94 for six years. Who named the Act? Prime Minister ("pm"): North Act 1773, Pitts India Act 1784. Secretary of State ("SoS"): Cross 1892, Morley Minto Reforms 1909, Montagu Chelmsford Reforms 1919. Viceroy beside them: "L 05-10" (Minto 05-10, for 1909) and "L 16-21" (Chelmsford 16-21, for 1919); "GoI" under the 1919 line. "Freedom" splits into "CS, MS" (civil and military services) and "[50:50 Br Indians]" (an equal British-Indian share).

items.t: 2 · The "indirect election" that was not called an election (handout Sec. 3)
items.x: Because the British wanted to look generous without sharing power, they invented 'nomination on recommendation'. Ask: why is a list from which someone else picks not an election? The "indirect election" that was not an election The most significant feature of ICA 1892: indirectly nominated members in the ILC (Imperial Legislative Council) and the PLCs (Provincial Legislative Councils). This was the first time something resembling representative membership appeared in these councils. But nominated, not elected. The word "election" was deliberately omitted from the Act. The legal mechanism was strictly "nomination on the basis of recommendation." It was selection, not election. Notable Indians who served under this framework: Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta, names that would dominate Moderate politics for the next two decades. 1861: the first GRAIN of popular character. 1892: SOME FORM of representative membership. One step up the ladder (Chapter 25: 1861 non-officers, 1909 proper indirect election, 1919 direct election). What a proper election means: choice of voters is final Proper election = the choice of the voters is FINAL. In ICA 1892 "Final" was missing. Example: 10 seats to fill; the bodies send a list of 50 names; the Viceroy or Governor picks 10 from the 50 = nominated. Direct against indirect elections: the 1892 chain In a 100% proper indirect election the chain would be: people elect local body members, local body members elect the Legislators of the province from among themselves, and the Legislators elect the next level from among themselves. In a proper election the choice of voters is final. Under ICA 1892 neither condition held: the recommending bodies only sent names, and the final pick was the Viceroy's or Governor's. The "election" was really a shortlist. Proper indirect election = the elected representative is not directly chosen by the people. Today's example: People (direct) elect MLAs; MLAs elect Rajya Sabha members (indirect). The 1892 chain: People, Local Bodies [Direct], PLCs [indirect] (Provinces), ILC [indirect] (Centre), with "elect" at each step. Local Bodies: four kinds Local Bodies are four kinds: Urban LBs (Municipalities), Rural LBs (Panchayats), Business Bodies, Others. District Boards = the rural local body (Panchayats). Business Bodies = Trade Associations and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. 2.1 How it worked: two levels (handout Sec. 3.1 and 3.2) How the nomination worked: two tiers Nomination flow from People to ILC For the PLCs: the Governors nominated non-official members on the recommendation of District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations and Zamindars. For the ILC: the Viceroy nominated non-officials on the recommendation of the non-official members of the PLCs and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce, not directly from local bodies. The two tiers of "nomination on recommendation" People elect (directly) the Local Bodies (Panchayats, Municipalities, Business Bodies, Others) Tier 1: District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations and Zamindars send a list of names to the Governor Governor nominates some from the list: the non-official PLC members Tier 2: the non-official PLC members + the Bengal Chamber of Commerce send a list of names to the Viceroy Viceroy nominates some from the lists: the non-official ILC members Choice of voters not final at both tiers: the lists only recommend PLC non-official members = "[* Politicians]" who then recommend the ILC non-officials. The Viceroy or Governor nominates only some names from the list: "Choice of voter not Final" (at both PLC and ILC levels). Exam Trap. "ILC members under ICA 1892 were directly recommended by Municipalities" is WRONG. Municipalities fed the PLCs; the PLCs fed the ILC. Two separate tiers. Direct recommendation to the ILC came only from the PLCs (their non-official members) and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce.

Because names now reached the councils, the next question is how many seats there were and who held the majority. Ask: who wins when promoters hold the vote? Both the ILC and the PLCs were expanded. In the ILC, the total number of additional members was now set at 10 to 16, and at least half could be non-officials. Compare 1861: the additional members were 6 to 12, of whom the non-officials were 3 to 6 (half). Key words: "additional members," "10 to 16," "at least half," "non-officials"; 1861: "half of the 6-12 additional," "i.e. 3 to 6." But the numbers hide the point: the Viceroy's Executive Council + the official additional members always comfortably outnumbered the non-official Indians. The official majority was mathematically guaranteed by the structure of the Act. Think of a board meeting where the promoter group always holds the majority regardless of how many independent directors are added: the independents may speak; they cannot win a vote. Officials = VEC + the official additional members. Additional members are half official, half non-official, so VEC + official additional members is usually more than the non-officials. Official majority in the ILC from ICA 1861 to ICA 1909. First non-officers' majority and first elected majority: GOI Act 1919 (Chapter 34).

items.t: 4 · The Viceroy's Executive Council: no change (handout Sec. 5)
items.x: Because the legislature grew, the executive had to be kept fixed. Ask: which box (VEC or ILC) changed in 1892? Concept structure of VEC and ILC: two boxes Whenever a question mentions the Indian Councils Acts (1861, 1892, 1909), split the government into two boxes: Box A, the Executive Council (VEC): the inner cabinet = GG + C-in-C + Ordinary Members. Box B, the Legislative Council (ILC): Box A plus the "Additional Members" (a mix of officials and non-officials). ILC = VEC + additional members; half of these must be non-officials. Box A: "[Law itself says they will be member]" (Ordinary Members are members by law). The C-in-C was "sent by CoD" and is the "extra-ordinary member" (Chapter 25: appointed by the Court of Directors). The word "choice" beside it is . VEC: no change, six portfolios The VEC did not change at all under ICA 1892 (unchanged from 1874). VEC = GG + C-in-C + the Ordinary Members (6). The Ordinary Members were the dedicated "ministers" who held specific administrative portfolios. In 1892 all were nominated by the British Crown. The six portfolios: Home, Revenue/Agriculture, Law, Military (an administrative counterpart to the C-in-C, that is, a Defence Minister), Finance (added 1861) and Public Works (added 1874). Pre 1861 GG + CIC + C1 to C4 Four Ordinary Members 1861 GG + CIC + C1 to C5 Finance is C5 1874 GG + CIC + C1 to C6 Public Works is C6 1892 No change Still C1 to C6

items.t: 5 · What the members could do (handout Sec. 6)
items.x: Because the room had new members, ask what they could do with the floor. Ask: which two powers were firsts, and which two were refused? Powers of the ILC: questions, resolutions, bills, ordinances, Budget Gained for the first time (starred): Questions and Budget. Not gained: Resolutions and Bills ("[Official Majority]"; "Non officers = inconsequential"). Beside Questions: "C1 to C6" with a "not equal" sign. 5.1 Questions For the first time, non-official members could ask questions to the executive (the VEC), a genuine new right. But with strict conditions: 6 days' prior notice was required, there could be no discussion of the answers, and no supplementary questions were allowed. You could ask. You could not follow up. 5.2 Resolutions Opposition members (the non-official, non-officer members, since the executive under the Viceroy was made up entirely of officers) could not bring any resolution before the council, nor demand a vote on a government resolution. Resolution = a formally declared intent of policy: a motion that the council endorses a direction. 5.3 Bills and legislation The government could make laws without the ILC or PLCs. The official majority meant that on every bill, Indian non-official members were outvoted. Their presence was advisory, not decisive: the legislative function was recommendatory, not mandatory. The Viceroy could veto any Bill. Ordinance power: no change. It remained as under ICA 1861: a 6-month emergency instrument. The council was recommendatory because of the official majority and the Viceroy's absolute veto, not because of any new bypass mechanism. 5.4 Budget The Budget could be discussed for the first time, another genuine new right. But members could neither vote on it nor amend it. "Taxation without Representation" (TWR) was the slogan that sparked the American Revolution (1776). Here Indians had a faint echo of representation: they could watch the Budget and speak to it, with zero power to change it. Traps in this section. (1) Supplementary questions: NO. (2) Discussion of the answers: NO. (3) Vote or amendment on the Budget: NO. (4) Resolutions by non-officials: NO, and no vote on a government resolution. (5) Ordinance power: unchanged from 1861 (6 months), not enlarged. (6) The ILC was not given an elected majority; the official majority stayed.

Because the Centre kept every key, the one small change stands out. Ask: which of BRASS's keys was handed back? ICA 1892 made one notable change in Centre-Province relations: the Governor no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate Non-Officers to the PLC. Until then (ICA 1861), even though Governors recommended names for their own Provincial Councils, the Viceroy's sanction was required. ICA 1892 ended this requirement. A small but genuine decentralisation: the first relaxation of the Viceroy's iron grip over provincial council composition since 1861. All other controls stayed exactly as under ICA 1861: rule-making powers; prior approval for certain bills; a single unified budget with no separate provincial budget; the power to create new provinces and to appoint Lieutenant-Governors. Unitary, federal and confederal: split of power A feature is federal if it shifts power from the Centre to the Provinces. Scale: Unitary = Centre 80% or more, Provinces 20% or less; Federal = about 50:50; Confederal = Centre 20% or less, Provinces 80% or more. "No mention of ppl in Topic of Federalism": people belong to Democracy; federalism is the law about Centre and Province. So the Governor's freedom from the Viceroy's sanction counts as a small federal step.

Because the details are many, one table anchors every provision. Ask: can you fill each row from memory before you look? Key names Lord Cross (SoS), Lansdowne 88-94 (Viceroy) Election principle Nomination on the basis of recommendation (the word "election" avoided) ILC size VEC + 10 to 16 additional members (up from 6 to 12 of 1861); at least half non-officials Official majority YES VEC Unchanged from 1874 Questions First: allowed with 6 days' notice; no discussion; no supplementary questions Budget First: discussion allowed; no vote Resolutions Opposition could not bring resolutions; no vote on a Government resolution Federalism Governor did not need the Viceroy's approval to nominate Non-Officers in the PLC Civil services reform NOT a provision of the Act: Aitchison Commission: CCS to ICS, UCS to PCS (done separately as an administrative measure)

items.t: 8 · A separate administrative reform of the same era (handout Sec. 9)
items.x: Because 1892 also saw civil service renaming, the exam sets a trap. Ask: was any of this written in the Councils Act? Classic exam trap: keep these separate from the Act. Under Lansdowne 88-94, on the Aitchison Commission (1886-88) recommendations, these civil-services changes were made as administrative orders, not provisions of ICA 1892. If listed under "provisions of ICA 1892": not a provision. Covenanted Civil Services (CCS) renamed ICS. Uncovenanted Civil Services (UCS) renamed Provincial Civil Services (PCS). Statutory Civil Services (created 1878): abolished. The "federal logic": Centre and province now had their own civil service cadre (ICS at the Centre, PCS in the Province). Handout vs slide, three points. (1) Statutory CS year: handout says created 1878; slide writes 1879 (Chapter 18: Act 1878, rules 1879); use 1878 for the Act, 1879 for the rules. (2) Subordinate CS: slide adds a third tier and says [UCS + Statutory CS posts] became (PCS + Subordinate CS); handout says only UCS to PCS and Statutory CS abolished. Both agree the Statutory CS ended and the PCS was formed. (3) Expansion of "ICS": handout and slide say "Imperial Civil Services"; Chapter 18 says Aitchison proposed "Imperial Civil Service" but 1892 kept "Indian Civil Service." Handout and teacher win here: CCS to ICS, UCS to PCS. For the spelling-out of ICS, check your notebook and Chapter 18.

items.t: 9 · Scorecard: what the Moderates won (handout Sec. 10)
items.x: Because the Moderates had asked for much, the scorecard counts what they got. Ask: which single row is a yes, and why 'but dissatisfactory'? Indianisation of Civil Services and Military No Non-official majority in the councils No Elected majority No Proper indirect election No (only nomination on recommendation) Expansion of ILC and PLCs Yes, but dissatisfactory Powerful Legislatures No Constitutionalism (Preamble + Basic Structure) No The word "election" did not even make it into the text of the Act. Only the Expansion of the ILC and PLCs scored a yes (and a dissatisfied one): 1 yes, 6 no. Handout says "six demands," but the scorecard has seven rows (one yes, six no). Read "six" as the six not met plus the one partly met. In an answer: "one demand (expansion) was partially met; the rest were refused." Moderates' demands: Chapter 26.

items.t: 10 · What the Moderates did next (handout Sec. 11)
items.x: Because the Act disappointed them, the Moderates changed the ask. Ask: how do Dominion status, Swaraj and the Drain Theory fit together? Impact: Moderates more assertive, Dominion demand and Swaraj Disappointed by ICA 1892, the Moderates raised their ceiling of demand. They began asking for Self-Government on the lines of Australia and Canada: the Dominion model, full self-governance within the British Empire without breaking from it. Their argument: Australia got self-government as a Dominion in 1901; Canada in 1867. Both were majority white-settler colonies. If those colonies could govern themselves, why not a civilisation far older and more complex than either? This officially became the goal of the INC at the 1906 Calcutta session, named Swaraj: Self-Government within the Empire, also called Home Rule. Alongside, the Moderates developed and propagated the Drain Theory: the economic argument that British rule was systematically extracting India's wealth to Britain. Political demand for Swaraj and economic critique through the Drain Theory became the twin pillars of Moderate politics in the years that followed. The Dominion demand (Australia and Canada) and Swaraj (1906 Calcutta) are the same idea. Dominion status = "Self-Government within Br Empire" = Swaraj = Home Rule. (Chapter 27: the Drain Theory in detail.)

items.t: 11 · Legacy: the catalyst for Extremism (handout Sec. 12)
items.x: Because the Moderates had played by every rule and still got a hollow Act, the method broke. Ask: what grew in the soil the Act left? ICA 1892 matters not only for what it contained, but for what it proved. Six demands, and one partially met. The Moderates had played by every British rule, used every permissible channel and mustered every rational argument. The Act they received was hollow: expanded councils with no real power, a budget discussion with no vote, questions with no follow-up. This was the moment the belief in British benevolence began to crack. If "prayers and petitions" could produce only this, the method itself was bankrupt. The disillusionment seeded by ICA 1892 was the soil in which Extremism would take root in the decade that followed. (The slide adds: the Bengal Partition of 1905 became the catalyst; see Chapter 29.) Failure listed: budget discussion with no vote; questions with no follow-up; no elections; no non-official majority. Method = 3Ps; consequence = street protests and mass politics under the Extremists. Soil (ICA 1892), then Catalyst (Bengal Partition 1905). From petitions to a hollow Act to Extremism 1885 to 1892: the Moderates use 3P (Prayer, Protest in Press, Petitions) for constitutional reform 1892: ICA 1892 (Lord Cross, Lansdowne 88-94): bigger councils, nomination on recommendation, Questions and Budget discussion, official majority The Act is hollow: no vote on the Budget, no follow-up to questions, no elections, no non-official majority The Moderates upgrade the demand: Dominion-style Swaraj (Calcutta 1906) and the Drain Theory Faith in "prayers and petitions" breaks; the method is bankrupt Extremism takes root: street protests and mass politics; Bengal Partition 1905 is the catalyst Additional members in the ILC 6 to 12 (non-officials 3 to 6, i.e. half) 10 to 16 (at least half non-officials) Representative principle The first GRAIN of popular character (non-officers nominated) Some form of representative membership: nomination on recommendation VEC Finance the 5th (C5) Unchanged from 1874 (C6 Public Works) Questions No First time: 6 days' notice, no discussion, no supplementaries Budget No discussion First time: discussion only, no vote, no amendment Governor's PLC nominations Needed the Viceroy's sanction No sanction needed Official majority Yes Yes (to 1909) Ordinance power 6-month ordinance No change

Seven years of polite asking. From 1885 to 1892 the Moderates used the 3P method (Prayer, Protest in Press, Petitions): carefully reasoned arguments for constitutional reform. The reply was the Indian Councils Act 1892, the Lord Cross Act, passed with Lord Cross as Secretary of State and Lansdowne 88-94 as Viceroy. It was a result of their struggle and proof of its failure. A shortlist called an election. The most significant feature was indirectly nominated members in the ILC and the PLCs, the first time something like representative membership appeared. But the word 'election' was deliberately left out: the mechanism was nomination on the basis of recommendation. In the teacher's example, if 10 seats were to be filled, names of 50 were asked and the Viceroy or Governor chose 10. Names climb the stairs. Tier 1: District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations and Zamindars sent names to the Governor, who nominated the non-official PLC members. Tier 2: the non-official PLC members and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce sent names to the Viceroy, who nominated the non-official ILC members. Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta were among those who served; Municipalities never recommended straight to the ILC. A bigger room, the same majority. The ILC's additional members rose to 10 to 16 (6 to 12 in 1861), and at least half had to be non-officials. But the VEC plus the official additional members always outnumbered the non-officials: like a board where the promoters always hold the vote, the independents may speak but cannot win. The inner cabinet stays put. The VEC did not change at all: GG + C-in-C + six Ordinary Members holding Home, Revenue/Agriculture, Law, Military, Finance (added 1861) and Public Works (added 1874). The ILC is the VEC plus the additional members: two boxes, one inside the other. Ask and browse, never vote. For the first time members could ask questions (6 days' notice, no discussion, no supplementaries) and discuss the Budget (no vote, no amendment): Taxation without Representation, the 1776 slogan, with a faint echo. They could not bring resolutions or demand a vote on a government resolution, the government could legislate over them, the Viceroy could veto any Bill, and the 6-month ordinance power was unchanged. One small step for the provinces. The Governor no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate non-officers to the PLC: the first relaxation of the Viceroy's grip since 1861. Rule-making powers, prior approval of certain bills, the single budget and the power to create provinces and appoint Lieutenant-Governors stayed as before. A reform from the same years, but not the Act. On the Aitchison Commission's recommendations (1886-88), in Lansdowne 88-94's time, the Covenanted Civil Services became the ICS, the Uncovenanted Civil Services became the PCS, and the Statutory Civil Services were abolished. These were administrative orders, not provisions of ICA 1892: a classic exam trap. The scorecard: one yes, six no. Indianisation of Civil Services and Military, a non-official majority, an elected majority, proper indirect election, powerful legislatures and constitutionalism were all refused. Only expansion of the ILC and PLCs scored a yes, and a dissatisfied one. The word 'election' did not make it into the text. Raising the ceiling. The Moderates began asking for self-government on the lines of Australia (1901) and Canada (1867): the Dominion model. Swaraj, self-government within the Empire (Home Rule), became the INC goal at Calcutta in 1906. They also developed the Drain Theory: the political demand and the economic critique became the twin pillars of their politics. The soil for Extremism. If prayers and petitions could produce only this hollow Act (a Budget talk with no vote, questions with no follow-up, no elections, no non-official majority), the method was bankrupt. Belief in British benevolence cracked; street protest and mass politics took root, with the Bengal Partition of 1905 as the catalyst.
