Story so far: a villain makes a hero. Keep the six numbered points on the title board in mind: Curzon 99-05, the reasons, the first mass protest, the 1905-08 people's phase, the Revolutionaries, Lal-Bal-Pal and Aurobindo. Chapter 29 title: Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement, board plan Curzon 99-05 is the villain and the villain makes the hero: "Stronger villain, stronger hero (INM)." His reasons: the Bengal Partition 1905 and his other authoritarian policies. Result: the first time the masses protest ("imp shift in methods of INM"). Timeline: [1905-08] the people's phase; [1907-11] the Revolutionaries (the ranges overlap by a year; the handout says the Revolutionaries rose 1908-11). Heads of the board: Lal, Bal, Pal, Sri Aurobindo (circled 6:).

Because the Moderates' petitions had failed, the Extremists look for a new recipe. Ask: which three causes (collapse, culture, Curzon 99-05) turn a failure into a movement? "Why Rise of the Extremists, Three Drivers": three reasons numbered 1 to 3; a CULTURE tree under the second: Religion, Indian Historical Heroes, etc. 1.1 Leaders and goal By 1905 the Moderate phase of the INM ended and the Extremist phase (1905-20) began under Lal-Bal-Pal and Sri Aurobindo: Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra), Bipin Chandra Pal and Sri Aurobindo Ghosh (Bengal). For most Extremists the goal was Swaraj within the British Raj; for a few, Sri Aurobindo and B.C Pal, it was Purna Swaraj (complete independence). INM and INC: who dominated when INM is the movie, INC is the hero. (1) INC dominated by Moderates 1885-1918, ~1920; (2) INM dominated by Moderates 1857-1905; (4) Extremists dominated the INM 1905-20; (5) MG dominated the INM [written like "1990-47": read as 1920-47; unclear, check your notebook]. So the Extremists led the movement but never the organisation, matching the handout's note that INC control passed to Gandhi at the 1920 Nagpur Session (section 8). Swaraj: meaning and practicality Swaraj = power of L, E, J (legislative, executive, judicial) split in two: the external part stays with the British; the domestic part comes "significantly" to Indians, 75% to 100%, called Dominion Status. The Extremists did not believe in the Providence of British rule (that it was a blessing). BUT Swaraj was more practical than Purna Swaraj, so most Extremists asked for Swaraj within the British Raj (the first word after "Sym for" is). 1.2 Sri Aurobindo and the first Purna Swaraj demand Sri Aurobindo studied in Cambridge and qualified for the CSE in 1890 but deliberately skipped the horse-riding test. He joined the Baroda Princely State civil service and later served as Vice-Principal of Baroda College. He was the first to publicly demand absolute independence in 1907, through his writings in Bande Mataram (not through an INC resolution). "1st formal Purna Swaraj resolution" = "in INC": the two firsts differ. Aurobindo = first public demand (1907, writings); Hasrat Mohani = first formal resolution in the INC (1921). The first formal resolution in the INC for Purna Swaraj was by Hasrat Mohani (with Swami Kumaranand) at the 1921 Ahmedabad Session. It was rejected by the INC, mainly on Mahatma Gandhi's opposition: he argued the demand was premature, irresponsible, and that the masses were not yet disciplined or prepared for a completely independent State. 1.3 The three drivers "Every phase of the INM was, in a sense, born from the failure of the phase before it." Chain: pre-1857 revolts → 1857 Revolt → modern INM → failure of conservative earlier organisations → WEMC-led regional organisations → INC under the Moderates → Moderates' failure → Extremists → Extremists' failure → Revolutionaries → and so on, until Gandhi. Each failure raised the temperature of the next response. Driver 1: The Moderates had failed. The Moderates led the INC since 1885. Their method was petition, prayer and press. By the early 1900s it had yielded nothing concrete: no self-governance, no economic relief, no political power. The Extremists read this as proof that gentle methods do not work against a colonial administration. Driver 2: mass mobilisation through religion and culture. The Moderates worked through newspapers, petitions and annual INC sessions, and their base was the Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC). The Extremists wanted the religious masses, and so spoke in cultural terms. Tilak organised the Ganapati Festival (1893) and the Shivaji Festival (1896) in Maharashtra as platforms for political mobilisation. Nationalism: cultural, economic, political Nationalism has three faces: Cultural, Economic (the Drain Theory), Political (power to the people or nation over the State). Extremists' recipe: Step 1: use culture to raise passion and emotion among the masses; Step 2: convert that cultural energy into political energy. Masses to gather: the non-Western-educated, motivated through Religion and Historical Heroes, then directed into the INM. "Emotion = energizer of Action." Netaji Bose: "Sv = Spiritual father of the INM in Bengal" = Cultural Nationalist [the slide writes only "Sv", probably Swami Vivekananda (section 3); check your notebook]. Handout: this was not a new idea in world history. Across colonised and occupied nations cultural nationalism has often been the first step toward political nationalism, especially when direct political organisation is suppressed. Tilak in the 1890s was doing what many European nationalists did in the 1820s and 1830s. Driver 3: Curzon 99-05 made mass anger unavoidable. Curzon 99-05 governed with an arrogance and authoritarianism that alienated even moderate opinion. His laws concentrated power and told educated Indians their opinions did not matter. Three reactionary laws (Calcutta Municipal Corporation Amendment Act 1899, Indian Universities Act 1904, Indian Official Secrets Amendment Act 1904) each hit a different pillar, local self-government, education and the press, and together showed that the administration would not reform itself. Section 2 gives the laws in detail. "Stronger the villain, Stronger the Hero." Handout version: Curzon 99-05's authoritarianism made even the Moderates of Bengal rethink their methods; he attacked local self-government, education and the press, and deployed DnR @ Bengal. PYQ 6, Prelims 2004: Viceroy chronology Prelims 2004: "Consider the following Viceroys: 1. Lord Curzon 99-05 2. Lord Chelmsford 3. Lord Hardinge 4. Lord Irwin. Correct chronological order?" Correct: (a) 1, 3, 2, 4 (Curzon 99-05, Hardinge 10-16, Chelmsford 16-21, Irwin 26-31). Tempting wrong option: (c) 1, 4, 2, 3 (puts Irwin second). (b) and (d) open with Chelmsford. Prelims 1998: "Which one of the following defines extremist ideology during the early phase?" Correct: (b) Obtaining self-government by aggressive means in place of petitions and constitutional ways. Traps: (a) preferring indigenous goods is Swadeshi, a method; (c) national education is one of the four Calcutta methods; (d) military coups belong to the Revolutionary stream. Extremism was about how self-government should be won.

items.t: 2 · The Swadeshi Movement: Curzon 99-05's measures and the road to 1905
items.x: Because Curzon 99-05 had already hit three pillars of public life, anger was ready before the Partition. Ask: which law attacked local self-government, which education, which the press? Before the Swadeshi Movement erupted, Curzon 99-05's own measures set the stage. Three laws built the frustration. Local bodies (Swaraj in 1882) and Official Secrets Pyramid: Centre, Provinces, Local Bodies. Local bodies = "Swaraj in 1882" under Ripon 80-84: the Resolution that gave Indians self-government at the lowest level; the 1899 Act rolled it back. Official secrets: an organisation (ORG) has private secrets (IPR, intellectual property rights) and State or Government secrets (Official Secrets): "such info which if in public domain can hurt the ORG's stability." Also: "1870: Bengal Govt expenditure on Higher Edu" (the verb is). Calcutta Municipal Corporation Amendment Act, 1899 Reduced the number of elected members in municipalities, rolling back the limited representative participation Indians had in local governance Local self-government Indian Universities Act, 1904 Brought universities under direct government control. Curzon 99-05 thought universities were "factories of sedition" (centres producing politically aware graduates who questioned British authority), so he clamped down Education Indian Official Secrets Amendment Act, 1904 Cut press freedom: power to censor and confiscate any publication hurting British interests; made communicating an "official secret" (broadly defined: anything relating to State affairs or specially notified) a criminal offence. In force until the Indian Official Secrets Act, 1923, even stricter The press Handout: educated Indians were the ones writing the petitions, editing the newspapers, running the INC and now leading the Swadeshi movement. So education policy was always also colonial control policy. Prelims 2015: "Which movement contributed to a split in the INC into Moderates and Extremists?" Correct: (a) Swadeshi Movement. The others come later: Quit India 1942, Non-Cooperation 1920-22 (when Gandhi united the factions), Civil Disobedience 1930-34. Prelims 2019: Swadeshi statements: 1. It contributed to the revival of indigenous artisan crafts and industries. 2. The National Council of Education was established as part of the Swadeshi Movement. Correct: (c) Both 1 and 2 (see section 5 for the National Council of Education and the Swadeshi enterprises). Prelims 2023: Statement-I: 7 August is National Handloom Day. Statement-II: the Swadeshi movement was launched on the same day in 1905. Correct: (a) Both correct, II explains I. The Boycott Resolution at Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905 launched the movement (section 4).

items.t: 3 · The Partition of Bengal (announced July 1905, effected 16 October 1905)
items.x: Because the anger was ready, one more act lit it. Ask: what did the British say, what did Indians believe, and why does the teacher call it Divide and Rule? 3.1 Bengal's administrative history before the Partition The British had redrawn Bengal's boundaries many times, each time for their own administrative or political convenience. 1765 The British obtained the Diwani of Bengal Suba (Bengal, Orissa, Bihar). In 1775 they annexed Benaras and ran it as part of the Bengal Presidency 1801 Half of Awadh ceded in a subordinate alliance treaty (Treaty of Lucknow 1801) and added to the Bengal Presidency as the "Ceded Provinces". Scindia's territory from the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) was added: now the "Ceded and Conquered Provinces" 1803 Orissa came under control by defeating the Bhonsle of Nagpur in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (the Diwani since 1765 had practically covered only Midnapore) 1826 Assam annexed by the Treaty of Yandabo 1826 after the 1st Anglo-Burma War (1824-26) and added to the Bengal Presidency 1836 North West Provinces (NWP 1836) created: the "Ceded and Conquered Provinces" separated from the Bengal Presidency 1874 Assam carved out as a separate Chief Commissioner (CC) Province (a UT equivalent: directly under central administration, not a full Lieutenant-Governor province) 1874-1905 Bengal Presidency = Bengal + Orissa + Bihar; Assam separate as a CC Province 1905 The Partition created Bengal (= WB + Bihar + Orissa) and the new province of East Bengal & Assam (EBA = EB + Assam) 1911 The Partition annulled: Bengal = WB + EB; Assam and "Bihar & Orissa" became separate 1936 Bihar & Orissa made full, separate provinces "SA" beside 1801 (the handout calls 1801 a subordinate alliance treaty with Awadh, Chapter 11); a small oval split in two with "1801" in the left half. On the 1874-1936 map: "1947: [EB + Sylhet from Assam] = EP" (East Pakistan). Quotation marks on "Bengal", "Assam" and "Bihar & Orissa" in the 1911 row = political names, not fixed geography. Map sketch: Bengal and East Bengal and Assam (EBA) before and after 1905 What moved in 1905. Before 1905 the Bengal Presidency covered Bihar, West Bengal, Orissa and East Bengal, with Assam beside it. The Partition (Oct 1905) cut the east off: East Bengal + Assam = EBA, holding the Assam Tea Gardens, the Assam-Bengal Railways and Chittagong Port; Calcutta Port stays in "Bengal." Quotation marks around a name = a political name. 1911 restored the pre-1905 map. Map: Partition of Bengal 1905 The handout numbers the administrative history 3.1 to 3.10 and then numbers the three British "benefits" again as 3.10 to 3.12. The slides split them correctly. 3.2 The British justification The official rationale was administrative. Undivided Bengal was the most populous province and too large for one administration. The British named three benefits: (1) Assam would grow and, as part of a proper Lieutenant-Governor province, get its own civil services cadre; (2) the Assam-Bengal Railways would come under the unified administration of EBA; (3) Assam's tea gardens would gain a cheaper maritime outlet via Chittagong port. 3.3 The real reason: what Indians believed Indians saw the Partition as Divide and Rule, meant to weaken the INM in Bengal. If administration were the goal, the logical fix was to reorganise Bengal on linguistic lines, not religious ones. Instead two provinces were divided along the Hindu-Muslim demographic fault line: it was communal engineering. How it weakened the INM: the movement in Bengal was led by the Bengali Bhadralok, upper-caste (UC) Hindu educated professionals. The Partition made Bengalis a minority in West Bengal (diluted by Bihar and Orissa) and Hindus a minority in EBA, so the support base shrank in both provinces at once. The second objective was to appease elite Muslims and counter the rising tide of Hindu cultural nationalism. EBA was designed as a new Muslim Majority Province (MMP). Stated reason (good governance) and real reason for the Partition Stated reason = good governance: (1) high population, (2) an officer cadre for Assam, (3) better railways, (4) cheaper tea exports ("ease of doing business"); "will get" and "when EBA" = promised only after EBA existed. Real reason, three parts: (1) Bengalis become a minority in Bengal, so Bengali INM leaders are weak: e.g. under indirect elections to the Imperial Legislative Council they would not win; (2) DnR = divide Bengalis, and Hindus against Muslims: Hindus become a minority in EBA, and the INM was dominated by Hindus; (3) co-opt Muslim elites. Language-based partition wanted by INM leaders INM leaders wanted a language-based partition (cf. States Reorganisation Act 1956), best for good governance: Orissa, Bihar, Bengal and Assam as provinces (each a language region), not a split of Bengal along religious lines. The teacher's board stresses the Bengali Bhadralok and indirect elections as the mechanics of weakness: the base is diluted. The handout states the same outcome as "a minority in Bengal (diluted by Bihar & Orissa)". 3.4 Hindu cultural nationalism and the Muslim response The British were watching Hindu cultural nationalism rise through the 1880s and 1890s. Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's Anandamath (1882) gave the idea of Bharat Mata and composed Bande Mataram. Swami Dayanand Saraswati (died 1883) and Swami Vivekananda built it ideologically; then came the Ganapati Festival (1893) and the Shivaji Festival (1896). Partitioning Bengal to appease elite Muslims was in part a response to this trend. Nawab Salimullah of Dacca and the elite Muslim leadership welcomed the Partition. The Muslim League (ML1906), formed a year later, actively supported it and worked with the Ulamas, who controlled the Muslim masses, deepening communal lines and reducing the chance of joint Hindu-Muslim resistance. Prelims 2009: "16 October 1905 is well-known because...?" Correct: (b) The Partition of Bengal took effect. Wrong options: (a) the Boycott Resolution at Calcutta Town Hall = "Aug 1905"; (c) Dadabhai Naoroji declaring Swaraj = "Dec 1906"; (d) Tilak did not start Swadeshi in Poona: it began in Bengal. Prelims 2010: "What was the immediate cause for the launch of the Swadeshi Movement?" Correct: (a) The Partition of Bengal done by Curzon 99-05. Traps: (b) Tilak's 18 months' imprisonment; (c) arrest and deportation of Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh with the Punjab Colonisation Bill (two years later); (d) the Chapekar brothers' death sentence (the 1897 Poona episode).

Because the Partition was announced, Bengal answered in steps. Ask: who initiated the movement (Moderates) and who led it (Extremists)? The movement did not begin on the day of Partition. It built over two years, changed character and spread beyond Bengal. How the Swadeshi movement unfolded, 1903-1907 "Who initiated the Swadeshi movement? Bengal Moderates" (7 August 1905 Boycott Resolution; 7 Aug 1905 = date of Swadeshi movt). "Who led it?" the Extremists ("Extremists take over"). Opposition to the Risley Papers was "by Mod + Ex" (both groups); a second note "By extremists". Desher Katha was in Bangla on the Drain Theory; "early 1900s: books on Drain published." At Barisal the police repression of the procession was a "Big Boost to movt" ["violent" above "SNB & Aurobindo" is unclear; check your notebook]. 1903: the Risley Papers. The Risley Papers 1903 (H.H Risley was Home Secretary) carried Curzon 99-05's Minute on Territorial Re-distribution with the Partition plan in detail. They were published in the Gazette of India to gauge public reaction, so Indians knew the scheme in 1903 itself (the slide gives Risley's letter of 3 Dec 1903 and the Gazette of 12 Dec 1903). 1903-05: the Moderate phase, press and Constructive Swadeshi. Surendranath Bannerjea (SNB) and C.R. Das ran a press campaign through Bengalee, Sanjibani and Hitabadi. Village-level mobilisation was attempted by Constructive Swadeshi, the best example being Rabindranath Tagore's ShantiNiketan Ashram (1901). These methods failed to stop the Partition, announced in July 1905 and effected on 16 October 1905. Partition as proof of the Moderates' failure: 1903-1905 "Proof of Moderates' Failure": the 1892 ICA (Indian Councils Act 1892) and the Partition of Bengal, which came after "Dec 1903 - July 1905: 1.5 yrs of 3 Ps" (the Moderates' petition, prayer and press). Oct 1905: the unit "Bi, WB, EB, Or" + "Assam (UT)" becomes "Bi, WB, Or" + "Assam + EB = MMP" (Muslim Majority Province). See Chapter 28 for the 1892 Act. Desher Katha (1904). Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar published Desher Katha (1904), documenting the economic exploitation of India under British rule. Its significance is that Deuskar used "Desh" for the entire Indian subcontinent, not just Bengal: a conscious attempt to build pan-Indian economic consciousness against the colonial drain. It was widely read in Bengal. 7 August 1905: the Boycott Resolution. In response to the July announcement, Moderates SNB, K.K Mitra, Anand Mohan Bose and P.C. Ray passed a resolution to boycott British goods and institutions at Calcutta Town Hall. The Moderates themselves had crossed a line. The Extremists take over. They widened both goal and method: to the demand for annulment of the Partition they added Swaraj; to Boycott and Swadeshi they added Passive Resistance (PR): non-cooperation with British institutions, civil disobedience (CD) and the threat of violent agitation if the government used repression. They also took the movement out of Bengal. Leaders across the country (the Extremists): Bengal C.R. Das and B.C. Pal Bombay Tilak Delhi Syed Haidar Raza Punjab Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh Madras V.O. Chidambaram Pillai April 1906: Barisal Conference. SNB and Aurobindo Ghosh distributed Bande Mataram badges. The police repressed the procession before it began. Bande Mataram, composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in Anandamath (1882), had become the anthem of the movement; its link with Bharat Mata and Hindu religious symbols would later cause tension with Muslim participation. PYQ 2, Prelims 1998: Partition and Surat (Assertion-Reason) Prelims 1998: Assertion [A] the Partition of Bengal in 1905 brought to an end the Moderates' role in the freedom movement. Reason [R] the Surat session separated the Extremists from the Moderates. Handout and bank key: (d) A is false, R is true. A is false because the Moderates passed the Boycott Resolution (7 Aug 1905) and stayed in the movement; R is true (Surat 1907; they reunited only in 1916). Conflict: the class slide marks "T" on both A and R. Use (d) (handout, bank key and answer slide agree); check your notebook for what the teacher said about A. Prelims 2008: "New Lamps for Old" (a systematic critique of the Moderates in a series of articles): (a) Aurobindo Ghosh. The others: R.C. Dutt (economic critique, drain), Syed Ahmad Khan (outside Congress politics), Viraraghavachari. Prelims 2016: "'Swadeshi' and 'Boycott' were adopted as methods of struggle for the first time during..." Correct: (a) the agitation against the Partition of Bengal (Boycott first at Calcutta Town Hall, 7 Aug 1905). Home Rule, Non-Cooperation and the Simon Commission boycott only reused them. Prelims 2002: which statement is NOT correct? Correct (the false one): (a) Liakat Hussain led the Muslim peasants of Barisal in their agitations. True statements: (b) the scheme of national education was formulated by Satish Chandra Mukherjee in 1889; (c) the Bengal National College was founded in 1906 with Aurobindo as Principal; (d) Tagore preached the cult of Atmasakti, whose main plank was the social and economic regeneration of villages. See the conflict note in section 5. Prelims 2018: biographer of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji and Shrikrishna, stayed in America, elected to the Central Assembly: (c) Lala Lajpat Rai (not Aurobindo, B.C Pal or Motilal Nehru). Prelims 2020, Desher Katha: (a) 1 and 2 only: it warned against the hypnotic conquest of the mind and inspired Swadeshi plays; "Desh" was the whole subcontinent.

items.t: 5 · Methods of the Extremists during Swadeshi 05-11
items.x: Because the Extremists wanted the masses, they built a many-sided toolkit. Ask: which methods are political (NC, CD) and which social (Constructive Work)? The Extremists used a wider and more confrontational toolkit than the Moderates. The teacher's boards sort it first, then the handout lists nine methods. Extremists' methods: Passive Resistance, Civil Disobedience, Constructive Work Passive Resistance = NC + CD + CW + violence if repression. Test = Step 1: Active Resistance = Step 1 is violence (the Revolutionaries' method); in Passive Resistance Step 1 is never violence; violence comes only if the government answers with repression. Civil Disobedience is always illegal (violent or non-violent): civilians breaking an unjust law or unjust orders of the Government. Constructive Work (CW) = SOCIAL domain; the other methods are POLITICAL action. CW has four strands: NGO-like activity; welfare of the poor (education in vernaculars, skill development for livelihood, health awareness); use of religion and spirituality for confidence; alcohol de-addiction. Its goal: the individual's Atmashakti (Atmanirbharta, self-reliance). Constructive Work: community Atmashakti and unity Second goal: Community Atmashakti via Hindu-Muslim unity, Upper Caste-Lower Caste unity and women's empowerment. "Unity is Power." Proofs: cooperatives (milk, Amul; banks) and SHGs (Self Help Groups: self + help = self-reliance; the group is the organisation of the community). CW "did": "SDS 1875" and "SV (RkMission 1897)"; "Service of Jiva = Worship of Shiva (Daridra Narayan)" [initials only; they fit Swami Dayanand Saraswati (Arya Samaj 1875) and Swami Vivekananda (Ramakrishna Mission 1897), section 3; check your notebook]. This is the Atmasakti Tagore preached in the 2002 PYQ (social and economic regeneration of villages). Constructive Work today, political movements tomorrow Today's CW leads to tomorrow's stronger political movements: a united community can be made politically aware while doing social work, as in Swadeshi. CW is a tool: used positively in the INM, negatively after 1947 by NGOs that act against the national interest. Non Cooperation: Boycott and Swadeshi, two sides of a coin Boycott and Swadeshi: legislature, executive, titles, education Boycott and Swadeshi in the judiciary Boycott of British goods: supply side and demand side Non Cooperation is always legal, so always non-violent (NV): NC = a coin with two sides, Boycott and Swadeshi. Boycott = do not cooperate with the three organs of the State (Legislature, Executive, Judiciary), plus titles, education institutions and British goods and services. Legislature: candidates do not fight elections, MLAs/MPs resign, voters do not vote. Executive: do not become a minister, CS or MS; holders resign. Title: renounce titles ("S+R" struck out). Education: do not teach or study the Brown Sahib syllabus. Judiciary: people do not file cases, lawyers strike, judges resign or do not join. Swadeshi is the matching construction: education = National Education / Swadeshi education (syllabus and books, schools, colleges for humanities and science; "1882: Edu was made a free enterprise"); civil cases = panchayats and arbitration courts. For Legislature and Executive: "NA [Sedition]: not applicable, i.e. nothing done by Indians" [link to "Sedition" unclear; check your notebook]. "People can give time to leaders: Sardar, Lokmanya, Mahatma." Boycott of British goods: imported goods are hit on the supply side (importers, port workers, domestic merchants) and the demand side (shops, people, picketing volunteers, social boycott); goods made in India by the British (FDI) are hit by strikes of workers in "browned" enterprises. Answer to both: Swadeshi: produce Indian goods and services and set up enterprises. 5.1 The nine methods i) Non Cooperation (NC), Boycott, Civil Disobedience (CD) and violent agitation. A call for NC (boycott of British institutions and goods) with Swadeshi (Indian-made goods), plus CD (deliberately violating unjust laws); if the government used police repression, violent agitation was to follow. ii) Constructive Work (CW). Continued alongside confrontation for awareness-building and mass mobilisation. iii) National Education. In response to the Indian Universities Act 1904, the Extremists set up parallel institutions: the Bengal National College (Aurobindo as principal), the National Council of Education (the teacher: an NCERT equivalent, and on the slide "NCERT + Sciences + Humanities") and the Bengal Technical Institute. Extremist methods (v-ix): Samitis, Jatras, religion iv) Swadeshi enterprises, to give Boycott economic teeth, across soap, matches, chemicals, steel, banking and shipping: Tata Iron & Steel Company (TISCO) Conceived by Jamsetji Tata; established by his son Dorabji Tata in 1907 Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals (BCPL) By P.C. Ray Bombay Swadeshi Stores (BSS) By Tilak and others Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (1906) By V.O. Chidambaram Pillai in Tuticorin, to challenge the British monopoly of coastal shipping (against the British India Steam Navigation Company) Punjab National Bank (PNB, 1894) and Lakshmi Insurance Company (1906) PNB by Dyal Singh Majithia and Lala Harkishen Lal, with significant involvement of Lala Lajpat Rai. L.L. Rai also promoted the D.A.V. (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) movement and, through his Lahore Indian Association (1878), led the Punjab Canal Colony Agitations (1907) PNB (1894) is older than the Swadeshi Movement. The handout and slide date it 1894, yet list it as a Swadeshi-era institution of economic nationalism; the Lakshmi Insurance Company (1906) is the one dated inside the movement. Do not date PNB to 1905-11. v) Picketing: physically preventing the sale of British goods at shops and liquor outlets; it also drew in women participants, so it mattered socially beyond its economic impact. vi) Samitis (volunteer corps). The INC under the Moderates had no ground-level structure, and the Samitis filled that gap. Example: the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (1905) of Ashwini Kumar Dutt in Barisal, which did Constructive Work among Muslim ryots and organised the Barisal Conference 1906. vii) Jatras (plays and theatre): traditional theatre to raise awareness and nationalist sentiment among audiences who would not read newspapers. viii) High use of religion. Prabhat Pheris (morning-worship processions), Tilaks, religious pledges and Kali worship; in Maharashtra, Tilak's Ganpati Festival (1893) and Shivaji Festival (1896) were the anchors. ix) Workers' strikes. C.R. Das, Liaqat Hussain and B.C Pal led strikes in foreign-owned enterprises; the logic hit the supply side too, by disrupting production and distribution. The INC was only a 3-day annual conference; PCCs (set up 1886) were dysfunctional on the ground, so Samitis mattered. Jatras: awareness + emotions leads to mobilization of masses. Prabhat Pheris = processions after morning worship. Conflict on Liaqat Hussain (Prelims 2002). The handout and slide (section 5, method ix) place Liaqat Hussain among those who led workers' strikes in foreign-owned enterprises during Swadeshi (with C.R. Das and B.C Pal). The answer slide and the bank, however, explain option (a) as false because the Barisal peasant agitation is "a later salt-breaking agitation of the Civil Disobedience era", a detail that is not in the handout. The answer stays (a) "Liakat Hussain led the Muslim peasants of Barisal" is NOT correct; remember him by the handout: Swadeshi workers' strikes, not Barisal peasants.

items.t: 6 · Why Swadeshi did not become a proper mass movement
items.x: Because a toolkit is not a movement, the mass base never formed. Ask: which reason is about cost, which about caste, which about religion and which about the INC? The Extremists attempted the first real mass movement in the history of the INC and did not fully succeed. How to judge any movement How to judge any movement, three columns. (1) Goal achieved or not; the ideology of nationalism. (2) Movement of the people (especially INM): level of participation by region (rural, urban; North, South, East, West) and by group (Lower Caste, Upper Caste; Hindu, Muslim; rich, poor; peasants, [Z: unclear, check your notebook], working class, capitalists; men, women). (3) Modern Politics as criterion: clear ideology, clear goals, a plan or programme (methods), strong united leadership, an organisation (ORG) and a voice. The next board adds money to the list. Modern Politics: criteria, with symbols as voice 6.1 Costly Swadeshi goods Too few enterprises to meet demand at affordable prices, so Swadeshi goods were dearer: low participation by the poor (Muslim ryots, Lower Castes (LC), blue-collar workers) 6.2 Force and social boycott Some student leaders and volunteers used force and social boycott against LC and Muslims who did not join, deepening alienation 6.3 Few Swadeshi institutions Arbitration courts, educational institutions and enterprises stayed thin relative to the ambition 6.4 Low Muslim participation (i) Jatras sometimes showed Muslims and the British as collaborators; (ii) the Muslim League (ML1906), led by elite Muslims like Nawab Salimullah of Dacca, backed the Partition and partnered with the Ulamas; (iii) the heavy Hindu symbolism (Bande Mataram, Kali worship) alienated Muslims 6.5 Capturing the INC over the masses Internal factionalism: the effort to take over the INC organisation distracted energy from ground mobilisation The result: overall mass mobilisation failed; British goods imports were not significantly impacted; the boycott failed on its primary economic objective. "(Costly)" goods: the poor who could not afford them include peasants (ryots) as well as workers. "In Bengal ~50% Muslims" (low Muslim participation hurt Bengal most). "i.e. British imports not impacted" under the boycott's failure. Handout: the recurring problem: Upper Caste (UC) leadership produces low Lower Caste (LC) participation. It showed up in the criticism of Social Reformers (Chapter 19), in the limits of the Moderates (Chapter 26) and now in the Extremists' movement. It is a structural problem of Indian social hierarchy meeting political organisation. Prelims 1998: "The Indian Muslims in general were not attracted to the Extremist movement because of the..." Correct: (d) Extremists' policy of harping on the Hindu past. Board key: (a) Sir Syed's influence F, (b) anti-Muslim attitude F, (c) indifference F, (d) T. The cause is the heavy Hindu symbolism (Bande Mataram, Kali worship, Ganapati and Shivaji festivals), not personal hostility. 6.1 After Surat: leaders scattered, Revolutionaries rise After the Surat Split of 1907 (section 7) the Extremist leadership was repressed and scattered: Tilak was deported to Mandalay, Burma (1908-14); Aurobindo retired from active politics; B.C Pal retired temporarily; L.L Rai went abroad from 1914 to 1920, to London and then the United States, where he set up the 'Indian Home Rule League of America'. With the movement leaderless by 1908, the Revolutionaries rose (1908-11): those who concluded that even the Extremists' passive resistance and mass politics had failed. Each failed approach bred a more radical successor. (Chapter 30 begins here.) "When Pen failed, People came out; when People failed, Guns came out; when Guns failed, MG came out [1920+]." Pen = the Moderates' petitions; People = the Extremists' mass politics; Guns = the Revolutionaries; MG = Mahatma Gandhi, 1920 onwards. After Surat (1907): leaders scattered, Revolutionaries The class transcription labels slide 22 "Chapter 30", but the handout's section 6 for this chapter carries exactly the same text (Tilak, Aurobindo, Pal, Rai, then the Revolutionaries of 1908-11), so it is placed and cited once, here. The detailed Revolutionary story is Chapter 30.

Because the Moderates feared losing the INC, the split came at Surat. Ask: did the two wings differ on goal or on method? How did the INC fracture, and why did it matter? Tension between Moderates and Extremists had been building since Swadeshi gave the Extremists a platform. The Bombay-based Moderates opposed Extremist methods on principle: they feared confrontation would provoke repression and damage the constitutional progress they believed in. Calcutta 1906: mid path between Moderates and Extremists Background: Calcutta 1906 was a "mid path" between two camps. Bombay and Madras Moderates: constitutional; opposed violence, CD, Boycott and mass politics; did not want Swadeshi taken outside Bengal. Bengal Moderates: pro non-violent Boycott, not in favour of CD or violence. Extremists: CD, NC and violence as Step 2. Calcutta 1906: President Dadabhai Naoroji ("Bheeshma Pitamah," the elder statesman respected by both sides); goal (no dispute) = Swaraj; methods = Boycott, Swadeshi, National Education, with no CD and no violence = the 4 Calcutta Resolutions (Boycott and Swadeshi ticked). Moderates' fear: armchair intellectuals losing control over the INC to the Extremists' mass politics. The 1906 INC session was held in Calcutta with Dadabhai Naoroji as President. The Extremists got four resolutions passed: (1) Swaraj (the goal), (2) Boycott, (3) Swadeshi, (4) National Education (methods). The Bengal Partition was condemned separately. Tilak also set up an Extremist/Nationalist party within the INC to convert it from within into an extremist organisation. Prelims 2010: "Which was NOT one of the four resolutions?" Correct: (a) Annulment of the Partition of Bengal (condemned separately). The four are one goal (Swaraj) and three methods (Boycott, Swadeshi, National Education). The question stem says the retention or rejection of these four split the Congress at Surat. Surat 1907: failure of the mid path, choice of venue "Surat Split 1907 = failure of the mid path = success of the British DnR." Surat is in Gujarat, in the Bombay Presidency (the President does not come from the host region). Nagpur or Poona, both Extremist strongholds, would have given the Extremists, with mass pressure, the upper hand; so the Moderates chose Surat. Regional pattern: "uneven growth of Western education leads to uneven growth of the INM": (Marathi) Bombay and Poona, Madras, Calcutta. For 1907 the session was originally planned for Poona or Nagpur, both Extremist strongholds. The Moderates shifted the venue to Surat, where they had more control. Morley's 1906 Budget speech and the Surat Split as DnR Morley's 1906 Budget speech is the British move behind Surat. In 1906 the Secretary of State Morley, in the British Parliament on the Budget of the Government of India, hinted at council reforms: expansion and more powers for the ILC and PLCs by amending the ICA 1892. The Moderates' mouths watered. Both the 1906 session and the 1907 Surat Split are DnR: Moderates against Extremists (second bracket "Royal vs Royal":). The Moderates wanted no violence, so the reforms would not be derailed, especially in Bombay and Madras. (Reform: Chapter 31.) Handout: Morley's Budget speech of 1906 as Secretary of State hinted at forthcoming council reforms. This gave the British the opening for Divide and Rule (DnR): the hint motivated Moderates to show the British that the INC was cooperative and in favour of a truce, while the Extremists wanted nothing to do with such optics. British empire built and sustained by Divide and Rule "The British empire was created and sustained via DnR policies." Under the EIC: PoRF (Policy of Ring Fence), SA (Subsidiary Alliance), misuse of succession disputes (Chapter 10, Chapter 11); Peel Commissions; Martial Races + Cantonments. From 1857 onward: PS 1793 (Permanent Settlement), Macaulay's minute, the Bengal Partition (PS 1793 and Macaulay's minute are listed under 1857+ though earlier). The Bengal Partition divided three ways: Bengalis divided, Hindus against Muslims, Moderates against Extremists. Surat 1907: the presidential contest and the split At Surat the immediate flashpoint was a fight over the presidency: L.L Rai (Extremist) against Rash Behari Ghosh (Moderate). L.L Rai withdrew to prevent a split, but the Extremists refused any compromise unless the four Calcutta resolutions were re-adopted. The session collapsed: shoes were hurled, chairs were broken and the Extremists were expelled from the INC. Presidency contest: L.L Rai (Extremist) against Rash Behari Ghosh (Moderate), "not Bose" (not Anand Mohan Bose). L.L Rai withdrew from fear of an INC split, BUT on the condition that the four Calcutta Resolutions be re-adopted, especially Boycott by the masses. The Moderates did not agree: self-government within the empire was fine for them; they opposed mass politics by the INC. Chairs broken, shoes hurled. Extremists expelled from the INC [Dec 1907 to the Lucknow session of Dec 1916]. Extremists as Lok Sabha MPs, Moderates as Rajya Sabha MPs Analogy: Extremists = Lok Sabha MPs (the people's leaders); Moderates = Rajya Sabha MPs (the intellectuals). In 1908 the Allahabad Convention (Mehta Congress), a small meeting of senior INC leaders as distinct from the annual December session, declared "we are loyal to the Raj." The 1908 INC Annual Session was held at Madras with Rash Behari Ghosh as President. The INC remained divided until 1920, when Mahatma Gandhi united the Moderates and Extremists. The Extremists re-entered the INC in 1916 (Lucknow), but re-entry is not agreement on methods. The Surat Split was the INC's first organisational crisis. Both factions wanted Swaraj; they split over method: Moderates believed in petition, Extremists in confrontation. The 1907 split lasted 13 years until 1920, when Gandhi reunified the Congress. PYQ 4, Prelims 1999: end of pray and petition Prelims 1999: "The Congress policy of pray and petition ultimately came to an end under the guidance of: (a) Aurobindo Ghosh (b) Bal Gangadhar Tilak (c) Lala Lajpat Rai (d) Mahatma Gandhi." Conflict: handout and bank key vs the teacher's board. The handout and bank key give (b) Tilak (he built the Extremist party within the INC to convert it from within). The board gives (d) Gandhi: "ultimately" with "1906 TEMPORARY" (the end of petitions in 1906 was only temporary: the Moderates came back, Surat 1907, Allahabad Convention 1908) and "INC: 1885-1918, ~1920" (Moderate-dominated INC until about 1920). Follow the teacher's board: (d) Gandhi; keep (b) Tilak in mind [key and board disagree; check your notebook]. Prelims 2016: "Main reason for the split at Surat 1907?" Correct: (b) Extremists' lack of faith in the capacity of the Moderates to negotiate with the British Government. Board: "METHODS" beside (b): the split was about method, not goal. Traps: (a) Minto's communalism (1909 reforms, after Surat), (c) the founding of the Muslim League (separate track), (d) no Aurobindo presidency bid.

items.t: 8 · Impact of the Swadeshi Movement and the Curzonian administration
items.x: Because the movement failed in its main aim but not in what it taught, its impact is mostly future use. Ask: which impacts are positive and which two are negative? The Swadeshi Movement and Curzon 99-05's administration reshaped the INM in ways that outlasted the movement. 8.1 A nationalism that never came down Nationalist consciousness, especially in Bengal and Maharashtra, did not subside even after the movement ended and leaders scattered 8.2 The foundation of mass politics For the first time the attempt was made to involve not just the WEMC but the Working Class (WC), the masses and ordinary people. Incomplete, but the first attempt: the Working Class movement and Revolutionary activities grew from it 8.3 Economic awareness spread People grasped the Drain of Wealth and the role of British goods in impoverishing Indian industry; Boycott became a major tool of the future INM. To convince the poor to buy costlier Swadeshi goods, Extremists had to explain the Drain in simple language 8.4 Nationalistic symbols Bande Mataram became the anthem of the INM; Tagore's 'Amar Sonar Bangla' (My Golden Bengal), written in protest against the Partition, later became the national anthem of Bangladesh 8.5 New methods for future use Passive Resistance (NC and CD), Constructive Work (CW), Jatras and Prabhat Pheris were all later used heavily by Gandhi: he inherited a tested toolkit, not a blank slate 8.6 From petitions to mass action The INM moved from the Moderates' petition-and-pray model to mass action under Extremist leadership, but the INC itself remained under Moderate control until the 1920 Nagpur Session, when Gandhi took over (not "Extremist control of the INC in 1905") "To convince the poor to buy costlier Swadeshi, leaders must explain Drain" (8.3 links back to the cost problem of section 6): the economic education was itself a lasting contribution. Beside 8.5: "methods" and "for mass mobilization" (the toolkit was meant for mass mobilization). Handout: recall that political symbols, grand marches, the idea of the fatherland and songs had also played a major role as positives of the peasant revolts of earlier periods (Chapter 22). Delhi Durbar, capital politics and the Partition's goal 8.7 Capital shifted to Delhi (1911). It reduced Bengal's dominance in the INM: Curzon 99-05 got his strategic outcome. It was announced at the Delhi Durbar, December 1911, during the coronation of King George V and Queen Mary as Emperor and Empress of India. Three linked points. A new King or Queen means an Imperial (Delhi) Durbar. The goal of the Bengal Partition 1905 = weaken the INM in Bengal. Politics done in the capital gets extra TRACTION: when the capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911, Bengal lost that extra traction and the INM's centre of gravity shifted, which is how Curzon 99-05 got his strategic outcome. 8.8 Birth of the Muslim League (ML1906): it led to the formal, organised beginning of communal politics in India, a long shadow stretching to 1947. Prelims 2014: "The Partition of Bengal made by Curzon 99-05 in 1905 lasted until...?" Correct: (b) King George V abrogated Curzon 99-05's Act at the Royal Durbar in Delhi, in 1911. The teacher's notes on the traps: (a) the I World War is 1914-19 and (c) Gandhi's Civil Disobedience Movement is 1930-34; (d) confuses the 1905 Partition with the 1947 Partition of India. From Curzon 99-05 to Gandhi's toolkit Moderates fail: petition, prayer, press yield nothing by the early 1900s Curzon 99-05: Municipal 1899, Universities 1904, Official Secrets 1904; Risley Papers 1903 Partition of Bengal: announced July 1905, effected 16 October 1905; DnR, EBA as a Muslim-majority province 7 Aug 1905: the Moderates' Boycott Resolution; then the Extremists add Swaraj and Passive Resistance Swadeshi methods: boycott, Swadeshi, national education, enterprises, Samitis, Jatras, religion, strikes Not a mass movement: costly goods, force, thin institutions, low Muslim participation, INC capture Surat Split 1907: leaders scattered; Revolutionaries 1908-11; Delhi Durbar 1911 annuls the Partition 1920: Gandhi inherits the tested toolkit Goal Self-government within the empire Swaraj within the Raj (most); Purna Swaraj (Aurobindo, Pal) Method Petition, prayer, press Boycott, Swadeshi, Passive Resistance (NC + CD + CW), violent agitation only if repression Base WEMC, newspapers, annual sessions The religious masses through culture, Samitis, Jatras View of mass politics Opposed (Bombay and Madras especially) The method Leaders Naoroji, SNB, Rash Behari Ghosh Lal-Bal-Pal, Sri Aurobindo Teacher's analogy Like Rajya Sabha MPs: intellectuals Like Lok Sabha MPs: the people's leaders

1882 Anandamath: Bankim gives Bharat Mata and Bande Mataram 1883 Swami Dayanand Saraswati dies 1885 INC founded; Moderate-led (to 1918, about 1920) 1890 Aurobindo qualifies for the CSE but skips the riding test 1893 Tilak's Ganapati Festival 1896 Tilak's Shivaji Festival 1899 Curzon 99-05 begins; Calcutta Municipal Corporation Amendment Act ★ 1901 Tagore's ShantiNiketan Ashram 1903 Risley Papers published in the Gazette of India (12 Dec) ★ 1904 Indian Universities Act; Indian Official Secrets Amendment Act; Desher Katha ★ 1905 July: Partition announced; 7 Aug: Boycott Resolution, Calcutta Town Hall; 16 Oct: Partition effected; EBA created ★ 1906 April: Barisal Conference; Dec: Calcutta session (Naoroji, four resolutions); Muslim League founded; Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company; Bengal National College ★ 1907 Surat Split; Aurobindo demands absolute independence in Bande Mataram; TISCO; Punjab Canal Colony Agitations ★ 1908 Tilak deported to Mandalay (to 1914); Allahabad Convention (Mehta Congress); Madras session; Revolutionaries rise (to 1911) ★ 1911 Delhi Durbar (Dec): Partition annulled, capital to Delhi ★ 1914 L.L Rai abroad (to 1920) 1916 Extremists re-enter the INC at Lucknow 1920 Gandhi unites the INC; Nagpur Session ★ 1921 Hasrat Mohani's Purna Swaraj resolution rejected at Ahmedabad 1936 Bihar and Orissa made separate provinces

The petitions that went nowhere. The Moderates have led the INC since 1885, and their method is petition, prayer and press. By the early 1900s it has brought no self-governance, no economic relief and no political power. The Extremists read this as proof that gentle methods do not work against a colonial administration. Culture becomes a weapon. Lal-Bal-Pal and Sri Aurobindo lead the Extremist phase: Lajpat Rai in Punjab, Tilak in Maharashtra, Pal and Aurobindo in Bengal. Tilak had already turned the Ganapati Festival (1893) and the Shivaji Festival (1896) into political platforms: culture first, then political energy. Most want Swaraj within the Raj; Aurobindo (1907, in Bande Mataram) and Pal want Purna Swaraj. Curzon 99-05's three orders. In 1899 the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Amendment Act cuts elected members; in 1904 the Indian Universities Act takes the universities under direct control, calling them factories of sedition; and in 1904 the Indian Official Secrets Amendment Act cuts press freedom. Local self-government, education and the press are all hit. The teacher: the stronger the villain, the stronger the hero. The Partition of Bengal. The Risley Papers of 1903 reveal the plan. It is announced in July 1905 and takes effect on 16 October 1905: Bengal (West Bengal, Bihar, Orissa) and East Bengal and Assam, a new Muslim-majority province. The stated reason is good governance; the Indian view is Divide and Rule, since Bengalis become a minority in Bengal and Hindus a minority in EBA. Nawab Salimullah welcomes it and the Muslim League follows in 1906. The pen, then the boycott. From 1903 to 1905 Surendranath Bannerjea and C.R. Das run a press campaign and Tagore tries Constructive Swadeshi at Shantiniketan; Deuskar's Desher Katha (1904) uses 'Desh' for all India. After about 1.5 years of the Moderates' three Ps the Partition still comes, and on 7 August 1905 the Moderates themselves pass the Boycott Resolution at Calcutta Town Hall. The Extremists take over. The Extremists add Swaraj to the goal and Passive Resistance (NC + CD + CW, with violence only if the government uses repression) to the method, and carry the movement out of Bengal: Das and Pal, Tilak, Haidar Raza, Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh, and V.O. Chidambaram Pillai. At Barisal in April 1906 the police stop a procession of Bande Mataram badges, and it becomes a big boost to the movement. The toolkit. Boycott and Swadeshi (two sides of one coin), national education with the Bengal National College under Aurobindo, enterprises such as TISCO (1907) and the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (1906), picketing, Samitis, Jatras, religious symbols and workers' strikes. Constructive Work aims at Atmashakti, the individual and then the community. Why it fell short. Swadeshi goods are costly, so the poor stay out; student volunteers use force and social boycott on Lower Castes and Muslims; institutions are thin; Muslims are put off by Jatras, the Muslim League and the heavy Hindu symbolism; and the Extremists spend energy trying to capture the INC. British imports are not hit. Calcutta, then Surat. At Calcutta (1906) Naoroji presides and the Extremists pass Swaraj, Boycott, Swadeshi and National Education. Morley's 1906 Budget speech hints at council reforms, and the Moderates move the 1907 session from Poona or Nagpur to Surat. A fight over the presidency between L.L. Rai and Rash Behari Ghosh ends with shoes hurled and the Extremists expelled; in 1908 the Allahabad Convention declares loyalty to the Raj. Leaders scattered, guns appear. Tilak is deported to Mandalay (1908-14), Aurobindo retires, Pal retires for a time, and Rai goes abroad (1914-20). Leaderless, the movement gives way to the Revolutionaries (1908-11). The teacher's chain: when the pen failed people came out, when people failed guns, when guns failed MG. What was left. Nationalism stays lit, mass politics has begun, the Drain is explained to the poor, Bande Mataram becomes the INM's anthem, and Passive Resistance, Constructive Work, Jatras and Prabhat Pheris are a toolkit Gandhi inherits in 1920. At the Delhi Durbar of December 1911 the Partition is annulled and the capital moves to Delhi; the Muslim League's birth leaves communal politics as the long shadow.

Prelims 1995 The Barrah Dacoity was the first major venture of the revolutionary terrorists of the freedom movement in: (a) Bombay-Karnataka (b) Punjab (c) East Bengal (d) The Madras Presidency (c) East Bengal. Barrah, near Dhaka, was the work of the Dacca Anushilan Samiti under Pulin Behari Das (1908). Bombay-Karnataka is the Savarkar stream; Punjab is the later Ghadar current.
