Because the Extremists were scattered after Surat and the Swadeshi movement stood leaderless, someone had to answer what next. Ask: what did the Pen, the People and the Guns each try? Chapter 30 title: Revolutionary Activities and Repression of Extremists Priority: Mains = potential future question, no past question; Prelims = some questions. A list-and-link chapter: who founded what, when, with which method, and what the British did in reply. After Surat (1907): leaders scattered, Revolutionaries rise Chain of failed approaches: "When Pen failed, People came out; when People failed, Guns came out; when Guns failed, MG came out [1920+]." Pen = the earlier phase that failed; People = the Extremists' mass politics; Guns = the Revolutionaries; MG = mass politics returning from 1920+. Each failed approach bred a more radical successor. The Extremist leaders were scattered after Surat (1907). Tilak was deported to Mandalay, Burma (1908-14); Aurobindo retired from active politics; B.C. Pal retired temporarily; L.L. Rai went abroad (1914-20) and set up the Indian Home Rule League of America. With the movement leaderless by 1908, the Revolutionaries rose (1908-11): those who concluded that even the Extremists' passive resistance had failed.

Because mass politics had failed, a small committed group chose arms with two aims. Ask: which aim is long term and which is immediate? Mass politics versus armed struggle Two models of struggle. Mass politics = Extremists; method = the people (NC = non-cooperation, CD = civil disobedience, violence only if repression, and then only stones and burning, not an AK-47). Armed struggle = Revolutionaries; method = a committed small group; tool = AK-47. By 1908 the Swadeshi Movement was leaderless: its prominent Extremist leaders had been arrested, deported, or forced into exile. The question facing the radicalised Indians: if mass politics has failed, what next? The Revolutionaries had two answers and pursued both at once. Long-term goal: repeat 1857, that is, start a civil rebellion and cause disaffection within the army, eroding the British military foundation in India. Immediate method: individual heroic action, assassinating hated British officials to strike fear in British hearts, to remove the fear of the British from among Indians, and to arouse nationalist sentiment. If caught, the courtroom itself became a platform: a public trial was an opportunity for propaganda, and a death sentence was an act of supreme sacrifice that could inspire others. Goal = Repeat 1857 = LTM (long term) = not immediate action. Assassination is the method of now; the 1857-style army rebellion is the goal of later. "Repeat 1857" points to the Dhaka Anushilan's long-term preparation. 'Propaganda by deed' is not unique to India. Russian groups of the 1870s-80s (Narodniks, later the Socialist Revolutionary Party) used similar tactics. The Indian Revolutionaries knew these examples and consciously drew from them; Savarkar's admiration for Mazzini shows the same internationalist consciousness.

Because heroic action needed structure, they built societies at home and centres abroad. Ask: why did the teacher say go abroad (VOICE)? The logic of individual heroic action needed structure. The Revolutionaries built two types of organisations: secret societies inside India and centres abroad that could operate with greater freedom, acquire weapons and produce propaganda. The two networks were linked and fed each other. Secret societies: in India versus outside India Five reasons to set up societies outside India ("Voice"): (1) Diplomatic pressure by highlighting colonialism. (2) Greater freedom of speech, newspapers: "Voice" (the modern-politics word for a platform). (3) Procure weapons and send them to India (Arms Act 1878 made weapons hard to get inside India). (4) Assassinate British officers at their home, in England (India is one stage, "Home in England" the other). (5) NRIs: awareness and nationalism (NRIs and relatives exchange letters). International help from enemies of the British supplies "Weapons and Rupee." Abroad an organisation can be "PUBLIC ORG (not secret org)"; the example in the handout is the IHRS (Section 2.5). 2.1 The birth of organised militant nationalism in Bengal (1902 onwards) Because the Samiti began with physical training and armed resistance, an impatient inner circle broke away around a newspaper. Ask: who stood behind Jugantar? Anushilan Samiti 1902 and the Jugantar branch 1906 One body in 1902, two branches by 1906. Anushilan Samiti (1902) is the parent; it splits into the continuing Anushilan Samiti and Jugantar (1906). Backdrop: 1905 Bengal Partition. The roots of organised militant nationalism in Bengal go back to 1902, when Pramathanath Mitra (P. Mitra) founded the Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta. Outer form: a body for physical training and character building. Inner purpose: to cultivate the spirit of armed resistance. By 1906 an impatient radical inner circle had formed within the Samiti, driven by the conviction that immediate armed action could not wait. This faction coalesced around a fiercely anti-British newspaper, Jugantar ("New Era"), established by Barindra Kumar Ghosh (younger brother of Aurobindo Ghosh), Bhupendranath Datta and Abinash Bhattacharya. The network that grew around it became known independently as the Jugantar party. Who is who. Jugantar: B.K. Ghosh, Bhupendra Dutt, Abhinash Bhattacharya. Anushilan Samiti: P. Mitra, S C Basu. Dacca Anushilan Samiti: Pulin Behari Das. Two brothers, two responses. Aurobindo worked through writing, philosophy and the INC; Barindra went straight into revolutionary conspiracy. After the Alipore Case broke Jugantar, Aurobindo escaped to Pondicherry and turned to spiritualism; Barindra was transported to the Cellular Jail (Section 3.4). Prelims 2000 (Tripura). Answer (b): the Bengal revolutionaries took shelter in Tripura. Organised militant nationalism was a Bengal story from 1902; Tripura, next door, was the shelter. Distractors: (a) kings not standing anti-British rebels, (c) tribal temperament not the recorded reason, (d) no anti-kingship insurgency in the account. Read the handout figure as a list of boxes, not arrows of descent. Correct lines: Anushilan 1902 gives Jugantar 1906; Dacca Anushilan 1906 is a separate East Bengal offshoot; Abhinav Bharat is a Western-India stream from Mitra Mela 1899. The Ghadar box is "next chapter" (Chapter 32: Ghadar Movement (1913-15)). Organisational network of the Revolutionaries The network with names. Anushilan: P. Mitra, S C Basu. Jugantar: B.K. Ghosh. Dacca Anushilan: Pulin Behari Das. Abhinav Bharat: [Pune], Nasik; Ganesh and Vinayak = Savarkar. India House: Shyamji Krishna Varma, 1905 (year partly unclear). Ghadar seed: USA and Canada, NRIs who came back to India to repeat the 1857 revolt (Chapter 32: Ghadar Movement (1913-15)). Beside Anushilan: "Goal = Repeat 1857 = LTM = not immediate Action." 2.2 The British intelligence response: CID (1903) Exam hooks on the CID slides: Fraser Police Commission of 1902 and the word "infiltrate." The British were not passive observers. Recognising the need for a specialised intelligence apparatus beyond the foundational Indian Police Act of 1861, the colonial government formally established the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) in 1903, following the recommendations of the Fraser Police Commission of 1902. What it was: a professionalised network of spies and informers, embedded within Indian society, designed to track, infiltrate and dismantle political dissent and secret societies. The CID (1903) was a structural response, not just a legal one. The British did not only pass sedition laws; they built intelligence machinery to identify threats early, and the CID remained central to colonial repression throughout the INM. 2.3 Inside India: the Revolutionary organisations Because Bengal and the west each built their own society, the streams diverged in method. Ask: which stream matches Repeat 1857? Abhinav Bharat 1904 [Pune]; Mitra Mela 1899 [Nasik]; brothers Ganesh and Vinayak = Savarkar; London branch 1906. "Narrative" - "imp": Savarkar's The Indian War of Independence 1857 (1909) recast the 1857 Revolt as a planned war of national liberation, not a mere "mutiny" (banned before publication, yet circulated underground as essential revolutionary reading). A Revolutionary movement also needs a narrative, a story of why it fights; the same idea recurs for the IHRS ("Building Narrative in favor of Home Rule") and The Indian Sociologist ("Narrative for ideology of Nationalism"), Section 2.5. Abhinav Bharat (1904): the Savarkar brothers, Vinayak (Veer Savarkar) and Ganesh, set up a secret society called Mitra Mela in 1899 in Nasik. It was renamed Abhinav Bharat, or Young India, in 1904 in Pune. When Veer Savarkar went to London to study law in 1906, he opened a branch of Abhinav Bharat there and compiled Mazzini Charitra (1906), a translation of Mazzini's writings. Savarkar also wrote The Indian War of Independence 1857 (1909), which recast 1857 as a planned war of national liberation rather than a mere "mutiny." The British banned it before publication, but copies circulated underground. Why "Young India"? Mazzini's "Young Italy." It was active in the revolts of 1830 to overthrow Austrian colonialism in northern Italy and unify the Italian kingdoms; unification finally succeeded in 1870. Mazzini's method was guerrilla warfare. Savarkar saw a parallel between Austrian colonialism over Italy and British colonialism over India. Prelims 1999 (Abhinava Bharat). Answer (b) V.D. Savarkar. Distractors: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki (Muzzafarpur bombers, Bengal stream); Bhagat Singh (1920s generation). Hook: Mitra Mela 1899 Nasik, then Abhinav Bharat 1904 Pune = Savarkar. "Good Relations between Revolutionaries and Extremists": not enemies. The Dacca Anushilan Samiti had the backing of Bipin Chandra Pal (an Extremist) and P. Mitra. "& P. MITRA (main)" beside the Calcutta Anushilan Samiti of Satish Chandra Basu: P. Mitra is the main figure. The Anushilan Samiti of Satish Chandra Basu operated from Calcutta (the teacher adds: and P. Mitra, main). Dacca Anushilan Samiti (1906): a massive and distinct offshoot in East Bengal, founded by Pulin Behari Das with the backing of P. Mitra and Bipin Chandra Pal. The Jugantar faction: a third major strand, built around the newspaper of the same name (1906). After the police repression of the Barisal Conference in April 1906, Yugantar wrote defiantly: "30 crore Indians should raise their 60 crore hands to end oppression." The message: force must be stopped by force. The two major streams developed completely distinct operational philosophies and effectively broke apart (the two models below). Jugantar versus Dhaka Anushilan: two models Structure Loose, decentralised confederation of local revolutionary groups Rigidly hierarchical, highly centralised, strictly disciplined Method 'Propaganda of the deed': immediate, spectacular acts of violence, individual heroic action and martyrdom to awaken the masses Long-term military preparation, deep infiltration of society, mass organisation for a future coordinated rebellion Focus Demonstrate that the British were not invincible through assassination of hated British officials Less interested in isolated assassinations; built for slow mass action Global debate Dramatic individual action NOW Slow mass organisation for LATER Model table to learn. Jugantar: decentralised; propaganda of the deed / individual heroic action; the stream of the immediate method. Dhaka Anushilan: centralised; long-term military preparation; matches the goal "Repeat 1857." A recurring global debate: dramatic individual action now versus slow mass organisation for later. Neither fully succeeded, but together they kept the British intelligence machinery stretched and anxious. Prelims 1995 (Barrah Dacoity). Answer (c) East Bengal. Done by the Dacca Anushilan Samiti under Pulin Behari Das (Section 3.2). Distractors: (a) Bombay-Karnataka = Savarkar's Abhinav Bharat, (b) Punjab = later Ghadar current, (d) Madras Presidency not a centre of the early dacoity phase. Prelims 1996 and 2000: the DASH pegs. Society-and-leader pairs: Abhinav Bharat = Savarkar; Anushilan = Aurobindo (exam key, not the handout's founder; see the Exam lens alert); Ghadar Party = Lala Hardayal; Swaraj Party = C.R. Das. In 2000: Chittagong Armoury Raid = Kalpana Dutt; Kuka Movement = Guru Ram Singh. 2.4 Centres abroad Exam hooks on the Centres Abroad slides: "secret societies inside India and centres abroad" (the two types), "first version of Indian national flag", "International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany." Reasons for going abroad: the VOICE list in Section 2. The Revolutionaries understood that operating freely required bases outside British jurisdiction. The key figures: 1. Veer Savarkar: London (Abhinav Bharat branch, from 1906). 2. Lala Hardayal: eventually reached the United States, where he became a key organiser. 3. Shyamji Krishna Varma: London (he moved to Paris in 1907, Section 2.5). 4. Madame Cama: Paris. In August 1907, Madame Bhikaji Cama unfurled the first version of the Indian national flag at the International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany, a dramatic assertion of Indian sovereignty on a global stage, years before any official tricolour was adopted. 5. Ajit Singh: abroad after the Swadeshi period. Also in 1906, an All Bengal Conference of Revolutionary Groups was held, a coordination meeting that led to the formation of the weekly newspaper Yugantar / Jugantar (1906). 2.5 Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS), 1905: revolutionary activity in Britain Because London was free of British jurisdiction, Shyamji built a public organisation with a hostel and a journal. Ask: how is it different from Tilak's 1916 League? Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS), 1905, London Indian Home Rule Society. Home Rule = Swaraj (self-rule); Society = ORG. Not the Indian Home Rule League of 1916, which is Tilak's (League = ORG; Chapter 33: Home Rule League Movement (1916-18) and Lucknow Pact (1916)). Goal's second half, "propaganda in Britain" = "Building Narrative in favor of Home Rule." "All practicable means" = "to prevent factionalism @ methods": groups with different methods can stay in one body. Written constitution = sign of a modern institution, like today's political parties. In 1905, Shyamji Krishna Varma founded the Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS) in London, with support from Bhikaji Cama (the handout spells it "Kama" in this line), Dadabhai Naoroji (who was not a revolutionary himself) and S.R. Rana. Its key features: 1. Goal: secure self-rule in India and do propaganda in Britain. 2. Method: all practicable means. 3. Only Indians could become members. 4. Organised as a modern institution: a written constitution, modelled on British public institutions of the time. 5. Strong support among Indian students and other Indians in Britain. 6. Maintained close contact with revolutionaries in India. 7. Set up India House in London, a student hostel that actively promoted nationalist views among students. 8. The IHRS and Shyamji's journal The Indian Sociologist (not socialist in ideology: the name is misleading) laid the foundation of the militant Indian nationalist movement in Britain. After Shyamji shifted to Paris in 1907, the lead role at India House passed to the Abhinav Bharat Mandal / Society, Veer Savarkar's secret nationalist society (the teacher's note: the 1906 London branch). Criteria for fighting elections to the British Parliament Side board on Dadabhai Naoroji (the handout says he was not a revolutionary). Criteria for fighting British Parliament elections, for people of the empire who are not British citizens: (1) land or property ownership, (2) duration of stay. Naoroji served as an MP for one term [1892-95] on a Liberal Party ticket. IHRS, 1905, London (contd.): India House and The Indian Sociologist Why Indian students were in Britain: (1) to prepare for or give the CSE; (2) other degrees, e.g. law, medicine; (3) for jobs. That was India House's support base. The Indian Sociologist: "Modern Politics: Voice" (a journal is a voice) and "Narrative for ideology of Nationalism." So the IHRS gave the movement in Britain an organisation, a hostel and a voice. Prelims 1999 (persons and journals). Answer (a) A-2 B-3 C-4 D-1: Shyamji Krishna Varma = The Indian Sociologist; Madam Bhikaji Cama = The Talwar; Annie Besant = Commonwealth; Aurobindo Ghosh = Bande Mataram. Only the Varma journal is in the handout; the other three links come from the slide explanation only. Distractors swap Varma and Cama (d), swap the last two (c), or reassign all four (b).

Because the networks were ready, a chain of actions began, each triggering a British reply. Ask: which of the seven cards is a 1908 event? With the network in place, the next phase was action. The period produced a series of dramatic events, best understood in sequence: each event triggered a British response, which triggered the next escalation. Key Revolutionary Actions, 1907 to 1912 The seven cards. (1) 1907: attempt on the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal. (2) 1908 Barrah Dacoity = a Swadeshi dacoity; the Zamindar of Barrah. (3) 1908 Muzzafarpur: Bihar, not Muzaffar Nagar in UP. (4) 1908 Alipore: Aurobindo Ghosh, case fought by C.R. Das. (5) 1908 Tilak Trial: sedition, article "Arrival of Bomb," condemned violence but put the blame on the British, defended Chaki and Bose. (6) 1909 Abhinav Bharat: London, Dhingra, and the Nasik Conspiracy Case. (7) 1912: Delhi Conspiracy. Cards 3, 4, 5 form one chain: the Muzzafarpur bomb, the Alipore crackdown that followed, Tilak's article on Muzzafarpur. 3.1 1907: the attempt on the life of the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal An attempt on the life of the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal in 1907: it failed. 3.2 Barrah Dacoity, 1908 "For revolution I need ARMS": three routes. (1) Dacoity at an armoury: 1930-33 Chittagong Armoury Raid by the IRA of Surya Sen. (2) Dacoity at the British Government of India or at loyalists ("Zlenders", most likely zamindars and money-lenders, as the handout says), then use the money to buy arms in India or abroad: Barrah Dacoity 1908 (the money route), Kakori Robbery 1925. (3) Alliance with enemies of the British (Germany, Russia, France; depends on geopolitics), as in WWI (1914-18); e.g. the Zimmerman Plan, linked to the Ghadar Movement. A Swadeshi dacoity in Dhaka, East Bengal, carried out by the Dacca Anushilan Samiti under Pulin Behari Das. The residence of the Zamindar of Barrah was looted; the funds were intended to finance revolutionary activities. "Dacoity" (armed robbery) to fund operations was deliberate. The Revolutionaries needed money for weapons, printing and travel; with no wealthy backers, they targeted zamindars and moneylenders seen as collaborators of the colonial order. "For revolution I need ARMS": three routes Chittagong Armoury Raid: board and PYQ name different people. The board says "1930-33 Chittagong Armoury Raid by IRA of Surya Sen." The Prelims 2000 key pairs the raid with Kalpana Dutt (answer (a)). Not rival answers: use Kalpana Dutt in a match-the-following and Surya Sen's IRA from the board. The raid itself falls after this chapter (Chapter 39: Revolutionaries Post 1922). 3.3 1908 Muzzafarpur Conspiracy Case "Two English women were killed instead" (the bomb killed the wrong people). Prafulla Chaki: "(OR) he ate CYANIDE": the handout says he shot himself in the mouth with his own revolver; another version says cyanide. Both agree he killed himself to avoid capture. Muzzafarpur is in Bihar, not Muzaffar Nagar in UP. Target: a failed attempt on the life of Magistrate Kingsford, a particularly hated colonial official. Attack: Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose threw a bomb at his carriage, but Kingsford was not inside. Two English women were killed instead. 1908 Muzzafarpur Conspiracy Case Prafulla Chaki shot himself in the mouth with his own revolver to avoid capture (the teacher: or he ate cyanide). Khudiram Bose was arrested, tried and given the death sentence. Khudiram Bose was 18 when executed in 1908. He became an instant martyr across Bengal: songs were written, his image was printed on cloth and sold as mourning wear. The British intended deterrence; it had "the opposite effect!!!!" 3.4 1908 Alipore Conspiracy Case (also the Murari Pukur / Manick Tolla Conspiracy Case) Because the Muzzafarpur bomb alarmed the British, they went after the masterminds. Ask: why could Aurobindo not be convicted, and what became of Barindra? 1908 Alipore Conspiracy Case "A home was raided." The case is named after the raided house: Murari Pukur Road, Manicktolla colony, Alipore (house number unclear in the ink; check your notebook). Hence three names: Alipore, Murari Pukur, Manick Tolla. "Aurobindo Ghosh: case fought by C.R. Das." Trigger: the Muzzafarpur bombing alarmed the British into a broader crackdown; they wanted to go after the masterminds, not just the foot soldiers. This led to the Alipore Conspiracy Case: mass arrests, including Aurobindo Ghosh from his address on Murari Pukur Road in Manick Tolla. Defence: Aurobindo was defended by C.R. Das. B.C. Pal refused to testify, and without his testimony Aurobindo could not be convicted. After acquittal, Aurobindo wrote further anti-British articles but, sensing imminent re-arrest, escaped to Pondicherry, then under French control and therefore outside British jurisdiction. There he turned to spiritualism and withdrew permanently from politics. The case did far more damage to the Jugantar network. Barindra Kumar Ghosh (Aurobindo's younger brother and the principal organiser of Jugantar), Ullaskar Dutta and several others were found guilty and sentenced to death. Their sentences were later commuted to "transportation for life" in the Cellular Jail (Kala Pani) in the Andaman Islands. The Alipore Case heavily decimated the early Jugantar leadership, the very faction that had built the most active network of armed revolutionary cells in Bengal. B.C. Pal was forced to retire temporarily from active politics as a result of the case. Ghadar PYQ trap (Barindra Kumar Ghosh). Barindra was transported to the Cellular Jail from 1908, so he could not have joined the Ghadar Movement (1913-15). Any UPSC option linking him to Ghadar is an elimination trap. Once transported, he was cut off from revolutionary activity on the mainland. "Transportation for life" to the Cellular Jail was seen as worse than death: isolation, brutal conditions, permanent removal from the mainland. Savarkar got this sentence in 1910. The Andamans let the state eliminate revolutionary leadership without creating more martyrs by public hanging. 3.5 Tilak Trial, 1908 Kesari article (Marathi): in Kesari, Tilak's Marathi newspaper. Case points: sedition; article "Arrival of Bomb"; "Condemned violence but put blame on Br"; "Defended Chaki & Bose." Imp: sedition, six years, Mandalay, Jinnah. In his newspaper Kesari, Tilak condemned the violence of Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose in the Muzzafarpur case, but simultaneously defended both men on a deeper ground: that the British should understand that sustained oppression will produce violence. The article was titled "Arrival of Bomb." This nuanced position (condemn the act, explain the cause) was enough for the colonial government to charge him with sedition. Tilak was sentenced to six years' imprisonment and deported to Mandalay, Burma. His legal defence was conducted by Jinnah, an early and significant meeting of two men whose later relationship would define the partition of India. Jinnah defending Tilak, 1908. Jinnah was then a young constitutional lawyer with nationalist sympathies, not yet the Muslim League leader; he took the case on principle. The two disagreed fundamentally on methods but stood on the same side of the anti-colonial divide. The gap to 1940 (the Pakistan demand) measures how much communal politics transformed in three decades. 3.6 Actions credited to Abhinav Bharat Imp names and phrases: Madan Lal Dhingra, Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie, "worked with Secretary of State for India," District Magistrate Jackson, Anant Laxman Kanhere, "Savarkar had sent pistols to India," transportation for life, Cellular Jail, Nasik Conspiracy Case (1909). Banner: ABHINAV BHARAT over London, 1909 Dhingra and the Nasik Conspiracy Case. The Abhinav Bharat network, operating across India and London, was responsible for two major actions: 1. 1909, London: Madan Lal Dhingra killed Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie (not Curzon 99-05 the Viceroy: Curzon-Wyllie was a different person, who worked with the Secretary of State for India). 2. 1909, Nasik Conspiracy Case: District Magistrate Jackson was killed by Anant Laxman Kanhere. Savarkar had sent pistols to India from London, one of which was used by Kanhere. As a consequence, in 1910 Savarkar was sentenced to transportation for life (imprisonment in the Cellular Jail in the Andaman Islands) in connection with the Nasik Conspiracy Case (1909). Two traps. Curzon-Wyllie is not Curzon 99-05 the Viceroy (who imposed the Partition); Dhingra killed an adviser to the Secretary of State for India, in London. Savarkar was sentenced in 1910, not 1909: the Nasik killing is 1909.

Because the phase was repressed, we ask what it still achieved. Ask: how did pride, Morley-Minto and 1911 link back to the Revolutionaries? The Revolutionary phase was repressed by the British. But its impact was not nothing. 4.1 Pride and dignity, and the Morley-Minto Reforms 4.1 The Revolutionaries gave back a sense of pride and dignity to Indians: the feeling that Indians were not passive subjects but active agents capable of fighting back. Many contemporaries felt that the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 were partly a result of British anxiety about the spread of revolutionary activities: a reform offered to buy peace. (The reforms are the subject of Chapter 31: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms.) 4.2 1911: the Partition annulled and the capital moved to Delhi "Bihar & Orissa" (1912) is marked in quotation marks and a brace; no reason is written (check your notebook). In 1911 the Partition of Bengal was annulled and Delhi was made the new capital, which ended Bengal's dominance in the INM. The shift was announced at the Delhi Durbar of December 1911, where King George V and Queen Mary were crowned as Emperor and Empress. The reading: the annulment of the Partition was the political concession; the capital shift was the strategic correction, reducing Bengal's outsized influence over the national movement. 1911: Partition annulled, capital to Delhi 1912: the province of "Bihar and Orissa" was separated from the Bengal Presidency, and Assam was made a full province from "East Bengal and Assam" (EBA 1905). (Assam had originally been made a Chief Commissioner Province in 1874.) These changes were the post-1911 tidying up of Bengal's territorial structure. Curzon 99-05's legacy is contradictory. The Partition he imposed was reversed in 1911, and the capital he governed from was shifted away from Calcutta. In that narrow sense the Swadeshi agitation succeeded: Bengal was reunited. But the larger design of 1905 (divide Hindus and Muslims, undercut Bengal's dominance, shift capital) was substantially achieved: Curzon was successful on the strategic questions. 4.3 Delhi Conspiracy Case, 1912, and the line to the INA Because the capital moved to Delhi, a bomb greeted the procession, and its thrower lived on. Ask: how did Rash Behari Bose connect 1912 to the INA of 1943? Rash Behari Bose (1912) to the INA (1943) "- RB Bose": in the last box, Rash Behari Bose took over INA leadership after Mohan Singh's arrest and, because of old age, handed it to Netaji in 1943. "He" is not Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose. Occasion: when the capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911, a grand procession was organised in Delhi. Attempt: Rash Behari Bose planned and executed a failed assassination attempt against Viceroy Hardinge 10-16 in Chandni Chowk. Hardinge was seated on an elephant during the procession. Rash Behari Bose threw a bomb from a balcony; Hardinge was wounded but survived. Rash Behari Bose subsequently provided leadership to the Ghadar Movement (1913-15) (see Chapter 32: Ghadar Movement (1913-15)) and escaped to Japan in 1915. Later, in 1942, he convened conferences in Tokyo and Bangkok to establish the Indian Independence League (IIL), which became the supreme political organisation for Indians living in Southeast Asia. Under the political backing and guidance of the IIL, Captain Mohan Singh organised Indian Prisoners of War (captured by the Japanese) into the First Indian National Army (INA). After the arrest of Captain Mohan Singh, Rash Behari Bose took over the leadership of the INA; due to old age he handed over its reign to Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose in 1943, who reorganised the INA into the Azad Hind Fauj. The through-line from the Delhi Conspiracy Case (1912) to the INA (1943) passes through Rash Behari Bose. The generation of 1905-12 did not vanish after repression; several resurfaced in later movements, in more organised, internationally connected forms. Pen, People, Guns. By 1908 the Swadeshi Movement was leaderless: Tilak was deported to Mandalay, Aurobindo retired, B.C. Pal retired temporarily and L.L. Rai went abroad. The politically radicalised asked what next if mass politics had failed. The teacher's chain says it all: when the Pen failed, People came out; when People failed, Guns came out; when Guns failed, MG came out (1920+). Two answers: a long game and a quick strike. The long-term goal was to repeat 1857: a civil rebellion and disaffection within the army. The immediate method was individual heroic action: assassinate hated officials to strike fear in British hearts, remove fear from Indians and arouse nationalism. If caught, the trial became a stage and a death sentence a supreme sacrifice. Bengal builds the Anushilan. In 1902 Pramathanath Mitra founded the Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta for physical training and character building, with armed resistance as its inner purpose. By 1906 an impatient inner circle formed around the newspaper Jugantar of Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Bhupendranath Datta and Abinash Bhattacharya. The British replied in 1903 with the CID, after the Fraser Police Commission of 1902. Jolt now, drill for later. Jugantar was a loose, decentralised confederation that believed in propaganda of the deed and assassination to show the British were not invincible. The Dacca Anushilan Samiti of Pulin Behari Das (1906) was rigidly hierarchical and built for long-term military preparation, the teacher's 'Repeat 1857'. In the west the Savarkar brothers turned Mitra Mela (1899, Nasik) into Abhinav Bharat (1904, Pune), copying Mazzini's Young Italy. Why go abroad? VOICE. Abroad they could speak freely in newspapers, procure weapons despite the Arms Act 1878, assassinate officers at Home in England, win diplomatic pressure by highlighting colonialism and raise awareness among NRIs. Savarkar sat in London, Hardayal reached the USA, Shyamji Krishna Varma ran the IHRS and India House (1905) before moving to Paris in 1907, and Madame Cama unfurled the first Indian flag at Stuttgart in August 1907. 1908: Barrah, Muzzafarpur and the bomb that missed. The Dacca Anushilan looted the Zamindar of Barrah to fund the revolution, since dacoity targeted collaborators. At Muzzafarpur Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose bombed Magistrate Kingsford's carriage, but he was not inside and two English women died. Chaki killed himself and Khudiram, 18, was executed and became an instant martyr, the opposite of what the British intended. Alipore and the Andamans. The Alipore Case brought mass arrests, including Aurobindo from Murari Pukur Road. C.R. Das defended him and B.C. Pal refused to testify, so he could not be convicted; he fled to Pondicherry and spiritualism. Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Ullaskar Dutta were sentenced to death, commuted to transportation for life in the Cellular Jail, which broke the early Jugantar. Tilak, Kesari and Jinnah. In Kesari, Tilak condemned the Muzzafarpur violence but defended Chaki and Bose on the ground that sustained oppression breeds violence, in an article titled 'Arrival of Bomb'. He was charged with sedition, sentenced to six years and sent to Mandalay, Burma, with Jinnah, a young constitutional lawyer, conducting his defence. 1909: Dhingra, Nasik and Savarkar's sentence. In London in 1909 Madan Lal Dhingra killed Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie, who was not Curzon 99-05 but worked with the Secretary of State for India. In Nasik, Anant Laxman Kanhere killed District Magistrate Jackson with a pistol that Savarkar had sent from London. In 1910 Savarkar was sentenced to transportation for life in the Cellular Jail. Pride, reform and Delhi. The Revolutionaries gave back pride and dignity, and many felt the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 were a reform offered to buy peace. In 1911 the Partition was annulled and Delhi became the capital at the Durbar of December 1911, reducing Bengal's outsized influence; in 1912 Bihar and Orissa and a full province of Assam followed. Curzon 99-05 lost the map but won the plan. Rash Behari Bose to the INA. In 1912 Rash Behari Bose threw a bomb from a balcony at Viceroy Hardinge 10-16 on an elephant in Chandni Chowk; Hardinge was wounded but survived. He led the Ghadar Movement (1913-15), escaped to Japan in 1915 and in 1942 convened the Tokyo and Bangkok conferences forming the IIL. Under it Captain Mohan Singh organised the first INA; after Mohan Singh's arrest Rash Behari Bose took over and, for old age, handed it to Netaji in 1943.

ICA 1861 was the longest (30 years), ICA 1892 ran 17, GOI Act 1919 ran 16. The Aga Khan led the 1906 Simla Deputation at home; Liaquat Ali Khan is of the 1940s generation; in 1908 Jinnah was still a Congress constitutional lawyer (slide's reason) Section 5.4 Prelims 2002 (PYQ 3) "Which one of the following statements is not correct?" (a) Hakim Ajmal Khan was one of the leaders to start the nationalist and militant Ahrar movement (b) When the INC was formed, Sayyid Ahmad Khan opposed it (c) The All-India Muslim League formed in 1906 vehemently opposed the partition of Bengal and separate electorates (d) Barakatullah and Obeidullah Sindhi were among those who formed a Provisional Government of India in Kabul (c). (a), (b) and (d) are true history; (a) and (d) are outside this chapter Sections 2, 5 and 6 Prelims 2026 (related; the slide labels it Ch 34) Assertion: "The genesis of political alliances based on community lay in the very nature of the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms, 1919." Statements: 1. Reforms retained and extended the principle of separate electorates 2. Separate electorates were supposed to counter Indian nationalism, which was growing stronger 3. Deprived classes rallied around the favours inherent in separate electorates (d) 1, 2 and 3. Teacher's ink: "T" after each statement. The question is about the 1919 Act (Chapter 34), but it tests the same logic this chapter starts: separate electorates, Divide & Rule against nationalism. The slide's reasons: the 1919 Act made separate electorates watertight and extended them to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians and Christians; it fitted DnR against a nationalism that had just united Hindus and Muslims (Lucknow 1916); Depressed Classes got nominated seats Section 8 (a Chapter 34 question, kept here as a related PYQ) Mains No Mains PYQ is solved on the slides or listed in the bank for this chapter Two practice skeletons built only from these notes are given below Sections 7 and 4

Story so far: the chapter is two halves, the rise of an organised Muslim politics and the Act that wrote it into law. Ask: which thread joins them (Divide & Rule), and where does each later section fit? Chapter 31 title: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and the Morley-Minto Reforms One story, two halves. First: how a separate organised Muslim politics rose (Census 1881, religion-wise reports, low Western education, Hunter, Sir Syed, Hindu revivalism, Simla Deputation 1906, ML1906). Second: ICA 1909 ("ICA 1909" box), the council reform through which the British turned that politics into law with separate electorates. The link is Divide & Rule (DnR). The chapter in one chain Census 1881 and religion-wise reports: one homogeneous Muslim group, and a sense of relative deprivation Low Western education (cost, Ulamas, Persian, landlords): Hindus gain the new middle-class jobs British DnR: Hunter 1871, job reservation 1897, Partition 1905 Sir Syed and the Muslim elite: qaums, MAO College 1875, Educational Congress 1886 Hindu revivalism after 1883: Cow Killing Riots 1893, Hindi-Urdu 1900, Swadeshi symbols 1905-11 Simla Deputation 1906: keep the Partition, population-proportional reservation, separate electorates ML1906 at Dacca: hold the British to Simla; London branch 1908; ICA 1909 grants separate electorates Foundation of Partition: organised communal politics never reversed until 1947

items.t: 1 · Background: census, education and communal consciousness
items.x: Because the teacher frames imperialism as loot with Divide & Rule as the tool, the British needed groups to work on. Ask: how did the Census, the religion-wise reports and low Western education make Muslims one deprived group? 1.0 The teacher's frame: the goal of imperialism Goal of imperialism = economic: loot or drain the wealth of the colony, that is its masses. Tool = DnR (Divide & Rule), especially against the leadership (one group of leaders favoured, one not). Masses split into majority and minority: if the majority is co-opted, the minority is looted; if the minority is co-opted, the majority is looted. Example: Rwanda (colonial power Belgium, majority Hutus, minority Tutsis circled, which fits the "minority co-opted" branch; that link is a reading). Comes just before the Census slide. 1.1 Census 1881 and communal consciousness Census 1881 was the first full census of British India. The first attempt, in 1872, was not completed for all of British India. From 1881 it ran every 10 years: 1881, 1891, 1901... Muslims were roughly 20% overall, with a majority in Punjab and roughly 50% in Bengal. Goal of imperialism and the tool of Divide and Rule Hold three numbers: Muslims about 20% overall; a majority in Punjab (~54%, the handout only says "majority"); about 50% in Bengal. 20% is the base against which the 30% of ICA 1909 is later called appeasement (Section 7.4.6). 1.2 The Census as a Divide & Rule contribution The Census had a deep DnR contribution: it created and reinforced a consciousness of being a homogeneous religious group among an otherwise heterogeneous Muslim community. Before mass enumeration, a poor Muslim weaver in Bengal and a rich Muslim landlord in Punjab had very different daily realities. The Census told both that they were part of one community with one set of interests, and that Hindus and Muslims were two separate communities with separate, potentially competing interests. Shia-Sunni differences and Worker-Peasant class differences all came later; Muslim identity was put first by the census logic. 1.3 Religion-wise reports and relative deprivation The British government published reports on education, employment and poverty religion-wise. This created a sense of relative deprivation among Muslims: the data showed them behind Hindus in government jobs, education and the new middle-class professions. Whether the cause was discrimination or other factors, the published comparison reinforced a feeling that Hindus were gaining at Muslims' expense. Communalism is the organisation of society on the basis of religion and the ideology that every religious group has its own separate interests, which may be mutually exclusive: that the two communities cannot co-exist happily, and that meeting one community's interests will necessarily hurt the other's. This is the logic that underpinned the demand for Separate Electorates and the demand for Pakistan. 1.4 Why Western education uptake was low among Muslims The low representation of Muslims in the new middle-class professions was partly the result of lower uptake of Western education. The reasons were structural, not simply backwardness: i) Cost Western education was expensive, and most Muslims in Bengal were poor ryots who could not afford it ii) The Ulamas resisted it The Ulamas (the Muslim clerical class) actively resisted Western education. Their concern was cultural and religious: the Western curriculum, through Western literature, exposed students to a way of life, family structures and social values that contradicted Islamic teaching and would erode their community control (the handout's reminder: literature has stories, values, attitudes and religious beliefs that shape the way we think) iii) Preserve Persian A desire to preserve Persian, the language of Muslim high culture and administration under the Mughals, against the encroachment of English and Hindi iv) Landlords' low incentive Rich Muslim landlords had low utility for middle-class government jobs and therefore little incentive to pursue Western education v) Consequence Hindus benefitted more from the new middle-class professions created by British administration, because they accepted Western education more readily and in greater numbers Key line: "Hindus benefitted more from the new middle-class professions." The four causes (i to iv) are why; (v) is the result that feeds the relative deprivation of Section 1.3. 1.5 Hunter's Indian Musalmans and the British Divide & Rule W.W. Hunter's book Indian Musalmans (1871) argued that the neglect of Muslims, specifically their economic decline since the end of Mughal rule, had contributed to the Faraizi movement of the 1830s-70s in Bengal, and therefore the British should appease Muslims for greater political stability. This argument became a justification for the DnR approach of favouring Muslim interests against Hindu-dominated political formations. 1.6 The specific DnR measures toward Muslims 1871 Hunter's Indian Musalmans The argument above: appease Muslims for political stability 1897 Reservation in government jobs for Muslims The first named reservation 1905 Bengal Partition Created East Bengal and Assam as a Muslim Majority Province (MMP), appeasing elite Muslims and countering rising Hindu nationalism Stressed: "appease Muslims for political stability," "1897 - Job reservation," "elite Muslims." Elite matters: appeasement went to the elite, not the common Muslim; the next board (Section 1.7) asks what the common Muslim got. 1.7 The teacher's question: what did the common Muslim get? Question: "What did the common Muslim get from Pakistan?" Board answer: a KATORA (bowl) with KHOON (blood) in it. The rest was spoken. After the slide on elite-directed measures (1871, 1897, 1905), read it as the cost to the common Muslim of an elite-led politics.

items.t: 2 · Muslim WEMC demands: from association to organisation
items.x: Because the DnR measures opened space for elite demands, the Muslim elite organised step by step. Ask: how did Sir Syed's qaums become the architecture of the Two Nation Theory, and why was he not a full separatist? The British DnR measures opened space for elite Muslim political demands. The Muslim upper and middle class, those who had accepted Western education (the WEMC, Western-Educated Middle Class, as the teacher abbreviates it), began demanding special political status. The demand built gradually through the 19th century: What did the common Muslim get from Pakistan? From association to organisation: the Muslim elite Mohammadan Association (1855) Pro-British; it opposed the 1857 revolts. It sought benefits for Muslims through loyalty to the British, not through joining the nationalist cause Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817-98) The pivotal figure. He argued that India was not a single nation but a summation of qaums (qaum = community or nation, a distinct ethno-religious group), and that the Hindu qaum and the Muslim qaum were separate, with separate interests (the early form of the Two Nation Theory). He further argued that the Muslim qaum, as the ruling community before the British, deserved special status, and that to claim it Muslims needed Western education ii.i) Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College (MAO), 1875 Later Aligarh Muslim University. It combined Western education with Islamic values, to build a Muslim middle class that could compete for government positions without abandoning core religious identity ii.ii) Mohammadan Educational Congress, 1886 Set up as a rival to the INC, because Sir Syed believed the INC was a Hindu organisation. He actively discouraged Muslim participation in the INC Sir Syed Ahmed Khan was not a separatist in the full 1940s sense. He still believed in a unity of qaums. But his framing, that Muslims are a separate qaum with separate interests, provided the intellectual architecture that later leaders used to build the full Two Nation Theory. Short argument, partly unclear. (1) Row 1: "nationalist" replaced by "anti colonial": the Association stayed out of the anti-colonial cause. (2) "WEMC Hindus Pro-Br Rule", with aim 2 = benefits for Muslims: the early Muslim WEMC was pro-British rule, as the early Hindu WEMC also was. (3) Sir Syed row: "2N1S" (a label for the Two Nation idea; reading uncertain). (4) MAO College: "PRO-Br." (5) "India = Developed in future" (meaning not clear). Stressed: "Two Nation Theory," "a rival to the INC," "INC was a Hindu organisation," "discouraged Muslim participation."

items.t: 3 · Post-1883: Hindu revivalism and Muslim alienation
items.x: Because the Muslim elite was building a separate identity, Hindu revivalism widened the gap in three waves. Ask: which wave did the INC not condemn, and why? Hindu cultural revivalism of the late 19th and early 20th centuries (the Shuddhi movement, the Cow Protection Movement, the Swadeshi period's use of Hindu religious symbolism) alienated Muslims from the Congress-led national movement in successive waves. Hindu revivalism and Muslim alienation after 1883 3.1 Wave i: Shuddhi and the Cow Protection Movement The Shuddhi movement and the Cow Protection Movement were run by the Arya Samaj (1875) and became more aggressive after Swami Dayanand Saraswati died in 1883. The result was the Cow Killing Riots of 1893. The INC did not condemn these riots, because its 1886 rule was to take up only political issues. This non-condemnation produced a sharp decline in Muslim participation in the INC. 3.2 Wave ii: the Hindi-Urdu Controversy (1880s to 1900) The controversy was in the North West Provinces and Awadh (1877), led by the moderate Madan Mohan Malviya. It demanded official language status for Hindi (spoken by the majority) equivalent to Urdu. Success came in 1900. The unintended byproduct: Hindi became associated with Hindus and Urdu with Muslims. Language board: Punjabi and Bangla are the two big languages, yet "Jinnah chose URDU" and its script is Arabic. Pakistan was linguistically dominated by Punjabis and Bengalis, but Jinnah made Urdu official for an Islamic image, not a linguistic majority; the Arabic script gave Urdu that image. Remember the place and year "NWP" and "(1877)." 3.3 Wave iii: Hindu symbolism in the Swadeshi movement (1905-11) Bande Mataram, Kali worship, Prabhat Pheris, Ganpati and Shivaji festivals contributed further to Muslim alienation from the movement, leading to low participation (as already discussed).

Because the Partition of 1905 had favoured the elite, elite Muslims went to the Viceroy to secure it. Ask: why is Separate Electorates called the hinge of partition history? The Simla Deputation (1906) 4.1 What the Deputation was and what it demanded In 1906, elite Muslims led by the Aga Khan met Viceroy Minto 05-10 (1905-1910) in Shimla to secure Muslim elite interests. Their demands: i) Keep the Partition No annulment of the Bengal Partition ii) Reservation by population As a separate qaum and an overall minority, reservation proportional to population in the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC), the Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) and government jobs iii) Separate Electorates Separate Electorates in future council reforms. Separate Electorates = only Muslims have the right to vote (R2V) in a seat reserved for a Muslim candidate. This structurally promotes the Two Nation Theory: it tells every Muslim voter that their representative must be Muslim and their interests are separate from Hindu interests The demand for Separate Electorates is the hinge of partition history. Once you accept that Muslims must elect Muslim representatives from Muslim-only constituencies, you have institutionally accepted the Two Nation Theory. The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 granted this demand, and that grant was the legislative seed of 1947. Chain: Aug 1905 Swadeshi Movement, Oct 1905 Partition, elite Muslims went to Simla to meet Minto 05-10. Bottom: "Partition" under the hinge box. Demand ii precedent: "1897: Reservation for Muslims in Govt Jobs" and "Here in proportion to % in pop" (the 1906 job demand was proportional to population). "Separate Electorates" is the key demand. Source conflict: Swadeshi and Partition order. The teacher's chain puts Aug 1905 Swadeshi before Oct 1905 Partition; the handout says the Partition set off the Swadeshi Movement. For cause and effect write Partition 1905 gave rise to the Swadeshi Movement 1905-11; for dates use August and October. 4.2 Reservation with Separate Electorates: the teacher's boards State or Country = sum of its constituencies. Reservation with Separate Elections: MLA/MP = Muslim and voters = only Muslim, a representative "of the m, for the m, by the m" = "Pak within India." Our Constitution chose Reservation with Joint Electorates: the voter list is mixed, the MLA/MP is from the reserved community (example: SC), but all communities vote ("For Indians, by Indians"; last words unclear). RwSE (Reservation with Separate Electorates) and ICA 1909 Reservation with separate electorates versus joint electorates Four verdicts on RwSE (ICA 1909): (1) anti-democracy ("takes away R&V", perhaps right to vote); (2) DnR, hurts Indian-ness; (3) "Pak within India"; (4) landmark on the Partition journey. "WHY (RwSE)?" Separate electorates do not raise the chances of Muslim MLA/MPs in general ("No"), but do raise those of the ML1906 Muslim MLA/MPs ("Yes"): the system helped the communal party, not Muslims as such (arrow direction unclear). Example: INP versus MJP, reservation for women Made-up example: reservation for women; general party INP (Indian National Party), women's party MJP (Mahila Janshakti Party). (1) Separate electorates: males have no vote in the women's seat; most females vote MJP; winner = female of MJP. (2) Joint electorates: males vote INP, some females too, most females MJP; the pie is mostly INP, so the winner is a female (by the pie, the INP's candidate: a reading). Lesson: under separate electorates only the group's own voters decide, so the group's own party wins; under joint electorates a party must win beyond its group. Hence ML1906 wanted separate electorates.

items.t: 5 · Formation of the All India Muslim League (ML1906)
items.x: Because Simla needed someone to hold the British to its promises, the League was born at Dacca. Ask: what head start did the League's provincial structures give it over the PCCs? Formation of the Muslim League (ML1906) The All India Muslim League was set up by elite Muslims in Dacca, in December 1906, immediately following the Simla Deputation. 5.1 Goal To ensure the British did not go back on the promises made at the Simla Deputation (1906). To promote Muslim interests. To promote Muslim loyalty to the British. 5.2 The Green Book The League's constitution, called the Green Book, was written by Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Mohammed Ali Jauhar, both of the Aligarh movement. Green Book row: "main" = the authors are an important point. "Aligarh" and "movement": the League's constitution came out of Sir Syed's Aligarh movement (Section 2). 5.3 1907-09: Provincial Muslim Leagues and the head start Provincial Muslim Leagues were set up in 1907-09. ML1906 had functional provincial structures reaching ground-level Muslim communities for more than a decade before the INC's PCCs became effective mass instruments. This gave communal politics an organisational head start on the ground. Handout only (no class slide): PCCs existed since the INC's 1908 Constitution (as the handout writes it; see alert below) but were mapped to British provinces and ran in English, keeping the Congress elite. At the 1920 Nagpur Session, Gandhi redrew PCC borders on linguistic lines, so local work ran in the mother tongue and the INC could penetrate the villages. "1886 PCCs setup BUT they don't go to masses." "1920 [MG?] era began for PCCs, they became mass politics" (the two letters look like "MG", Mahatma Gandhi; unclear). Sum: "LOST 13 YEARS" and "-ve of INC under moderates." The 13 years run from the provincial Leagues of 1907 to the PCCs' mass role in 1920. Source conflict: PCC year. The typed slide said PCCs existed from "the 1908 INC Constitution"; the teacher replaced it with "1886." The handout says 1908. Follow 1886 in answers, and keep the trap: PCCs were not created at Nagpur 1920; they were reorganised on linguistic lines there. Prelims trap (handout). If a statement says "PCCs were established for the first time at the 1920 Nagpur Session": False. If it says "PCCs were reorganised on linguistic lines at the 1920 Nagpur Session": True. 5.4 1908: the London branch under Ameer Ali A London branch of the ML1906 was set up in 1908 under the presidency of Ameer Ali. It influenced the Indian Councils Act 1909 (ICA1909), which laid the foundation of partition politics by introducing Separate Electorates for Muslims in the reformed councils. Prelims 2001 (UPSC tested this). Answer (B) Ameer Ali. Wrong options: (A) Aga Khan (he led the 1906 Simla Deputation at home); (C) Liaquat Ali Khan (the League's later 1940s generation); (D) MA Jinnah (in 1908 still a Congress constitutional lawyer, the slide adds).

Because the League kept its goal of Partition and Separate Electorates, organised communal politics never reversed. Ask: why is any option saying the League opposed them false (Prelims 2002)? ML1906 was set up in 1906 to preserve the Bengal Partition and to secure Separate Electorates. Separate Electorates were granted by ICA1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms). The INC's PCCs only became effective mass instruments in 1920; ML had functional provincial structures for 13 years before the INC caught up. The formal, organised beginning of communal politics that ML1906 represented never reversed: it deepened decade by decade until 1947. Handout only (no class slide): the handout closes Section 6 with a point not on the slides. "This is why the birth of ML1906 is listed as one of the negative impacts of the Swadeshi period." It was not simply a reaction to Swadeshi, but the Swadeshi period's Hindu symbolism and the British DnR response together created the conditions for it. Prelims 2002 (UPSC tested this). Answer (C): "The All-India Muslim League formed in 1906 vehemently opposed the partition of Bengal and separate electorates" is NOT correct (marked "F" on the slide). Correct statements: (A) Hakim Ajmal Khan was a leader to start the nationalist and militant Ahrar movement; (B) Sayyid Ahmad Khan opposed the INC when it was formed (marked "T"); (D) Maulana Barakatullah and Maulana Obeidullah Sindhi were among those who formed a Provisional Government of India in Kabul.

Because the British ran repression and reform together, the reform came packaged with Divide & Rule. Ask: what did Move 1 split, and what did Move 2 split? 7.1 Names behind the reform, and where ICA 1909 sits Hallmarks: what each council Act is remembered for (ICA 1861 and ICA 1892 are Chapters 25 and 28): ICA 1861 ILC with the VEC; PLCs with the GEC; a grain of popular representation; first: non-officers (nominated); the Portfolio System; 6 to 12 additional members, half at least non-officers ICA 1892 First: questions can be asked; first: the Budget (BD) can be discussed; selection and not election (nominated non-officers from recommended lists); first: some popular representation; 10 to 16 additional members ICA 1909 First: proper indirect elections; Reservation with Separate electorates; in the PLC a majority of non-officers, but most were nominated, not elected; first: one Indian in the VEC; brought Limited Self-Government (LTD SG); first: supplementary questions; resolutions can be passed; Budget vote on individual items, not on the Budget as a whole Hallmarks of ICA 1861, 1892 and 1909 Source conflict: 1861 range. This board writes "6 to 12", a later board writes "6 to 10". Use 6 to 12 (as in Chapter 25); treat "6 to 10" as a slip. Two men gave the reform its name: John Morley was the Secretary of State for India, sitting in London. Lord Minto 05-10 (1905-1910) was the Viceroy and Governor-General in India. Together their names became attached to what is formally called the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (ICA1909). 7.2 Context: why this reform happened India in 1905 was not quiet. The partition of Bengal in 1905 had set off the Swadeshi Movement (1905-11), which pushed Indian politics in a sharper, angrier direction. 1905-1908 saw the rise of Extremist politics within the INC, and from 1908 Revolutionary Activities became a real and growing force that worried the British. The British response had two tracks, repression and reform, and they ran simultaneously. ICA1909 was the reform track. But reform, in British hands, always came packaged with a political strategy. There was also a personal dimension: Morley was a Liberal in the British political tradition, less authoritarian than many predecessors and open to giving Indians more participation. His disposition, with political necessity, shaped the reform. 7.3 The Divide & Rule (DnR) strategy behind ICA1909 The British wanted to split the Indian political movement, specifically to separate the Moderates from the Extremists within the INC. The strategy played out in two moves. Move 1: Split the INC. In 1906, Morley gave a speech in the British Parliament during the debate on India's Budget and hinted strongly at upcoming council reforms. The message landed exactly as intended. Moderate leaders began to worry that Extremist agitation would harden British opinion and kill the chances of reform. This fault line widened until the Surat Split of 1907, where the Extremists were expelled from the INC. With the Extremists outside the tent, the British moved to repress them directly. Morley's 1906 Budget speech and the Moderates Move 2: Divide Hindus and Muslims. The vehicle was the introduction of separate electorates for Muslims, a demand formally placed before Minto 05-10 by a delegation of Muslim elites at the Shimla Deputation of 1906. The Shimla Deputation: a group of Muslim leaders met Minto 05-10 and asked not just for reserved seats, but for a system where only Muslims could vote for Muslim representatives. The British were happy to oblige: it suited their DnR strategy perfectly. Move 1 (circles A, B, C). (A) In 1906 Secretary of State Morley spoke in the British Parliament on the Budget of the Government of India. (B) He hinted at council reforms, ILC and PLCs, "by amending ICA 1892," through expansion and powers. (C) Result: "Moderates' mouth watered." Links: "1906 session" and "1907 Surat Split" = DnR (Moderates against Extremists). Moderates "don't want any kind of violence so reforms aint derailed." Unclear: two words after "esp" (like "Br Madras") and "A Royal vs Royal". The transcription reads "DnR" on this board as "Dadabhai Naoroji"; it stands for Divide and Rule (as in the handout and Move 1). Read DnR = Divide and Rule. 7.4 Provisions of ICA1909 7.4.1 Nature of government introduced Formula of fully responsible government ICA1909: nature of government Morley stated explicitly: "There is no intent of Responsible Govt in India via ICA1909." Fully Responsible Government means every minister must first be an elected member of the legislature: the Executive is the child of Parliament, and a child is always accountable to its mother. That is, no minister had to be an MP or MLA first. ICA1909 gave nothing of the sort. What ICA1909 did introduce was Representative Government, also called Limited Self-Government (LTD SG): people get to elect representatives to sit in a council and talk and advise, meaning some partnership in domestic affairs, but not self-rule, not Self Government, not Responsible Government. This had been the goal of the INC until 1906. From the 1906 Calcutta Session onward the INC's goal shifted to Swaraj. So even by the Moderates' own older standard, the reform arrived too late. It was the second failure of the Moderate approach. Formula: "Fully Responsible Government: every minister must be MP/MLA first." The Executive does not need the legislature's membership or confidence, so ICA1909 is not responsible government. "[not fully Representative how]" beside Representative Government (last word unclear; likely the handout's point that most non-official members were nominated, not elected). Goal ladder: 1885-1906: LTD SG (Limited Self-Government); 1906-16/28: SG within the empire, Home Rule, Swaraj (1906 stressed); 1916/28: Dominion Status; 1929: Purna Swaraj. ICA1909 delivered the 1885-1906 goal in 1909, after the INC had already moved up the ladder. 7.4.2 The Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) The structure of the VEC remained GG + Commander-in-Chief (CIC) + 6 ordinary members, the same as under ICA1892 (the teacher: "same since 1874"). 7.4.3 The Imperial Legislative Council (ILC): composition The ILC tree: VEC plus additional members ICA1909: the VEC and the ILC The ILC was expanded to 69 members in total (9 + 60). It was structured as follows: a) 8 ex-officio members Drawn from the VEC (GG + CIC + 6 Ordinary Members, since 1874) b) 1 additional ex-officio member The rotating Governor or Lieutenant-Governor of the province where the ILC session was held, so the 9th ex-officio slot changed with the location of the session c) 60 additional members 27 elected and 33 nominated (28 officials + 5 non-officials) Result: an Officer majority was maintained at the Centre. Officers = 9 ex-officio + 28 nominated officials = 37. Non-Officers = 27 elected + 5 nominated non-officials = 32. The British were not giving up control at the top. The word 'election' was used officially for the first time in ICA1909. Proper indirect elections were introduced: taxpayers and rent payers who met threshold criteria elected local bodies; the local bodies elected an electoral college from among themselves; the electoral college elected Members of PLCs, who elected Members of the ILC. The indirect election chain (the teacher's board, slide 61) Rent / tax payers (who meet the income threshold) elect Local bodies Electoral college (the local bodies and the college are boxed together: the college is the voters) PLCs (Members of the Provincial Legislative Councils) ILC (Members of the Imperial Legislative Council) Right to vote with income criteria: voters to ILC ILC = VEC + additional members (e.g. 60). VEC side [9], "= 8" ex-officio from the VEC, plus the rotating one ("[not imp]"). The 60 additional split into Officers 28 (always nominated) and Non-officers: Nominated 5, Elected 27. 28 + 5 = 33 nominated. "(imp)": the 27 elected + 33 nominated split, so learn the numbers. The 5 nominated non-officials: "PRO-Br" "MOST PROBABLY" (partly unclear). "[1861: 6 to 10; 1892: 10 to 16; 1909: 60]" compares additional members across the three Acts (use 6 to 12 for 1861; Section 7.1). Elected: unreserved seats indirectly, Muslim reserved seats directly (Section 7.4.6). Source conflict: 1861 range. This board writes "1861: 6 to 10"; the hallmarks board and Chapter 25 give 6 to 12. The 1892 range 10 to 16 matches both. Treat "6 to 10" as a slip. 7.4.4 Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) For the first time, a non-official majority was introduced, but only in the PLCs, not in the ILC. However, most non-official members were nominated, not elected. (Nominated non-officials are chosen by the government, not by the people: the difference between a government selecting a friendly face and the people actually electing their representative.) Bengal exception: the Bengal PLC got an elected majority, the first province to have this. But 4 of those elected seats were reserved for European Businesses. 7.4.5 Indians in the Executive: a first For the first time, Indians were inducted into executive branches. One Indian entered the VEC, the first Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council: Satyendra Prasanna Sinha (S.P. Sinha), Law Member. (An Indian as Minister was new.) Two Indians had already been appointed to the Secretary of State's India Council in London in August 1907: K.G. Gupta and Syed Hussain Bilgrami. This was a precursor action, not a provision of ICA1909 itself, but it led to an Indian presence in the London administration for the first time. Stressed: "One Indian," "entered the VEC," "S.P. Sinha as Law Member," "the first Indian." August 1907 row: "Not Imp": learn Sinha, skip Gupta and Bilgrami (though they appear in the summary card, so know them once). 7.4.6 The Muslim separate electorate: communal appeasement For the first time, separate electorates for Muslims were introduced, in the ILC, PLCs and local bodies. In the ILC, 8 of the 27 elected seats were reserved for Muslims: about 30% of the elected seats. Muslim population in India was about 20%. The INC's own 1889 Minority Clause had asked for minority reservation proportional to population, that is 20% for Muslims. The extra 10% beyond the population share was pure appeasement politics. Due to separate electorates, only Muslims could vote in Muslim reserved seats. However, Muslims also had the right to vote in general (unreserved) seats, so they were not excluded from unreserved constituencies. Muslims effectively had a double advantage: they could influence both their own reserved seats and the unreserved seats. Compare with today's India: reservation exists for Scheduled Castes (SCs) in Parliament and state legislatures, but with joint electorates: non-SC voters also vote in SC-reserved seats. What ICA1909 gave Muslims was institutionally far more separatist. The conceptual difference is crucial. Reservation with Joint Electorates = Candidate of the People, For the People, By a Community. Reservation with Separate Electorates = Candidate of a Group, For a Group, By a Group. Country = Sum of Constituencies: thus today it is our Constituencies and tomorrow it is Our Pakistan. The right to vote (R2Vote) was linked to income criteria. The income threshold was set lower for Muslims than for other communities, making it easier for Muslims to qualify. A mix of direct and indirect elections: unreserved seats = the first proper indirect elections; Muslim reserved seats = the first direct elections (but only for Muslim seats). (Compare: ICA1892 had used the word "selection," a fake indirect election where bodies nominated rather than elected.) "EXTRA 10% = appeasement": 8 of 27 seats (about 30%) against 20% of the population. The 1889 Minority Clause (the INC itself had asked for the proportional 20%) shows the extra 10% is the British gift. Also stressed: "LOWER for Muslims" (income threshold) and "the 1st direct elections (but only for Muslim seats)." Handout formula: "of the m, for the m, by the m" (Joint against Separate: Section 4.2). 7.4.7 Powers of the legislature Budget (BD) Discussion allowed, no voting Members could vote on individual items of the Budget, but not on the Budget as a whole (voting to reject the whole Budget would amount to a No Confidence Motion, which the British would not allow) Questions No supplementary questions Members could ask supplementary questions, but only the member who asked the original question could ask the supplementary Resolutions The opposition could not move resolutions and no voting on government resolutions Members could initiate and pass resolutions, but the government was under no obligation to follow them: recommendatory only 7.4.8 Powers of the executive The government retained the power to reject or disqualify any candidate it considered politically dangerous (nationalists). In 1892 the British had the power of selection, choosing who could stand; by 1909 they had the power of rejection, removing those they did not want. Either way, nationalist leaders could be kept out of the councils. The Executive remained non-responsible to the Legislature. The Viceroy's powers continued as before. This was not even remotely close to the position of a ceremonial President in a democracy. 7.5 Impact of ICA1909 Was ICA1909 a success? No, and by almost every measure it failed. 7.5.1 The shortest-lived reform ICA1909: impact, the shortest-lived reform ICA 1861 30 years ICA 1892 17 years ICA 1909 10 years: the shortest of all council reforms GOI Act 1919 16 years GOI Act 1935 15 years, then the Constitution of India 1950 ICA1909 is the most short-lived of all the council reforms. It satisfied nobody: The Moderates wanted real legislative power; what they got was still toothless. The INC's goal since 1906 was Swaraj, and ICA1909 was nowhere near it. The Extremists had never cared for council reforms. The Muslims had been given separate electorates, which planted its own long-term disaster. Dropped: "the Extremists never cared for councils" and "a long-term disaster." Added: "BUT powerless legislatures." Why it failed: (1) the Moderates wanted real power, (2) the goal was already Swaraj, (3) the Muslims got separate electorates, (4) the legislatures were powerless. For the PYQ: "10 years" and "1919" (the Act that replaced it). Source conflict: reasons for failure. The handout keeps all four reasons, including "Extremists never cared for councils" and "a long-term disaster"; the teacher strikes both and adds "BUT powerless legislatures." Use the teacher's four points (Moderates, Swaraj, separate electorates, powerless legislatures); "long-term disaster" is covered in Section 7.5.2. Prelims 1999 (UPSC tested this). Q: "The most short lived of all of Britain's constitutional experiments in India was the ..." Answer (C) Indian Councils Act of 1909. Wrong options: (A) ICA 1861 (the longest, 30 years); (B) ICA 1892 (17 years); (D) GOI Act 1919 (16 years). 7.5.2 The long shadow: foundation of Partition The most consequential impact of ICA1909 was not what it gave but what it planted. Separate electorates for Muslims, introduced here for the first time in the ILC, PLCs and local bodies, laid the direct foundation for the partition of India in 1947. When you tell a community that they must vote separately, you are telling them they are separate. Over decades this institutional separation hardened into political reality. ICA1909: the long shadow and Benevolent Despotism Minto 05-10 became known as the "Father of Communal Electorate", a title history has not handed down with pride. 7.5.3 Benevolent Despotism, again Since there was no responsible government, ICA1909 produced what we can call Benevolent Despotism. "Benevolent" because ICA1909 was more democratic than ICA1892: more participation, more discussion rights, more elections. "Despotism" because real power remained entirely with the British Executive, answerable to nobody in India. We saw the same phrase for ICA1861: "Despotism Controlled from Home" was the core feature then. Nearly five decades later, the core had not changed: the packaging had become slightly friendlier, but the structure of power was the same. Foundation row: "10 to 16 ADDNL" then "60 ''": additional members rose from 10 to 16 in 1892 to 60 in 1909; size grew sharply, power did not. Benevolent Despotism: "Better Than 1892" (benevolent) and "= DICTATORSHIP, No Resp GOVT" (despotism). 7.6 ICA1909: summary card ICA1909: summary card Key Names Morley (SoS, Liberal), Minto 05-10 (Viceroy): the Morley-Minto Reforms ILC size 69 (8 ex-officio + 1 rotating + 27 elected + 33 nominated); the teacher adds 60 ADDNL Official majority Yes in the ILC (37 against 32); first non-official majority in the PLCs Elections First proper indirect (unreserved seats); direct (Muslim seats only) Separate electorates 8/27 Muslim seats in the ILC; only Muslims vote in Muslim seats; Muslims also vote in unreserved seats; lower income threshold Indians in the Executive S.P. Sinha (VEC, under ICA1909); K.G. Gupta and Bilgrami (India Council, London, August 1907, precursor) Budget / Questions / Resolutions Vote on individual items (not whole); supplementary questions (original questioner); resolutions non-binding Nature / Lifespan / Legacy Limited Self-Government = Benevolent Despotism; 10 years (shortest); Foundation of Partition; Minto = Father of Communal Electorate The handout page for this chapter ends with the index of the next chapter (the Ghadar Movement, Sections 1 to 11). That belongs to Chapter 32; it is not part of this chapter.

items.x: Because the 1919 Act kept the same communal design, a Prelims 2026 question about it fits here. Ask: which three actions (retain, counter, rally) did the British repeat from 1909? This question is about the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 (Chapter 34) and is kept here only because the same lecture solved it straight after the ICA 1909 PYQs, and because it tests the same logic: separate electorates as a Divide-and-Rule device. There are no class notes on the 1919 Act in this chapter; read Chapter 34 for its content. Assertion "The genesis of political alliances based on community lay in the very nature of the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms, 1919." Which of the following statements support the assertion? Statement 1 Reforms retained and extended the principle of separate electorates Statement 2 Separate electorates were supposed to counter Indian nationalism, which was growing stronger Statement 3 Deprived classes rallied around the favours inherent in separate electorates Options (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 2 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 "T" after every statement: all three support the assertion, answer (d). Statement 1: the 1919 Act made separate electorates watertight and extended them to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians and Christians. Statement 2: it fitted British Divide-and-Rule against a nationalism that had just united Hindus and Muslims (Lucknow 1916). Statement 3: the Depressed Classes got nominated seats, so every community had a favour to rally around. Other options: (a) stops at statement 1; (b) drops statement 1, the core (the Muslim separate electorate retained and made watertight); (c) drops statement 3. From separate qaum to separate electorate Census 1881 and religion-wise data: one homogeneous Muslim group, relative deprivation British DnR: Hunter 1871, jobs 1897, Partition 1905 Sir Syed: the Muslim qaum is separate; MAO College 1875; Educational Congress 1886 Hindu revivalism: cow riots 1893, Hindi-Urdu 1900, Swadeshi symbols: alienation Simla Deputation 1906: Partition kept, population-proportional seats, Separate Electorates ML1906 and its London branch 1908: the lobby for separate electorates ICA 1909 grants Separate Electorates: the hinge and the seed of 1947 Who is the candidate From the reserved community (the teacher: SC) A Muslim (the teacher: MLA or MP = Muslim) Who votes All communities in the seat (mixed voter list) Only the group's own voters (only Muslim) The handout's formula Candidate of the People, for the People, by a Community Candidate of a Group, for a Group, by a Group The teacher's phrase "For Indians, by (voters) Indians of SC community" (the last words unclear) "of the m, for the m, by the m": Pak within India Example in this notebook Our Constitution's SC seats ICA 1909's 8 of 27 Muslim seats
